questions.explanation: Earthwork paid by unit price is normally measured in place: in the finished work or at the borrow pit. Separate unit prices for excavating, stockpiling, and placing would follow the work more closely but make the owner pay for much more measuring, and truckload or loose-volume measurements should be avoided whenever possible. Bid-form quantities are only estimates for comparing bids.

questions.question: Which scenario most clearly calls for a UNIT PRICE rather than an allowance or an alternate?

options.A: The owner may delete the entry canopy if bids run over budget
options.B: Rock excavation volume is unknown until digging begins
options.C: The owner wants a separate price to add rooftop solar
options.D: A light fixture's make is still undecided
options.E: Lobby finish selections have not yet been made
options.F: The contractor offers a cheaper roofing product

questions.explanation: A unit price fits work whose quantity cannot be known until it is performed, such as rock excavation, because the contract sum is adjusted to the measured quantity. Adding or deleting scope for a separate price, like a canopy or rooftop solar, is an alternate; an undecided fixture or finish selection is handled by an allowance; and a contractor's offer of a cheaper product is a substitution.

questions.question: Which document must state which alternates the owner has accepted?

options.A: The executed agreement
options.B: The invitation to bidders
options.C: Section 01 23 00, Alternates
options.D: The instructions to bidders
options.E: The supplementary conditions
options.F: The bid form

questions.explanation: The executed agreement must show, as part of its description of the work, which alternates the owner accepted, and the contract sum must reflect those choices; accepted alternates then become part of the work without changes to the general conditions. Section 01 23 00 describes every alternate offered, accepted or not, and the bid form only collects their prices.

questions.question: Two alternates propose different cladding for the same first-floor surface. The owner would:

options.A: Not select both, since they are mutually exclusive
options.B: Convert both into unit prices for the surface
options.C: Select both to compare the cladding
options.D: Merge them into one combined deduct alternate
options.E: Let each bidder pick which one it prices
options.F: Accept whichever alternate is priced lower

questions.explanation: Two alternates that put different cladding on the same surface are mutually exclusive: the owner can accept one or the other, but not both. Each alternate should describe its scope against the base bid clearly enough that this is plain to bidders. Converting them to unit prices, merging them, or letting bidders choose would defeat the purpose of pricing each option separately.

questions.question: Which pair of terms is preferred when describing alternates?

options.A: 'Baseline' and 'Alternative'
options.B: 'Base/base bid' and 'Alternative'
options.C: 'Baseline' and 'Alternate'
options.D: 'Base/base bid' and 'Alternate'
options.E: 'Baseline' and 'Option'
options.F: 'Base/base bid' and 'Option'

questions.explanation: The preferred terms are 'base' or 'base bid' for the work priced without alternates and 'alternate' for each separately priced change, rather than 'baseline,' 'alternative,' or 'option.' Whichever terms appear, they must be used the same way on the bid form, in Section 01 23 00, and on the drawings, so bidders are not left guessing what is included.

questions.question: If an alternate's extent is not shown on the drawings, Section 01 23 00 may:

options.A: Refer bidders to the base-bid drawings for its scope
options.B: Leave the location for the contractor to propose
options.C: Describe the affected areas or portions of the work
options.D: Show it on a sketch issued after award
options.E: Have each affected section locate it in PART 3
options.F: Carry it as an allowance until its extent is drawn

questions.explanation: Section 01 23 00 identifies each alternate and the changes it makes, referring to the affected sections where possible; when the drawings do not show an alternate's extent, the section may describe the affected areas or portions of the work so bidders know where the changes occur. Bidders cannot price an alternate whose location is left for the contractor to propose or shown only after award.

questions.question: Under AIA A201, addenda may be issued up until:

options.A: Receipt of bids
options.B: Notice of award
options.C: Execution of the agreement
options.D: Issuance of the notice to proceed
options.E: The prebid conference
options.F: The date of commencement of the Work

questions.explanation: A201 treats addenda as instruments issued before the agreement is executed, which reflects a private owner who may negotiate with a bidder and issue addenda after bids are opened, right up to signing. EJCDC C-700 cuts addenda off at the opening of bids, and changes after execution are modifications, not addenda.

questions.question: Under EJCDC C-700, addenda may be issued up until:

options.A: Receipt of bids
options.B: The prebid conference
options.C: Notice of award
options.D: Execution of the agreement
options.E: Issuance of the notice to proceed
options.F: Ten days before bid opening

questions.explanation: EJCDC C-700 defines addenda as written or graphic instruments issued before the opening of bids. That reflects public works, where the procurement documents may not be changed in the gap between bid opening and signing of the agreement. A201's later cutoff, at execution of the agreement, reflects a private owner who can negotiate after bids.

questions.question: A bidder submits a written question nine days before bid opening on a project using AIA A701. The question is:

options.A: Timely; the A701 cutoff is 7 days before bids
options.B: Untimely; the A701 cutoff is 10 days before bids
options.C: Untimely; the A701 cutoff is 14 days before bids
options.D: Timely only if the owner extends the bid date
options.E: Untimely; the A701 cutoff is 15 days before bids
options.F: Untimely; the A701 cutoff is 21 days before bids

questions.explanation: AIA A701, Instructions to Bidders, requires questions and substitution requests at least seven days before the date bids are received, so a question nine days out is on time. The 10-day period is what EJCDC C-200 recommends for questions, not A701's rule.

questions.question: A minor addendum can sometimes be issued, without imposing hardship on bidders, as late as:

options.A: The morning of bid opening
options.B: Four days before the bid or proposal due date
options.C: Ten days before the bid or proposal due date
options.D: Seven days before the bid or proposal due date
options.E: Fifteen days before the bid or proposal due date
options.F: The day before the bid or proposal due date

questions.explanation: Addenda should reach bidders with enough time to prepare prices, but a minor addendum can sometimes go out as late as four days before bids or proposals are due without causing hardship. A significant last-minute change is different: the owner should be told and, if possible, the bid date postponed rather than relying on a hasty addendum.

questions.question: Where separate prime contracts will be awarded on one project, addenda are numbered:

options.A: Only by date, omitting sequential numbers to avoid confusion
options.B: By affected specification section number rather than sequentially
options.C: In a separate consecutive series for each prime contract
options.D: In a single continuous series shared across all the contracts
options.E: In one series, with a prefix marking each contract's items
options.F: With a revision identifier such as CO-01 for each contract

questions.explanation: Addenda are numbered consecutively, and where separate prime contracts will be awarded, each contract gets its own series of addendum numbers, so each contract's addenda can be tracked as a complete set. A simple numbering of items within each addendum also helps later cross-referencing. A single shared series, date-only numbering, or numbering by section would blur which addenda belong to which contract.

questions.question: The instructions to bidders should state that issuing partial sets of documents is:

options.A: Permitted for subcontractors bidding one trade
options.B: Permitted when the bidder pays printing costs
options.C: Required on public work for each trade
options.D: To be avoided for every bidder
options.E: Permitted for prime bidders on separate contracts
options.F: Permitted once the bid solicitation lists them

questions.explanation: Under the documents topic of the instructions to bidders, the A/E states whether documents will go to anyone besides prime bidders, explains the return of documents and refund of deposits, and makes clear that partial sets of documents should not be issued. The rule applies to every bidder, including subcontractors bidding a single trade, whoever pays for printing.

questions.question: A public agency receives a sealed bid a few minutes after the bid deadline in the invitation. Which statements about late and withdrawn bids are correct?

options.A: A bid received after the established time is sufficient cause for complete rejection
options.B: Late bids are usually marked as late, left unopened, and may be returned
options.C: A postmark dated before the deadline cures a late delivery
options.D: A bidder may withdraw its bid if it asks before the time set for receipt of bids
options.E: Both {A} and {B}
options.F: {A}, {B} and {D}

questions.explanation: A bid received after the time set for receipt is sufficient cause for complete rejection, especially on public projects, and late bids are usually marked as late, left unopened, and may be returned. A bidder may withdraw its bid by asking before the time set for receipt, though not after. That makes {F} correct. Lateness is judged by when the bid is received, so an earlier postmark does not cure it.

questions.question: All bids for a public contract exceed the budget. Which statements about what follows are correct?

options.A: The bids are rejected and bid security is returned to the bidders
options.B: The project may be redesigned in a value analysis process
options.C: The owner may abandon the project
options.D: The owner keeps the document deposits to offset rebidding costs
options.E: Both {A} and {B}
options.F: {A}, {B} and {C}

questions.explanation: When every bid for a public contract exceeds the budget, the bids are rejected and the bidders get back their bid security and document deposits. Once the cause is evaluated, the owner generally has three choices: raise the budget, redesign the project through value analysis to fit the budget, or abandon it, and a redesigned project may be rebid. That makes {F} correct; the owner does not keep the deposits.

questions.question: At a public bid opening, the bid amounts are read aloud. At that moment, the owner knows:

options.A: The successful bidder
options.B: The apparent low bidder
options.C: The lowest responsive and responsible bidder
options.D: The bidder that will receive the notice of award
options.E: The bidder the A/E will recommend
options.F: The bidder the board will approve

questions.explanation: Because public bids are opened and read aloud, the apparent low bidder is known immediately. The successful bidder, the one awarded the contract, is known only after the agency and A/E check the bids and supplements for strict compliance, which can take days or weeks, and after any A/E recommendation or board approval. Until then, no one knows who is responsive and responsible or who will get the notice of award.

questions.question: In the standard arrangement of an addendum, which group of changes comes first?

options.A: Changes to prior addenda
options.B: Changes to procurement requirements
options.C: Changes to contracting requirements
options.D: Changes to specifications
options.E: Changes to drawings
options.F: Approved substitutions

questions.explanation: An addendum opens with its number and date, project identification, the A/E's name and address, the recipients, and opening remarks. The changes then follow in the order of the project manual and drawings: changes to prior addenda first, then procurement requirements, contracting requirements, specifications (including approved substitutions), and finally drawings.

questions.question: Provisions that are an inherent part of the agreement and, with it, govern the entire project belong in:

options.A: The conditions of the contract
options.B: Division 01—General Requirements
options.C: PART 1—GENERAL of each section
options.D: The procurement requirements
options.E: Section 01 10 00—Summary
options.F: The bid form and its supplements

questions.explanation: The conditions of the contract are an inherent part of the agreement and together with it govern the entire contract; they set contractual principles that apply to most projects, supplemented for the particular one, and they are not specifications. Division 01 is part of the specifications and holds the project's administrative and procedural requirements, and PART 1 of each section covers only that section's work.

questions.question: General administrative and procedural requirements are stated at three levels in the contract documents. Which sequence runs from BROADEST to most specific?

options.A: Conditions of the contract, Division 01, technical sections
options.B: Technical sections, Division 01, conditions of the contract
options.C: Conditions of the contract, technical sections, Division 01
options.D: Division 01, conditions of the contract, technical sections
options.E: Division 01, technical sections, conditions of the contract
options.F: Technical sections, conditions of the contract, Division 01

questions.explanation: The general conditions state administrative and procedural provisions in broad terms; Division 01 expands on them with requirements that apply to the whole project; and each technical section states the details for its own work. For testing, for example, the conditions say tests may be required, Division 01 covers who selects and pays the laboratory, and the section names the particular tests and how many.

questions.question: Which items do NOT belong in the instructions to bidders?

options.A: Information about liquidated damages provisions
options.B: Whether performance and payment bonds will be required
options.C: Conditions under which a bidder may be disqualified
options.D: The schedule of values format for payment applications
options.E: Conditions for modifying or withdrawing a bid
options.F: Requirements for the daily construction reports

questions.explanation: Instructions to bidders cover procurement matters such as whether performance and payment bonds will be required, conditions for disqualifying bidders, information about liquidated damages provisions, modification or withdrawal of bids, and bid security. The schedule of values for payment applications and daily construction reports are construction-phase administrative requirements, specified in Division 01 and used after award.

questions.question: Which are true of supplementary conditions but NOT of general conditions?

options.A: They must be written separately for each project
options.B: They contain the constants that apply to most projects
options.C: Their static content allows published standard forms
options.D: They are part of the specifications
options.E: They take precedence over the general conditions
options.F: They are broad contractual conditions

questions.explanation: Supplementary conditions modify the general conditions for a particular region or project, so they must be written separately for each project and they take precedence over the general conditions. General conditions are the broad contractual constants, relatively static, which is why published standard forms can be used for them. Neither one is part of the specifications.

questions.question: General requirements for evaluating system performance, including testing, adjusting, and balancing within a facility-wide process, belong in:

options.A: Section 01 75 00—Starting and Adjusting
options.B: Section 01 91 00—Commissioning
options.C: Section 01 79 00—Demonstration and Training
options.D: Section 01 45 00—Quality Control
options.E: Section 01 92 00—Facility Operation
options.F: Section 01 81 00—Facility Performance Requirements

questions.explanation: Section 01 91 00, Commissioning, sets the general requirements for commissioning a facility and its systems: the commissioning agent's responsibilities, evaluation of system performance, and testing, adjusting, and balancing as part of the commissioning process. Section 01 75 00, Starting and Adjusting, covers starting and adjusting equipment before commissioning begins, and the two sections must be coordinated.

questions.question: Which statements about action and informational submittals are correct?

options.A: Action submittals require responsive action by the A/E
options.B: Test reports and qualification statements are action submittals
options.C: Approved shop drawings become Contract Documents
options.D: Informational submittals are approved, approved as noted, or rejected
options.E: Both {A} and {B}
options.F: {A}, {B} and {D}

questions.explanation: Action submittals require responsive action by the A/E, who may approve, approve as noted, ask for revision and resubmittal, or reject. Test reports and qualification statements are informational submittals, which need no responsive action and are largely kept as a record, so they are not approved or rejected. A201 §3.12.4 states that shop drawings and similar submittals are not Contract Documents.

questions.question: End-of-service-life shutdown requirements for a building are specified in:

options.A: Section 01 77 00—Closeout Procedures
options.B: Section 01 91 00—Commissioning
options.C: Section 01 94 00—Facility Decommissioning
options.D: Section 01 78 00—Closeout Submittals
options.E: Section 01 92 00—Facility Operation
options.F: Section 01 93 00—Facility Maintenance

questions.explanation: Section 01 94 00, Facility Decommissioning, specifies the basic requirements for taking a facility, its systems, or its equipment out of operation, including protecting deactivated facilities, deconstruction or demolition, removal, and the handling of hazardous materials. Commissioning and the closeout sections deal with bringing the work into service and turning it over, and facility operation and maintenance cover the building while it is in use.

questions.question: Participants, schedule, costs, evaluation and reports for a team study of cost-saving design changes are specified in which section?

options.A: Section 01 25 00—Substitution Procedures
options.B: Section 01 24 00—Value Analysis
options.C: Section 01 23 00—Alternates
options.D: Section 01 31 00—Project Management and Coordination
options.E: Section 01 26 00—Contract Modification Procedures
options.F: Section 01 21 00—Allowances

questions.explanation: Section 01 24 00—Value Analysis sets out how a value analysis study is run: who takes part, its schedule and costs, how proposals are evaluated and reported, and how accepted results are carried into the work. Section 01 25 00—Substitution Procedures handles a contractor's request to use a different product, which is not a team study of design changes.

questions.question: Work whose quantity cannot be determined before bidding, and which is paid at a stipulated rate times the quantity completed, is priced as:

options.A: A cash allowance
options.B: An alternate
options.C: A unit price
options.D: A stipulated sum
options.E: A cost-plus fee
options.F: A guaranteed maximum price

questions.explanation: A unit price fits work whose quantity cannot be fixed before it is done, such as excavation or utility work: the contractor is paid an agreed rate for each unit actually completed and measured. A cash allowance carries a sum for a product not yet selected, and a stipulated sum is a single fixed price for the defined work.

questions.question: An owner wants a defined scope item priced separately so it can be accepted or declined at award. This is specified as a(n):

options.A: Unit price in Section 01 22 00
options.B: Alternate in Section 01 23 00
options.C: Contract modification in Section 01 26 00
options.D: Allowance in Section 01 21 00
options.E: Value analysis proposal in Section 01 24 00
options.F: Substitution in Section 01 25 00

questions.explanation: An alternate is a defined change in scope priced separately on the bid form, so the owner can accept or reject it when the contract is awarded; Section 01 23 00—Alternates describes each one, and the affected technical sections refer to it. An allowance carries a sum for a selection not yet made, and a unit price pays a rate per measured quantity.

questions.question: A dollar sum is carried in the contract for finish hardware whose specific product the owner has not yet selected, to be reconciled against actual cost. This device is a:

options.A: Cash allowance
options.B: Quantity allowance
options.C: Deduct alternate
options.D: Unit price
options.E: Contingency allowance
options.F: Add alternate

questions.explanation: A cash allowance puts a stated sum in the contract for a product the owner has not yet chosen; under A201 it covers the materials delivered to the site plus taxes, and the difference from the actual cost is settled by change order. A quantity allowance instead fixes an estimated quantity of installed work, adjusted at unit prices, and an alternate is a separately priced scope option.

questions.question: In a technical section affected by an alternate, where does the statement calling attention to the alternate go?

options.A: PART 1, under the Summary article
options.B: PART 1, under the Submittals article
options.C: PART 2, in the affected product article
options.D: PART 3, under the Installation article
options.E: PART 1, under the Quality Assurance article
options.F: PART 3, under the Field Quality Control article

questions.explanation: Sections in Divisions 02 through 49 that an alternate affects should carry a short coordinating statement in PART 1—GENERAL, under the Summary article, pointing to Section 01 23 00—Alternates, which describes each alternate. The products and installation involved are specified in PARTS 2 and 3 as usual, but the statement that flags the alternate belongs in PART 1, not under submittals or quality assurance.

questions.question: To get a separate price for one floor tile product on a bid project, which section is edited along with the bid form and Section 09 30 00—Tiling?

options.A: Section 01 21 00—Allowances
options.B: Section 01 22 00—Unit Prices
options.C: Section 01 23 00—Alternates
options.D: Section 01 29 00—Payment Procedures
options.E: Section 01 25 00—Substitution Procedures
options.F: Section 01 24 00—Value Analysis

questions.explanation: A separate price for a defined item that the owner can accept or reject is an alternate, so the bid form gets a line for it, Section 01 23 00—Alternates describes it, and the tiling section flags it. Unit prices are for work whose quantity is uncertain, and allowances carry a sum for a selection not yet made.

questions.question: When the installed quantity of a quantity-allowance item differs from the stated quantity, the contract sum is adjusted by:

options.A: A change order at the stated unit prices
options.B: A construction change directive at cost plus fee
options.C: A credit at final payment with no change order
options.D: No adjustment, since the quantity is fixed
options.E: A change order at actual cost plus a fee
options.F: A minor change in the Work at the unit prices

questions.explanation: Quantities stated for allowances are estimates for fair bidding; when the installed quantity differs, the contract sum is adjusted at the unit prices given with the bid, and the adjustment is made by change order, often a final change order that also settles unit-price quantities. A construction change directive is for changes without agreed pricing, and a minor change cannot alter the contract sum.

questions.question: While bids are still being prepared, a bidder wants to propose a substitute for a specified product. On which form should the request be made?

options.A: AIA Document G701, Change Order
options.B: 00 43 25 Substitution Request Form (During Procurement)
options.C: 00 63 25 Substitution Request Form (During Construction)
options.D: 00 63 13 Requests for Information Form
options.E: AIA Document G709, Work Changes Proposal Request
options.F: AIA Document G710, Architect's Supplemental Instructions

questions.explanation: When substitutions are allowed during bidding, bidders use the procurement-phase substitution request form, which MasterFormat places among the procurement form supplements at 00 43 25, and submit it before or with the bid. The construction-phase version at 00 63 25 is for requests made after award, and the AIA forms listed are for changes to a contract already in place.

questions.question: Under AIA A201, the owner and contractor have not agreed on the cost and time impact of a directed change, but the work must proceed now. The proper instrument is the:

options.A: Construction change directive (AIA G714)
options.B: Architect's supplemental instructions (AIA G710)
options.C: Change order (AIA G701)
options.D: Minor change in the work
options.E: Work change directive (EJCDC C-940)
options.F: Interim directive (ConsensusDocs 203)

questions.explanation: A construction change directive, on AIA G714, lets the owner order a change within the general scope before the owner and contractor agree on the change in contract sum or time; the contractor must proceed while the adjustment is worked out. A change order records an agreement already reached, and a minor change involves no change in sum or time at all.

questions.question: Under AIA A201, a construction change directive is prepared by the architect and signed by:

options.A: The owner, architect, and contractor
options.B: The owner and contractor only
options.C: The owner and architect
options.D: The architect only
options.E: The owner only
options.F: The architect and contractor

questions.explanation: Under A201 the architect prepares a construction change directive, and the owner and architect sign it to order the change before the price or time adjustment is agreed. The contractor's signature is not needed; if the contractor later signs to accept the proposed adjustment, that agreement is recorded as a change order, which carries all three signatures.

questions.question: Which statements about signatures on AIA A201 change instruments are correct?

options.A: A change order is signed by the owner, contractor, and architect
options.B: An order for a minor change in the Work requires the owner's signature
options.C: A construction change directive is signed by the owner and architect
options.D: A construction change directive is invalid without the contractor's signature
options.E: Both {A} and {C}
options.F: {A}, {B} and {C}

questions.explanation: A change order rests on agreement of all three parties, so the owner, contractor and architect sign it, while a construction change directive needs only the owner and architect, which makes {E} right. The contractor may sign a directive to show agreement, but it is valid without that signature, and the architect alone may order a minor change, with no owner signature.

questions.question: Under A201, an order for a minor change in the Work is:

options.A: Signed by the architect alone and binding on owner and contractor
options.B: Signed by the owner and architect, with the price set later
options.C: Signed by the owner, the contractor, and the architect
options.D: Issued by the architect, but binding only once the owner countersigns
options.E: Signed by the architect alone, and it may extend the contract time
options.F: Signed by the owner alone, with no change in price or time

questions.explanation: The architect alone may order a minor change in the Work, provided it involves no change in the contract sum or time and fits the intent of the contract documents; the written order binds both the owner and the contractor. An order signed by the owner and architect with the price settled later is a construction change directive, and any time extension needs a change order.

questions.question: Under EJCDC C-700, the instrument that orders a change before agreement on price or time, signed by the owner and recommended by the engineer, is the:

options.A: Field order issued with no standard form
options.B: Work change directive, EJCDC C-940 form
options.C: Written amendment to the agreement terms
options.D: Change order, the EJCDC C-941 form
options.E: Interim directive, ConsensusDocs 203 form
options.F: Construction change directive, AIA G714 form

questions.explanation: In EJCDC C-700 a work change directive is the owner's written order, recommended by the engineer, to add, delete or revise work before its price or time effect is agreed; its form is EJCDC C-940, and the adjustment is later captured in a change order. The C-941 change order records an agreed adjustment, and a field order is the engineer's order for minor changes that need no adjustment.

questions.question: Which statements about adjusting the contract sum or contract time under AIA A201 are correct?

options.A: A change order is the document that records an agreed change in the contract sum or time
options.B: A construction change directive the contractor signs in agreement is recorded as a change order
options.C: Architect's supplemental instructions may extend the contract time
options.D: A minor change may adjust the contract sum when the amount is small
options.E: Both {A} and {B}
options.F: {A}, {B} and {C}

questions.explanation: Under A201 an agreed change in the contract sum or time is recorded in a written change order, and when a contractor signs a construction change directive to accept its proposed adjustment, that agreement is recorded as a change order, so {E} is right. Architect's supplemental instructions are used for minor changes, which by definition involve no change in the contract sum or time, however small the amount.

questions.question: What chiefly distinguishes a goods contractor under a purchasing contract from a construction contractor?

options.A: Little or no on-site construction or installation
options.B: A performance bond is always required
options.C: Selection by negotiation rather than bidding
options.D: Governed by A201 rather than the UCC
options.E: Installation under a subcontract with the contractor
options.F: Training of the owner's personnel

questions.explanation: A purchasing contract is for goods the owner buys, and the goods contractor does little or no work on site: no construction, installation or erection. When the supplier must take part in the construction, the goods are furnished and installed under a subcontract instead, and purchasing contracts are mostly governed by the Uniform Commercial Code, not A201.

questions.question: Under the UCC, mercantile terms such as FOB and CIF place responsibility for:

options.A: The buyer's right to reject nonconforming goods
options.B: Transportation costs, insurance, and risk of loss
options.C: The quantity term that must be stated for enforceability
options.D: The seller's implied warranty of merchantability only
options.E: Transfer of a clear title free of security interests
options.F: Price terms left open to be agreed at a later date

questions.explanation: Shorthand mercantile terms such as FOB (free on board) and CIF (cost, insurance and freight) are defined in the UCC and settle who pays for transportation and insurance and who bears the risk of loss. Where the parties do not agree otherwise, the UCC splits risk of loss according to how far the agreement has been performed; quantity, warranties and title are handled by other rules.

questions.question: Under UCC Article 2, which of the following must a written contract for the sale of goods include to be enforceable?

options.A: An express warranty of fitness
options.B: A delivery date certain
options.C: A stated quantity
options.D: The agreed unit price
options.E: The signature of the party to be charged
options.F: The place of delivery

questions.explanation: Article 2 of the UCC asks only three things of the writing: it shows that a contract for the sale of goods was made, it is signed by the party against whom it would be enforced, and it states a quantity. Price, payment and delivery terms can be supplied by the UCC if they are left out, and warranties come from the UCC rather than being required in the writing.

questions.question: Under the UCC, a contract for the sale of goods must be in writing to be enforceable when the goods cost more than:
questions.explanation: Under the UCC, a contract to sell goods priced at more than $500 can be enforced only if it is in writing; a clear written contract is then generally treated as the whole agreement. None of the other amounts, larger or smaller, is the UCC's threshold for requiring a writing.

questions.question: Which statements about the ConsensusDocs purchasing documents are correct?

options.A: They call the owner the Buyer and the party offering the Goods the Seller
options.B: They do not directly reference the UCC
options.C: ConsensusDocs 703 covers goods that include installation
options.D: They state that the agreement prevails over any conflict with the UCC
options.E: Both {A} and {B}
options.F: {A}, {B} and {C}

questions.explanation: ConsensusDocs purchasing forms use the same terms as EJCDC (the owner is the Buyer and the party supplying the Goods is the Seller), but unlike AIA and EJCDC they do not refer directly to the UCC, saying instead that the law where the project is located governs. ConsensusDocs 703 covers goods with installation, so {F} is right. The clause making the agreement prevail over the UCC is in AIA A151.

questions.question: Which EJCDC procurement document is the Agreement Between Buyer and Seller for Procurement?

options.A: EJCDC P-700
options.B: EJCDC P-520
options.C: EJCDC P-200
options.D: EJCDC P-400
options.E: EJCDC P-800
options.F: EJCDC C-520

questions.explanation: EJCDC's procurement series parallels its construction series: P-200 is the instructions to bidders, P-400 the bid form, P-520 the agreement between buyer and seller, P-700 the standard general conditions, and P-800 the guide to the supplementary conditions. C-520 is the construction agreement between owner and contractor, not a procurement form.

questions.question: The EJCDC procurement documents are NOT intended for use where:

options.A: The goods are competitively bid using a standard goods bid form
options.B: The manufacturer or supplier must participate in on-site installation
options.C: Multiple deliveries of the same engineered item are anticipated
options.D: The owner purchases engineered materials directly from the goods provider
options.E: A subcontractor at the site will install the furnished goods
options.F: The seller provides special services to assist the installing entity

questions.explanation: EJCDC's procurement documents assume the goods will be installed by the owner's own forces, a construction contractor or a subcontractor at the site; they are not meant for purchases where the manufacturer or supplier must take part in the installation. The seller may still provide limited special services to help the installer, and installation by a site subcontractor is exactly what the forms expect.

questions.question: On a purchasing contract, the bond usually required is a performance bond. It gives the owner:

options.A: Recourse if goods are not made, supplied, or delivered
options.B: Protection against liens by the seller's suppliers
options.C: Coverage for the goods while in transit
options.D: Assurance the buyer will accept the goods
options.E: Coverage for the goods after delivery to the site
options.F: Recourse if the contractor installs the goods poorly

questions.explanation: On a purchasing contract, the performance bond protects the owner if the goods contractor fails to manufacture, supply or deliver the goods as agreed. Damage to the goods during shipment is covered by transit insurance that the goods contractor provides, insurance after delivery is usually the owner's, and poor installation is the installing contractor's problem.

questions.question: Which of the following are reasons an owner may buy major equipment under a separate purchasing contract before construction?

options.A: Avoid having to coordinate the purchasing and construction documents
options.B: Gain lead time on goods requiring long fabrication periods and avoid construction delays
options.C: Transfer all risk of late or incomplete delivery to the construction contractor at no owner cost
options.D: Eliminate the need for submittals on the purchased goods
options.E: Take advantage of tax exemptions not available to a construction contractor
options.F: Reduce the administrative time the owner and A/E spend on the project

questions.explanation: Buying goods ahead of construction can secure items with long fabrication times so they do not hold up the work, and it can let the owner use tax exemptions a construction contractor could not claim. The drawbacks run the other way: more coordination for the A/E, more administrative time for the owner and A/E, and possible owner liability for late or incomplete delivery.

questions.question: Which AIA documents are used to purchase goods and reference the UCC?

options.A: AIA A101
options.B: AIA A152
options.C: AIA A312
options.D: AIA A701
options.E: AIA A151
options.F: AIA A141

questions.explanation: AIA A151 is the owner-vendor agreement for furniture, furnishings and equipment that include assembly or installation, and AIA A152 is the purchase order, with its companion terms and conditions, for FF&E without installation; both refer to the UCC. A101 is the owner-contractor agreement, A141 the owner-design-builder agreement, A312 the bond form, and A701 the instructions to bidders.

questions.question: When an owner buys goods under a purchasing contract for the construction contractor to install, which risks must the documents address?

options.A: The construction contractor may not warrant goods it did not supply
options.B: The goods contractor may carry builder's risk for the whole project
options.C: The owner is relieved of responsibility for delivery time and storage
options.D: The UCC may not apply to the purchase because installation is involved
options.E: Fault for a performance failure may be disputed between the two contracts
options.F: The goods contractor becomes liable for the installer's workmanship

questions.explanation: When separately purchased goods are installed by the construction contractor, the contractor may resist installing them and may not warrant them as it would goods it supplied, and blame for a failure can be disputed because the goods came under one contract and were installed under another. The owner is not relieved of anything; it may take on delivery timing, handling and storage.

questions.question: In a section that delegates the design of railings, the loads the contractor's engineer must design for are stated in:

options.A: PART 1, under the delegated-design submittal
options.B: PART 2, under Performance Requirements
options.C: PART 3, under Installation
options.D: Section 01 40 00—Quality Requirements
options.E: PART 1, under Quality Assurance
options.F: PART 2, under Source Quality Control

questions.explanation: When the design of an item such as railings is delegated, the section states the criteria the contractor's engineer must meet, including the loads, in PART 2 under Performance Requirements, since performance requirements belong in PART 2. PART 1 calls for the delegated-design submittal signed and sealed by that engineer, and Section 01 40 00 defines a qualified professional engineer.

questions.question: A shop drawing deviates from the contract documents, and the architect approves it. Under A201, the contractor stays responsible for the deviation unless:

options.A: It flagged the deviation in writing and the architect approved it
options.B: The architect's approval stamp appears on the deviating drawing
options.C: The deviation adds nothing to the contract sum or time
options.D: The owner accepted the shop drawing at a progress meeting
options.E: The architect did not reject it within the review period
options.F: Its subcontractor prepared and sealed the shop drawing

questions.explanation: Under A201, approval of a shop drawing does not relieve the contractor of a deviation from the contract documents unless the contractor pointed out that specific deviation in writing when it submitted and the architect approved it in writing, or a change order or construction change directive authorized it. A general approval stamp on a drawing that quietly deviates does not shift responsibility.

questions.question: Which statements about the surety on a construction bond are correct?

options.A: It is only secondarily liable, after the principal defaults
options.B: It holds an indemnity agreement from the principal
options.C: It should be licensed by the insurance department of the project's state
options.D: It takes primary responsibility for claims, like an insurer
options.E: Both {A} and {B}
options.F: {A}, {B} and {C}

questions.explanation: Unlike an insurer, the surety is only secondarily liable: it answers after the principal defaults, and the principal, which stays primarily liable, signs an indemnity agreement promising the surety will suffer no loss. The surety should also be licensed by the insurance department of the state where the project is, so {F} is right. Taking primary responsibility for claims is how insurance works, not a bond.

questions.question: The limit on the amount a bond guarantees, frequently 100 percent of the contract amount, is the:

options.A: Premium
options.B: Penal sum
options.C: Limit of liability
options.D: Contract sum
options.E: Deductible
options.F: General aggregate

questions.explanation: Every bond states the most the surety will pay, called the penal sum or penal amount, often set at 100 percent of the contract amount. The premium is the price paid for the bond, and limit of liability is the insurance term for the most an insurer will pay on a covered loss.

questions.question: Which statements about the payment bond are correct?

options.A: It protects the owner against mechanic's liens
options.B: It also covers capital goods the contractor uses on many projects
options.C: It guarantees payment of subcontractors and material suppliers
options.D: Claimants may file suit at any time after the project closes
options.E: Both {A} and {C}
options.F: {A}, {C} and {D}

questions.explanation: A payment bond, also called a labor and material payment bond, guarantees that subcontractors, suppliers and others who furnish labor, materials and equipment to the project get paid, which shields the owner from mechanic's liens and delays, so {E} is right. It covers only labor and material for the bonded project, not capital goods used on many jobs, and claimants usually must sue within a fairly short time.

questions.question: Which bond form combines the performance bond and the payment bond in a single document?

options.A: EJCDC C-610
options.B: EJCDC C-615
options.C: AIA A312
options.D: AIA A310
options.E: ConsensusDocs 260
options.F: EJCDC C-430

questions.explanation: AIA A312 contains both the performance bond and the payment bond in one document. EJCDC and ConsensusDocs publish a separate form for each, such as EJCDC C-610 Performance Bond and C-615 Payment Bond or ConsensusDocs 260 and 261, while AIA A310 and EJCDC C-430 are bid bonds.

questions.question: The purpose of a bid bond is to:

options.A: Guarantee completion of the work at the bid price
options.B: Guarantee payment of the low bidder's subcontractors
options.C: Cover any bidder who withdraws before bid opening
options.D: Protect the owner if the selected bidder won't sign
options.E: Cover the owner if all bids exceed the budget
options.F: Hold the bidder's subcontractors to their quotes

questions.explanation: A bid bond protects the owner if the bidder it selects refuses to sign the contract at the bid price or to furnish any required performance and payment bonds; the surety then covers the owner's loss up to the bond's penal amount. A bidder may withdraw before the deadline for receiving bids without default, and completing the work is what a performance bond guarantees.

questions.question: Which of the following describe workers' compensation laws?

options.A: Employers compensate employees for job-related injuries regardless of fault
options.B: The injured employee must prove the employer's negligence to collect
options.C: An insured employer may still be sued for unlimited damages
options.D: Benefits exclude any amount for permanent injuries
options.E: The employee cannot sue the employer for more than the statutory amount
options.F: Compensation covers lost wages but not medical costs

questions.explanation: Workers' compensation is a no-fault, limited-liability bargain set by statute: the employer pays for work-related injuries whatever their cause, and in exchange the employee cannot sue the employer for more than the statutory benefits. Those benefits include medical costs, lost wages and set amounts for certain permanent injuries; only an employer that lacks the coverage can face unlimited damages.

questions.question: Which of the following does the contractor's commercial general liability (CGL) insurance primarily cover?

options.A: The cost to repair the contractor's defective work
options.B: Fire, theft, or weather damage to the work in progress
options.C: Bodily injury to third parties
options.D: The contractor's failure to complete the work
options.E: Loss of the contractor's tools and equipment
options.F: Damage to others' property from the contractor's operations

questions.explanation: Commercial general liability insurance answers claims by others for bodily injury and property damage arising from the contractor's operations. It does not pay to fix the contractor's own defective work, only the damage that work causes; loss to the work in progress is a builder's risk matter, and failure to complete the work is what a performance bond covers.

questions.question: Before specific products can be researched and evaluated, what must first be identified?

options.A: A basis-of-design product
options.B: A preliminary list of manufacturers
options.C: A generic product type
options.D: A product cost range
options.E: The applicable reference standards
options.F: A local product representative

questions.explanation: Product research starts by identifying a generic product type, such as ductile iron pipe for a sewer force main, that satisfies the design criteria and the project conditions; only then are specific products compared. A basis-of-design product and a preliminary list of manufacturers come out of that later research.

questions.question: The main risk of relying on a printed manufacturer's catalog is that it:

options.A: Cannot legally be cited because the catalog text is copyrighted by the maker
options.B: Is organized by trade name rather than by the project's MasterFormat numbers
options.C: Can contain inaccurate product data if it is not the most recent version
options.D: Omits Safety Data Sheets that might be required for the project's materials
options.E: Is no longer issued in print by most product manufacturers
options.F: Contains guide specifications biased toward the maker's own products

questions.explanation: Printed catalogs and other printed product literature can go out of date, so their product data may be wrong unless the copy is the manufacturer's latest version. That is one reason office catalog libraries have largely given way to manufacturers' websites, although printed literature is still published.

questions.question: During design, the team summarizes product quotes mainly to:

options.A: Fix the contract sum before bidding
options.B: Set the contractor's product pricing
options.C: Satisfy the AHJ's permit requirements
options.D: Aid in estimating construction cost
options.E: Evaluate each product's sustainability
options.F: Draft the preliminary project description

questions.explanation: During design, the team gathers product information and summarizes product quotes to help estimate the project's construction cost. These are budgeting figures: they do not fix the contract sum, which comes from bids or negotiation, and they do not bind the contractor's own pricing.

questions.question: Which of the following are factors to research about the sourcing of selected products?

options.A: Manufacturer's financial stability
options.B: Owner's life cycle cost projection
options.C: Contractor's preferred installers
options.D: AHJ's prior code modifications
options.E: Country of origin
options.F: Trades needed for installation

questions.explanation: Sourcing research looks at where a product comes from and who stands behind it: country of origin (domestic or imported, which affects delivery, testing, parts and warranty service), the manufacturer's longevity, financial stability and track record, its distribution network and local representatives, and warranty and service. Installing trades belong to final selection, and the owner's life cycle projection to cost evaluation.

questions.question: Which of the following are major aspects to consider in the final selection of a product?

options.A: Bid spread between competing general contractors
options.B: Supply chain risk and equipment lead time
options.C: AHJ's permit-processing schedule
options.D: Design firm's professional-liability exposure
options.E: Compatibility with other selected products
options.F: Product representative's sales quota

questions.explanation: Final selection weighs the owner's requirements and project conditions, the product's characteristics and quality, the risk of supply chain problems and long equipment lead times, how well it works with the other products chosen, the manufacturer, installation needs, installed and operating cost, maintenance and warranty. Bid spread, permit timing, the design firm's liability exposure and a representative's quota are not product-selection criteria.

questions.question: Which are common sources or methods of obtaining product information?

options.A: Contractor submittal logs
options.B: Trade shows
options.C: Owner work-order records
options.D: Bid tabulations
options.E: Product standards websites
options.F: Schedules of values

questions.explanation: Common sources of product information include manufacturers' websites, authorities having jurisdiction, product standards websites, printed catalogs and datasheets, trade shows, and local product representatives. Submittal logs, bid tabulations and schedules of values are records produced later, during procurement and construction, not sources for researching products.

questions.question: Online catalogs of construction product manufacturers are typically organized by:

options.A: UniFormat
options.B: OmniClass
options.C: MasterFormat
options.D: Manufacturer name
options.E: SectionFormat
options.F: Product trade name

questions.explanation: Online catalogs of building product manufacturers usually list the makers by MasterFormat number and title, with links to each manufacturer's website. UniFormat arranges information by systems and assemblies for early design, and OmniClass is a much broader classification of the built environment, so neither is how these catalogs are usually arranged.

questions.question: The owner's primary goal is low capital cost. An enhanced product option costs more up front but lowers installation and maintenance costs. Which options are often specified?

options.A: Enhanced product options
options.B: Options the manufacturer recommends
options.C: Options chosen by the contractor
options.D: Basic product options
options.E: Options with the lowest maintenance cost
options.F: Custom product options

questions.explanation: When the owner's main goal is low capital cost, basic product options are usually specified. An enhanced option with a higher first cost but lower installation and maintenance costs makes sense when life cycle value is the goal; here the owner's stated priority, not the lower long-term cost, decides.

questions.question: The owner insists on a color available only from a manufacturer with a longer lead time. What must the owner weigh?

options.A: Whether it can wait for the product, at extra cost
options.B: Whether the A/E will absorb any delay costs
options.C: Whether the maker will expedite at no cost
options.D: Whether a domestic product avoids the delay
options.E: Whether the contractor will absorb the delay costs
options.F: Whether trained installers are available locally

questions.explanation: When meeting a design goal, such as a color only one maker offers, calls for a product that takes longer to arrive, the owner decides whether it can accept the extra time and the added cost that comes with it, since every day the project is late costs the owner money. The A/E, the contractor and the manufacturer do not absorb that delay for the owner.

questions.question: Which statements comparing domestic and imported products are correct?

options.A: Domestic products often have shorter, more reliable delivery schedules.
options.B: Domestic products are more cost-effective because their quality is higher.
options.C: Imported products can be more or less cost-effective than domestic ones.
options.D: Country of origin can affect delivery time, testing, parts availability, and warranty service.
options.E: Both {A} and {D}
options.F: {A}, {C} and {D}

questions.explanation: Domestic products tend to arrive sooner and more predictably, imported products can cost more or less than domestic ones because their quality varies, and a product's country of origin bears on delivery time, testing, spare parts and warranty service, so {F} is right. Nothing supports the claim that domestic products are cheaper because they are of higher quality.

questions.question: A project has a very short construction period, and early completion is crucial. Which product trait most argues against selecting a product?

options.A: A high embodied-carbon value
options.B: A guide spec naming competitors
options.C: A long delivery time
options.D: A specialized technique with ample local labor
options.E: A high cost for maintenance supplies
options.F: A low first cost but costly upkeep

questions.explanation: Products with long delivery times may not suit a project with a short construction period or one where early completion is crucial, so lead time weighs most heavily here. A specialized installation technique is a concern only where skilled local workers are scarce, and the option with ample local labor removes that concern; maintenance and carbon do not affect the schedule.

questions.question: Which statements about custom products are correct?

options.A: To overcome long lead times, the owner may buy custom products before construction and furnish them to the contractor.
options.B: Manufacturers often require prepayment on orders for custom products.
options.C: Custom products are usually stocked for shipment when a purchase order arrives.
options.D: A custom product needs no further testing if the standard product was already certified.
options.E: Both {A} and {B}
options.F: Both {B} and {D}

questions.explanation: Custom products are made to order and rarely stocked, so lead times can be long; the owner may buy them before construction and furnish them to the contractor to install, and manufacturers often ask for prepayment in case the product is never used, so {E} is right. Stock ready to ship describes standard products, and altering a certified standard product can call for more testing.

questions.question: Which costs can make a product with a low initial cost expensive over its service life?

options.A: Expensive, labor-intensive maintenance
options.B: Higher building permit fees
options.C: Substitution-request processing costs
options.D: Higher A/E detailing fees
options.E: Regular replacement of a high-cost component
options.F: Prepayment on a custom product order

questions.explanation: A cheap product can become costly to own if its maintenance is expensive and labor-intensive, or if routine service means regularly replacing a high-cost component. Permit fees, substitution processing, A/E detailing and custom-order prepayment are one-time costs of design, procurement or ordering, not costs that recur over the product's life.

questions.question: When should a product's expected maintenance cost be discussed with the owner?

options.A: During submittal review
options.B: Before the product is specified
options.C: During the bidding phase
options.D: At closeout, with the O&M manuals
options.E: At the preconstruction conference
options.F: During the one-year correction period

questions.explanation: Because the product chosen drives the cost and ease of operating and maintaining it, its expected upkeep cost should be looked into and talked over with the owner before the product goes into the specifications. By bidding, submittal review or closeout the choice has already been made, and the owner has lost the chance to weigh it.

questions.question: Which factors belong in estimating a product's life cycle cost?

options.A: Number of contractors expected to bid
options.B: Permit and inspection fees for the project
options.C: Local availability of qualified installers
options.D: The A/E's construction administration fees
options.E: Projected frequency of repair or replacement
options.F: Retainage withheld from progress payments

questions.explanation: Life cycle cost estimates should account for how often the product is expected to need repair or replacement from normal deterioration, and whether trained or authorized installers and service technicians can be found in the project area. Bidder counts, permit and A/E fees, and retainage are project or payment matters that do not change what the product costs to own.

questions.question: An unsprinklered office building (Group B, Type IIA construction) reaches 80 ft above grade. The adopted building code allows Type IIA, Group B buildings 65 ft without sprinklers and 85 ft with a sprinkler system throughout. To keep the 80-ft height, the team must:

options.A: Do nothing, since 80 ft is within the height limit
options.B: Change to Type IIB construction
options.C: Lower the building, since 80 ft is never allowed
options.D: Sprinkler the building throughout
options.E: Change to Type IIIA construction
options.F: Change to Type IV (HT) construction

questions.explanation: At 80 ft the building is over the 65-ft limit for an unsprinklered Type IIA building but within the 85-ft limit once it is sprinklered throughout, so adding sprinklers keeps the design. Type IIB has lower height limits, and Types IIIA and IV (HT) carry the same 65-ft and 85-ft limits as Type IIA, so changing construction type does not help.

questions.question: A sprinklered Type IIA office building could reach 85 ft under the 2018 IBC, but the code the jurisdiction has adopted allows 75 ft for Type IIA. Which code dictates the height?

options.A: The local code, which has jurisdiction
options.B: The 2018 IBC, as the model code
options.C: Whichever code allows the greater height
options.D: Whichever code the specifications cite first
options.E: The IBC, since an AHJ cannot modify it
options.F: The newest edition the ICC has published

questions.explanation: The code that governs is the one in force where the project is built, which here is the jurisdiction's adopted code. A model code such as the IBC has no legal force until an authority having jurisdiction adopts it, and the AHJ may adopt only parts of it and change them, as it did with this height limit.

questions.question: Why is 'insulation as required by code' inadequate in a specification?

options.A: Codes may not be cited in project specifications
options.B: It does not state the actual requirement
options.C: Thermal values must come from reference standards
options.D: Code citations need the AHJ's prior approval
options.E: It should cite the IECC section instead
options.F: Code requirements belong only on the drawings

questions.explanation: A specification has to state the actual requirement, such as a specific minimum R-value, so the contractor knows what to provide and the A/E can confirm the code is met. 'As required by code' leaves the requirement undefined; codes can be referenced in specifications, but the specific value still has to be written out.

questions.question: Where should a schedule that covers materials from several specification sections be placed?

options.A: At the end of PART 3 of each section
options.B: In PART 2 of the lead section
options.C: On the drawings or in a separate section
options.D: In PART 1, under submittals
options.E: At the end of PART 3 of the lead section
options.F: In PART 1, under related requirements

questions.explanation: A schedule that covers materials from several specification sections, such as a sealant or hardware schedule, belongs on the drawings or in a specification section of its own, where all the related sections can use it. A schedule that serves only one section goes at the end of that section's PART 3—EXECUTION.

questions.question: To find a list of the reference standards a building code incorporates, the specifier should consult:

options.A: ANSI's registry of approved standards
options.B: The AHJ's log of granted variances
options.C: The manufacturers' guide specifications
options.D: The building code's appendices
options.E: The References article in each section
options.F: The ICC's evaluation service reports

questions.explanation: Model codes adopt many voluntary reference standards, and each code's own appendices give a convenient list of the standards it references. A registry of approved standards does not show which ones a particular code adopts, and an evaluation report addresses one product's compliance with the code.

questions.question: Which project site characteristics should the specifier obtain from the other consultants' determinations?

options.A: The owner's maintenance program
options.B: Environmental severity classification
options.C: Expected frequency of use
options.D: Security, vandalism, and theft concerns
options.E: Energy code climate zone
options.F: Space constraints

questions.explanation: Site characteristics such as the environmental severity classification, the energy code climate zone, wind loads calculated under ASCE/SEI 7, and exposure to saltwater or de-icing chemicals are determined by other consultants, and the specifier should get them. Maintenance programs, frequency of use, space constraints and security concerns are project conditions the specifier compares directly with the manufacturer's data.

questions.question: A manufacturer's guide specification states its own test result, Smoke Developed 150 per ASTM E84, while the building code accepts Smoke Developed 450. What is the risk of copying 150 into the project specification?

options.A: It falls below the code minimum
options.B: It violates ASTM's copyright
options.C: It limits the comparable products
options.D: It conflicts with the energy code
options.E: It exceeds the code's flame spread limit
options.F: It requires an AHJ code modification

questions.explanation: Copying a manufacturer's own test result instead of the value the code accepts sets a stricter bar than the project needs, which can rule out comparable products and push the specification toward a proprietary one. A rating of 150 is stricter than 450, so it does not fall below the code minimum.

questions.question: A manufacturer's guide specification includes the line 'No Substitutions.' Who should decide whether substitutions are acceptable on the project?

options.A: The contractor, after award
options.B: The guide spec's manufacturer
options.C: The product representative
options.D: The owner and the designer
options.E: The owner and the contractor
options.F: The AHJ, during plan review

questions.explanation: Whether substitutions are allowed is a project decision for the owner and the design professional. A 'No Substitutions' line in a guide specification serves the manufacturer's interest, so guide specifications should be reviewed and edited for the project rather than dropped in as written; the contractor and the representative do not make that call.

questions.question: Most project specifications list more than one acceptable manufacturer. What should a product representative therefore be ready to do?

options.A: Name other qualified competitive sources
options.B: Match the lowest competing price
options.C: Prepare the contractor's substitution requests
options.D: Justify a sole-source specification
options.E: Write the specification section for the A/E
options.F: Register the project with the manufacturer

questions.explanation: Good representatives know competing products as well as their own and can name other qualified sources the specifier could list. They would rather compete against qualified products than against cheap, inferior ones, so helping build a sound list of acceptable manufacturers serves them too; they do not write the section or justify a sole source.

questions.question: During a code modification request, how can a product representative help the A/E?

options.A: A written guarantee of AHJ approval
options.B: Technical help and an equivalent product
options.C: A modification issued by the manufacturer
options.D: Indemnity for the modified design
options.E: An interpretation from the maker's R&D staff
options.F: Approval of the modification by the rep

questions.explanation: A product representative can give the A/E technical assistance and offer an equivalent product that helps the design meet code, and may help assemble product data and certifications for the meeting with the authority. Only the authority having jurisdiction can grant a modification or interpretation, so a representative cannot guarantee or approve one.

questions.question: Which kinds of organizations typically manage ecolabels?

options.A: Federal agencies
options.B: Model code bodies
options.C: Trade associations
options.D: Local AHJs
options.E: Environmental organizations
options.F: Code evaluation services

questions.explanation: Ecolabels are run mostly by private companies, trade associations and environmental organizations; examples include the Carpet and Rug Institute's Green Label Plus, UL's GREENGUARD and FSC Chain of Custody Certification. They are not government programs, code requirements or the evaluation reports that model code organizations issue.

questions.question: The GREENGUARD ecolabel is managed by:

options.A: Green Seal
options.B: Carpet and Rug Institute
options.C: Forest Stewardship Council
options.D: Underwriters Laboratories
options.E: ASTM International
options.F: International Code Council

questions.explanation: GREENGUARD is the ecolabel run by Underwriters Laboratories (UL). Green Seal is a separate ecolabel despite the similar name, the Carpet and Rug Institute runs Green Label Plus, and the Forest Stewardship Council runs FSC Chain of Custody Certification.

questions.question: An ecolabel is best described as:

options.A: A packaging mark showing environmental criteria are met
options.B: A summary of the product's complete life cycle assessment
options.C: A third-party report showing model code compliance
options.D: A sustainability standard used to rate whole buildings
options.E: A declaration of the product's material ingredients
options.F: A test report on the product's emissions

questions.explanation: An ecolabel is a mark on a product's packaging that lets buyers see at a glance that the product meets specific environmental performance criteria. A life cycle assessment is what most sustainability standards rely on, and a report showing that a product complies with the model code is an evaluation report.

questions.question: Three insulating glass units are compared. Visible light transmittance: Unit A 70%, Unit B 60%, Unit C 65%. Winter U-value: Unit A 0.48, Unit B 0.28, Unit C 0.33. Which units best meet 'high transparency' and 'thermal resistance,' in that order?

options.A: Unit B, then Unit A
options.B: Unit A, then Unit B
options.C: Unit C, then Unit C
options.D: Unit A, then Unit A
options.E: Unit C, then Unit B
options.F: Unit A, then Unit C

questions.explanation: Transparency is measured by visible light transmittance, so the highest value, Unit A at 70%, is best. Thermal resistance improves as the U-value falls, so the lowest U-value, Unit B at 0.28, is best. Picking Unit A for both reads the U-value backward, as if a higher number meant better insulation.

questions.question: A carpet tile specification requires cut loop pile. The submitted product has multi-level pattern loop pile, and its face weight and density meet the specified minimums. The product:

options.A: Complies, since face weight and density meet the spec
options.B: Complies, since pile type is an aesthetic choice
options.C: Does not comply, since the pile is not cut loop
options.D: Can't be judged until it is installed and inspected
options.E: Complies, since its fiber is solution-dyed nylon
options.F: Complies, since gauge and stitch rate are unspecified

questions.explanation: Each stated requirement must be met on its own. Cut loop and multi-level pattern loop are different pile constructions, so the product fails the pile requirement however well it meets the face weight and density minimums; pile type is a specified characteristic, not a matter of taste that the submittal can override.

questions.question: NFPA 1, Fire Code, and NFPA 13, Sprinkler Systems, are, respectively:

options.A: A reference standard and a code
options.B: A regulation and a reference standard
options.C: A reference standard and a reference standard
options.D: A code and a reference standard
options.E: A regulation and a code
options.F: A reference standard and a regulation

questions.explanation: NFPA 1, Fire Code, is a model code that authorities having jurisdiction can adopt and enforce, while NFPA 13, Standard for the Installation of Sprinkler Systems, is an installation standard. Codes often cite NFPA 13, which gives it legal force there, but it is still a standard, and neither document is a government regulation.

questions.question: New construction in a state must meet at least a baseline sustainability rating, and the design team is close to qualifying for the next level up, missing only a handful of credits. Which actions should the team take?

options.A: Weigh near credits' cost and time, then tell the owner
options.B: Proceed, since the state minimum is already met
options.C: Swap in lower-VOC paint though the current paint complies
options.D: Drop the target to the state minimum to avoid cost
options.E: Revisit credits not pursued to see if they are viable
options.F: Leave the extra credits to the contractor after award

questions.explanation: The team should find the credits it is close to earning, weigh what they would take in cost, availability and time, and report that to the owner, and it should revisit credits it had not pursued to see whether they could still be achieved. Simply proceeding at the minimum, or leaving credits to the contractor, skips the evaluation the owner needs to decide.

questions.question: A civil engineer specified a parking-lot striping paint with more than 50 g/L of VOCs. Will switching to a lower-VOC paint likely earn another sustainability credit?

options.A: Yes, low-VOC paint earns credit anywhere on the site
options.B: No, credits rarely cover VOCs outside the envelope
options.C: Yes, but only once the AHJ approves the change
options.D: No, VOC limits apply only to interior flooring
options.E: Yes, since its VOCs can drift in through open doors
options.F: No, since VOC content is not a sustainability metric

questions.explanation: Sustainability credits rarely set VOC limits for products used outside the building envelope, such as pavement markings in a parking lot, so the switch is unlikely to earn a credit. It may still be worth making, because VOCs from outdoor paint can drift into the building through open doors and windows and add to air pollution.

questions.question: On a six-scope project the owner signs separate prime contracts for site, general, masonry, mechanical, plumbing, and electrical work. Unless the documents assign coordination authority to a contractual entity, who most likely bears coordination responsibility?

options.A: The owner
options.B: The architect/engineer, who prepared the documents
options.C: The masonry contractor, whose work the others build on
options.D: The prime with the largest contract value
options.E: The general construction prime, as de facto general contractor
options.F: The site construction prime, whose work starts first

questions.explanation: In a multiple-prime arrangement each prime contracts only with the owner, so unless the documents give some contractual entity, such as a construction manager, the duty and authority to coordinate, the owner may end up with it. No prime has authority over the other primes, so neither contract size nor the order of the work makes one of them the coordinator.

questions.question: For a multiple-prime project, which of the following describe how the A/E's construction documents most commonly differ from those for a single-prime project?

options.A: A separate set of documents is prepared for each prime contract
options.B: The documents include a clear summary of the extent of each contract
options.C: Division 01 is omitted, since each prime writes its own requirements
options.D: Preparation is handed to the lowest qualified prime for each scope
options.E: One combined project manual applies identically to each prime
options.F: Dividing the work is left to the primes to settle with each other

questions.explanation: For multiple primes the A/E may prepare a separate set of documents for each contract, and the documents need a clear summary of what each contract includes so every prime knows its scope. How the work is divided and coordinated is set by the A/E, construction manager or owner-builder, not left to the primes, and Division 01 still carries the scope requirements.

questions.question: Multiple-prime contracts are often linked to which scheduling technique, and to what cost effect?

options.A: Fast-track scheduling, with detailed coordination adding to project cost
options.B: Linear sequencing, with reduced documentation cost from consolidating scopes
options.C: Critical-path scheduling, removing any need for construction management
options.D: Phased occupancy, with all coordination risk passed to the subcontractors
options.E: Fast-track scheduling, with separate scopes lowering overall project cost
options.F: Phased construction, with the A/E's document preparation time reduced

questions.explanation: Multiple-prime contracts often result from fast-track scheduling, where separate packages are let as their documents are ready. The detailed coordination of documents and contracts this demands can add to project cost, and claims between contracts are to be expected, so splitting the work into separate scopes does not by itself lower cost.

questions.question: On a multiple-prime project, the drawings may show the limits of each prime contract's work graphically. Where should the scope of each contract be described in writing?

options.A: In Division 01, General Requirements
options.B: In notes on the drawings beside the graphic limits
options.C: In PART 3, EXECUTION, of the specification section
options.D: In PART 1, GENERAL, of the specification section
options.E: In the general conditions of each prime contract
options.F: In the MasterFormat section titles, by trade

questions.explanation: Drawings can mark the limits of each contract's work, but the written description of each contract's scope belongs in Division 01—General Requirements and in PART 1—GENERAL of the specification sections. Notes on the drawings and MasterFormat section titles do not assign work to contractors or trades, and PART 3 covers execution rather than scope.

questions.question: Why do large or complex multiple-prime projects often require construction management, when a comparable single-prime project may not?

options.A: Multiple-prime contracts cannot be fast-tracked unless a CM holds contracts
options.B: Construction management is legally mandated when more than one trade is on site
options.C: No single contractor coordinates the primes, so inter-contract claims arise
options.D: The A/E is contractually barred from providing contract administration here
options.E: The A/E cannot prepare a separate set of documents for each prime contract
options.F: The owner is barred from coordinating the work between separate primes

questions.explanation: With several primes each contracting only with the owner, no single contractor coordinates the others, so coordination is critical and claims between contracts are to be expected; that is why large or complex multiple-prime projects often bring in construction management. On a single-prime project the contractor divides and coordinates the work itself, and nothing bars the owner from coordinating.

questions.question: An owner wants single-point responsibility for construction cost through a GMP, plus major-trade input during design. Which method fits?

options.A: CM as advisor, which binds the owner to a GMP
options.B: CMAR, which offers a GMP after design input
options.C: Design-bid-build, where the low bid sets the sum
options.D: Multiple-prime, where each prime sets a GMP
options.E: CM as agent, which guarantees a GMP to the owner
options.F: Owner-build, where specialty primes give a GMP

questions.explanation: Under construction manager at risk, the CM brings major trade subcontractors in during design and, once the documents are far enough along, takes on the cost risk and proposes a guaranteed maximum price. A CM as advisor cannot bind the owner or carry cost risk, and in design-bid-build the price comes from bids on completed documents, with no trade input during design.

questions.question: In design-bid-build, the A/E and contractor have no contract with each other. What do their separate agreements with the owner create between them?

options.A: A third-party relationship of mutual reliance
options.B: An implied contract that either party may enforce
options.C: A subcontract relationship running through the owner
options.D: No relationship of any kind during construction
options.E: A tripartite contract that all three parties sign
options.F: A direct contractual relationship for administration

questions.explanation: Although the A/E and contractor have no contract with each other, their separate agreements with the owner create a third-party relationship: the contractor relies on the A/E doing its duties under the owner-A/E agreement, and the A/E relies on the contractor doing its duties under the owner-contractor agreement.
