options.B: Quality control for the tested batch and quality assurance for concrete not yet placed
options.C: Quality control only, because any material test is an evaluation of completed work
options.D: Neither, because field tests count as informational submittals rather than quality steps
options.E: Quality assurance for the tested batch and quality control for the concrete once placed
options.F: Quality control by the supplier, performed before its materials ship to the site

questions.explanation: Quality control for one step can become quality assurance for the next, a pattern sometimes called a quality loop or spiral. The slump test checks the batch in the mixer, which makes it quality control for that batch, and it also assures the quality of that same concrete before it goes into the work. Calling it only one or the other misses that the two overlap.

questions.question: An owner wants 10 percent more floor area but will not raise the project budget. What must happen to keep the design and budget in balance?

options.A: Extend the design schedule so the cost estimates can be refined
options.B: Carry the added area in the contractor's contingency for pricing
options.C: Keep the components and settle the overrun later by change order
options.D: Reduce the cost of the components used to construct the project
options.E: Extend the construction time so it absorbs the cost of the added area
options.F: Increase the project budget to match the cost of the added area

questions.explanation: A change to the design's extent or to the budget must bring a matching change in the other: more floor area needs either a larger budget or less costly components. With the budget fixed, reducing the cost of the components is the only way to keep the two in balance. Settling the gap later by change order or contingency just defers the problem and leads to misunderstandings when the work is priced.

questions.question: With design development documents complete, an estimator applies costs per unit of assembled construction, such as the roof system, exterior wall and floor structure. Which estimating method is this, and how accurate is it?

options.A: Assemblies/systems estimate, accurate to about 10 percent
options.B: Unit of measure estimate, accurate to about 15 to 20 percent
options.C: Unit price estimate, accurate to about 3 to 5 percent
options.D: Order of magnitude estimate, accurate to about 20 to 25 percent
options.E: Assemblies/systems estimate, accurate to about 15 to 20 percent
options.F: Unit price estimate, accurate to about 10 percent

questions.explanation: An assemblies or systems estimate prices units of assembled construction, often organized by UniFormat, needs the information developed in design development, and is accurate to about 10 percent. A unit price estimate, the most accurate at about 3 to 5 percent, needs a full quantity takeoff from completed construction documents. An order of magnitude estimate, at 20 to 25 percent, uses costs per unit of occupancy, such as per bed or per seat.

questions.question: A value analysis workshop opens with the A/E presenting the background and decisions behind the design. What should the team establish next, before it generates ideas?

options.A: A short list of the alternatives that promise the most savings
options.B: Workable solutions whose costs are compared to the program
options.C: The owner's objectives, key criteria and definition of value
options.D: A written report of the recommendations and their costs
options.E: Items that can be left out now and added later without disruption
options.F: As many lower-cost product and system ideas as possible

questions.explanation: The workshop begins with the information phase: after the A/E explains the background and decisions behind the design, the team analyzes the key functional issues and sets the owner's objectives, key criteria and definition of value. Generating ideas is the next phase, and short-listing, developing solutions and writing the report all come after that, in the evaluation, development and presentation phases.

questions.question: During the speculation (creative) phase of a value analysis workshop, one team member starts rejecting each idea as soon as it is offered. Why is that out of step with this phase?

options.A: Ideas may be rejected only by the owner, who alone defines value during this phase
options.B: The phase develops ideas into workable solutions, so each must first be fully priced
options.C: Rejected ideas must be logged in the written report, which is prepared in this phase
options.D: The phase aims to generate as many ideas as possible, and screening comes next
options.E: Screening belongs to the information phase, which has already been completed
options.F: Ideas may be rejected only by the A/E, whose design decisions are under review

questions.explanation: The speculation (creative) phase exists to produce as many ideas as possible for products, materials, systems and equipment with lower first cost or better life cycle value. Judging ideas belongs to the next step, the evaluation (analysis) phase, where criteria are defined first and the unworthy ideas are then discarded. Neither the owner nor the A/E is the sole gatekeeper during brainstorming.

questions.question: In the five-phase value analysis workshop, what happens during the development phase?

options.A: Chosen ideas are made workable, with pros, cons and costs compared to the program
options.B: Ideas are judged against defined criteria, and the unworthy ones are thrown out
options.C: The owner's objectives, key criteria and definition of value are first established
options.D: The approved changes are carried out and later measured against other options
options.E: As many ideas as possible are generated for lower-cost products and systems
options.F: A written report with recommendations and their costs is prepared

questions.explanation: In the development phase, the ideas chosen during evaluation are expanded into workable solutions, their advantages and disadvantages are set out, and their costs are compared with the original program. Throwing out unworthy ideas happens one step earlier, in the evaluation (analysis) phase, and the written report with recommendations comes one step later, in the presentation phase.

questions.question: A value analysis team has expanded its best ideas into workable solutions and compared their costs with the program. What is the last workshop phase, and what does it produce?

options.A: The implementation phase, which produces revised construction documents for bidding
options.B: The presentation phase, which yields a written report with recommendations and costs
options.C: The evaluation phase, which produces a review of how the changes performed in use
options.D: The information phase, which produces a statement of the owner's definition of value
options.E: The development phase, which produces costed solutions with pros and cons
options.F: The speculation phase, which produces a list of alternative design ideas

questions.explanation: The workshop ends with the presentation phase, which produces a written report giving the team's recommendations and their costs. The five workshop phases are information, speculation, evaluation, development and presentation, so the costed solutions the team already has came from the development phase. Implementing the changes and reviewing how they performed are not phases of the workshop.

questions.question: Bids are in, and the team wants to implement two value analysis items: a simple product swap and a change to the structural system. How do these compare?

options.A: Both can go ahead without delay, since changes made at the bidding stage do not affect the design schedule
options.B: Neither can go ahead, since value analysis must be finished before the pricing stage of a project begins
options.C: The swap can likely go ahead without delay, but the structural change may force redesign and extend the schedule
options.D: The structural change is easier, since major structural systems are priced as allowances during bidding
options.E: The structural change can go ahead now, but the product swap must wait until construction begins
options.F: Both should wait for construction, when they can be made by change order with less risk to cost

questions.explanation: At the pricing stage, fairly simple value analysis decisions can usually still be made without upsetting the schedule, and competition still keeps prices in check, but complex changes may force redesign of parts of the project and extend the schedule. Value analysis is most efficient the earlier it happens; during construction, cost and schedule are at greater risk, so waiting for change orders is the wrong move.

questions.question: In the five-phase value analysis workshop, what does the evaluation (analysis) phase involve?

options.A: The built change's performance is measured, along with how other options might have done
options.B: Selected ideas are expanded into workable solutions whose costs are compared to the program
options.C: As many ideas as possible are generated for lower first cost or better life cycle value
options.D: After criteria are defined, weak ideas are discarded and the most promising carried forward
options.E: The owner's objectives, key criteria and definition of value are established for the team
options.F: A written report with the team's recommendations and their costs is prepared

questions.explanation: In the evaluation (analysis) phase, the team first defines its evaluation criteria, then judges the ideas from the speculation phase, discards the unworthy ones and carries forward those with the most potential for savings and better value. Expanding ideas into costed solutions is the development phase that follows. Measuring how a built change performed is not one of the five workshop phases at all.

questions.question: Which statements about common value analysis recommendations are accurate?

options.A: Reducing project size is the owner's usual preferred way to cut cost
options.B: Simplified detailing to cut cost can affect the project's aesthetic value
options.C: Deferring items to a later phase always disrupts the facility's operations
options.D: Cheaper substitute products reliably raise the project's life cycle value
options.E: New technologies tend to be higher-risk options with greater return potential
options.F: Changes in product types can proceed without the A/E or owner taking part

questions.explanation: Simplifying details to cut cost can affect the project's aesthetic value, and new technologies tend to be higher-risk alternatives with greater potential return. Swapping in cheaper products can lower life cycle value, changes in product types may need the A/E, sub-consultants and owner to judge whether they are practical, deferral suits only items that can be added later without disruption, and owners are usually reluctant to cut size.

questions.question: Beyond the owner's program, which of these is NOT one of the design considerations and constraints that guide the A/E?

options.A: The contractor's construction means and methods
options.B: Constructability of the proposed design decisions
options.C: Regulations such as codes and land-use rules
options.D: Sustainability required by the owner or by code
options.E: Functional requirements of the owner's spaces
options.F: The owner's budget for the project

questions.explanation: The design considerations and constraints that guide the A/E, beyond the owner's program, are aesthetics, functional requirements, regulations, sustainability, constructability and budget. Means and methods remain the contractor's responsibility. Constructability is the A/E's review of whether design decisions are practical and economical to build, not control over how the contractor builds them.

questions.question: Which statements about aesthetic requirements are accurate?

options.A: Acoustical and tactile qualities can shape a design's aesthetic effect, not only visual ones
options.B: Context requirements are advisory and cannot be grounds for withholding a building permit
options.C: Aesthetic requirements are refined in earnest during schematic design and design development
options.D: A skilled A/E translates the owner's vision exactly, keeping its own tastes out of the design
options.E: Both {A} and {C}
options.F: {A}, {C} and {D}

questions.explanation: {E} is right. Aesthetic effects are not only visual: acoustical, tactile and other qualities also shape them, and although their basis may be set in project conception, aesthetic requirements are refined in earnest during schematic design and design development. Authorities having jurisdiction can withhold zoning or building permits when a design ignores its context, and A/Es always bring their own tastes, so the owner's vision is seldom translated exactly.

questions.question: Midway through design, the A/E concludes that an adjacency required by the owner's program will hurt how the building works. Which statements reflect recommended practice?

options.A: The A/E should treat the owner's program like a contract document
options.B: The A/E should revise the layout on its own judgment and explain it later
options.C: The A/E should raise the issue with the owner and propose possible solutions
options.D: Conformance to the owner's program is the benchmark of the A/E's success
options.E: Both {A} and {C}
options.F: {A}, {C} and {D}

questions.explanation: {F} is right. How well the A/E conforms to the owner's program is the measure of its success, so it should treat the program as a contract document, much as a contractor treats the construction documents. When the A/E disagrees with part of the program, it should tell the owner and propose solutions for the owner to consider, not change the layout on its own and explain afterward.

questions.question: Which group consists entirely of items classified as materials rather than products or assemblies?

options.A: Sand, portland cement, lumber and glass
options.B: Brick, sealants, fasteners and stone
options.C: Stone, precast panels, drywall and metals
options.D: Glass, paint, roofing membranes and lumber
options.E: Sand, stone, metals and plumbing fixtures
options.F: Lumber, brick, glass and unitized curtain walls

questions.explanation: Materials are substances extracted, harvested, recycled or processed from a raw state into something with useful physical properties, such as sand, portland cement, stone, brick, lumber, metals and glass. Sealants, fasteners, paint, roofing membranes and plumbing fixtures are products, manufactured units made of several materials. Precast panels, drywall partitions and unitized curtain walls are assemblies or fabrications.

questions.question: A specifier is sorting items by product type. Which items fit the definition of equipment rather than a product or an assembly?

options.A: Plumbing fixture
options.B: Domestic water heater
options.C: Unitized curtain wall
options.D: Glazed concrete masonry unit
options.E: Packaged air conditioning unit
options.F: Precast concrete panel

questions.explanation: Equipment is a self-contained configuration of materials, products and assemblies with an operational function, often connected to a building utility; water heaters, pumps, elevators, fans and packaged air conditioning units are typical examples. Plumbing fixtures connect to utilities too, but they are classed as products, as are glazed masonry units, while unitized curtain walls and precast concrete panels are assemblies.

questions.question: Product decisions are made progressively through design. Which decision is typical of the schematic design phase?

options.A: Choosing the sealant manufacturer and joint width at the curtain wall perimeter
options.B: Confirming curtain wall anchor spacing shown on the fabricator's shop drawings
options.C: Choosing the glass coating and frame finish from the manufacturer's samples
options.D: Choosing an aluminum curtain wall or brick veneer for the exterior skin
options.E: Choosing among the listed curtain wall makers after contract award
options.F: Choosing the brick's color, texture and mortar joint profile

questions.explanation: Product decisions start at the level of building elements and grow more detailed as design proceeds. In schematic design, basic choices such as steel or concrete structure, or aluminum curtain wall or brick veneer skin, are made from basic information on aesthetics, form, function and budget. Choosing finishes, colors, sealants and manufacturers comes in design development and the construction documents, and shop drawings come during construction.

questions.question: A public owner that is not prequalifying bidders wants each to sign an owner-furnished affidavit that it does not maintain segregated facilities. In which Division 00 group does this form belong?

options.A: 00 43 00 Procurement Form Supplements
options.B: 00 21 00 Instructions for Procurement
options.C: 00 73 00 Supplementary Conditions
options.D: 00 45 00 Representations and Certifications
options.E: 00 62 00 Certificates and Other Forms
options.F: 00 41 00 Bid Forms

questions.explanation: Owner-furnished, single-purpose forms that verify a bidder has a qualification the project needs are representations and certifications, 00 45 00, and the non-segregated facilities affidavit is a standard example. They are common on public work and especially useful when bidders were not prequalified. Procurement form supplements, 00 43 00, are attachments that carry added bid information, such as the bid security form or a list of subcontractors.

questions.question: Division 00 procurement and contracting documents are not specifications, yet MasterFormat gives them standard numbers and locations. Why?

options.A: They are usually bound in the project manual with the specifications.
options.B: They become technical specifications once the agreement is signed.
options.C: They are prepared by the specifier rather than by the owner's counsel.
options.D: They govern Divisions 01 through 49 and so must share their numbering.
options.E: MasterFormat classifies them with Division 01 as general requirements.
options.F: They are written in SectionFormat's three-part structure.

questions.explanation: Division 00 items are documents, not specifications, but MasterFormat gives them standard numbers and locations because they are usually bound in the project manual with the specifications; the project manual concept gives every document a standard place. Divisions 01 through 49 are the specifications. Procurement and contracting documents are usually prepared by or with the owner and its legal counsel and insurance advisor, not by the specifier alone.

questions.question: A specifier is evaluating products against a project's sustainability criteria and plans to consult GreenFormat. How is GreenFormat best described?

options.A: A green building rating system that certifies whole projects
options.B: A website listed as a source of product information arranged by sustainability criteria
options.C: A standard format that arranges a specification section into three parts
options.D: A reference standard that defines laboratory tests for recycled content
options.E: An ecolabel placed on the packaging of products that meet environmental criteria
options.F: A life cycle assessment method used by most sustainability standards

questions.explanation: GreenFormat is one of several online resources, along with Building Green, Energy Star, GreenSeal and GreenSpec, that present product information organized by sustainability criteria, which makes it useful when evaluating a product's sustainable attributes. A green building rating system is a separate thing: a project may require products that meet its principles. SectionFormat, not GreenFormat, organizes a specification section into three parts.

questions.question: Which drawing types, once reserved for expressing design concepts, can now be produced easily from a digital model for construction use?

options.A: Diagrams
options.B: Perspectives
options.C: Schedules
options.D: Key plans
options.E: Isometrics
options.F: Wall sections

questions.explanation: The usual drawing types are plans, elevations, sections, details and schedules. Perspectives and isometrics once took special skill and time to draw, so they were kept for expressing design concepts; a digital model now produces them easily for construction use. Schedules, wall sections, diagrams and key plans were always part of ordinary construction drawings, so they are not the types that changed.

questions.question: Which view is paired with its correct classification?

options.A: Building wall section: non-scaled
options.B: Key plan: scaled
options.C: Single-line diagram: non-scaled
options.D: Room finish schedule: scaled
options.E: Isometric: scaled
options.F: Floor plan: non-scaled

questions.explanation: Views are either scaled or non-scaled. Scaled views are plans, elevations and cut views such as wall sections and floor plans, drawn to a stated scale. Schematic views, such as an electrical single-line diagram or a plumbing riser diagram, are non-scaled, along with key plans, schedules, perspectives, isometrics and title sheet drawings. A schedule is tabular information, so it is non-scaled even when it sits on a scaled sheet.

questions.question: How should the scale of a scaled view be shown on construction drawings?

options.A: With both a numerical scale and a graphic scale
options.B: With a graphic scale only, since it survives reduction
options.C: With a numerical scale only, stated under the title
options.D: With one sheet-wide scale noted in the title block
options.E: With a metric ratio such as 1:100 in place of both
options.F: With the scale of each view listed in the sheet index

questions.explanation: Scale is usually stated as a number, for example a 1:100 ratio or 1/8 inch to the foot, or drawn as a graphic scale. Because half-size prints are common on the construction site, good practice is to show both on the drawings. A graphic scale does stay correct when a print is reduced, but the recommendation is the pair, not either one alone.

questions.question: One floor of a large hospital is drawn at 1/8 inch scale and split across four sheets. Which non-scaled view helps a reader see which portion of the floor each sheet shows?

options.A: A riser diagram
options.B: An isometric
options.C: A key plan
options.D: A cover-sheet location map
options.E: A perspective
options.F: A schedule

questions.explanation: A key plan is a small, symbolic plan that shows how one portion of the project relates to the whole, so it is used alongside a larger-scale plan that covers only part of the building; it can also mark where sections or elevations are taken. A riser diagram depicts a whole plumbing system in one view, and a cover-sheet location map places the project on its site or in its city, not a part within the building.

questions.question: A university requires its consultants to follow the university's own drawing standard. How should this requirement be viewed?

options.A: As unusual, since the NCS governs all construction drawings
options.B: As common for large organizations and public agencies
options.C: As improper, since each firm's office standard governs
options.D: As acceptable for public agencies but not private owners
options.E: As acceptable only if the standard is based on the UDS
options.F: As proper for in-house staff but not for consultants

questions.explanation: Many large organizations and public agencies have their own drawing standards for in-house staff and consultants, so the university's requirement is common. Some private owners also require a particular standard, their own or another organization's, so it is not limited to public agencies. Every firm keeps its own office standard, but an owner may still require its own on its projects.

questions.question: In a set numbered by discipline and sheet type, what does sheet number A-201 indicate?

options.A: Architectural, elevations series, first sheet of that series
options.B: Architectural, second floor level, first sheet for that floor
options.C: Addendum A, second revision, sheet 01 of the addendum
options.D: Architectural, floor plans series, sheet 201 of that series
options.E: Architectural, sections series, first sheet of that series
options.F: Architectural, elevations series, sheet 201 of the whole set

questions.explanation: In discipline-and-sheet-type numbering, the A marks the architectural discipline, the 200 series marks elevations, and the last two digits, 01, show it is the first elevation sheet. The 2 identifies the type of sheet, not a floor level, and the 201 is not a sequential count through the whole set. Individual drawings on the sheet then get their own identifiers so each can be located easily.

questions.question: Solid lines on a drawing are most often used to designate which of the following?

options.A: Construction to be demolished
options.B: Existing conditions to be modified
options.C: Furniture not included in the contract
options.D: Elements behind the plane of the view
options.E: New construction
options.F: Match lines between drawing sheets

questions.explanation: Solid lines most often show new construction and existing conditions that are to be modified. Dashed lines show demolition work, elements lying in front of or behind the plane of the view, and items not in the agreement, such as furniture or equipment. Match lines are a special line type, made by combining solid and dashed segments, for joining drawings across sheets.

questions.question: A toilet room plan dimensions the required wheelchair turning space. Is this a proper use of dimensions?

options.A: No, dimensions should give only the actual size of built objects.
options.B: No, required clearances belong in the specifications, not on drawings.
options.C: Yes, but only on a non-scaled diagram rather than on the plan.
options.D: Yes, dimensions may also show extent or required clearances.
options.E: Yes, but only on an enlarged plan drawn at a larger scale.
options.F: No, required clearances should be listed in a schedule instead.

questions.explanation: Dimensions on drawings can give the actual size of an object, and they can also show extent or required clearances, such as a wheelchair turning space; their end points are marked with arrowheads or slash marks. Showing location, size and dimension is part of what drawings are for, so the clearance belongs on the plan rather than only in the specifications or a schedule.

questions.question: Which of the following are NOT parts of the U.S. National CAD Standard?

options.A: AIA CAD Layer Guidelines
options.B: BIM Implementation
options.C: MasterFormat
options.D: Plotting Guidelines
options.E: Uniform Drawing System
options.F: UniFormat

questions.explanation: The U.S. National CAD Standard is made up of the NIBS foreword, introduction and administration, the AIA CAD Layer Guidelines, the Uniform Drawing System, BIM Implementation and the Plotting Guidelines. MasterFormat and UniFormat are separate classification systems; they can be inserted into the Uniform Drawing System's application chapters, but they are not parts of the NCS itself.

questions.question: Who administers the U.S. National CAD Standard?

options.A: The organization that publishes the Uniform Drawing System
options.B: The AIA, which publishes the CAD Layer Guidelines
options.C: The buildingSMART alliance, a council of NIBS
options.D: The U.S. General Services Administration
options.E: ASTM International, as a consensus standard
options.F: The Department of Defense, for federal projects

questions.explanation: The buildingSMART alliance administers the NCS; the alliance is one of the councils of the National Institute of Building Sciences (NIBS). The Uniform Drawing System and the AIA CAD Layer Guidelines are component parts of the NCS, but the organizations that publish those parts do not administer the standard as a whole, and it is not a federal agency or ASTM standard.

questions.question: In a renovation, the CAD team must put existing walls to remain and new walls on separate layers. Under the AIA CAD Layer Guidelines, which layer-name field carries that distinction?

options.A: Discipline designator
options.B: Major group
options.C: Minor group
options.D: Status
options.E: Sheet type designator
options.F: Sheet sequence number

questions.explanation: AIA CAD Layer Guidelines layer names have four fields: discipline designator, major group, minor group and status. The status field identifies the condition or phase of the work, such as new, existing, temporary, not in contract or a phase number, so existing walls to remain and new walls separate there. The major group names the building system, such as walls, and the minor group only refines it.

questions.question: How is the Uniform Drawing System (UDS) structured?

options.A: As four-field hierarchical names for drawing layers
options.B: As open application chapters organized by life-cycle stage
options.C: As tables linking line widths to gray-scale and color plotting
options.D: As fixed divisions of work results with six-digit numbers
options.E: As a hierarchy of systems and assemblies, like UniFormat
options.F: As one fixed sequence of disciplines that allows no additions

questions.explanation: UDS is an open structure of application chapters organized around the stages of a facility's life cycle, into which MasterFormat, UniFormat, keynotes and specifications can be inserted. It sets the content and order of the drawing set, how sheets are identified and how files are named, so drawing information can be retrieved and reused later. Four-field layer names belong to the AIA CAD Layer Guidelines, and line-width tables to the Plotting Guidelines.

questions.question: Under the NCS plotting guidelines, each color used in CAD should be coordinated with what?

options.A: A specific line width and screening
options.B: A specific discipline designator
options.C: A specific sheet type number
options.D: A specific layer status code
options.E: A specific layer major group
options.F: A specific drawing scale

questions.explanation: Drawings rely on the printed line, and a line's width and style tell the reader what it is, such as a profile, a section cut or a hidden line. Because CAD works in colored lines, each color should be tied to a specific line width and screening, from black through gray tones, so plots read correctly. Discipline designators and status codes belong to layer naming, not plotting.

questions.question: An owner's request for qualifications asks for each firm's bonding capacity, though no performance or payment bonds will be required. Why ask?

options.A: It sets the amount of bid security each firm must furnish.
options.B: It shows the retainage the owner may withhold from payments.
options.C: It reveals both financial stability and past performance.
options.D: It replaces the firm's financial statements in the review.
options.E: It confirms licensing in the project's jurisdiction.
options.F: It shows experience in the selected delivery method.

questions.explanation: Bonding capacity is a useful qualification factor even when the owner will not require bonds, because a firm's ability to get bonded reflects both its financial stability and its record of performance. It does not set the amount of bid security or retainage. Financial statements remain a separate factor, alongside experience, capacity, licensing, personnel and equipment.

questions.question: An A/E is advising a private owner on the length of the bidding period. Which activities does the bidding period NOT need to allow time for?

options.A: Obtaining bid security when the procurement requirements call for it
options.B: Furnishing the performance and payment bonds required by the contract
options.C: Preparing qualification statements when the procurement requirements call for them
options.D: Proposing substitutions when the procurement documents permit them
options.E: Executing the owner-contractor agreement for the work
options.F: Soliciting and compiling prices from subcontractors and suppliers

questions.explanation: The bidding period should give bidders time to study the documents, attend the prebid meeting, visit the site, ask questions, propose substitutions where allowed, receive addenda, gather subcontractor and supplier prices, obtain bid security and prepare any required qualification statements. Executing the agreement and furnishing performance and payment bonds come after a bid is accepted; bid security is the guarantee that the winning bidder will do both.

questions.question: Under a public owner's bid depository for mechanical and electrical subcontracts, how do subcontractors submit prices, and what does it mainly curb?

options.A: To each prime bidder, sealed until opening, to curb collusion among primes
options.B: To the A/E for technical review, to curb unauthorized substitutions
options.C: To the owner, independently of the prime, to curb bid shopping
options.D: To the surety along with their bonds, to curb subcontractor default
options.E: Listed on the prime's bid form, to curb later changes of subcontractor
options.F: To the owner with non-collusion affidavits, to curb price fixing

questions.explanation: With a bid depository, prequalified subcontractors send their prices straight to the owner rather than through the prime contractor, a method used with some success on public work to prevent bid shopping. Because a prime cannot use one sub's price to push another lower, subs are not pressed to cut a quote after submitting it. Collusion and price fixing are dealt with through non-collusion affidavits, a different tool.

questions.question: A private owner has negotiated for two weeks with one contractor and is unhappy with its responsiveness. The owner may:

options.A: Open talks with other contractors and choose among them
options.B: Continue, since a negotiated project must stay with the first contractor invited
options.C: Hand the negotiation to the A/E, who then selects the contractor
options.D: Switch to public bidding, since private owners must bid once talks stall
options.E: Continue, since negotiation is a dialog between just two parties
options.F: Continue, since only public owners may negotiate with several firms

questions.explanation: An owner does not have to negotiate with just one contractor: it can negotiate with several, choose the one that is most responsive, and run the process however it wishes. Negotiations may be limited and restricted on public projects, but private projects have no such limits. Nothing ties this owner to the first contractor it invited or forces it into public bidding.

questions.question: In a negotiated project, the contractor's offer exceeds the owner's budget, and the owner counteroffers with a lower sum. How does the contractor usually decide whether it can accept?

options.A: It performs value analysis and repricing to test the counteroffer.
options.B: It must accept or reject at once, since only one counteroffer is allowed.
options.C: It asks the A/E to issue an addendum reducing the scope of work.
options.D: It resubmits a sealed price for a public bid opening.
options.E: It repeats the discovery step to exchange new drawings.
options.F: It treats the counteroffer as a new request for proposal.

questions.explanation: Unlike formal bidding, negotiation lets the owner make counteroffers, and the contractor may perform value analysis and repricing to judge whether a counteroffer is acceptable. The exchange can repeat several times as long as it is making progress, so there is no single take-it-or-leave-it round. Addenda, sealed rebids and new requests for proposal belong to competitive procedures, not to negotiation.

questions.question: A school district wants the lowest prices on janitorial supplies but cannot run its own public bid for each order. Which approach fits and still complies with laws on public funds?

options.A: Set up a national account with one manufacturer at a fixed price
options.B: Negotiate privately with a single preferred local supplier
options.C: Have its general contractor furnish the supplies under an allowance
options.D: Join a purchasing cooperative that solicits bids from many sellers
options.E: Assign a purchasing contract to its contractor to fill a cash allowance
options.F: Buy under a single-source proprietary purchasing contract

questions.explanation: A purchasing cooperative is a group of buyers that jointly seeks bids for goods and services from multiple sellers, which raises their purchasing power and lowers prices. Public buyers can use one to skip the expense of running their own bids while still complying with the laws that govern public funds. A national account instead gives one owner or contractor fixed pricing directly from a single manufacturer or supplier.

questions.question: A prime bidder's stipulated-sum price is built from which two pricing sources?

options.A: The A/E's estimate of probable cost and the bidder's markup
options.B: Subcontractor and supplier bids, plus the bidder's own estimates
options.C: Unit prices on the bid form and allowances stated in Division 01
options.D: Published cost databases and the owner's construction contingency
options.E: The owner's project budget and the bidder's overhead and profit
options.F: Supplier quotations and the A/E's estimate of probable cost

questions.explanation: A bidder builds its price from two sources: bids from subcontractors and suppliers for parts of the work, and its own internal estimates for the rest. Together they become the stipulated sum, the price the bidder will charge, overhead and profit included, to do the work. The A/E's estimate of probable cost serves the owner and is not one of the bidder's pricing sources.

questions.question: Which items in a contractor's bid estimate are NOT construction costs?

options.A: Royalties and license fees for using a patented product
options.B: Engineering for a delegated-design curtain wall
options.C: Rent and utilities at the contractor's head office
options.D: Premiums for the project's insurance and bonds
options.E: Salaries of the contractor's general management staff
options.F: Temporary field offices and heat for the project

questions.explanation: Construction costs are the calculable costs of doing the project's work, including royalties and licenses, delegated design engineering, insurance and bonds, permits, mobilization, temporary facilities such as field offices and heat, and taxes. Rent and utilities at the contractor's place of business and salaries of office and general management staff are overhead: the cost of running the business that is not tied to one project.

questions.question: The project contingency is held by the owner rather than built into the contract sum, and part of it is unspent at closeout. What happens to the unspent amount?

options.A: It goes to the contractor as added profit.
options.B: It must be split equally between owner and contractor.
options.C: It is released to the surety to close out the bonds.
options.D: It goes to the owner as a lower construction cost.
options.E: It is held back to fund the correction period.
options.F: It is paid to the subcontractors in proportion to their work.

questions.explanation: When the owner holds the contingency outside the contract sum, money left unspent at closeout stays with the owner and shows up as a lower construction cost. Unspent contingency goes to the contractor only when the fund sits inside its contract sum, and sharing the savings is one possible arrangement, not a required equal split.

questions.question: Why must procurement documents be readily available to subcontractors and suppliers, not only to prime bidders?

options.A: Their prices feed the bid that becomes the contract's basis of payment.
options.B: Their prices replace the A/E's estimate as the owner's construction budget.
options.C: They also sign the owner-contractor agreement along with the prime.
options.D: They must attend the prebid meeting and visit the site before pricing.
options.E: Their bids are opened publicly along with the prime bids.
options.F: They may receive documents only from the owner, never from bidders.

questions.explanation: Subcontractors and suppliers price the work too, and their prices are built into the bid that becomes the basis of payment under the construction contract. That is why the procurement documents must reach every bidder in time for efficient, accurate pricing. Subcontractors do not sign the owner-contractor agreement, and their prices do not replace the A/E's estimate.

questions.question: An A/E drafts an information control plan for the start of procurement. Which provisions conflict with good practice for such a plan?

options.A: Document every oral inquiry received from bidders.
options.B: Name the reporting and distribution services to be used.
options.C: Issue supplemental information in time for pricing.
options.D: Post editable native files so bidders can mark them up.
options.E: Exchange documents as paper or read-only electronic files.
options.F: Send supplemental information only to bidders who ask for it.

questions.explanation: An information control plan keeps distribution fair: it names the reporting and distribution services, issues supplemental information in time for pricing, records oral inquiries, and protects the documents by exchanging them as paper or read-only files. Posting editable native files invites altered documents, and sending supplemental information only to bidders who ask breaks the aim that every bidder gets the same information in time to price it.

questions.question: A contractor buys sealant from a firm that only delivers product but sends a manufacturer's representative to train the installers on site. The project manager says that site visit makes the firm a subcontractor. Which statement is accurate?

options.A: It remains a supplier; suppliers typically furnish no on-site labor, but a product representative may visit to train installers.
options.B: It becomes a subcontractor, because any firm that sends its personnel to assist with installation is furnishing labor on the project.
options.C: It becomes a separate contractor of the owner, because training the installers falls outside the contractor's own scope of work.
options.D: It remains a supplier, because suppliers are not bound by the terms of the agreement that binds the contractor and its subcontractors.
options.E: It becomes a subcontractor, because it now furnishes both the materials and on-site services for the sealant work.
options.F: It becomes a subcontractor, because its representative oversees the installation of the product it furnished.

questions.explanation: A supplier furnishes materials for others to install and typically puts no labor on site; a manufacturer's representative who visits to train, oversee or assist the installers is a recognized exception that does not change the firm's role. The answer resting on suppliers not being bound by the contractor's agreement reaches the right label for the wrong reason: work by subcontractors and suppliers alike is bound by the terms that bind the contractor.

questions.question: On a large phased campus project, the contractor proposes skipping the preconstruction meeting and covering procedures at the first progress meeting. Which response is best?

options.A: Agree; on phased work the first progress meeting serves that role
options.B: Agree, if Division 01 already describes the meeting procedures
options.C: Disagree; hold it before site work starts, perhaps more than once
options.D: Disagree; hold it once, before bids are due, for all bidders
options.E: Disagree; hold it after mobilization, once site work is under way
options.F: Disagree; hold it after the first application for payment

questions.explanation: The preconstruction meeting is in effect the unofficial start of construction, held before work begins on the site so the parties can go over procedures; a large or complex project may need more than one. Division 01 lists the meetings to be held but does not replace them, and a meeting with all bidders before bids are due is a prebid conference.

questions.question: A retail fit-out has a six-week construction period and a fixed opening date. How often should progress meetings be held?

options.A: Monthly, in step with the payment cycle
options.B: Daily or weekly, given the short duration
options.C: Only at schedule milestones, to spare the crews
options.D: As Division 01 says, regardless of duration
options.E: Twice monthly, in step with a faster payment cycle
options.F: Only before installation of certain products

questions.explanation: How often progress meetings are held depends on the extent of the project and the delivery method, and complex or short-duration projects may need them daily or weekly. A six-week fit-out with a fixed opening date is that case. Monthly is a common payment interval, not a rule for meetings, and meetings before certain products are installed are preinstallation meetings.

questions.question: The owner's representative asks to sit in on the contractor's weekly meetings with its subcontractors. Which statement is accurate?

options.A: They usually cover progress and scheduling, but not payment requests
options.B: The A/E usually attends them to interpret the RFIs raised there
options.C: They often cover payment and RFIs, but owner and A/E rarely attend
options.D: The owner usually attends them to approve subcontractor pay requests
options.E: They cover only coordination between two or more subcontractors
options.F: The owner and A/E chair them, since modifications are raised there

questions.explanation: Meetings between the contractor and its subcontractors deal with progress, scheduling and coordination, and they often take up contract matters such as payment applications, site safety, RFIs and modifications. Even so, the owner and A/E typically do not attend; these are the contractor's working sessions with its own subcontractors, not meetings the owner or A/E chairs.

questions.question: An A/E is preparing the invitation list for the closeout meeting on a new laboratory. Which parties are NOT minimum attendees for that meeting?

options.A: The facility manager
options.B: The commissioning authority
options.C: The authority having jurisdiction
options.D: The contractor's major subcontractors
options.E: The sustainability consultant
options.F: The contractor's surety

questions.explanation: The minimum attendees for the closeout meeting are the owner and its advisors, the facility manager, the A/E and its consultants, the sustainability consultant, the commissioning authority, the contractor, and its major subcontractors. Requirements of the authorities having jurisdiction are an agenda topic, but the AHJ is not a listed attendee, and neither is the contractor's surety.

questions.question: Which as-needed meeting would the owner typically schedule?

options.A: A meeting to coordinate separate contractors, color selections, and move-in plans
options.B: A meeting to address the contractor's internal organization, operation, and safety issues
options.C: A meeting to coordinate overlapping work among two or more of the contractor's subcontractors
options.D: A meeting to coordinate the builder and the A/E under a design-build contract
options.E: A meeting between the contractor and its subcontractors on applications for payment
options.F: A meeting required by a technical section before certain products are installed

questions.explanation: The owner calls as-needed meetings on matters it controls: coordinating its separate contractors and owner-furnished, contractor-installed items, choosing colors, and planning move-in. Meetings on the contractor's internal organization, operation and safety are the contractor's own, and a design-builder calls the meetings that coordinate its builder and A/E.

questions.question: An owner on a design-bid-build project expects the A/E to catch every defect before it is covered. Which of the following are purposes of the A/E's periodic site visits?

options.A: Inspecting all work continuously to certify each portion free of defects
options.B: Becoming generally familiar with the progress and quality of the work
options.C: Supervising the contractor's crews during critical operations
options.D: Visiting only when the contractor requests completion inspections
options.E: Informing the owner of known deviations and defects observed
options.F: Controlling construction means, methods and sequences

questions.explanation: The A/E visits the site at intervals suited to the stage of construction to learn, in general, how far the work has progressed and how good it is, and it tells the owner of known deviations and defects it sees. It is not required to make exhaustive or continuous inspections, so it cannot certify every portion free of defects, and supervising crews or controlling means, methods and sequences stays with the contractor.

questions.question: A contractor builds stair guards exactly as detailed. The building inspector red-tags them because the openings violate the code, and the contractor did not know of the violation. How is the correction handled?

options.A: The contractor corrects them at its own cost, because it must confirm that the documents comply with code.
options.B: The inspector must accept the guards, because the permit was issued from the approved construction documents.
options.C: The owner may accept the guards as nonconforming work, which ends the contractor's duty to correct them.
options.D: The work is redone to meet code, and the contractor may be entitled to a change order for it.
options.E: The A/E rebuilds the guards at its own cost, since code compliance of the documents is its responsibility.
options.F: The contractor corrects them at its own cost, since it pays for all corrective work and retesting.

questions.explanation: Code compliance of the documents is the A/E's responsibility; the contractor is not required to verify it. When work built as the documents direct is rejected by the authority having jurisdiction, it is rebuilt to code and the contractor may be entitled to a change order. The contractor pays only for work it knew violated code, and the owner cannot accept nonconforming work that violates code.

questions.question: On an occupied campus, a subcontractor's crew keeps blocking walkways and harassing passersby. Which party is responsible for enforcing discipline and good order among the workers on the site?

options.A: The A/E, as the owner's representative during construction
options.B: The owner, since the campus stays occupied during the work
options.C: The contractor, as one of its listed duties during construction
options.D: The subcontractor alone, since the crew members are its employees
options.E: The owner's facility manager, who controls access to the campus
options.F: The resident project representative assigned to assist at the site

questions.explanation: Enforcing strict discipline and good order on the site is one of the contractor's construction-phase duties under the standard general conditions, and it reaches the subcontractor crews working under the contractor. The A/E observes and reports but does not control the workforce, and the subcontractor answers to the contractor rather than standing alone.

questions.question: An A/E firm is sending three junior staff members to the construction site for the first time. Which of the following are the A/E's safety obligations?

options.A: Brief its staff on the procedures to be followed at the site
options.B: Follow the safety procedures the contractor has established
options.C: Take part in planning the contractor's safety program
options.D: Supervise the contractor's construction safety measures
options.E: Apply its own firm rules wherever they conflict with site rules
options.F: Leave its staff's site safety entirely to the contractor

questions.explanation: The contractor plans, maintains and supervises safety measures and programs, but the owner and A/E remain responsible for their own employees on site. They should brief staff who will visit on the procedures to follow and then follow the contractor's safety procedures, without taking part in planning the contractor's program or supervising its measures.

questions.question: Under the standardized general conditions, which work stoppage is NOT authorized?

options.A: The owner orders a stop after the contractor repeatedly fails to correct nonconforming work.
options.B: The contractor stops after notice when the owner fails to pay within the stipulated time.
options.C: The contractor stops after finding hazardous materials the contract documents do not address.
options.D: The A/E orders a stop after seeing installed work that does not conform to the documents.
options.E: The owner orders a written suspension of the work for its own convenience, without cause.
options.F: The contractor stops after notice when the A/E fails to issue a payment certificate on time.

questions.explanation: No standard general conditions give the A/E authority to order the contractor to stop work; the A/E can reject nonconforming work, but ordering a stop when the contractor keeps failing to correct it is the owner's right. The contractor's own rights to stop work, after notice for nonpayment and when it finds hazardous materials the documents do not address, are recognized.

questions.question: Before each site visit, the A/E reviews the contractor's construction progress schedule and submittal schedule. Which are NOT benefits of this review?

options.A: Judging the percentage of completion when evaluating payment requests
options.B: Anticipating when products are due to arrive at the site
options.C: Targeting areas of the work that will soon be concealed
options.D: Setting the sequence in which the contractor performs the work
options.E: Recalling the current status of the contractor's submittals
options.F: Choosing the construction methods the contractor will use

questions.explanation: Reviewing the progress and submittal schedules before a site visit helps the A/E judge percent complete (essential for lump-sum pay requests), recall where submittals stand, anticipate product deliveries, and look at work that will soon be concealed. Sequences and methods are not the A/E's to set: the contractor alone is responsible for construction means, methods, techniques and sequences.

questions.question: After a prototype store opens, the A/E holds a closeout meeting with its own project design team. What is the main objective of that meeting?

options.A: Gathering feedback to repeat successes and avoid design mistakes on future projects
options.B: Reviewing closeout procedures with the owner, contractor, and commissioning authority
options.C: Setting the schedule for the punch list and the inspection for substantial completion
options.D: Obtaining the client's view of the firm's performance before any dispute can arise
options.E: Confirming that systems have been started and the owner's staff have been trained
options.F: Assembling the project record documents and operation and maintenance data

questions.explanation: A closeout meeting with the firm's own design team collects lessons learned so the firm can repeat its design and construction successes and avoid mistakes and design deficiencies on later projects. Asking the client how the firm performed belongs to the meeting with the owner before closeout, and reviewing closeout procedures with the owner, contractor and commissioning authority is the project closeout meeting.

questions.question: The owner-contractor agreement has just been executed, and the A/E is logging the preconstruction submittals. Which items do NOT belong in that log?

options.A: Payment bond
options.B: Bid bond
options.C: Schedule of values
options.D: Traffic control plan
options.E: Non-collusion affidavit
options.F: Building permit

questions.explanation: Preconstruction submittals start once the agreement is signed: insurance certificates, performance and payment bonds, the schedule of values, submittal and progress schedules, the building permit, the stormwater pollution prevention plan and the traffic control plan, among others. A bid bond and a non-collusion affidavit are submitted with the bid during procurement, so neither belongs in the preconstruction log.

questions.question: Under a team approach to project quality, which contribution belongs to the A/E?

options.A: Setting realistic goals and a reasonable program, budget, and schedule
options.B: Turning the owner's requirements into a design that sets the basis for evaluation
options.C: Controlling the means, methods, and sequences so that the finished work meets requirements
options.D: Selecting the delivery method and the extent of the design team's basic services
options.E: Being evaluated on how well the completed project meets the contract documents
options.F: Supervising and directing the work using its own expertise, skill, and attention

questions.explanation: In the team approach, the A/E's part is translating the owner's requirements into a documented design, which defines the expected quality and the measures for judging it, such as standards and tolerances. Setting realistic goals, a reasonable program, budget and schedule, and choosing the delivery method and the scope of design services fall to the owner; the contractor's performance is what gets judged against the contract documents.

questions.question: A large fast-track data center project will spend very large sums over brief periods on a regular basis. Which payment interval may be appropriate?

options.A: Monthly progress payments, required on all large projects
options.B: Twice-monthly or weekly progress payments to match the rapid rate of spending
options.C: Provisional payments of fixed amounts tied to identifiable project milestones
options.D: A single payment, since most of the cost accrues late on a fast-track job
options.E: A single payment at completion, since spending occurs over brief periods
options.F: Provisional payments tied to percentages of the total project quantities

questions.explanation: Twice-monthly or even weekly progress payments may suit large fast-track projects that spend large sums over short periods on a regular basis, as well as small projects by small contractors. Monthly payments fit most projects but are not required on all large ones. Provisional payments are tied to milestones or quantity percentages, and a single payment suits small, short contracts or ones where most cost comes late.

questions.question: After a leak appears, the owner argues that the A/E's certification of a pay application guaranteed the billed work was free of defects. On what is the A/E's certification based?

options.A: A warranty that all of the billed work is complete and free of any defects
options.B: The A/E's knowledge, information, and belief from observations and the application
options.C: The contractor's sworn statement of conformance, which the A/E simply forwards
options.D: Exhaustive inspection of the billed work by the A/E's consultants and testing agencies
options.E: The testing agency's reports certifying that the billed work meets the documents
options.F: The schedule of values alone, applied to the percentages the contractor claims

questions.explanation: The A/E certifies amounts due from its site observations and its evaluation of the application, and the certificate rests only on its knowledge, information and belief that the work has reached the stage claimed and conforms to the documents. It is not a warranty that the work is free of defects, and it does not depend on exhaustive inspection or on simply forwarding the contractor's statement.

questions.question: Which situations are NOT grounds for the A/E to withhold certification of all or part of a payment application?

options.A: The contractor has not properly paid its subcontractors from earlier payments.
options.B: The unpaid balance would not cover liquidated damages for an expected delay.
options.C: The contractor damaged work installed by one of the owner's separate contractors.
options.D: The owner's lender has delayed releasing the next construction-loan draw.
options.E: Third-party claims have been filed, or are expected to be filed.
options.F: The contractor has disagreed with a construction change directive's pricing method.

questions.explanation: The A/E may withhold certification to protect the owner from loss the contractor is responsible for: uncorrected defective work, third-party claims, unpaid subcontractors, a balance too small to finish the work or cover delay damages, damage to the owner or a separate contractor, and repeated failure to perform. A lender's delay is the owner's financing problem, and a contractor that disputes a construction change directive's pricing must still proceed while the adjustment is determined.

questions.question: The A/E certified a payment on time, but the owner, without cause under the contract, has not paid within the prescribed period. Which statement is accurate?

options.A: The contractor may stop work immediately and without notice, since the owner is in breach.
options.B: The contractor must keep working and may only file a claim for interest on the late payment.
options.C: Upon prior notice, the contractor may stop work, and the owner may owe remobilization costs.
options.D: The contractor may terminate at once and recover its lost profit, even if the owner cures the breach.
options.E: Upon prior notice, the contractor may stop work, and the owner then owes its lost profit.
options.F: The contractor may stop work only after the A/E certifies that the owner is in breach.

questions.explanation: An owner that fails to pay on time without cause may be in material breach. After giving written notice, the contractor may stop work if payment still has not arrived when the notice period ends, and the owner may then owe the costs of shutting down, delay and starting up again. Lost profit comes into play only if the breach goes uncured and the contract is terminated.

questions.question: On a site walk, the owner's project manager sees an unguarded floor opening and tells the foreman exactly how to barricade it, down to the materials and layout. Which statement best describes the owner's action?

options.A: It is risky, because an owner that directs the contractor on safety may be liable for the results.
options.B: It is proper, because the owner shares with the contractor the planning of site safety measures.
options.C: It is proper, but only the A/E, as the owner's representative, should give such safety directions.
options.D: It is harmless, because the contractor stays solely liable for all safety outcomes on the site.
options.E: It is required, because the owner is responsible for the safety of its employees at the site.
options.F: It is risky only if the A/E has not first approved the barricade's design and layout.

questions.explanation: Owners and A/Es should not tell the contractor how to handle safety, because whoever gives that direction can become liable for what results. The contractor plans and runs the safety program, and the owner and A/E follow its procedures; the owner's duty for its own employees' safety does not extend to directing the contractor's crews.

questions.question: A contractor asserts that it is owed more money under the contract for rock it hit during excavation, and the A/E must decide whether the contractor actually has a right to that benefit under the contract or law. The assertion and the right being judged are, respectively:

options.A: a claim and an entitlement
options.B: an entitlement and a claim
options.C: a dispute and an entitlement
options.D: a claim and a dispute
options.E: a dispute and a claim
options.F: an entitlement and a dispute

questions.explanation: A claim is a party's demand asserting a right under the contract, here the contractor's demand for more money for the rock. An entitlement is a right to benefits that the law or the contract provides, which is what the A/E must judge. A claim becomes a dispute only when it is left unresolved, so nothing here is a dispute yet.

questions.question: A contractor installs extra in-wall blocking it believes is outside its scope, then first tells the A/E about it months later in its final pay request. The blocking cannot reasonably be inferred from the documents. What is the main risk to the contractor's claim?

options.A: None, because work that cannot be inferred from the documents entitles the contractor to payment.
options.B: The claim converts at once into a dispute, which must go directly to binding arbitration.
options.C: Its failure to give proper and timely notice can forfeit its entitlement to the claim.
options.D: The claim is valid only if the A/E observed the blocking during one of its site visits.
options.E: None, because the general conditions require notice only for claims for delay.
options.F: The contractor must first prove the blocking was reasonably inferred from the documents.

questions.explanation: Contractor entitlement turns on two separate tests: whether the work lies outside what the documents reasonably require, and whether the claim was made on time. The general conditions require notice before the extra work is done, so first raising it months later in a final pay request can forfeit the claim even though the scope test favors the contractor.

questions.question: The owner insists the contractor add tamper-resistant fasteners at no cost, saying they are implied by the documents. The A/E finds they cannot be reasonably inferred from the contract documents. What follows?

options.A: The owner's claim is upheld, and the contractor provides the fasteners without a modification.
options.B: The owner's claim is denied; the fasteners are dropped or added by a contract modification.
options.C: The contractor must provide the fasteners, since an owner's demand controls until a dispute ends.
options.D: The A/E issues a minor change to add the fasteners, since minor changes carry no added cost.
options.E: The owner's claim is upheld, because owner claims need no reasonable inference from the documents.
options.F: The claim goes straight to mediation, since the A/E cannot judge whether work is inferred.

questions.explanation: For an owner's claim, the test is whether the contract documents reasonably imply the work demanded. If they do, the claim can be upheld with no modification; if they do not, as here, the claim is denied and the work is either dropped or added by a contract modification. A minor change cannot add work that changes the contract sum.

questions.question: An owner's new policy sets a goal of 'zero claims on every project.' How should the goal be reframed, and what is the first step?

options.A: Dispute avoidance; start with mutual understanding of interests and limits
options.B: Claim avoidance; start by having the A/E reject undocumented claims
options.C: Dispute avoidance; start by naming a mediator in the agreement
options.D: Claim avoidance; start by sending every claim to the initial decision maker
options.E: Claim avoidance; start with mutual understanding of interests and limits
options.F: Dispute avoidance; start by having the A/E reject undocumented claims

questions.explanation: A claim is simply a party asserting a right under the contract, and claims arise even on well-run projects, so the realistic goal is avoiding disputes, not avoiding claims. Avoiding disputes starts with each party understanding the other's interests and limitations. Naming a mediator plans for a dispute rather than preventing one, and having the A/E reject claims does nothing to build that understanding.

questions.question: A contractor proposes holding the HVAC demonstration and training sessions a month after substantial completion, once the staff has moved in. How should the A/E respond?

options.A: Accept it, because training belongs in the one-year correction period after occupancy.
options.B: Reject it, because training must wait until final completion and the final payment.
options.C: Accept it, as long as the O&M manuals are delivered before substantial completion.
options.D: Reject it, because training should precede substantial completion, with approved O&M data.
options.E: Reject it, because training belongs to the final inspection for final completion.
options.F: Accept it, because the A/E may certify substantial completion before any training.

questions.explanation: The owner needs to understand its systems before it occupies the building, so the A/E should not treat the project as substantially complete until the contractor has demonstrated the systems, trained the owner's and facility manager's staff, and submitted O&M data that the A/E has approved and sent to the owner. Training a month after substantial completion reverses that order; it belongs neither to the correction period nor to final completion.

questions.question: The contractor asks the A/E to walk the building and write the punch list so that the contractor can request substantial completion. How should the punch list process work?

options.A: The A/E prepares the list; the contractor reviews it and adds any items it disputes.
options.B: The commissioning authority prepares the list from the results of functional testing.
options.C: The owner and facility manager prepare the list at the closeout meeting with the A/E.
options.D: The contractor prepares the list; the A/E inspects, reviews it, and may add more items.
options.E: The A/E prepares the list only after the contractor certifies final completion.
options.F: The contractor prepares the list, and the owner alone approves it as final.

questions.explanation: When the contractor believes the work is substantially complete, it prepares the punch list of incomplete work and notifies the A/E and owner. The A/E then inspects the work, reviews the contractor's list and may add items to set the final punch list. Asking the A/E to write the first list reverses those roles, and the owner does not approve the list alone.

questions.question: As a new facility nears occupancy, the owner asks what it must handle with the authorities having jurisdiction. Which of the following may the owner be required to do?

options.A: Dedicate easements to local utility providers
options.B: Leave the signed-off permits with the AHJ to archive
options.C: Post certificates such as elevator and boiler certificates
options.D: Leave requirements missing from the contract to the contractor
options.E: Treat emergency plans as contractor closeout submittals
options.F: Leave bonds for future landscaping work to the contractor

questions.explanation: Even when the construction contract does not cover them, the owner must meet the regulatory requirements for use and occupancy. That can mean dedicating easements to utility providers and posting certificates such as the certificate of occupancy and elevator and boiler certificates. The owner also submits and posts emergency plans, provides any bonds for future landscaping or plantings, and keeps the original signed-off permits, since some agencies do not archive them.

questions.question: Which pairings of facility work and maintenance type are correct?

options.A: Converting a storage room to house a new lab function: routine maintenance
options.B: Postponing a planned roof replacement for lack of funds: deferred maintenance
options.C: Quarterly inspection, lubrication, and testing of air handlers: general maintenance
options.D: Tightening a loose cabinet pull that a user reported: emergency maintenance
options.E: Replacing worn, inoperative pump components on a schedule: routine maintenance
options.F: Replacing a broken door closer at a user's request: preventive maintenance

questions.explanation: Deferred maintenance is work put off, planned or not, often for lack of money, and routine maintenance repairs or replaces worn, broken, obsolete or inoperative parts, whether scheduled or requested by a user. Converting a room for a new function is renovation or modification, periodic inspection, lubrication and testing is preventive maintenance, and a minor fix reported by a user is general maintenance, not emergency work.

questions.question: A facility manager is setting up maintenance management software. Which of the following are among the minimum data the maintenance records should document?

options.A: The date the component was installed
options.B: The source for parts and service
options.C: The installer's original bid price
options.D: The length of the special warranty
options.E: The approved shop drawing number
options.F: The end date of the correction period

questions.explanation: At a minimum, maintenance records identify each component and its location, its installation date and source, who maintains it, where parts and service come from, its routine maintenance and monitoring needs, required regulatory tests and inspections, and its maintenance history. Bid prices, warranty lengths, shop drawing numbers and correction-period dates are not on that list; cost data is captured through the maintenance history.

questions.question: The owner of a just-completed office building plans to install new systems furniture the week before staff move in. The contract documents had no off-gassing period. What should the owner do?

options.A: Allow time for the furniture to off-gas before full occupancy, accepting some schedule impact.
options.B: Move in at once, since off-gassing matters only when the contract documents required it.
options.C: Have the contractor flush out the building under the one-year correction period at no added cost.
options.D: Move in on schedule and rely on periodic VOC sampling afterward instead of delaying.
options.E: Move in on schedule and rely on routine air-handling maintenance by facility staff.
options.F: Replace the order with green furnishings so the move-in can stay on schedule.

questions.explanation: When the contract did not build in off-gassing time, or the owner brings in new materials such as furniture, the owner should let them off-gas before full occupancy. The schedule and cost impact is usually outweighed by avoiding indoor air quality problems after move-in. The contractor's correction period covers defective work, not owner-furnished items, and testing after move-in does not keep occupants from the emissions.

questions.question: Which statements about regulatory requirements during facility operation are accurate?

options.A: Fees for compliance monitoring and life safety inspections are one-time costs paid at the time of occupancy.
options.B: OSHA workplace inspections typically result from accidents and from health or safety complaints.
options.C: The fire department, not the facility manager, is responsible for accident prevention on site.
options.D: Previously approved conditions that fall short of current requirements are often accepted if not modified or replaced.
options.E: Both {A} and {C}
options.F: Both {B} and {D}

questions.explanation: OSHA workplace inspections are usually triggered by accidents and by health or safety complaints, and conditions approved earlier that fall short of current rules are often accepted until they are modified or replaced. Regulatory fees for monitoring and inspections recur and belong in the annual budget, and accident prevention, including OSHA compliance, is the facility manager's job, so {E} is wrong.

questions.question: A facility manager wants data that assigns a cost to every maintenance activity, both to measure crew productivity and to find where added funds would cut long-term spending. Which practice provides this?

options.A: Life cycle costing
options.B: Value analysis
options.C: Cost accounting
options.D: Facility condition assessment
options.E: Post-occupancy evaluation
options.F: Preventive maintenance planning

questions.explanation: Cost accounting assigns a cost to every activity, producing data for measuring productivity and for finding opportunity costs, the places where added money can lower long-term spending. Life cycle costing compares the present and future value of facilities and equipment, usually to guide capital investments, and a facility condition assessment documents physical condition rather than the cost of each activity.

questions.question: A facility manager is organizing the archive of resource materials for a new building. Which are NOT among the four standard categories for storing and archiving that information?

options.A: Permanent record information
options.B: Regular use information
options.C: Equipment and systems information
options.D: Warranty information
options.E: Commissioning information
options.F: Cleaning and regular maintenance information

questions.explanation: Facility information is best stored and archived in four categories: permanent records, information in regular use, equipment and systems information, and cleaning and regular maintenance information. Warranties and commissioning data are among the documents handed over to the facility manager at the end of construction, but neither is one of the four categories.

questions.question: A hospital's engineering office holds the only complete set of record documents, warranties and O&M data, in boxes with no index. What should the facility manager have established around substantial completion?

options.A: Return of the originals to the A/E for archiving
options.B: A permanent, protected and accessible archive
options.C: Retention by the contractor through the correction period
options.D: Filing of the originals with the AHJ's permit records
options.E: Turnover of the files to the commissioning agent
options.F: A project file kept until final completion only

questions.explanation: Around substantial completion, the facility manager should take possession of the owner's project files and set up a permanent archive that is protected against loss or damage and stays accessible for the life of the facility. The owner's side keeps these records, not the A/E, the contractor or the AHJ, and some agencies do not archive permit records at all.

questions.question: A facility manager is setting the evaluation cycle for each component of a large campus. What affects the length of time between condition assessments?

options.A: The length of each component's special warranty
options.B: The AHJ's cycle for renewing operating certificates
options.C: The original installed cost of each component
options.D: The facility's age and how often users change operations
options.E: The cost recorded in each component's maintenance history
options.F: The manufacturer's recommended replacement cycle

questions.explanation: Each facility component should have its own evaluation cycle, and the interval between assessments depends on how old the facility is and how often its users change the way they operate. Condition assessment starts with the post-occupancy evaluation and runs for the life of the facility; warranty length, certificate renewals and installed cost do not set the interval.

questions.question: When is a post-occupancy evaluation best performed, and what role does it play afterward?

options.A: About three to six months after initial occupancy; it is the baseline for ongoing evaluation.
