questions.explanation: Coordination drawings are prepared by the contractor to fit all the trades' requirements together in a congested area, such as a tight ceiling cavity, and Section 01 31 00 Project Management and Coordination specifies requirements for them. A shop drawing shows how one part of the work is fabricated and installed, and a record drawing documents what was built.

questions.question: Drawings of an existing structure, provided to show existing conditions related to the work but not included in the contract, are called:

options.A: Resource drawings
options.B: Supplemental drawings
options.C: Construction drawings
options.D: Coordination drawings
options.E: Shop drawings
options.F: Contract drawings

questions.explanation: Resource drawings, such as record drawings of an existing building, show existing conditions or construction related to the work but are not part of the contract. Construction drawings describe the work of the project, and supplemental drawings are issued by the A/E during construction to change or clarify the contract documents.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the 'Related Requirements' paragraph in a section's PART 1 Summary?

options.A: To help readers locate requirements specified elsewhere
options.B: To define the scope of the work included in this section
options.C: To assign related work to particular subcontracts or trades
options.D: To state which section governs when two sections conflict
options.E: To separate the work among trade jurisdictions
options.F: To list the reference standards the section cites

questions.explanation: Related Requirements briefly lists other sections or documents that hold information a reader might expect to find in this section but that is specified elsewhere. The cross-reference is for information only: it does not define the section's scope, divide the work among contracts or subcontracts, or set trade jurisdictions.

questions.question: Which reference does NOT belong in a section's 'Related Requirements' paragraph?

options.A: Division 01 procedural sections, such as submittals
options.B: Another section that specifies closely related work
options.C: Section 01 11 16, Work by Owner, for related owner work
options.D: Sections with other components of the same rated assembly
options.E: Section 01 11 00, Summary of Work, for related owner work
options.F: The aluminum entrance section, cited from finish hardware

questions.explanation: Related Requirements should not list Division 01 procedural sections such as submittals, since those general requirements already govern every section. Cross-references to closely related work, to related work by the owner in Section 01 11 00 or 01 11 16, and to other components of an assembly that spans several sections are all appropriate.

questions.question: In SectionFormat, products to be 'installed by others' outside the contract, or noted 'not in contract' (N.I.C.), are considered to be installed by:

options.A: The Owner
options.B: The installer named in the section
options.C: The contractor, under another section
options.D: The supplier who furnishes them
options.E: The construction manager as advisor
options.F: A subcontractor chosen by the contractor

questions.explanation: Installation 'by others' outside the contract, or marked 'not in contract,' is treated as installation by the Owner, and it is coordinated with Section 01 11 00 Summary of Work or 01 11 16 Work by Owner. Work by the contractor under another section is still part of the contract, so it is not work by others.

questions.question: Owner-furnished products that the contractor installs under a section are listed in that section's Summary under:

options.A: Section Includes
options.B: Products Furnished But Not Installed Under This Section
options.C: Products Installed But Not Furnished Under This Section
options.D: Related Requirements
options.E: Owner-Furnished/Owner-Supplied Products
options.F: Work by Owner, under Section 01 11 16

questions.explanation: 'Products Installed But Not Furnished Under This Section' lists products installed under this section but supplied elsewhere, and products supplied 'by others' outside the contract count as furnished by the Owner; they are coordinated with Section 01 64 00 Owner-Furnished Products. The reverse heading, 'Products Furnished But Not Installed,' lists products supplied here and installed under another section.

questions.question: In SectionFormat, where are compatibility and transitions to adjacent materials, such as special separation or bonding, described?

options.A: PART 1, Coordination
options.B: PART 1, Related Requirements
options.C: PART 3, Interface with Other Work
options.D: PART 3, Systems Integration
options.E: PART 3, Special Techniques
options.F: PART 3, Tolerances

questions.explanation: Interface with Other Work, an article in PART 3, describes compatibility and transitions to other materials, including accessories, anchorage and any special separation or bonding. Systems Integration covers linking a system's components into a complete working system, and PART 1 Coordination covers administrative coordination, not physical transitions between materials.

questions.question: Two separate contracts on the same site include sections of similar scope, and their crews will work at the same time. In SectionFormat, where are the requirements for hand-offs between those sections specified?

options.A: PART 1, Coordination
options.B: PART 1, Related Requirements
options.C: PART 3, Interface with Other Work
options.D: PART 3, Systems Integration
options.E: PART 1, Sequencing
options.F: PART 1, Preinstallation Meetings

questions.explanation: The Coordination article in PART 1 is for unusual or detailed coordination affecting the section, such as hand-offs between similar sections in separate contracts working on one site at the same time, and it is coordinated with Section 01 31 00 Project Management and Coordination. Interface with Other Work in PART 3 covers physical transitions between materials, not administrative hand-offs.

questions.question: In the general conditions, calling the contract documents 'complementary' means:

options.A: Each document governs only the subject matter it covers
options.B: The most recently issued document governs any conflict
options.C: The specifications govern whenever they conflict with drawings
options.D: What one requires is as binding as if all required it
options.E: The printed record version governs the electronic version
options.F: The engineer issues all clarifications and interpretations

questions.explanation: AIA A201 and EJCDC C-700 both state that the contract documents are complementary: what one requires is as binding as if all of them required it. That is why precedence statements between drawings and specifications are discouraged and conflicts go to the A/E for a documented interpretation; no document governs only its own subject matter.

questions.question: Conflicting information shown in two or more places in the drawings and specifications is called a(n):

options.A: Duplication
options.B: Omission
options.C: Terminology difference
options.D: Discrepancy
options.E: Overlap
options.F: Latent defect

questions.explanation: A discrepancy is conflicting information shown in two or more places in the drawings and specifications. A duplication is the same work specified or shown more than once; it is not yet a conflict, but it invites one. An omission is information left out of the documents.

questions.question: If the standard contract forms do not fully define 'alternate,' where does SectionFormat place the definition?

options.A: Section 01 23 00, Alternates
options.B: The supplementary conditions
options.C: The instructions to bidders
options.D: The bid form
options.E: The general conditions
options.F: The agreement

questions.explanation: The use and meaning of 'alternate' and 'alternative' vary by region and between standard contract forms, so the specifier must settle the definitions. If the standard forms do not fully define them, the definitions go in the supplementary conditions, and Section 01 23 00 Alternates is coordinated with them to describe the alternates themselves.

questions.question: In a unit price schedule, pipe fittings that are not measured separately but are paid within the pipe's per-foot price are treated as:

options.A: Subsidiary obligations
options.B: Incidental allowances
options.C: Measured quantities
options.D: Contingency items
options.E: Quantity allowances
options.F: Estimated quantities

questions.explanation: In a unit price schedule, some items are measured directly while related work, such as the fittings on a pipe run, is a subsidiary obligation paid within another item's unit price. Here the measured quantity is the linear feet of pipe, and the fittings are covered by that price, not by an allowance or a contingency.

questions.question: A bonding company issues a performance bond on a contractor's work for a school district. In bonding terms, the bonding company is the:

options.A: Obligee
options.B: Principal
options.C: Surety
options.D: Claimant
options.E: Indemnitor
options.F: Bonding agent

questions.explanation: The surety, also called the bonding company, guarantees the principal's performance and agrees to be bound to the principal's obligations if the principal fails to perform. On this bond the school district is the obligee, the party the bond protects, and the contractor is the principal, the party whose performance is bonded.

questions.question: The party for whose benefit a bond is written is the:

options.A: Principal
options.B: Surety
options.C: Obligee
options.D: Indemnitor
options.E: Indemnitee
options.F: Named insured

questions.explanation: The obligee is the party the bond protects, usually the owner on a performance bond. The principal is the party whose performance is bonded, such as the contractor, and the surety is the bonding company that guarantees that performance; indemnitor and indemnitee are hold-harmless terms.

questions.question: A subcontractor furnishes a performance bond for the benefit of the general contractor. The principal on that bond is the:

options.A: General contractor
options.B: Owner
options.C: Surety
options.D: Subcontractor
options.E: Project lender
options.F: Indemnitee

questions.explanation: The principal is the party with the primary obligation to perform the bonded work, so on a subcontractor's bond the subcontractor is the principal. The general contractor it protects is the obligee, and a bond written for both the owner and the general contractor is called a dual obligee bond.

questions.question: Which three-party agreement makes one party answerable for another party's debt or default?

options.A: A surety bond
options.B: An indemnity agreement
options.C: An insurance policy
options.D: A hold-harmless agreement
options.E: A power of attorney
options.F: A waiver of subrogation

questions.explanation: A surety bond is a three-party arrangement among principal, surety and obligee in which the surety stands behind the principal's debt or default, much like a cosigner on a note; it is not an insurance policy. An indemnity agreement is the separate promise by the principal to keep the surety from any loss.

questions.question: The agreement by which the principal guarantees that the surety will incur no loss from providing the bond is the:

options.A: Hold-harmless agreement
options.B: Power of attorney
options.C: Surety bond
options.D: Indemnity agreement
options.E: Waiver of subrogation
options.F: Contractual liability

questions.explanation: In the indemnity agreement, the principal, and often its owners or officers, promise the surety that it will suffer no loss from issuing the bond, so the surety expects to be repaid for anything it pays out. A power of attorney shows an agent's authority to sign for the surety, and a hold-harmless clause shifts liability between contracting parties.

questions.question: An unpaid supplier seeking recovery under the contractor's payment bond is, in bonding terms, the:

options.A: Claimant
options.B: Obligee
options.C: Principal
options.D: Indemnitee
options.E: Surety
options.F: Insured

questions.explanation: A claimant is a party that files a claim against a bond, such as the owner, or an unpaid subcontractor or supplier seeking recovery under the payment bond. The obligee is the party the bond is written for, usually the owner, and the contractor whose obligations are bonded is the principal.

questions.question: An unpaid subcontractor's legal right to hold a security interest in the property it improved, or to have that property sold to satisfy its claim, is a:

options.A: Claim
options.B: Lien
options.C: Set-off
options.D: Retainage
options.E: Subrogation
options.F: Mortgage

questions.explanation: A lien gives a party such as an unpaid subcontractor or supplier a security interest in the improved property, with the right to have it sold to pay the claim; nearly every state allows mechanic's liens. Liens often outrank most mortgages, which is why owners want a lien-free project and payment bonds protect against them. A claim is only the demand itself.

questions.question: Which bond guarantees that, if the contractor defaults, the surety will complete the contract or fund completion up to the penal sum?

options.A: Payment bond
options.B: Bid bond
options.C: Performance bond
options.D: Maintenance bond
options.E: Warranty bond
options.F: Labor and materials bond

questions.explanation: A performance bond is the owner's most important bond protection: if the contractor defaults, the surety either completes the contract or provides funds, up to the penal sum, to complete it. A payment bond, also called a labor and materials bond, guarantees that subcontractors and suppliers are paid, and a bid bond protects the owner's benefit of an accepted bid.

questions.question: Bid bonds are required on a project. Which statements about them are correct?

options.A: A bid bond is a procurement requirement, while performance and payment bonds are contract documents
options.B: A bid submitted without the required bid bond is non-responsive and rejected
options.C: Missing bid security is a minor irregularity the owner may waive
options.D: Sureties usually charge separately for the bid bond when the other bonds are also required
options.E: Both {A} and {B}
options.F: {A}, {B} and {C}

questions.explanation: A bid bond, if required, is a procurement requirement, while performance and payment bonds are contract documents. When bid bonds are required, a bid without one is non-responsive and is rejected, because missing bid security is a material irregularity, not a minor one the owner may waive. Sureties usually include the bid bond at no added charge when they also write the performance and payment bonds.

questions.question: When is a bid bond discharged, with no liability to the surety?

options.A: The bidder finds its bid well below the others
options.B: The owner did not accept the bid within the stated time
options.C: The other bidders have already withdrawn
options.D: The owner must rebid the project
options.E: The bidder shows a mistake that gave it the right to withdraw
options.F: The owner asks the bidder to sign at the bid price

questions.explanation: A bid bond is liable only if the bidder's refusal to sign at its bid price is unjustified. It is discharged if the owner failed to accept the bid within the time the procurement documents allowed, if the bidder proves a mistake that gave it the right to withdraw, or if the owner tries on its own to change the bid terms. A low bid is no excuse, and if a rebid is needed because other bidders withdrew, the surety may also owe the reprocurement cost.

questions.question: In a hold-harmless clause in which the contractor protects the owner, the contractor is the:

options.A: Indemnitee
options.B: Obligee
options.C: Indemnitor
options.D: Named insured
options.E: Principal
options.F: Surety

questions.explanation: In a hold-harmless clause, the indemnitor is the party that holds the other harmless, and the indemnitee is the party protected. Here the contractor is the indemnitor and the owner the indemnitee; obligee, principal and surety are bond terms, not indemnity terms.

questions.question: A fixed amount per day, agreed in advance, that compensates the owner when the contractor fails to reach substantial completion on time is:

options.A: Liquidated damages
options.B: A penalty
options.C: Consequential damages
options.D: Actual damages
options.E: Retainage
options.F: Contingency

questions.explanation: Liquidated damages are a daily amount agreed in advance as the measure of the owner's injury from inexcusable late completion, used because actual damages would be hard to prove. A penalty is an amount not based on loss; it may be unenforceable, and courts generally will not enforce a delay penalty without a matching bonus for early completion.

questions.question: Under A201, the owner's lost rental income caused by late completion is:

options.A: Recoverable as actual damages on top of LDs
options.B: A consequential damage the owner waives
options.C: Recoverable only through the performance bond
options.D: Withheld from the contractor's retainage
options.E: Recoverable from the A/E as a design delay
options.F: Payable by the contractor as a penalty

questions.explanation: A201's mutual waiver of consequential damages includes the owner's rental expenses and its losses of use, income, profit and financing, so lost rent from late completion is waived. The waiver expressly does not prevent liquidated damages where the contract provides them, which is how an owner usually recovers for delay.

questions.question: Which statements about liquidated damages are correct?

options.A: A liquidated damages clause is generally in lieu of actual damages for delay
options.B: Without an LD clause, the contractor is immune from claims for delay damages
options.C: An LD clause is a penalty that needs a matching early-completion bonus
options.D: LDs suit multiple-prime projects well, since each contract has its own time
options.E: Both {A} and {B}
options.F: {A}, {B} and {D}

questions.explanation: Liquidated damages are not a penalty, and an LD clause is generally treated as replacing actual damages for delay. Without an LD clause the contractor is not immune: the owner can document and claim actual damages, which may far exceed an LD amount. The early-completion bonus rule applies to penalty clauses, and multiple-prime projects suit LDs poorly because responsibility for delay is hard to assign across contracts.

questions.question: A201 makes the contract's time limits 'of the essence.' By executing the agreement, the contractor also confirms that:

options.A: Liquidated damages reflect the owner's actual loss
options.B: The Contract Time is a reasonable period for the Work
options.C: The schedule of values fairly allocates the sum
options.D: The date of commencement can never change
options.E: The Contract Time runs to final completion and payment
options.F: The submittal schedule gives the architect enough time

questions.explanation: A201 makes the time limits in the Contract Documents of the essence and states that, by signing the agreement, the contractor confirms the Contract Time is a reasonable period for performing the Work. It makes no such confirmation about liquidated damages, the schedule of values or the architect's review time, and Contract Time runs to Substantial Completion, not to final completion.

questions.question: Under A201, the Contract Time is the period allotted for:

options.A: Final completion of the Work
options.B: Completion and final payment
options.C: Substantial Completion of the Work
options.D: Commencement through the correction period
options.E: Achieving Milestones and completing the Work
options.F: Final acceptance of the Work by the owner

questions.explanation: A201 defines Contract Time as the period, including authorized adjustments, allotted in the Contract Documents for Substantial Completion of the Work. Final completion and final payment come later. EJCDC C-700 uses the plural Contract Times, which cover milestones, Substantial Completion and completion of the Work.

questions.question: Under EJCDC C-700, a principal event the contractor must achieve by an intermediate completion date is a:

options.A: Milestone
options.B: Progress Schedule
options.C: Substantial Completion
options.D: Notice to Proceed
options.E: Contract Times
options.F: Effective Date

questions.explanation: C-700 defines a Milestone as a principal event the contract requires the contractor to achieve by an intermediate completion date, or at some time before Substantial Completion of all the Work. Milestones are one of the three things the Contract Times set dates for, along with Substantial Completion and completion of the Work.

questions.question: Under EJCDC C-700, the written notice that fixes the date on which the Contract Times start to run is the:

options.A: Notice of Award
options.B: Effective Date of the Contract
options.C: Notice to Proceed
options.D: Agreement
options.E: Field Order
options.F: Work Change Directive

questions.explanation: The Notice to Proceed is the owner's written notice fixing the date the Contract Times start to run and the contractor begins work. The Notice of Award is the owner's written acceptance of a bid, and the Effective Date of the Contract, stated in the Agreement, is when the Contract takes effect.

questions.question: Under A201, the stage when the Work is sufficiently complete for the owner to occupy or use it for its intended use is:

options.A: Final completion
options.B: Partial occupancy
options.C: Substantial Completion
options.D: Final acceptance
options.E: Date of commencement
options.F: Milestone

questions.explanation: A201 defines Substantial Completion as the stage when the Work, or a designated portion, is complete enough under the Contract Documents for the owner to occupy or use it for its intended use. Final completion comes later, after the remaining work is finished, the A/E has confirmed it, and final payment has been made and accepted.

questions.question: Which of the following are conditions of final completion?

options.A: The A/E certifies the owner can use the Work as intended
options.B: The punch list is attached to the certificate of completion
options.C: The contractor has accepted the owner's final payment
options.D: The one-year correction period has expired
options.E: The A/E has inspected and found the project complete
options.F: Retainage is held until the correction period expires

questions.explanation: Final completion requires that the contractor has completed the contract requirements, the A/E has inspected the project and found it complete, the owner has made final payment, and the contractor has accepted it. Use for the intended purpose, with a punch list attached, marks substantial completion, which is also when the one-year correction period starts, so neither that period's end nor held retainage is a condition.

questions.question: Which statements about the A201 one-year period for correction of Work are correct?

options.A: It runs from the date of Substantial Completion of the Work
options.B: It is extended for work first performed after Substantial Completion
options.C: It is not extended by corrective work the contractor performs
options.D: It limits the owner's time to enforce the contractor's other duties
options.E: Both {A} and {B}
options.F: {A}, {B} and {C}

questions.explanation: Under A201 12.2.2, the one-year correction period runs from Substantial Completion, is extended for work first performed after Substantial Completion, and is not extended by the contractor's corrective work, so the three statements together are correct. The period applies only to the duty to correct the Work; it does not limit the time for enforcing the contractor's other obligations.

questions.question: Under A201, payment of retainage at substantial completion follows the parties' acceptance of the certificate's responsibilities and:

options.A: Final lien releases from every sub-subcontractor
options.B: Expiration of the one-year correction period
options.C: Consent of surety, if any
options.D: The architect's final Certificate for Payment
options.E: Completion of every punch-list item
options.F: Delivery of all O&M manuals

questions.explanation: Under A201, once the owner and contractor accept in writing the responsibilities in the Certificate of Substantial Completion, and the surety consents if there is one, the owner pays the retainage for that work, adjusted for incomplete or nonconforming work. Lien releases and the architect's final Certificate for Payment belong to final payment, and the correction period only begins at Substantial Completion.

questions.question: Under A201, a contractor's acceptance of final payment waives:

options.A: Claims not already made in writing and listed as unsettled
options.B: Every claim, including those listed as unsettled
options.C: Only claims for an extension of the Contract Time
options.D: Nothing until the one-year correction period ends
options.E: The owner's claims for nonconforming work
options.F: Only claims arising after the final application

questions.explanation: Under A201, a contractor, subcontractor or supplier that accepts final payment waives its claims except those already made in writing and identified as unsettled at the time of the final Application for Payment. The owner's making of final payment is a separate waiver with its own exceptions, such as liens, nonconforming work and special warranties.

questions.question: A percentage of each progress payment withheld to protect the owner against estimating errors and defective work is:

options.A: Set-off
options.B: Contingency
options.C: Bid security
options.D: Retainage
options.E: Liquidated damages
options.F: Penal sum

questions.explanation: Retainage is a set percentage withheld from each progress payment. It is not meant to force performance; it protects the owner against errors in valuing completed work and against defective work, and it helps settle third-party claims before final payment. Owners traditionally pay 90 to 95 percent of earned sums. Liquidated damages compensate for late completion instead, and a contingency is a budget reserve for changes.

questions.question: A contractor-prepared allocation of the contract sum to portions of the Work, used as the basis for reviewing payment applications, is the:

options.A: Application for payment
options.B: Schedule of values
options.C: Cost of the Work
options.D: Schedule of unit prices
options.E: Schedule of submittals
options.F: Construction progress schedule

questions.explanation: The schedule of values divides the contract sum among portions of the work so the lines add up to the total, often following the project manual table of contents. The contractor submits it after award and before the first payment, and it becomes the basis for submitting and reviewing progress payments; the application for payment is the request built on it.

questions.question: Under cost-plus with a guaranteed maximum price, costs that push the total above the GMP, other than owner and design changes, are borne by the:

options.A: Owner
options.B: Contractor
options.C: Owner and contractor equally
options.D: Contractor's surety
options.E: A/E
options.F: Subcontractors

questions.explanation: The GMP is the ceiling on the owner's cost exposure for the direct costs of the work, so the contractor is at risk for costs that push the total above it. Owner changes and design changes fall outside the cost of the work and the GMP, which is why the owner should carry a budget contingency for them.

questions.question: In a cost-plus contract, the 'fee' is the contractor's:

options.A: Reimbursable direct cost of labor and materials
options.B: Overhead and profit, as a percentage or a sum
options.C: Contingency for incomplete documents
options.D: Premiums for bonds and insurance
options.E: Share of the savings below the GMP
options.F: Field office and temporary facility costs

questions.explanation: A cost-plus contract reimburses the actual direct costs of the work and adds a fee for the contractor's overhead and profit, usually a percentage of the direct costs but sometimes a fixed amount. Bonds, insurance, labor and materials are reimbursable costs of the work, not part of the fee.

questions.question: Which basis of payment is usually closed book, with the contractor's cost information not shared with the owner?

options.A: Guaranteed maximum price
options.B: Cost-plus with a GMP
options.C: Stipulated sum
options.D: Cost-plus without a GMP
options.E: Target price
options.F: Cost-plus with an incentive bonus

questions.explanation: A stipulated sum is a single fixed price and is usually closed book: the owner does not see how the contractor built up the price. GMP contracts are usually open book and open to audit, and cost-plus contracts require detailed cost documentation with each payment application.

questions.question: On an IPD project with a target price, actual costs overrun the target. What happens?

options.A: The contractor absorbs the overrun, as under a GMP
options.B: The owner pays, but contractor and A/E earn no more fee
options.C: The overrun is split equally among the parties
options.D: The parties' surety pays the overrun
options.E: The owner pays, plus added fees to contractor and A/E
options.F: The A/E absorbs the overrun as design liability

questions.explanation: Under a target price, the owner pays the direct cost of the work, and when costs overrun the target the owner bears the overrun but the contractor and A/E receive no further fees; when costs come in under, they share the savings. This pain and gain sharing replaces a GMP, under which the contractor would absorb the overrun.

questions.question: Under EJCDC C-700, a contractor's written request seeking an adjustment in Contract Price or Contract Times is a:

options.A: Claim
options.B: Change Order
options.C: Change Proposal
options.D: Work Change Directive
options.E: Proposal Request
options.F: Field Order

questions.explanation: C-700 calls the contractor's written request for an adjustment in Contract Price or Contract Times a Change Proposal. A Claim, in C-700 terms, is a later step, such as the contractor's demand to the owner contesting the engineer's decision on a Change Proposal; A201, by contrast, uses Claim for the initial demand itself.

questions.question: Under A201, a Claim must be initiated within how many days after the event, or after the claimant first recognizes the condition, whichever is later?

options.A: 10 days
options.B: 21 days
options.C: 30 days
options.D: 7 days
options.E: 14 days
options.F: 60 days

questions.explanation: A201 requires a Claim to be started by written notice within 21 days after the event giving rise to it, or within 21 days after the claimant first recognizes the condition, whichever is later. Ten days is the time the Initial Decision Maker has to act on a Claim it receives.

questions.question: Under A201, unless the agreement names someone else, the Initial Decision Maker on Claims is the:

options.A: Owner
options.B: Architect
options.C: Mediator
options.D: Construction manager
options.E: Dispute resolution board
options.F: Arbitrator

questions.explanation: A201 names the architect as Initial Decision Maker unless the agreement names someone else, and an initial decision is generally required before a Claim can go to mediation. Mediators and arbitrators come later in the dispute process, and under EJCDC C-700 the engineer decides only claims about the work, the design or engineering matters.

questions.question: Which dispute resolution process is non-binding, with the parties, not the neutral, setting the terms of any settlement?

options.A: Arbitration
options.B: Mediation
options.C: Dispute resolution board
options.D: Initial decision
options.E: Litigation
options.F: Engineer's decision on a Change Proposal

questions.explanation: Mediation is non-binding: a neutral facilitates discussion between the parties, and if they settle, they set the terms themselves. An arbitrator, by contrast, is empowered to make an enforceable decision, and dispute resolution board decisions are generally final and binding on the parties.

questions.question: Under A201, which of the following are NOT Modifications?

options.A: A Construction Change Directive
options.B: A written order for a minor change in the Work
options.C: An addendum issued before the Contract is executed
options.D: A written amendment signed by both parties
options.E: A Change Order
options.F: A shop drawing the architect has approved

questions.explanation: Under A201 1.1.1, a Modification is a written amendment signed by both parties, a Change Order, a Construction Change Directive, or the architect's written order for a minor change, issued after the Contract is executed. Addenda issued before execution are Contract Documents but not Modifications, and shop drawings, even approved ones, are not Contract Documents at all.

questions.question: Which term do both EJCDC and DBIA use for an order to make a change before price or time is agreed?

options.A: Construction change directive
options.B: Interim directive
options.C: Work change directive
options.D: Field order
options.E: Minor change
options.F: Owner's written order

questions.explanation: EJCDC and DBIA both use the term work change directive; AIA calls the same document a construction change directive, and ConsensusDocs calls it an interim directive. Each one directs the change now, with the price or time adjustment recorded later in a change order. A field order, by contrast, makes a minor change with no adjustment at all.

questions.question: The low bidder completed every blank, followed the instructions, and attached every supplement, but lacks the financial capacity to finish the work. The bid is:

options.A: Responsible but not responsive
options.B: Responsive but not responsible
options.C: Neither responsive nor responsible
options.D: Both, until bonds are furnished
options.E: Responsive, so it must be awarded
options.F: Non-responsive, as a supplement is missing

questions.explanation: A responsive bid completes every blank, follows the instructions to bidders, and includes the required supplements, so this bid is responsive. A responsible bidder also has the financial capacity, skills, workforce, equipment and integrity to do the work; a bidder that cannot finance the job fails that test, so the bid is responsive but not responsible.

questions.question: A prime bidder reveals one subcontractor's price to another subcontractor to get a lower price. This is:

options.A: Collusion
options.B: Bid shopping
options.C: Buyout
options.D: A bid depository
options.E: Bid listing
options.F: Value analysis

questions.explanation: Bid shopping is the unethical practice of revealing one subcontractor's price to get a lower price from another, or pressing a subcontractor to cut a price it already submitted. Collusion is bidders agreeing to fix prices, and a bid depository, where prequalified subcontractors submit prices to the owner independently, is one way to prevent bid shopping.

questions.question: After award, the contractor's issuing of subcontracts, supply contracts, and purchase orders is called:

options.A: Mobilization
options.B: Bid shopping
options.C: Prequalification
options.D: Buyout
options.E: Preconstruction
options.F: Bid listing

questions.explanation: Buyout is the contractor issuing subcontracts for the work, and supply contracts and purchase orders for products and equipment, after award, ideally early for long-lead items; it is one of the contractor's main preconstruction activities. Mobilization is moving people and equipment onto the site, and bid shopping is an unethical practice during procurement.

questions.question: Under the UCC, any written warranty is a(n):

options.A: Implied warranty of merchantability
options.B: Express warranty
options.C: Implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose
options.D: Warranty of title
options.E: Implied warranty
options.F: Correction-of-Work obligation

questions.explanation: Under the Uniform Commercial Code, any written warranty is an express warranty, and express warranties can also come from an affirmation of fact, a description such as drawings or specifications, or a sample that becomes part of the deal. Implied warranties, such as merchantability, arise from the nature of the transaction and state law, not from written terms.

questions.question: Under A201, the Contract Documents create a contractual relationship between the owner and:

options.A: The contractor and its subcontractors
options.B: The contractor only
options.C: The contractor and the architect
options.D: Every party named in the documents
options.E: The architect only
options.F: The contractor and its suppliers

questions.explanation: A201 states that the Contract Documents create no contractual relationship between the contractor and the architect, the owner and subcontractors, or the owner and the architect; the Contract for Construction is between owner and contractor only. The owner and the A/E deal with subcontractors and suppliers through the contractor.

questions.question: In contract terms, a supplier's quote and the contractor's purchase order are, respectively, the:

options.A: Acceptance and the offer
options.B: Offer and the acceptance
options.C: Consideration and the offer
options.D: Offer and the consideration
options.E: Consideration and the acceptance
options.F: Acceptance and the consideration

questions.explanation: A purchase order reflects the terms of the supplier's quote: the quote is the offer, and the contractor's purchase order accepts it, forming the contract. Consideration is the exchange of something of value, usually money, that an agreement also needs; it is not either document.

questions.question: A subcontractor's bond is written for the benefit of both the owner and the contractor. What is it called?

options.A: A co-surety bond
options.B: A dual obligee bond
options.C: A joint principal bond
options.D: A two-party surety bond
options.E: A labor and materials bond
options.F: A bid bond

questions.explanation: A bond written for the benefit of more than one obligee, such as a subcontractor's bond for both owner and contractor or a contractor's bond for owner and lender, is a dual obligee bond. It is still a three-party arrangement of principal, surety and obligee; the extra obligee does not add a principal or a surety.

questions.question: A city building department is a statutory AHJ because its authority comes from:

options.A: Federal procurement regulations
options.B: Legislative enabling acts
options.C: A business relationship with the owner
options.D: Accreditation by ANSI
options.E: A direct grant from the federal government
options.F: Membership in the International Code Council

questions.explanation: The federal government gives states authority over activities within their borders, and states pass authority to counties and cities through legislative enabling acts, which makes those local departments statutory AHJs. The authority does not come directly from the federal government or from a code-writing organization, and a business relationship with the owner is what defines a contractual AHJ.

questions.question: Which of these are contractual AHJs?

options.A: The city building inspection department
options.B: The state fire marshal's office
options.C: The utility company serving the building
options.D: The county environmental health department
options.E: The owner's property insurance carrier
options.F: The International Code Council

questions.explanation: Contractual AHJs are nongovernmental entities with a business relationship to the owner, such as the utility that will serve the building and the insurer that will cover it. They may impose requirements beyond the code and run their own plan reviews. Government departments are statutory AHJs, and the ICC writes model codes but has no authority over a project by itself.

questions.question: Which statements about regulations, sometimes called ordinances, are correct?

options.A: Regulations are written by model code organizations such as the ICC.
options.B: Unlike codes, regulations may impose fines for noncompliance.
options.C: Regulations are voluntary until a code adopts them.
options.D: CC&Rs are regulations enforced by the local building department.
options.E: Both {B} and {C}
options.F: {A}, {B} and {D}

questions.explanation: Regulations (ordinances) are written by authorities having jurisdiction for a specific purpose, and unlike codes they can carry fines for noncompliance. Model code organizations such as the ICC write codes, not regulations. Being voluntary until a code adopts them describes reference standards, and CC&Rs are deed restrictions enforced by homeowner or condominium associations, not by the building department.

questions.question: Publicly recorded deed restrictions enforced by a homeowners or condominium association are:

options.A: CC&Rs
options.B: Zoning ordinances
options.C: Allowable site coverage limits
options.D: Local code amendments
options.E: Zoning height restrictions
options.F: Site runoff regulations

questions.explanation: CC&Rs (codes, covenants, and restrictions, also read as covenants, conditions, and restrictions) are deed restrictions recorded against a property or development and enforced by a homeowners or condominium association. They can further limit lot size, height, setbacks and appearance. Zoning ordinances and zoning height limits are land-use rules the jurisdiction itself enforces, not an association.

questions.question: Manufacturers of similar products voluntarily agree to be bound by a standard they developed together. What is this called?

options.A: Company standard
options.B: Consensus standard
options.C: Manufacturer certification
options.D: Evaluation report
options.E: Ecolabel
options.F: Performance-based standard

questions.explanation: A consensus standard is a variation of a company standard: several makers of similar products agree, of their own accord, to be bound by a standard they reached together by consensus. A company standard is one maker's own standard, stricter than the common one, and a manufacturer certification qualifies the fabricators or installers of a product.

questions.question: A fabricator imposes on its own production a standard stricter than the commonly used industry standard. This is called a:

options.A: Consensus standard
options.B: Reference standard
options.C: Company standard
options.D: Manufacturer certification
options.E: Evaluation report
options.F: Performance-based standard

questions.explanation: A company standard is one a manufacturer or fabricator develops and imposes on its own production, more restrictive than the commonly used standard. A consensus standard binds a group of manufacturers that agreed on it together, and a manufacturer certification is a maker's requirement that fabricators or installers of its products be certified.

questions.question: A product evaluation report is issued when:

options.A: The local AHJ approves the product for a single project
options.B: A testing lab certifies the product's installers
options.C: The manufacturer publishes its own test results
options.D: A model code body finds the product code-compliant
options.E: ANSI accredits the product's test method
options.F: An ecolabel program verifies its claims

questions.explanation: Model code-writing organizations evaluate products that manufacturers submit, with samples and test reports, and issue an evaluation report when the product is found to comply with the model code. Some jurisdictions run their own evaluation services, but a report is a general finding of code compliance, not an approval by the local official for one project.

questions.question: A specified product has an evaluation report. Which statements are true?

options.A: Local approval is still not guaranteed.
options.B: Local building officials are bound to approve it.
options.C: Many AHJs require the report to be listed in the specifications and submitted.
options.D: It is exempt from the specified reference standards.
options.E: Both {A} and {C}
options.F: {A}, {C} and {D}

questions.explanation: Building officials may rely on evaluation reports to approve products, but having a report does not guarantee local approval, and many authorities having jurisdiction require the report to be named in the specifications and submitted. A report does not bind local officials, and nothing about it exempts the product from the reference standards the specifications require.

questions.question: A group of business competitors interested in commercially promoting their products or services is a:

options.A: Manufacturing association
options.B: Trade association
options.C: Professional association
options.D: Standards development organization
options.E: Governmental standards agency
options.F: Model code-writing organization

questions.explanation: A trade association is made up of business competitors who join to promote their products or services commercially. A manufacturing association is a consortium of manufacturers working to raise their industry's visibility and set up quality programs, and a professional association is a voluntary group of professionals advancing knowledge in a shared field.

questions.question: In ANSI's United States Standards Strategy, which principle means no one interest dominates the process?

options.A: Openness
options.B: Consensus
options.C: Impartiality
options.D: Transparency
options.E: Due process
options.F: Coherence

questions.explanation: Impartiality means no single interest dominates the standards process or is favored over another. Openness is about who may take part (all affected interests may participate), and consensus is about how decisions are reached (by agreement among those affected), so neither one addresses domination by an interest.

questions.question: Which United States Standards Strategy principle requires that essential information on standards activities be accessible to all interested parties?

options.A: Openness
options.B: Due process
options.C: Coherence
options.D: Transparency
options.E: Impartiality
options.F: Effectiveness and relevance

questions.explanation: Transparency means essential information about standardization activities is available to everyone interested. Openness is about who may take part, which is all affected interests. Coherence avoids overlapping and conflicting standards, and due process lets all views be considered and appealed.

questions.question: Which statements about field samples and mockups are correct?

options.A: Field samples are representative applications of finish materials.
options.B: Mockups demonstrate the coordination and interfacing of different products.
options.C: Mockups may be built for preconstruction testing in a lab or on the project site.
options.D: A field sample is an assembly such as a window built into a masonry wall.
options.E: Both {A} and {B}
options.F: {A}, {B} and {C}

questions.explanation: Mockups are representative assemblies built to show how different products fit and work together, such as a window set into a masonry wall, or built for preconstruction testing in a laboratory or at the site. Field samples are representative applications of finish materials. Describing an assembly like a window in a masonry wall as a field sample confuses the two terms.

questions.question: A material becomes a commodity when it is:

options.A: Made to the maker's own company standard
options.B: Specified without naming any manufacturer
options.C: Bought by the owner for the contractor
options.D: Specified with three named manufacturers
options.E: Produced in quantity and stocked for shipment
options.F: Specified by one named product 'or equal'

questions.explanation: A commodity is a good that various manufacturers can produce uniformly to the same predetermined quality. A material becomes a commodity when it is specified without naming any manufacturer, so any maker's product is acceptable. Naming three manufacturers, or one product 'or equal', still steers the choice to particular makers.

questions.question: Unique, high-performance materials with no comparable, competitively priced equivalents are called:

options.A: Custom products
options.B: Standard products
options.C: Proprietary products
options.D: Commodities
options.E: Owner-furnished products
options.F: Assemblies/fabrications

questions.explanation: Proprietary products are often unique, high-performance materials with no competitively priced or functionally equivalent alternatives. They may have limited distribution and few approved installers, and may be required when they are part of an existing system. Custom products are those with nonstandard characteristics, which is a different distinction.

questions.question: Product standards influence product selection by introducing:

options.A: Price competition among makers
options.B: Mandatory code minimums
options.C: Environmental performance marks
options.D: Quality control of the product
options.E: Life cycle cost comparisons
options.F: Delivery and lead-time limits

questions.explanation: Product standards influence selection by bringing quality control of the product into it. They are a series of related standards that the industry accepts as the framework for a baseline of product quality. Marks on packaging that identify environmental performance are ecolabels, and code minimums come from codes, not product standards.

questions.question: Uniform criteria and practices that most manufacturers or installers in an industry agree are their standard of care are:

options.A: Reference standards
options.B: Model codes
options.C: Regulations
options.D: Guide specifications
options.E: Company standards
options.F: Evaluation reports

questions.explanation: Reference standards set uniform guidelines, criteria, methods and practices for a product, assembly or installation, and they can reflect what most manufacturers or installers agree is the standard of care in their industry. Model codes and regulations are mandatory rules adopted by authorities, and a company standard is one maker's own rule.

questions.question: Which statements about model building codes are correct?

options.A: A model code is enforceable in a jurisdiction only after a local AHJ formally adopts it.
options.B: An AHJ may adopt only portions of a model code and modify them for its own purposes.
options.C: A model code takes effect in a jurisdiction when the ICC publishes the new edition.
options.D: Model codes are typically updated about every five years.
options.E: Both {A} and {B}
options.F: {A}, {B} and {D}

questions.explanation: A model code becomes enforceable in a jurisdiction only when a local authority having jurisdiction formally adopts it, and the authority may adopt any portion and modify it for its own purposes. Publishing a new edition changes nothing locally until it is adopted, and model codes are updated about every three years, not every five.

questions.question: The adopted building code would allow a building 75 ft tall. The site's zoning regulation limits height to 50 ft. Which limit applies?

options.A: The 75-ft code limit
options.B: 75 ft, with an AHJ code modification
options.C: The 50-ft zoning limit
options.D: Whichever limit the specifications cite
options.E: 75 ft, since codes override zoning
options.F: The 75-ft limit, if the building is sprinklered

questions.explanation: Height limits in local zoning regulations can be stricter than those in the adopted building code, and a project must meet every local requirement, so the 50-ft zoning limit governs. A building code modification or sprinkler allowance only affects what the code permits; it does nothing to relax a separate zoning restriction.

questions.question: Which organization is a property insurer that also writes standards, tests assemblies, and certifies products?

options.A: Underwriters Laboratories
options.B: ASTM International
options.C: National Fire Protection Association
options.D: FM Global
options.E: American National Standards Institute
options.F: International Code Council

questions.explanation: FM Global provides commercial and industrial property insurance and loss-prevention research, and it also publishes standards, tests materials, products and assemblies, and certifies them. Underwriters Laboratories is an independent product safety testing and certification organization, not an insurer, and NFPA and ASTM develop standards without insuring property.

questions.question: Which accessibility document is a reference standard incorporated into the IBC and enforced by the local jurisdiction?

options.A: ICC/ANSI A117.1
options.B: 2010 ADA Standards
options.C: ADA-ABA Accessibility Guidelines
options.D: Fair Housing Accessibility Guidelines
options.E: ABA Accessibility Standards
options.F: ADA Standards for Transportation Facilities

questions.explanation: ICC/ANSI A117.1 is the basis for accessibility in construction documents; the International Building Code adopts it by reference, so the local jurisdiction enforces it unless an amendment substitutes another standard. The 2010 ADA Standards are enforced by the Department of Justice, the ABA standards by federal agencies, and the Fair Housing guidelines come from HUD.

questions.question: Under EJCDC C-700, which of the following separate an 'or-equal' item from a substitute?

options.A: An or-equal may be proposed only during bidding; a substitute only after award
options.B: An or-equal needs the owner's consent in writing; a substitute does not
options.C: An or-equal is approved by addendum to the documents; a substitute by Change Order
options.D: An or-equal is shown by an approved Shop Drawing; a substitute by a Field Order or proposed Change Order
options.E: An or-equal needs a special performance guarantee from the contractor; a substitute does not
options.F: An or-equal's approval or denial changes no Contract Price; a substitute's approval may change it

questions.explanation: C-700 7.05.C says the engineer's or-equal determination is evidenced by an approved Shop Drawing or other written communication, and 7.05.D says neither approval nor denial of an or-equal changes the Contract Price. Under 7.06.B a substitute determination is evidenced by a Field Order or a proposed Change Order covering all related impacts, including Contract Price or Times. The owner may require a special performance guarantee for a substitute, not an or-equal.

questions.question: Which terms are other names for value analysis?

options.A: Life cycle costing
options.B: Constructability review
options.C: Value engineering
options.D: Cost accounting
options.E: Value management
options.F: Total cost of ownership

questions.explanation: Value analysis is also known as value engineering, value management and value-enhanced design: evaluating a design for alternative methods, systems or materials that improve life cycle value. Life cycle costing (total cost of ownership) can look similar but is a different process, and a constructability review judges how practical the design is to build, not its value.

questions.question: An estimate is not a price. What is a price based on?

options.A: Published cost data adjusted for local conditions
options.B: Costs of similar projects already constructed
options.C: Input from construction participants and a contingency
options.D: Bids from contractors, subcontractors, and suppliers
options.E: Economic conditions expected at the time of construction
options.F: The A/E's opinion of the probable cost of construction

questions.explanation: A price comes from bids by contractors, subcontractors and suppliers. An estimate is only an opinion of probable construction cost, built from sources such as costs of similar projects, published cost data, input from construction participants, expected economic conditions and a contingency, so each of those other choices describes an estimate input, not a price.

questions.question: An early estimate for a nursing home is built from a cost per bed. Which estimating method is this?

options.A: Unit of measure
options.B: Order of magnitude
options.C: Assemblies/systems
options.D: Unit price
options.E: Quantity survey (takeoff)
options.F: Life cycle costing

questions.explanation: An order of magnitude estimate uses costs per unit of occupancy, such as per bed or per seat; it is the quickest and least accurate method, within about 20 to 25 percent. A unit of measure estimate uses cost per square or cubic foot, and an assemblies estimate prices units of assembled construction such as roof or wall systems.

questions.question: Cost and value mean different things in design and construction. Which describes value?

options.A: The price paid to acquire and maintain a structure
options.B: The total cost of owning a facility over its life
options.C: The lowest first cost that meets the owner's program
options.D: Relative worth or importance, which may be intangible
options.E: An outlay of money, time, and labor for a structure
options.F: The price set by bids from contractors and suppliers

questions.explanation: Value is relative worth, merit or importance, and it can exceed what was paid for intangible reasons, such as exposure to a particular market. Cost is the price paid to acquire, produce or maintain a structure, an outlay of money, time and labor. The total cost of owning a facility over its life is life cycle cost, not value.

questions.question: A testing agency's report confirming that installed work meets the specified quality is usually which kind of submittal?

options.A: Action, needing approval by the A/E
options.B: Closeout, filed with the project record documents
options.C: Action, needing approval by the owner
options.D: Informational, needing no responsive action
options.E: Informational, needing approval by the owner
options.F: Action, needing the contractor's approval only

questions.explanation: Informational submittals need no responsive action by the architect/engineer; they generally verify or certify that installed work meets the specified quality, and test reports and qualification statements are typical examples. Action submittals, such as shop drawings, are the ones the architect/engineer approves, approves as noted, returns for resubmittal or rejects.

questions.question: A fabricator prepares drawings and schedules showing in detail how a portion of the work will be fabricated and fit adjacent construction. What are these?

options.A: Coordination drawings
options.B: Product data
options.C: Shop drawings
options.D: Delegated design submittals
options.E: Samples
options.F: Manufacturer's instructions

questions.explanation: Shop drawings are drawings, illustrations and schedules that show a portion of the work in more detail, including how it will be fabricated and how it meets adjacent construction; a subcontractor, fabricator or supplier usually prepares them for the contractor. Product data is the manufacturer's standard literature, and coordination drawings show how the work of several trades fits in shared space.

questions.question: Which submittal type sets the benchmark against which the finished work will be judged?

options.A: Product data
options.B: Samples
options.C: Shop drawings
options.D: Certificates
options.E: Qualification statements
options.F: Test and evaluation reports

questions.explanation: Samples are physical examples of materials, equipment or workmanship that show color, texture and other functional and aesthetic characteristics, and the approved sample becomes the standard the work is judged against. Product data describes a product in printed literature, and shop drawings show how a portion of the work is fabricated and installed.

questions.question: Which activities are quality control rather than quality assurance?

options.A: Taking field measurements and verifying site conditions
options.B: Obtaining manufacturers' certifications
options.C: Holding a preconstruction conference on procedures
options.D: Checking installed items against a tolerance
options.E: Checking the work against a list of contract requirements
options.F: Submitting evidence of the kind and quality of products

questions.explanation: Quality control evaluates completed work against the contract; common forms include checking whether items fall within an acceptable tolerance and checking the work against a list of contract requirements. Verifying site conditions, obtaining manufacturers' certifications, submitting evidence of product quality and holding a preconstruction conference are quality assurance, which guards against defects before and during the work.

questions.question: How does commissioning differ from the A/E's construction contract administration?

options.A: It checks the work's compliance with the contract documents
options.B: It is performed by the contractor's quality control staff
options.C: It verifies performance meets the owner's requirements
options.D: It begins at substantial completion and ends at closeout
options.E: It is limited to testing the mechanical and electrical systems
options.F: It replaces the contractor's field quality control testing

questions.explanation: Commissioning, usually by an independent authority the owner retains, is a quality process that achieves, verifies and documents that a facility and its systems and assemblies perform to defined objectives and criteria, starting with the owner's project requirements. The architect/engineer's contract administration instead verifies quality by checking compliance with the contract documents. Commissioning does not begin at substantial completion and is not limited to mechanical and electrical systems.

questions.question: Which type of commissioning starts when a facility is first conceived and continues through its management and use?

options.A: Systems and equipment commissioning
options.B: Building envelope commissioning
options.C: Limited commissioning
options.D: Total project commissioning
options.E: Facility condition assessment
options.F: Post-occupancy evaluation

questions.explanation: Total project commissioning, also called total facility or building commissioning, runs from project conception through facility management and use, and it includes both systems and equipment commissioning and building envelope commissioning. Systems and equipment commissioning covers testing, adjusting and training for specific systems, and a limited version added late cannot account for the original program and design.

questions.question: In commissioning, what is the document in which the design team explains how the owner's project requirements will be met?

options.A: Commissioning plan
options.B: Owner's project requirements
options.C: Final commissioning report
options.D: Basis of design
options.E: Commissioning specifications
options.F: Systems manual

questions.explanation: The design team analyzes the owner's project requirements and prepares a basis of design explaining how they will be met, including system selections, integration and sequences of operation. The owner's project requirements are the criteria themselves, and the commissioning plan, developed afterward, sets out how performance will be verified.

questions.question: Which statements correctly contrast design-assist with delegated design?

options.A: A design-assist subcontractor consults without taking design responsibility
options.B: Delegated design makes the contractor responsible for a component's design
options.C: Design-assist results come back as sealed drawings and calculations for review
options.D: Both {A} and {B}
options.E: Both {A} and {C}
options.F: {A}, {B} and {C}

questions.explanation: A design-assist subcontractor is brought in early to advise the design team on materials, installation, budget and similar matters, but it takes no responsibility for the design. In delegated design the specifications make the contractor responsible for designing and engineering a component through a licensed professional. Sealed drawings and calculations reviewed as a submittal are the product of delegated design, not design-assist.

questions.question: On a CMAR project with a GMP, the final cost of the work comes in below the GMP. What happens to the difference?

options.A: Kept by the CMAR as added profit
options.B: Held as retainage until the warranty ends
options.C: Split among the trade subcontractors who bid it
options.D: Credited to the owner or shared with the CMAR
options.E: Held in the CMAR's contingency for later changes
options.F: Paid to the A/E as a value analysis incentive

questions.explanation: The CMAR guarantees the project will cost no more than the guaranteed maximum price as long as the scope and its pricing assumptions hold. If the cost runs over, the CMAR pays the excess; if it comes in under, the difference is credited to the owner or shared between the owner and the CMAR, as the agreement provides. The CMAR does not simply keep it as profit.

questions.question: An owner contracts with an architect, who then subcontracts with a contractor for construction. Which design-build variation is this?

options.A: Constructor-based design-build
options.B: Developer-based design-build
options.C: Pure design-build
options.D: Designer-based design-build
options.E: Joint venture design-build
options.F: Single-purpose entity design-build

questions.explanation: Design-build variations are named for whoever holds the owner's contract. In designer-based design-build the owner contracts with the architect/engineer, who subcontracts the construction. Constructor-based design-build is the reverse, with the contractor subcontracting the design; developer-based puts a developer over both; and pure design-build is one integrated firm providing both with its own staff.

questions.question: Which pairings of term and meaning are correct?

options.A: Bid shopping: the owner comparing bids to find the lowest responsible bidder
options.B: Bid-day surprise: a low bid far below the others, suggesting an error
options.C: Scope creep: modifications that become time and cost change orders
options.D: Bid-day surprise: every bid received exceeds the owner's budget
options.E: Buyout: the owner's choice of which subcontractors the contractor uses
options.F: Bid shopping: bidders leaving out work that the documents only imply

questions.explanation: Scope creep is the name for modifications to the contract documents that turn into change orders affecting time and cost, and bid-day surprise is when every bid received exceeds the owner's budget. Bid shopping is the contractor shopping its subcontractors and suppliers to improve its own profit, not the owner comparing bids, and the owner has no say in how the contractor buys out the work.

questions.question: An architect hires a structural engineer for a project it is designing under an agreement with the owner. What is the architect-engineer agreement?

options.A: A second prime agreement with the owner
options.B: A joint venture between the two firms
options.C: A modification of the owner-architect agreement
options.D: A subcontract under the prime agreement
options.E: A tripartite agreement with the owner
options.F: A direct owner-engineer prime agreement

questions.explanation: A prime agreement is the original agreement between the two original parties for the original purpose, here the owner and the architect. When one of them contracts with someone else for work that is part of that purpose, the new agreement is a subcontract. A party may have any number of subcontracts, and none of them modifies the prime agreement.

questions.question: Why is procurement under the CMAR delivery method described as 'open book'?

options.A: Bidders see the CMAR's GMP before they price packages
options.B: The owner takes part in and knows how trades are selected
options.C: Bid results are published to the public after each opening
options.D: The A/E reviews each subcontract before it is signed
options.E: The owner holds the trade contracts and pays each directly
options.F: The CMAR's subcontracts are assigned to the owner at award

questions.explanation: CMAR procurement is called open book because the owner takes an active part in the construction management work the CMAR performs and knows exactly how the trade contractors, subcontractors and suppliers are chosen. Even so, the owner's only contract is with the CMAR, which holds the trade agreements, so the owner does not hold or pay the trade contracts directly.

questions.question: A project had no commissioning, and at closeout the owner hires an independent commissioning authority. Which statements about this limited commissioning are correct?

options.A: It brings expertise in system and equipment operation and performance
options.B: It cannot account for decisions made in the original program and design
options.C: It begins by documenting the owner's project requirements
options.D: It includes building envelope oversight from design onward
options.E: Both {A} and {B}
options.F: {A}, {B} and {C}

questions.explanation: An independent commissioning authority hired late can still bring specialized expertise in how systems and equipment operate and perform. Because this limited version never evaluates the original program or design, it cannot account for the decisions made early on. Documenting the owner's project requirements and overseeing the envelope from design onward belong to commissioning that begins at the start of the project.

questions.question: Which sentence uses 'shall' in its traditional sense of 'has a duty to'?

options.A: The Contractor shall protect adjacent finishes.
options.B: Adjacent finishes shall be protected.
options.C: Sealant shall cure for at least 7 days before painting.
options.D: Joints shall be 1/4 inch wide.
options.E: Two coats of paint shall be applied to each surface.
options.F: Equipment shall be installed plumb and level.

questions.explanation: 'The Contractor shall' can correctly be read as 'the Contractor has a duty to,' because the Contractor is a party that can be bound. Finishes, sealant, joints, paint and equipment cannot have a legal duty, so 'shall' with those subjects departs from its traditional meaning, which is one reason 'shall' is discouraged when specifying products and their installation.

questions.question: A paragraph assigns temporary power to the Owner. Which sentence follows standard specification usage of 'shall,' 'will,' 'must,' and 'is to'?

options.A: The Owner shall provide temporary power.
options.B: The Owner must provide temporary power.
options.C: The Owner is to provide temporary power.
options.D: The Owner will provide temporary power.
options.E: Temporary power shall be provided by the Owner.
options.F: Provide temporary power for the Owner.

questions.explanation: In specifications 'shall' is used for work required of the contractor, and 'will', the less obligatory form, for acts required of the owner or the architect/engineer, so the Owner 'will' provide temporary power. 'Must' and 'is to' are not recommended in specifications, and an imperative such as 'Provide temporary power' is addressed to the Contractor, not the Owner.

questions.question: In specifications, the indicative mood typically requires the use of:

options.A: A colon after the subject
options.B: The verb as the first word
options.C: 'Shall' or 'will'
options.D: 'Must' or 'is to'
options.E: An action verb before its object
options.F: Omitting articles such as 'the'

questions.explanation: Sentences in the indicative mood typically need 'shall' or 'will', which makes specifications wordy and monotonous. Putting the action verb first is the imperative mood, the recommended alternative, and the colon after a subject belongs to streamlining. 'Must' and 'is to' are not recommended in specifications at all.

questions.question: Which statements about the imperative mood are correct?

options.A: It should generally be maintained throughout a specification.
options.B: The verb that defines the action is the first word of the sentence.
options.C: It should be paired with 'shall' for clarity.
options.D: It should be limited to the installation statements in PART 3.
options.E: Both {A} and {B}
options.F: {A}, {B} and {D}

questions.explanation: The imperative mood is the recommended style for the whole specification: the verb that defines the action comes first, as in 'Install equipment plumb and level.' It is concise and easy to understand. It is not confined to the installation statements in PART 3, and it replaces 'shall' rather than being paired with it.

questions.question: In a specification, an imperative instruction such as 'Seal joints watertight' is addressed to:

options.A: The subcontractor doing the work
options.B: The installer named in PART 3
options.C: Whoever the A/E designates
options.D: The Contractor
options.E: The manufacturer of the sealant
options.F: The Owner's representative

questions.explanation: The owner and the contractor are the only parties to the owner-contractor agreement, so every instruction in the specifications is addressed to the Contractor, and 'Contractor shall' is normally left out in favor of the imperative. A subcontractor or installer may actually do the work, but dividing the work among them is the Contractor's responsibility.

questions.question: Which streamlined entry follows the standard streamlining form?

options.A: Install equipment: Plumb and level.
options.B: Equipment: Install plumb and level.
options.C: Equipment: Must be installed plumb and level.
options.D: Equipment: Shall be installed plumb and level.
options.E: Equipment: To be installed plumb and level.
options.F: Equipment: Is to be installed plumb and level.

questions.explanation: Streamlining puts the subject first, then a colon, then the requirement in the imperative, as in 'Equipment: Install plumb and level.' The colon stands in for 'shall' or 'shall be', so adding 'shall', 'must' or 'is to' after it is redundant, and leading with the verb before the colon loses the subject-first keyword.

questions.question: Every specification paragraph should end with:

options.A: A period only
options.B: A period, colon, or semicolon
options.C: A period or a colon
options.D: A period, unless it is a list item
options.E: A period or a semicolon
options.F: A colon, unless it ends the Article

questions.explanation: Every paragraph ends with either a period or a colon. A colon ends a parent paragraph that must be linked to the subparagraphs under it, and each item in a list of subparagraphs ends with a period to show nothing is missing. Semicolons are not used to end paragraphs or list items.

questions.question: Which statements about punctuation in specifications are correct?

options.A: The formal rules of punctuation must be observed.
options.B: Sentences should be built so a misplaced punctuation mark does not change the meaning.
options.C: Commas are used only between the items in a series.
options.D: The comma before the conjunction in a series is optional.
options.E: Both {A} and {B}
options.F: {A}, {B} and {D}

questions.explanation: Specifications are legal documents, so the formal rules of punctuation apply, and sentences should be built so that a misplaced or dropped mark cannot change the meaning. Commas are also used wherever they make a statement clearer, not only in series, and the serial (Oxford) comma before the conjunction is required, not optional.

questions.question: A draft specification reads: 'Seal joints between frames, sills and walls.' What change does good specification practice require?

options.A: None; the final comma is optional
options.B: Add a comma after 'joints'
options.C: Replace the commas with semicolons
options.D: Add a comma after 'sills'
options.E: Replace 'and' with 'and/or'
options.F: Remove the comma after 'frames'

questions.explanation: Specifications use the serial (Oxford) comma: every item in a series is followed by a comma, including the one just before the conjunction, so the text should read 'frames, sills, and walls.' Many general style guides treat that last comma as optional, but in a legal document such as a specification it is required to keep the items unambiguous.

questions.question: Recommended practice for parentheses and quotation marks in specification text is that they should be:

options.A: Minimized or avoided
options.B: Never used
options.C: Used to set off defined terms
options.D: Used instead of underlining for emphasis
options.E: Used freely wherever they aid clarity
options.F: Used only within PART 1 articles

questions.explanation: Parentheses and quotation marks should be minimized or avoided in specification text. The flat 'do not use' rule applies to underlining, not to these marks, and parentheses still appear in accepted forms such as '10 degrees C (50 degrees F).' Using them freely, or to set off defined terms or add emphasis, goes against the guidance.

questions.question: In the sentence 'Comply with article 3.04 of this section.', which words should be capitalized?

options.A: Neither word
options.B: Article only
options.C: Both Article and Section
options.D: Section only
options.E: ARTICLE in all capitals, like PART, and Section
options.F: Article, and SECTION in all capitals, like PART

questions.explanation: Article takes an initial capital when it refers to an article of the specifications or conditions of the contract, and Section takes one when it refers to a specific section of the specifications. Both words point to specific parts here, so both are capitalized: 'Comply with Article 3.04 of this Section.' Only PART is written in all capitals.

questions.question: Which statements follow standard capitalization practice for references such as 'See paragraph 2.03.B and subparagraph 2.03.B.1'?

options.A: Paragraph is capitalized when it refers to a paragraph in the specifications.
options.B: Subparagraph is usually not capitalized.
options.C: Clause is capitalized when it refers to a clause of the general conditions.
options.D: Paragraph is written in all capitals, like PART.
options.E: Both {A} and {B}
options.F: {A}, {B} and {C}

questions.explanation: Paragraph is capitalized when it refers to a specific paragraph of the specifications or other contract documents, but subparagraph and clause are usually left lowercase. Only PART is written in all capitals. The trap is assuming paragraph, subparagraph and clause are all treated the same way.

questions.question: In the sentence 'Install louvers in the north wall of the library.', which words should be capitalized?

options.A: Library only
options.B: North and Library
options.C: Neither north nor library
options.D: North and Wall
options.E: North only
options.F: North, Wall, and Library

questions.explanation: Room names such as Library, Science Room or Chemistry Laboratory are capitalized in specifications. Compass directions such as north or northwest stay lowercase unless they form part of a proper noun, and wall is an ordinary noun, so the sentence reads 'Install louvers in the north wall of the Library.'

questions.question: In the sentence 'Coordinate the work with the drawings and the project manual.', which words should be capitalized when they refer to this contract?
