options.D: Their standard bid forms
options.E: Their performance and payment bond forms
options.F: Their standard change order forms

questions.explanation: The AIA, EJCDC, ConsensusDocs, and DBIA conditions of the contract expressly set out how the A/E or owner issues interpretations and orders minor modifications consistent with them. Instructions to bidders and bid forms govern procurement, bond and change order forms record obligations or changes rather than set these procedures, and subcontracts do not set the A/E's or owner's authority under the prime contract.

questions.question: The A/E issues a written interpretation of an ambiguous detail that requires the contractor to add blocking. The contractor believes the interpretation justifies an increase in the contract sum. Under the standard conditions of the contract, which statement is accurate?

options.A: Either the contractor or the owner may claim a change they consider justified
options.B: Only the owner may claim a change arising from an A/E interpretation
options.C: No claim is possible because A/E interpretations are final and binding
options.D: The contractor may claim only after a change order has been executed
options.E: Only the contractor may claim; the owner is bound by the A/E's decision
options.F: Neither may claim; the A/E's interpretation adjusts the contract sum itself

questions.explanation: The standard conditions let both the contractor and the owner claim a change in contract sum or time when they believe a written A/E interpretation justifies it. The right is not limited to either party, an interpretation neither forecloses claims nor adjusts the sum by itself, and a claim does not wait for an executed change order.

questions.question: During construction, the contractor asks for clarification of an ambiguous detail. Under the standard conditions of the contract, which parties have procedures to issue an interpretation and order minor modifications consistent with it?

options.A: The A/E or the contractor
options.B: The A/E or the owner
options.C: The owner or the contractor
options.D: The A/E or the building official
options.E: The A/E or the contractor's surety
options.F: The contractor or the owner's lender

questions.explanation: The standard conditions of the contract give the A/E or the owner the procedures to issue interpretations and to order minor modifications consistent with them. The contractor receives interpretations and may claim changes based on them but does not issue them, and the building official, a surety, and a lender are not parties with that authority under the contract.

questions.question: A change order revises the paint finish requirements in Section 09 91 23. How does this modification relate to the original contract?

options.A: It replaces the entire original contract with a new contract
options.B: It creates a separate contract covering only the revised work
options.C: It interprets the contract but does not change any of its terms
options.D: It substitutes for part of the contract; the rest stays in effect
options.E: It suspends the original contract until the revised work is complete
options.F: It applies only to the subcontractor who performs the revised work

questions.explanation: Modifying a contract changes the original by adding, deleting, or correcting portions of the contract documents, but the modification does not replace the whole contract; it typically substitutes for a part of it while the rest stays in effect. It does not create a separate contract, suspend the original, or bind only a subcontractor, and a change order revising paint requirements alters terms rather than merely interpreting them.

questions.question: During construction, the manufacturer discontinues the specified rooftop air-handling unit model, and the contractor proposes a different product. Which frequent reason for contract modifications does this represent?

options.A: Changes in the owner's requirements
options.B: Unforeseen field conditions
options.C: Changes in market conditions
options.D: Correction of errors or omissions
options.E: Changes in code provisions or AHJ requirements
options.F: Owner-directed acceleration of the schedule

questions.explanation: Changes in market conditions are a frequent reason for modifications, and they expressly include specified products that are no longer available as well as new products offering price or other advantages. Changes in owner requirements (such as an owner-directed acceleration), unforeseen field conditions, code or AHJ changes, and correction of errors or omissions are separate categories that do not describe a discontinued product.

questions.question: Midway through construction, the city adopts an amended fire protection ordinance that took effect after the contract documents were issued, and the fire marshal now requires an added sprinkler zone. Which frequent reason for contract modifications does this represent?

options.A: Changes in code provisions or AHJ requirements
options.B: Correction of errors, omissions, or discrepancies
options.C: Unforeseen field conditions discovered in the work
options.D: Changes in market conditions affecting products
options.E: Changes in the owner's program or requirements
options.F: Owner-directed acceleration of the schedule

questions.explanation: New regulatory code provisions or other new requirements of the authorities having jurisdiction are a distinct, frequent reason for modifications. Because the ordinance took effect after the documents were issued, the documents were not in error, so correcting errors or omissions does not fit; nothing was uncovered in the field, no product became unavailable, and the owner did not change its program or schedule.

questions.question: The owner decides to upgrade the lobby flooring and asks whether to initiate the change now, early in construction, or wait until the lobby work is about to begin. What is the main advantage of initiating it early?

options.A: It avoids the need for a signed change order and cost proposal
options.B: It allows time to weigh proposals and alternatives without delaying progress
options.C: It lets the A/E process the change as an addendum to the documents
options.D: It shifts the cost of the change into the contractor's own construction contingency
options.E: It allows the change to skip the A/E's review of the contractor's proposal
options.F: It removes any need to adjust the contract time for the change

questions.explanation: Contract modifications should be issued in a timely, orderly way to minimize delays and added costs; a change started early in construction leaves time to consider proposals and alternatives and reach a mutually acceptable change without disrupting progress. Starting early does not eliminate the change order, turn it into an addendum, shift costs to the contractor, bypass the A/E's review, or rule out a time adjustment.

questions.question: An A/E is preparing a change order that revises several specification sections and adjusts the contract sum based on a lengthy pricing proposal from the contractor. How can the change order document itself be kept concise?

options.A: State only the net change in contract sum and omit the supporting pricing
options.B: Describe the changes in the work and defer pricing to the next pay application
options.C: List only the affected section numbers and have the contractor infer the revisions
options.D: Refer to attachments that describe the changes and cost breakdowns in detail
options.E: Restate each revised section in full within the body of the change order
options.F: Issue a separate change order for each specification section revised

questions.explanation: Contract modifications can usually stay concise by referring to attachments that describe the changes and the cost breakdowns in detail. Omitting or deferring the pricing leaves the sum adjustment undocumented, bare section numbers leave the revisions undefined, and restating whole sections or splitting the change into many change orders makes the record longer, not more concise.

questions.question: Section 01 26 00 specifies the procedural requirements for initiating and processing modifications. With which documents must that section be closely coordinated?

options.A: The conditions of the contract and the agreement
options.B: The instructions to bidders and the bid/proposal form
options.C: Section 01 25 00 and Section 01 31 00
options.D: The drawings and the schedule of values
options.E: The construction schedule and the submittal register
options.F: The owner-A/E agreement and the A/E's fee schedule

questions.explanation: Section 01 26 00—Contract Modification Procedures holds the procedural requirements for starting and processing modifications, and it must line up closely with the general and supplementary conditions and with the owner-contractor agreement. The instructions to bidders and bid form govern procurement, and other Division 01 sections, the drawings, schedules, logs, and the owner-A/E agreement are not where modification terms are set.

questions.question: When describing the revisions in a contract modification, which method does industry guidance suggest the A/E may follow?

options.A: The format used for a submittal review transmittal
options.B: The layout of the original bid or proposal form
options.C: An approach similar to the one used for an addendum
options.D: A narrative style like a field observation report
options.E: The format of a request for information log
options.F: The arrangement of the schedule of values

questions.explanation: Revisions in a contract modification may be described much the way an addendum describes them, with items arranged in the same order as the project manual and drawings. Submittal transmittals, bid form layouts, narrative field reports, RFI logs, and the schedule of values are not models for describing modifications.

questions.question: A specifier is editing Section 01 26 00 for a project whose general conditions are AIA Document A201. Which set lists the recognized ways to modify the contract documents under A201?

options.A: Change order, work change directive, field order, and written interpretation
options.B: Change order, construction change directive, and minor changes in the work
options.C: Change order, construction change directive, and field order
options.D: Change order, addendum, and minor changes in the work
options.E: Change order, construction change directive, and architect's interpretation
options.F: Change order, field order, and minor changes in the work

questions.explanation: A201 recognizes three ways to modify the contract documents: change order, construction change directive, and minor changes in the work. Work change directives, field orders, and written interpretations come from the EJCDC C-700 list, an architect's interpretation is not a modification method in the A201 list, and addenda are issued before the agreement is executed, so they do not modify the contract.

questions.question: The owner, contractor, and architect have agreed on an added entrance canopy, a $42,000 increase in the contract sum, and a 10-day time extension. Which AIA form does industry guidance identify as the standard form for documenting this?

options.A: AIA Document G710
options.B: AIA Document G714
options.C: AIA Document G702
options.D: AIA Document G701
options.E: AIA Document G709
options.F: AIA Document G703

questions.explanation: Because the parties agree on the change, the cost, and the time, a change order is the instrument, and AIA Document G701 is its standard form. G710, Architect's Supplemental Instructions, is for minor changes with no sum or time adjustment, G714 is the construction change directive used when sum or time is not agreed, G709 requests a proposal for a change, and G702 and G703 are payment application forms.

questions.question: On an A201 project, the owner and contractor have settled a revision to the work and its cost, but they still disagree about the extension of contract time the contractor requests. The contractor asks the architect to process a change order now and settle the time later. Under A201, which response is correct?

options.A: Process it; a change order requires agreement only on the change in the work
options.B: Process it; the time adjustment can be added later as a minor change in the work
options.C: Hold it; a change order states agreement on the work, the sum, and the time
options.D: Hold it; a change order may adjust the contract sum or the time, but not both
options.E: Process it; the contractor can claim the time later through a field order
options.F: Hold it; only the owner may sign a change order that adds contract time

questions.explanation: Under A201 a change order is a written instrument in which the owner, contractor, and architect state their agreement on the change in the work, the amount of any sum adjustment, and the extent of any time adjustment. With time still disputed, that condition is not met. One change order can adjust both sum and time, minor changes involve no sum or time adjustment, field orders are EJCDC instruments, and all three parties sign.

questions.question: On an AIA A201 project, the contractor emails the owner a change order it drafted for added work that has already been priced and agreed. Under A201, which party is responsible for preparing the change order instrument?

options.A: The architect
options.B: The contractor
options.C: The owner
options.D: The owner and contractor jointly
options.E: The owner's legal counsel
options.F: The contractor's surety

questions.explanation: Under A201, the architect prepares the change order as a written instrument, and the owner, the contractor, and the architect then sign it. A document drafted by the contractor, the owner, the two jointly, the owner's attorney, or a surety does not match that description, even when the pricing is already agreed.

questions.question: An architect's office prefers to issue minor changes in the work on its own field bulletin form instead of AIA Document G710. Where should the use of that alternate form be indicated?

options.A: Section 01 31 00—Project Management and Coordination
options.B: Section 01 26 00—Contract Modification Procedures
options.C: Section 01 33 00—Submittal Procedures
options.D: Section 01 25 00—Substitution Procedures
options.E: Section 01 35 00—Special Procedures
options.F: Section 01 77 00—Closeout Procedures

questions.explanation: AIA Document G710, Architect's Supplemental Instructions, is the standard form for minor changes, but if the architect chooses another document, that document should be named in Section 01 26 00—Contract Modification Procedures. Sections 01 25 00, 01 31 00, 01 33 00, 01 35 00, and 01 77 00 address substitutions, coordination, submittals, special procedures, and closeout, not the instruments for modifying the contract.

questions.question: A specifier is converting Section 01 26 00 from an AIA-based project to a project using EJCDC C-700 general conditions. Which list correctly identifies the recognized ways to change the contract documents under C-700?

options.A: Change order, construction change directive, field order, and minor change in the work
options.B: Change order, work change directive, engineer's supplemental instruction, and minor change in the work
options.C: Change order, work change directive, field order, and minor change in the work
options.D: Change order, work change directive, field order, and written interpretation or clarification
options.E: Change order, construction change directive, field order, and written interpretation or clarification
options.F: Change order, work change directive, field order, and architect's supplemental instruction

questions.explanation: C-700 recognizes four ways to modify the contract documents: the change order, the work change directive, the field order, and the written interpretation or clarification. Construction change directives and minor changes in the work are A201 terms, and supplemental instructions belong to the AIA G710 form; under C-700 minor changes are ordered by field order rather than listed as a separate method.

questions.question: For change orders under EJCDC documents, which statement correctly matches each party to its role?

options.A: Engineer recommends; owner authorizes; contractor accepts
options.B: Engineer authorizes; owner accepts; contractor recommends
options.C: Engineer accepts; owner recommends; contractor authorizes
options.D: Engineer recommends; owner accepts; contractor authorizes
options.E: Engineer accepts; owner authorizes; contractor recommends
options.F: Engineer authorizes; owner recommends; contractor accepts

questions.explanation: An EJCDC change order is recommended by the engineer, authorized by the owner, and accepted by the contractor, and all three sign it. Every other pairing swaps these roles: the engineer neither authorizes nor accepts the change, the owner neither recommends nor merely accepts it, and the contractor neither recommends nor authorizes it.

questions.question: On a project using EJCDC C-700, the engineer is preparing the instrument to add work with an agreed increase in contract price and time. Which EJCDC form does industry guidance identify as the standard form for it?

options.A: EJCDC C-940
options.B: EJCDC C-700
options.C: EJCDC C-941
options.D: EJCDC C-200
options.E: EJCDC C-520
options.F: EJCDC C-430

questions.explanation: An agreed adjustment in price and time is made by change order, and EJCDC C-941, Change Order, is the standard form. C-940 is the work change directive form, used before price or time is agreed; C-700 is the standard general conditions, C-200 the suggested instructions to bidders, C-520 the owner-contractor agreement, and C-430 a bid bond form.

questions.question: Under the EJCDC C-700 definition, from what point in the project may a change order be issued?

options.A: Only after the notice to proceed has been given
options.B: On or after the effective date of the agreement
options.C: At any time after the bids have been opened
options.D: Only after the notice of award has been issued
options.E: Only after substantial completion has been certified
options.F: As soon as the bidding documents have been issued

questions.explanation: Under the C-700 definition, a change order is recommended by the engineer, signed by owner and contractor, and may be issued once the agreement has taken effect, on its effective date or later. Issuing the bidding documents, bid opening, and the notice of award all come before the agreement takes effect, nothing requires waiting for a notice to proceed, and change orders are not held until substantial completion.

questions.question: An engineer on a project using EJCDC C-700 suggests issuing a work change directive to revise the scope of a pump station while bids are still being received. Based on how industry guidance summarizes the C-700 definition of a work change directive, why is this inappropriate?

options.A: It is signed by the owner and issued on or after the agreement's effective date
options.B: It is signed by the engineer and may be issued only after substantial completion
options.C: It is signed by the contractor and issued only after the notice to proceed
options.D: It is signed by the owner and contractor and issued only after bid opening
options.E: It is signed by the bidders and issued only during the bidding period
options.F: It is signed by the engineer alone and issued at any time after bid opening

questions.explanation: Industry guidance, summarizing EJCDC C-700, describes the work change directive as a written directive to the contractor, signed by the owner and issued on or after the agreement's effective date. While bids are still being received no agreement is in effect, so a directive cannot be used; revisions during bidding go out by addendum. The other options misstate who signs it, when it may be issued, or both.

questions.question: During excavation on an EJCDC C-700 project, the contractor uncovers buried foundations not shown in the contract documents. The owner wants work to continue now, with cost and time effects to be negotiated later. Which statement correctly describes the appropriate instrument?

options.A: A field order issued by the engineer, because the change involves no price or time effect
options.B: A change order on EJCDC C-941, because the owner must sign before any added work proceeds
options.C: A work change directive on EJCDC C-940, as evidence that a change order will follow
options.D: A written interpretation by the engineer, because the conditions differ from the documents
options.E: A construction change directive on AIA G714, because the owner signs it alone
options.F: An addendum issued to the contractor, because the conditions were unknown at bidding

questions.explanation: Under C-700, a work change directive can order changes or deal with differing or unforeseen subsurface or physical conditions, and its form is EJCDC C-940; it signals that a change order will follow once price and time are negotiated. A field order cannot change price or time, a C-941 change order needs agreed terms, an interpretation does not order changed work, G714 is the AIA counterpart, and addenda come before the contract.

questions.question: On an EJCDC C-700 project, the engineer wants to shift a floor drain 300 mm to clear a beam, with no effect on cost or schedule. The owner's representative is unavailable for two weeks. How should this change be handled?

options.A: The engineer prepares a change order for later signature by owner and contractor
options.B: The engineer gives verbal direction and records it in the next meeting minutes
options.C: The owner issues a work change directive upon returning, before the work proceeds
options.D: The engineer issues a written field order; the owner's signature is not required
options.E: The engineer issues an architect's supplemental instruction on AIA G710
options.F: The contractor moves the drain and notes the change on the record drawings

questions.explanation: An EJCDC field order is a written order from the engineer for minor changes that do not alter contract price or times. It must be in writing, but it needs neither an executed change order nor the owner's signature. Verbal direction or an unrecorded field change fails the writing requirement, a work change directive or change order is unnecessary for a change with no cost or time effect, and G710 is the AIA instrument.

questions.question: A specifier preparing the Division 01 section on contract modification procedures for an EJCDC-based project wants to name the form commonly used for field orders. Which should it cite?

options.A: EJCDC C-940 with the owner's signature block deleted
options.B: EJCDC C-941 with the price and time entries shown as zero
options.C: EJCDC C-942, Field Order
options.D: No form at all, since field orders may be given verbally
options.E: AIA G710, Architect's Supplemental Instructions
options.F: EJCDC C-200, which includes a field order form

questions.explanation: C-700 does not prescribe a particular document for minor changes, but the EJCDC Field Order form, C-942, is the one commonly used, and whichever form the project names, a field order must be in writing. C-940 is the work change directive and C-941 the change order, so neither is adapted for field orders; G710 is the AIA form for minor changes, C-200 is the suggested instructions to bidders, and verbal direction is not acceptable.

questions.question: A specifier is editing a Division 01 section on modification procedures for a project using ConsensusDocs 200 general conditions. Which set of modification methods matches that document?

options.A: Change order, construction change directive, and minor change
options.B: Change order, work change directive, and minor changes
options.C: Change order, work change directive, and field order
options.D: Change order, interim directive, and written amendment
options.E: Change order, interim directive, and field order
options.F: Change order, written amendment, and construction change directive

questions.explanation: ConsensusDocs 200 provides three ways to change the contract documents: the change order, the interim directive, and the written amendment. Construction change directives and minor changes are AIA terms, the work change directive with minor changes is the DBIA set, and field orders and work change directives come from EJCDC, so any set mixing in those terms is wrong.

questions.question: On a ConsensusDocs 200 project, the owner wants a firestopping detail redone; the contractor says the work is extra, but the owner believes it is already required. Which instrument lets the owner direct the work to proceed while the disagreement remains?

options.A: A change order recording the disputed work at no change in price
options.B: An interim directive, ordering the work before any adjustment is agreed
options.C: A written amendment issued by the owner under the general conditions' changes article
options.D: A field order, since the owner considers the work already required
options.E: A work change directive signed by the owner and the contractor
options.F: A construction change directive issued by the architect

questions.explanation: The ConsensusDocs interim directive orders work before the parties agree on price or time, and the owner also uses it for work the owner believes is not a change; only the owner must sign it. A change order needs the contractor's signature, which a disputing contractor will not give, the written amendment is not a formal change document in ConsensusDocs 200, and field orders, work change directives, and construction change directives belong to other document families.

questions.question: An owner's project manager on a ConsensusDocs 200 project needs to order work to begin before price and time adjustments are agreed. Which standard form does industry guidance identify for this purpose?

options.A: ConsensusDocs 202
options.B: ConsensusDocs 200
options.C: ConsensusDocs 203
options.D: DBIA Document No. 500D5
options.E: DBIA Document No. 500D2
options.F: AIA Document G714

questions.explanation: ConsensusDocs 203 is the standard form for the interim directive, which orders work before the time or price adjustment is agreed. ConsensusDocs 202 is the change order form, ConsensusDocs 200 is the general conditions, DBIA 500D5 is the design-build work change directive form, DBIA 500D2 the design-build change order, and AIA G714 the AIA construction change directive.

questions.question: A contractor on a ConsensusDocs 200 project refuses to proceed with directed work because it has not countersigned the interim directive. Whose signature is required on that directive?

options.A: The owner and the contractor
options.B: The owner, contractor, and A/E
options.C: The owner, then the contractor on acceptance
options.D: The owner only, as the directing party
options.E: The owner and the A/E
options.F: The contractor only, as the performing party

questions.explanation: Only the owner is required to sign a ConsensusDocs interim directive, so the contractor's missing signature does not make it invalid. The owner-and-contractor pairing describes the ConsensusDocs change order, a design-builder signature on acceptance describes the DBIA work change directive, and neither the A/E nor the contractor alone signs an interim directive.

questions.question: A specifier searches ConsensusDocs 200 for the procedure and form for a written amendment. What will the specifier find?

options.A: A dedicated changes article with its own standard amendment form
options.B: A brief mention in the order-of-precedence provisions, with no standard form
options.C: A required attachment to the agreement, completed at contract execution
options.D: A provision in the dispute resolution article, used to record mediation results
options.E: A standard form, ConsensusDocs 203, used for all written amendments
options.F: A definition in the changes article, with ConsensusDocs 202 as its form

questions.explanation: ConsensusDocs 200 does not treat the written amendment as a formal change document; it is mentioned only near the end, where the order of precedence is set out, listed alongside change orders, and ConsensusDocs has no standard form for it. ConsensusDocs 203 is the interim directive and 202 the change order, and no dedicated article, agreement attachment, or dispute-resolution role exists for it.

questions.question: A specifier's draft Division 01 section for a design-build project governed by DBIA Document No. 535 lists the modification methods as change order, interim directive, and field order. What correction is needed?

options.A: Replace interim directive with work change directive, and field order with minor changes
options.B: Replace interim directive with construction change directive, and field order with minor changes
options.C: Replace field order with written amendment, and keep interim directive as drafted
options.D: Replace interim directive with work change directive, and keep field order as drafted
options.E: Replace field order with minor changes, and keep interim directive as drafted
options.F: Replace interim directive with work change directive, and field order with written interpretation

questions.explanation: DBIA Document No. 535 changes the contract documents three ways: by change order, by work change directive, and by minor changes. The interim directive and written amendment are ConsensusDocs terms, field orders and written interpretations are EJCDC terms, and the construction change directive is an AIA term, so each wrong correction leaves at least one term from another document family in place.

questions.question: On a design-build project using DBIA documents, the design-builder's architect asks to sign each change order as the recommending party, as on design-bid-build work. Which form and signatories does industry guidance identify for the DBIA change order?

options.A: DBIA 500D5, signed by the owner alone
options.B: DBIA 500D2, signed by the owner, design-builder, and A/E
options.C: DBIA 500D2, signed by the owner and the design-builder
options.D: DBIA 535, signed by the owner and the design-builder
options.E: DBIA 500D2, signed by the design-builder and its A/E
options.F: AIA G701, signed by the owner, design-builder, and A/E

questions.explanation: The DBIA change order is Document No. 500D2, the Design-Build Change Order Form, and it requires only the owner's and the design-builder's signatures. Unlike AIA and EJCDC change orders, it calls for no separate A/E signature as a recommending party. DBIA 500D5 is the work change directive form, DBIA 535 the general conditions, and G701 the AIA change order form.

questions.question: An owner on a DBIA design-build project issues a work change directive for added paving. Which signatures does the DBIA work change directive require?

options.A: The owner only, as for the EJCDC directive
options.B: The owner, and the design-builder upon acceptance
options.C: The owner and the design-builder's A/E
options.D: The design-builder only, with written notice to the owner
options.E: The owner and the architect, as for the AIA directive
options.F: The design-builder first, then the owner once the price is agreed

questions.explanation: The DBIA work change directive is prepared and signed by the owner and then signed by the design-builder upon acceptance. An owner-only signature describes the EJCDC directive and the ConsensusDocs interim directive, the owner and architect sign the AIA construction change directive, and written notice to the owner by the design-builder describes the DBIA minor change procedure. Agreement on price comes later, in a change order.

questions.question: After a DBIA work change directive is issued for added site lighting, the owner and design-builder disagree on the cost. What do the DBIA general conditions require next?

options.A: The owner sets the final amount by issuing a second work change directive
options.B: The design-builder records the cost as a minor change with written notice
options.C: The parties negotiate in good faith and record the result in a change order
options.D: The parties execute a written amendment listed in the order of precedence
options.E: The A/E determines the adjustment from reasonable costs and savings
options.F: The design-builder stops the added work until a change order is signed

questions.explanation: DBIA general conditions require the owner and design-builder to negotiate in good faith after a work change directive, and the agreed cost and time are recorded in a written change order. The owner cannot fix the amount with another directive, a priced change is not a minor change, and the written amendment is a ConsensusDocs concept. Having the A/E set the amount from reasonable expenditures is the AIA rule, and a directive exists so the work goes ahead before price is agreed.

questions.question: An owner's project manager pulls DBIA Document No. 500D2 to direct the design-builder to start added work before the price is settled. What does industry guidance indicate about this choice?

options.A: 500D2 is the change order form; the directive belongs on DBIA 500D5
options.B: 500D2 is correct, but the A/E must also sign it as recommending party
options.C: DBIA has no directive form, so a letter from the owner must be used
options.D: The directive belongs on DBIA 535, the general conditions document
options.E: The directive belongs on ConsensusDocs 203, the interim directive form
options.F: The directive belongs on AIA G714, the construction change directive form

questions.explanation: DBIA 500D2 is the Design-Build Change Order Form, which records agreed changes. To direct a change before price and time are agreed, DBIA provides 500D5, the Design-Build Work Change Directive Form. DBIA does publish a directive form, its change order needs no A/E signature, DBIA 535 is the general conditions, and ConsensusDocs 203 and AIA G714 are the directive forms of other document families.

questions.question: A design-builder working under DBIA general conditions wants to adjust a pipe hanger layout. The adjustment is consistent with the documents' intent and will not materially or adversely affect design, quality, performance, or workmanship. What procedure applies?

options.A: The owner and design-builder must execute a change order on DBIA 500D2
options.B: The owner must issue a work change directive before the work proceeds
options.C: The A/E must issue a written order, binding on both owner and design-builder
options.D: The design-builder may proceed but must promptly inform the owner in writing
options.E: The engineer must issue a field order, without the owner's signature
options.F: The owner and design-builder must sign a written amendment first

questions.explanation: DBIA general conditions let the design-builder make minor changes that keep to the documents' intent and do not materially or adversely affect design, quality, performance, or workmanship, as long as it promptly informs the owner in writing. No change order or work change directive is needed. A written order by the A/E is the AIA approach, the engineer's field order is the EJCDC approach, and the written amendment belongs to ConsensusDocs.

questions.question: A specifier is engaged on a federal project whose general conditions were written by the owner rather than taken from AIA, EJCDC, ConsensusDocs, or DBIA. What is the best approach to the Division 01 modification procedures?

options.A: Default to AIA modification forms, since they are the most widely recognized
options.B: Confirm the owner's own modification methods, supporting documents, and forms
options.C: Use EJCDC methods, since they were developed for public works projects
options.D: Adapt the ConsensusDocs 200 methods, since they reflect industry consensus
options.E: Use the A/E's office master forms, since they suit any owner
options.F: Write new modification procedures in Division 01 to replace the owner's

questions.explanation: Entities such as GSA, DOD, and state public works agencies write their own general conditions. When a standard contract document is not used, the specifier must confirm the owner's modification method, procedures, supporting documents, and forms. Defaulting to AIA, EJCDC, or ConsensusDocs procedures or to office forms ignores what the owner's documents require, and Division 01 expands on the general conditions rather than replacing them.

questions.question: A state public works agency uses its own non-standard general conditions. With the bid date approaching and the documents still being finalized, the A/E needs to issue revisions. What does industry guidance emphasize for this situation?

options.A: Check for special requirements on modifications made before final bidding
options.B: Hold all revisions until after award and process them by change order
options.C: Issue revisions on standard AIA forms, since pre-bid procedures are uniform
options.D: Issue revisions as field orders, since no contract yet exists to modify
options.E: Issue revisions as change orders, since public agencies require them
options.F: Issue revisions as minor changes, since no price has been set yet

questions.explanation: For non-standard contract documents, the specifier should watch for any special requirements that apply to modifications made before final bidding or contract negotiation. Holding revisions until after award, assuming AIA pre-bid procedures apply, or using field orders before a contract exists all skip that check. Change orders and minor changes modify a contract already in place, so neither fits a revision issued before bids.

questions.question: Which public project most clearly falls within the 'other' category of contract modification methods, where the specifier must confirm the applicable method, procedures, and forms?

options.A: A county courthouse using AIA A201 general conditions
options.B: A municipal water plant using EJCDC C-700 general conditions
options.C: A state university lab using ConsensusDocs 200 general conditions
options.D: A military base using Department of Defense general conditions
options.E: A design-build fire station using DBIA 535 general conditions
options.F: A public school using AIA A201 with supplementary conditions

questions.explanation: The 'other' category covers general conditions written by entities such as GSA, DOD, and state or other public works agencies, where no standard contract document is used. A public owner that adopts AIA A201, EJCDC C-700, ConsensusDocs 200, or DBIA 535, even with supplementary conditions added, is still using a standard document, so that family's modification methods apply. The deciding factor is the document, not whether the owner is public.

questions.question: An architect issues AIA G709 to price a revised storefront layout. The contractor immediately stops storefront installation, claiming the request suspends that work. How should the architect respond?

options.A: The request is informational only and neither orders the change nor stops the work
options.B: The request suspends affected work until the change order is signed
options.C: The request acts as a construction change directive once the contractor receives it
options.D: The request obligates the contractor to begin the proposed change without delay
options.E: The request becomes a change order once the contractor returns a price
options.F: The request is a minor change the architect may order without the owner

questions.explanation: A change order proposal request, such as AIA G709, is for information only; it does not instruct the contractor to carry out the proposed changes or to stop work in progress. It only asks for the contractor's proposed adjustment of contract sum, time, or both. A returned price is not a change order, which needs the owner's signature, and a minor change involves no price adjustment at all.

questions.question: An architect with broad contract-administration duties signs a change order and tells the contractor the change is now authorized, though the owner has not yet signed. Which principle does industry guidance state that applies across AIA, EJCDC, ConsensusDocs, and DBIA?

options.A: The A/E's signature authorizes the change; the owner's confirms funding
options.B: The contractor's signature authorizes it once the A/E has recommended it
options.C: Authority to execute a change order rests with the owner alone
options.D: Either the owner or the A/E may execute it once both have been notified
options.E: The A/E and contractor may execute it if the cost is below a set limit
options.F: The initial decision maker may execute it when the parties disagree

questions.explanation: AIA, EJCDC, ConsensusDocs, and DBIA all treat it as an axiom that only the owner has authority to execute, or authorize, a change order. The A/E signs to recommend the change and the contractor signs to accept it; neither signature authorizes it, and no cost threshold changes that. The initial decision maker rules on claims and does not execute change orders.

questions.question: An A/E wants to obtain the contractor's proposed adjustment in contract sum and time for a possible revision, without directing any work. Which AIA document does industry guidance cite for initiating this?

options.A: AIA Document G701, Change Order
options.B: AIA Document G714, Construction Change Directive
options.C: AIA Document G710, Architect's Supplemental Instructions
options.D: AIA Document G709, Work Changes Proposal Request
options.E: AIA Document G702, Application and Certificate for Payment
options.F: AIA Document G705, List of Subcontractors

questions.explanation: The A/E can start a change order proposal request with AIA Document G709, Work Changes Proposal Request, which describes the proposed change and asks for a proposed adjustment without directing work. G701 records an agreed change, G714 directs work before agreement, and G710 issues supplemental instructions rather than requesting pricing. G702 is the contractor's payment application and G705 lists subcontractors.

questions.question: An owner wants a lab equipment vendor to furnish fume hoods and also build them into the walls and ductwork on site. How should the vendor's work be contracted?

options.A: Under a purchasing contract with the owner, listing installation as a special service
options.B: Under a subcontract agreement between the vendor and the construction contractor
options.C: Under a purchasing contract with the owner, later assigned to the A/E for administration
options.D: Under a purchasing contract, with the construction contractor coordinating the vendor's site work
options.E: Under an owner-furnished, contractor-installed arrangement in Division 01
options.F: Under a purchase order, with the vendor's crews acting as the owner's forces

questions.explanation: When the goods contractor must take part in actual construction, the goods are furnished and installed under a subcontract between the goods contractor and the construction contractor, not under a purchasing contract. Purchasing contracts involve little or no on-site work, and special services such as technical assistance stop short of building items into the work. An owner-furnished, contractor-installed arrangement leaves the installing to the contractor, not the vendor.

questions.question: A specifier preparing purchasing documents for an owner's FF&E package is asked why the documents use the term goods. The term keeps the specifications consistent with which source of terminology?

options.A: The Uniform Commercial Code
options.B: The Federal Acquisition Regulation
options.C: The MasterFormat numbering system
options.D: The construction contract's general conditions
options.E: The International Building Code
options.F: The OmniClass classification tables

questions.explanation: Purchasing specifications use the term goods because the Uniform Commercial Code, which governs most purchasing contracts, uses the same term, so the specifications stay consistent with the governing law. The FAR, MasterFormat, OmniClass, the building code, and construction general conditions are not where this terminology comes from.

questions.question: A university's facilities department buys the same light fixtures from fourteen vendors to maximize competition, but struggles with inconsistent quality. Under traditional management theory, which action is recommended?

options.A: Split orders evenly among the vendors to spread supply risk
options.B: Transfer fixture purchasing to the construction contractor on each job
options.C: Rebid every order among all fourteen vendors on a short-term basis
options.D: Reduce the number of suppliers used for the same or similar products
options.E: Make only short-term commitments to each vendor to keep prices low
options.F: Add vendors so that wider competition offsets the quality problems

questions.explanation: Traditional management theory holds that keeping a large pool of suppliers for the same or similar products usually costs more to manage than extensive competition saves, and it makes quality and consistent performance harder to control. Reducing the number of suppliers is the recommended action. Splitting orders evenly, rebidding short-term, or adding vendors keeps the large supplier base, and shifting purchasing to contractors ignores the problem.

questions.question: An owner has negotiated long-term contracts with a few preferred suppliers to gain cost savings. Under the traditional management theory industry guidance describes, what accompanies these large purchase commitments?

options.A: Reduced oversight, since long-term partners are trusted to self-manage
options.B: Periodic rebidding of each order to a broad pool of competing suppliers
options.C: More rigorous tracking of their timelines and quality
options.D: Fewer quality requirements, offset by the lower negotiated prices
options.E: Shorter commitments so that weak suppliers can be dropped quickly
options.F: Quality control handed over to the construction contractor on each job

questions.explanation: Under the traditional management theory, the large commitments made to a few preferred suppliers come with more rigorous and detailed tracking of their timelines and quality, along with higher quality and performance requirements. Relaxing oversight, returning to broad rebidding, or lowering quality requirements contradicts that approach, short-term commitments are what the long-term contracts replace, and the tracking stays with the buyer.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects how supply chain management concepts, as industry guidance describes them, view the acquisition function?

options.A: As a support function that responds to requisitions as they arrive
options.B: As a transactional function judged mainly by the unit prices it manages to obtain
options.C: As one part of a larger system linking customer needs and supplier capabilities
options.D: As an independent unit that operates apart from the organization's other processes
options.E: As a clerical function that places orders once others choose the goods
options.F: As a function judged mainly by how quickly it issues purchase orders

questions.explanation: Supply chain management concepts hold that acquisition does not work in a reactive vacuum: it is one component of a broader management system that adds value and profit by bringing customer needs and supplier capabilities together with the organization's own value-added processes. Responding to requisitions as they arrive is the reactive view it rejects, and judging acquisition by price, speed, or clerical output, or isolating it, misses the system view.

questions.question: A purchasing agent has formally notified a vendor that it is the successful bidder for an equipment package. The vendor asks whether a legally binding agreement now exists. Under typical procurement steps, what is the correct answer?

options.A: Yes; the agreement becomes legally binding when the award is made
options.B: No; it is formed at contract execution, the step after award
options.C: Yes; the agreement became legally binding when the bids were opened
options.D: No; the agreement becomes binding only when the goods are delivered
options.E: No; it is formed when the notice to proceed is issued
options.F: Yes; for goods, award and contract execution are a single step

questions.explanation: In the typical procurement steps, Award (step 4) is when the buyer formally awards the contract, and Execution of Contract (step 5) is when the buyer enters a legally binding agreement with the goods contractor. Award and execution are separate steps, and bid opening, delivery, and a notice to proceed are not the points where the binding agreement is formed.

questions.question: During the bid/proposal evaluation step of a goods procurement, the buyer tabulates the submissions. What does the buyer review them for?

options.A: Responsiveness and responsibility
options.B: Lowest price and earliest delivery
options.C: Completeness and lowest cost
options.D: Qualifications and references
options.E: Lead time and warranty terms
options.F: Installation methods and workmanship

questions.explanation: In the bid/proposal evaluation step, the buyer tabulates all bids or proposals and reviews them for responsiveness and responsibility. Price, delivery, lead time, warranty terms, completeness, and references may matter in a given procurement, but they are not the review criteria named for this step, and installation methods hardly apply to a goods contractor who does little or no on-site work.

questions.question: In the bidding or accepting-proposals step, bidders receive the complete set of procurement documents. Which item does industry guidance list among the contents of that project manual?

options.A: The bid tabulation from prior procurements
options.B: The notice of award
options.C: The buyer's evaluation scoring sheets
options.D: Certifications and representations
options.E: The goods contractor's delivery receipts
options.F: The bidders' financial statements

questions.explanation: The project manual issued for the bidding step includes certifications and representations, alongside the solicitation, instructions, bid forms, general provisions, contract conditions, a copy of the contract, drawings, and specifications. Bid tabulation and evaluation belong to the later evaluation step, the notice of award follows evaluation, delivery receipts come after execution, and financial statements come from bidders rather than being issued to them.

questions.question: A county's purchasing office publishes a Notice to Bidders for library shelving. In typical procurement steps, which step does this document represent?

options.A: Step 4, Award
options.B: Step 2, Bidding or Accepting Proposals
options.C: Step 1, Solicitation
options.D: Step 3, Bid/Proposal Evaluation
options.E: Step 5, Execution of Contract
options.F: Step 6, Delivery of Goods

questions.explanation: The first typical procurement step is Solicitation, Request for Bids, or Request for Proposals, also known as the Advertisement or Notice to Bidders. Bidding, evaluation, award, and contract execution follow as steps 2 through 5, and delivery is not one of the five steps, so a published notice inviting bids belongs to step 1.

questions.question: An owner pre-purchases lobby light fixtures and wants them to satisfy a cash allowance already carried in the contractor's agreement. Which mechanism does industry guidance identify for this use of purchasing?

options.A: Assigning the purchasing contract to the construction contractor
options.B: Issuing a field order directing the contractor to accept the owner's fixtures
options.C: Converting the allowance to a unit price based on the fixture count
options.D: Assigning the purchasing contract to the A/E for administration
options.E: Retaining the fixtures for the owner's own use and installation
options.F: Paying the goods contractor out of the construction contract's retainage

questions.explanation: One listed use of purchasing is acquiring goods to fulfill cash allowances in a construction contract by assigning the purchasing contract to the construction contractor. A field order cannot involve price, so it cannot settle an allowance; converting to a unit price does not fulfill the allowance; assignment to the A/E is not the mechanism; and retention for the owner's own use is a separate disposition that leaves the allowance unused.

questions.question: An owner is buying long-lead switchgear through its own purchasing contract, and the construction contractor will install it. Late delivery could expose the owner to delay claims from the construction contractor. What does industry guidance suggest considering in the purchasing documents?

options.A: Liquidated damages in the construction contract, payable by the goods contractor
options.B: Liquidated damages in the purchasing contract that reflect that claim exposure
options.C: A waiver of delay claims by the construction contractor in the purchasing contract
options.D: Transfer of delivery responsibility to the A/E under its design contract
options.E: A cash allowance in the construction contract to absorb delay costs
options.F: A performance bond from the construction contractor covering delivery

questions.explanation: When the owner buys goods for installation by the construction contractor, the owner becomes responsible for the time of delivery and may be liable to that contractor for late or incomplete delivery, so this exposure should be considered when setting liquidated damages in the purchasing contract. Damages or an allowance in the construction contract, a waiver, the installer's bond, or shifting delivery to the A/E do not make the supplier answer for late delivery.

questions.question: Commercial kitchen equipment will be bought under a purchasing contract and set in place by the construction contractor. Which task can properly be assigned to the goods contractor in the purchasing documents?

options.A: Setting and connecting the equipment as the installer of record
options.B: Building the equipment's concrete pads and wall blocking on site
options.C: Field checking and testing the equipment after others install it
options.D: Erecting the exhaust hood and ductwork during construction
options.E: Anchoring the equipment and making its final utility connections
options.F: Cutting and patching finishes where the equipment is set

questions.explanation: Purchasing documents may include special services such as field checking or testing goods after installation by others, start-up, and training, but these activities stop short of on-site construction or installation by the goods contractor. Setting equipment as installer, building pads and blocking, erecting hoods and ductwork, anchoring, utility connections, and cutting and patching are all construction activities.

questions.question: Comparing a purchasing project manual with a construction project manual, a specifier finds most differences are readily apparent. In which documents do the more subtle differences occur?

options.A: The solicitation and procurement instructions
options.B: The conditions of the contract
options.C: The bid or proposal forms
options.D: Division 01—General Requirements
options.E: The agreement between owner and goods contractor
options.F: The technical specification sections

questions.explanation: The solicitation, procurement instructions, bid forms, agreement, contract conditions, and Division 01 used for purchasing all differ from their construction counterparts. Most of those differences are obvious; the subtler ones occur in the conditions of the contract. Technical sections are chosen by project requirements, just as they are for construction.
questions.source: purchasing contract and construction contract differences

questions.question: To save time, a specifier proposes reusing the Division 01 sections from a recent construction project manual, unchanged, in a purchasing project manual for laboratory equipment. What does industry guidance indicate?

options.A: Acceptable, because Division 01 is the same for purchasing and construction
options.B: Unacceptable, because purchasing project manuals do not include Division 01
options.C: Acceptable, because only the conditions of the contract differ between the two
options.D: Unacceptable, because Division 01 for purchasing differs from construction
options.E: Acceptable, if the goods contractor will also install the equipment
options.F: Acceptable, if the supplementary conditions note the differences

questions.explanation: The Division 01 General Requirements used for purchasing contracts differ from those used for construction, along with the solicitation, forms, agreement, and conditions. Reusing construction Division 01 unchanged ignores those differences, and a note in the conditions does not fix it. Division 01 is still part of a purchasing project manual, and a goods contractor that installs would need a subcontract rather than a purchasing contract.
questions.source: purchasing contract and construction contract differences

questions.question: A school district requires its contractor to buy classroom casework through the district's established purchase contract. The casework arrives damaged, and the contractor argues it bears no responsibility because the district chose the source. Is the contractor correct?

options.A: Yes; buying through the owner's contract relieves the contractor of product responsibility
options.B: No; the contractor keeps the same responsibilities as for products from other sources
options.C: Yes; responsibility rests with the supplier alone under the owner's contract
options.D: No; responsibility is split equally, as with owner-furnished products
options.E: No; but the district must replace damaged casework at its own cost
options.F: Yes; casework bought this way becomes an owner-furnished product

questions.explanation: When a contractor buys products through the owner's established purchase contract, the contractor is not relieved of the responsibilities it would have for products bought through other sources. The owner's choice of source does not shift product responsibility to the owner or the supplier, no equal split is described, and the casework does not become owner-furnished: the contractor still purchases and installs it.

questions.question: A project includes contractor-furnished, owner-installed shelving and owner-furnished, owner-installed kitchen appliances needing utility rough-ins. Which section does industry guidance identify for listing these items and the parties' responsibilities?

options.A: Section 01 10 00
options.B: Section 01 64 00
options.C: Section 01 33 00
options.D: Section 01 60 00
options.E: Section 01 14 00
options.F: Section 01 31 00

questions.explanation: Section 01 10 00 (Summary) can list contractor-furnished, owner-installed and owner-furnished, owner-installed products and state each party's responsibilities for them. Section 01 64 00 (Owner-Furnished Products) is offered only as an alternative for owner-furnished, contractor-installed products, while 01 14 00 (Work Restrictions), 01 31 00 (Project Management and Coordination), 01 33 00 (Submittal Procedures), and 01 60 00 (Product Requirements) do not serve this purpose.

questions.question: A specifier is adapting an owner's standard general-conditions definitions article for a purchasing contract for factory-built switchgear. Which group of definitions is most likely to be inapplicable and should be avoided in the purchasing documents?

options.A: Definitions tied to submittals, shop drawings, and product data
options.B: Definitions tied to on-site construction or installation activities
options.C: Definitions tied to payment, delivery, and final acceptance of goods
options.D: Definitions tied to referenced ASTM, ANSI, ASME, or NEMA standards
options.E: Definitions tied to warranties and guarantees for the goods
options.F: Definitions tied to the parties: owner, buyer, and seller

questions.explanation: Definitions written for construction documents, especially those about on-site construction or installation work, often do not fit a purchasing contract, and the ones that do not apply must be left out. Submittals, payment and acceptance, warranties, the parties, and reference standards all remain relevant to a goods purchase, so their definitions still have a place in the purchasing documents.

questions.question: An owner has a purchasing contract for air-handling units and a separate construction contract under which another contractor installs them. Both project manuals define the term "Provide." How should the two definitions relate?

options.A: They must be identical word for word, so one text is copied into both manuals.
options.B: Only the construction contract may define it; the purchasing manual omits it.
options.C: Each contract stands alone, so the definitions need no coordination at all.
options.D: They may differ slightly between the documents but must not conflict.
options.E: The construction definition governs both, by the order of precedence.
options.F: The purchasing definition governs, since the goods are bought first.

questions.explanation: The same term may be defined in both contracts' documents with slight differences, and avoiding conflict between those definitions is treated as imperative. Requiring identical text overstates the rule, dropping the term from one manual or skipping coordination ignores the two contracts running at once, and neither contract's definition is set up to override the other: the point is that they must not conflict.

questions.question: An owner's attorney believes a purchasing contract for kitchen equipment must be closed out before any contract to install that equipment can take effect. Which response reflects industry guidance?

options.A: Both contracts may be in force at the same time for the same products.
options.B: Installation must instead be folded into the purchasing contract itself.
options.C: Installation may be contracted only after title transfers at the plant.
options.D: Installation may be contracted only after final payment for the goods.
options.E: The purchasing contract must first be assigned to the installer.
options.F: Installation may be contracted only before the goods are ordered.

questions.explanation: A purchasing contract and a construction contract that includes installing the purchased goods can both be in place at the same time for the same products, which is why their definitions must not conflict. Nothing requires closeout, title transfer, final payment, or a particular ordering sequence first, and assignment to the construction contractor is one disposition option, not a precondition.

questions.question: An owner is purchasing custom-fabricated sunshade assemblies that will be delivered to the site for installation by others. Which bond should usually be required of the goods contractor, and what does it protect against?

options.A: A payment bond, protecting against unpaid claims of the goods contractor's suppliers
options.B: A bid bond, protecting against refusal to sign the purchasing contract after award
options.C: A performance bond, protecting against failure to manufacture, supply, or deliver
options.D: A maintenance bond, protecting against defects found after the goods are installed
options.E: A performance bond from the installer, covering the goods' delivery
options.F: No bond, since the Uniform Commercial Code already protects the owner

questions.explanation: A performance bond should usually be required of the goods contractor, with the decision shaped by what the goods are and how they will be disposed of, because it gives the owner recourse if the goods contractor fails to manufacture, supply, or deliver them. Payment, bid, and maintenance bonds address other risks, a bond from the installer answers for the installer's own work, and the recommendation stands even though the UCC governs most purchasing contracts.

questions.question: Under a purchasing contract, the owner has paid for the first lot of transformers, which are finished but still stored at the goods contractor's plant awaiting shipment. Which insurance stipulation does industry guidance support?

options.A: Property insurance protecting the owner's interest in the paid, undelivered goods
options.B: General liability limits matching those required of every contractor working on site
options.C: Workers' compensation limits for the plant employees who fabricate the goods
options.D: Builder's risk insurance on the goods carried by the installing contractor
options.E: Automobile liability for the trucks that will ship the goods
options.F: Professional liability covering the goods contractor's shop drawings

questions.explanation: Insurance stipulations for work at the goods contractor's plant are generally inappropriate: the owner does not control that work, and liability coverage belongs to the goods contractor's normal business. The exception is property insurance, required when the owner asks for it, covering the owner's interest in goods it has paid for but not yet received. Liability, workers' compensation, automobile, and professional coverages for plant work are not stipulated, and goods still at the plant are not the installer's to insure.

questions.question: A purchasing contract requires the goods contractor to deliver rooftop units to the project site, where the construction contractor receives them. Which allocation of insurance responsibility is typical?

options.A: Goods contractor insures in transit and until installation is complete
options.B: Construction contractor insures in transit; owner insures after receipt
options.C: Goods contractor insures in transit; owner insures after delivery
options.D: Owner insures in transit; goods contractor insures until placed in service
options.E: Owner insures in transit; construction contractor insures after receipt
options.F: Construction contractor insures from shipment through final completion

questions.explanation: When the goods contractor delivers to a designated location, industry guidance calls for the goods contractor to carry transit insurance during shipment, particularly if payment has already been made. Receipt at the delivery point generally shifts responsibility, and insurance after delivery usually falls to the owner, so extending the goods contractor's coverage to installation or service, or assigning transit coverage to someone else, is inconsistent with recommended practice.

questions.question: A purchasing contract for a packaged chiller plant requires the manufacturer's field technicians to supervise start-up and train the owner's operators on site. Which coverages should the documents require of the goods contractor during these activities?

options.A: Property, transit, and general liability insurance
options.B: Workers' compensation, general liability, and automobile liability
options.C: Builder's risk, workers' compensation, and professional liability
options.D: Transit, automobile liability, and product warranty coverage
options.E: Workers' compensation, property, and professional liability
options.F: General liability, transit, and builder's risk insurance

questions.explanation: For on-site work such as start-up assistance and owner training, industry guidance notes that the goods contractor's insurable exposure, though smaller than under a construction contract, still exists, so liability coverage similar to a construction contract should be required. Industry guidance names workers' compensation, general liability, and automobile liability; property and transit insurance protect the goods rather than on-site exposure, and builder's risk and professional liability are not in its list.

questions.question: A specifier is drafting purchasing documents for custom millwork panels. Which condition would justify requiring the goods contractor to visit the site?

options.A: The need to obtain a construction permit for installing the panels
options.B: The need to set up temporary storage facilities at the site
options.C: The need to coordinate with the jobsite safety program
options.D: The chance that existing field conditions affect panel production
options.E: The need to provide hoisting equipment for setting the panels
options.F: The need to obtain a business license for work at the site

questions.explanation: The goods contractor should be required to visit the site or investigate conditions there only when field measurements are needed, technical assistance is specified, or existing field conditions may affect production of the goods. Permits, licenses, construction equipment, temporary facilities, and safety are the construction contractor's responsibility, so none of them justifies a site-visit requirement for the goods contractor.

questions.question: When does industry guidance suggest a purchasing contract might need stipulations governing subcontractor relationships?

options.A: When the goods are exceptionally expensive or complicated
options.B: When the goods are delivered to a designated location
options.C: When the owner makes progress payments during fabrication
options.D: When the goods contractor provides on-site start-up services
options.E: When the goods require transit insurance during shipment
options.F: When the goods are acquired from a single source

questions.explanation: Subcontractors are usually not involved in a purchasing contract unless the goods are exceptionally expensive or complicated, so most purchasing documents leave out subcontractor provisions. Delivery location, transit insurance, progress payments, single-source acquisition, and on-site start-up shape the insurance, payment, and acceptance provisions instead of creating a need for subcontractor stipulations.

questions.question: Purchasing documents are being prepared for standard low-voltage switchboards. Which requirement does industry guidance consider appropriate to stipulate for the goods contractor?

options.A: Compliance with all laws regulating the plant's manufacturing processes
options.B: Safety and protection provisions governing fabrication at the plant
options.C: Compliance with applicable industry standards, such as those of NEMA
options.D: Owner supervision of fabrication to verify workmanship at the plant
options.E: Compliance with the construction permits issued for the project site
options.F: Temporary facilities and protection for the goods at the site

questions.explanation: Unless unique codes or laws govern, as with nuclear components, pressure vessels, or fire protection systems, there should be no need to stipulate compliance with manufacturing-process laws or safety and protection provisions, because fabrication is the goods contractor's own business responsibility. Requiring compliance with applicable standards such as ASTM, ANSI, ASME, or NEMA is appropriate. Owner supervision at the plant is not part of the approach, and permits and temporary facilities belong to the construction contractor.

questions.question: An A/E is preparing the construction documents under which owner-purchased emergency generators will be installed by the electrical contractor. What must the A/E do regarding the purchasing provisions?

options.A: Leave receipt and start-up issues for the two parties to resolve in the field
options.B: Coordinate both contracts so no item is omitted or duplicated between them
options.C: Assign receipt, start-up, and training to the goods contractor by default
options.D: Repeat every purchasing provision in the construction contract so nothing is missed
options.E: Defer the purchasing provisions to the owner's purchasing agent
options.F: Let installers rely on the goods contractor's literature for start-up

questions.explanation: An A/E who prepares the documents for installing purchased goods must coordinate the construction contract's purchasing provisions, so that the two contracts fit together and nothing pertinent is left out or covered twice. Receipt and handling, utility connections, start-up, and owner training must be stated clearly. Leaving them to the field, to one party by default, to the purchasing agent, or to product literature skips that coordination, and repeating every provision creates the duplication to avoid.

questions.question: The A/E's responsibilities for a purchasing contract are determined by which factors, and who must thoroughly understand them?

options.A: UCC Article 2 and state law; the goods contractor and the A/E
options.B: The A/E's standard of care; the owner and the construction contractor
options.C: The goods contractor's scope; the owner and the goods contractor
options.D: Project requirements and the owner's desires; the owner and the A/E
options.E: The construction schedule; the owner and the installing contractor
options.F: The A/E's fee; the A/E and its consultants

questions.explanation: The A/E's responsibilities for a purchasing contract vary with the project requirements and what the owner wants, and both the owner and the A/E must carefully establish and fully understand them. The wrong answers substitute the UCC, a standard of care, the goods contractor's scope, the schedule, or the fee, and they name parties other than the owner and the A/E as the ones who must understand the arrangement.

questions.question: Midway through fabrication under a purchasing contract, the owner asks the A/E to travel to the goods contractor's plant to witness shop tests. Neither the A/E agreement nor the purchasing contract addresses this. Which course of action does industry guidance indicate should have been followed?

options.A: Settle with the owner beforehand whether the A/E will attend shop tests
options.B: Treat shop-test witnessing as part of basic contract administration
options.C: Assume the duty applies, since the A/E approved the shop drawings
options.D: Decide on witnessing once fabrication starts and test dates are known
options.E: Have the goods contractor witness its own tests and certify the results
options.F: Send the construction contractor to witness the tests for the A/E

questions.explanation: Whether the A/E must visit the goods contractor's plant, witness shop tests, or check the goods at delivery is not automatic. Because these items materially affect both the purchasing contract and the A/E's professional services agreement, they must be settled with the owner in advance. Treating witnessing as a basic service, inferring the duty from shop drawing approval, handing it to others, or deciding once fabrication starts all skip that up-front clarification.

questions.question: A specifier is editing the submittal procedures for a purchasing contract for owner-furnished laboratory casework that a separate contractor will install. How should the quantity of approved submittals compare with a typical construction contract?

options.A: Fewer copies, since the goods contractor performs no installation
options.B: The same number, with the goods contractor retaining the records
options.C: More copies than usual, for records and for transmittal to end users
options.D: Electronic copies only, distributed later by the construction contractor
options.E: One record copy, kept by the owner's purchasing agent
options.F: No approved copies, since O&M manuals take their place

questions.explanation: Under a purchasing contract, more approved submittals than usual may be collected, both for the records and to pass along to the construction contractor or other users of the purchased goods. Reducing the quantity, matching it, keeping a single record copy, or relying on other documents ignores the installer's need for the information, and shifting distribution to the construction contractor has no basis in recommended practice.
questions.source: shop drawings, product data, and samples

questions.question: An owner purchased elevator machinery early, and the A/E has already approved the goods contractor's shop drawings. The construction contract for installing the machinery has not yet been bid. What may be advantageous?

options.A: Withholding the approved drawings until the installer is under contract
options.B: Making the approved drawings available to bidders on the installation work
options.C: Returning the approved drawings to the goods contractor until delivery
options.D: Reissuing the drawings for re-approval once the installer is selected
options.E: Asking installation bidders to approve the drawings with their bids
options.F: Keeping the approved drawings only in the owner's purchasing file

questions.explanation: It may be advantageous to make approved purchasing-contract submittals available during solicitation for the construction contract, so installation bidders can price the work with the actual equipment information. Withholding the drawings, returning them to the goods contractor, keeping them in a purchasing file, or sending them back through approval keeps that information from bidders, and approving submittals is the A/E's job, not the bidders'.
questions.source: shop drawings, product data, and samples

questions.question: How does industry guidance characterize submittal requirements for shop drawings and product data in a purchasing contract?

options.A: Generally omitted, since the goods are fabricated away from the site
options.B: Reviewed and approved by the installing construction contractor
options.C: Replaced by the implied warranties that the UCC attaches to sales
options.D: Similar to construction contracts, with review managed by the A/E
options.E: Reviewed and approved by the owner's purchasing agent
options.F: Left to the goods contractor's own quality control program

questions.explanation: Shop drawing and product data stipulations in purchasing contracts resemble those in construction contracts, and the A/E typically manages submittal review and approval. Off-site fabrication does not eliminate submittals, the installer is not the reviewing party, UCC warranties do not substitute for submittal requirements, and neither a purchasing agent nor the goods contractor's own quality control takes the A/E's place.
questions.source: shop drawings, product data, and samples

questions.question: Why might operation and maintenance manuals be of critical importance under a purchasing contract?

options.A: The goods contractor may have little direct contact with the eventual installer
options.B: The UCC makes delivery of manuals a condition of transferring clear title
options.C: Purchasing contracts generally exclude the A/E from reviewing submittals
options.D: The goods contractor usually performs installation and start-up on site
options.E: Purchased goods usually come with no manufacturer warranty
options.F: The A/E prepares the O&M manuals under a purchasing contract

questions.explanation: Because the goods contractor and the eventual installer or erector may have little direct contact, the information delivered through O&M manuals can be critical. The UCC title warranty has nothing to do with manuals, the A/E typically does manage purchasing submittals, on-site installation by the goods contractor is the exception, purchased goods still carry warranties, and compiling O&M data is a service of the goods contractor, not the A/E.
