questions.question: During a project manual review, a team member proposes deleting the O&M manual requirement from a purchasing contract for a packaged boiler, arguing that manuals matter mainly in traditional construction contracts. Which response is consistent with industry guidance?

options.A: Agree; manuals belong only in the contract of whoever installs the boiler
options.B: Agree; manuals are needed under purchasing only for owner-installed goods
options.C: Disagree; manuals may be even more critical under a purchasing contract
options.D: Disagree; the UCC requires manuals for every sale of complex equipment
options.E: Agree; the approved shop drawings already carry that information
options.F: Disagree; manuals are needed only when the goods contractor installs

questions.explanation: O&M manuals, frequently required in traditional construction contracts, might be even more critical under a purchasing contract, because the goods contractor and the eventual installer may have little direct contact. Moving the requirement to the installer's contract, limiting it to certain goods, or relying on shop drawings ignores that the goods contractor is the source of the information, and the requirement comes from the contract documents rather than the UCC.

questions.question: In traditional construction contracts, industry guidance notes that operation and maintenance manual requirements are particularly common for which type of work?

options.A: Finishes requiring periodic cleaning or care
options.B: Complex equipment or systems
options.C: Products covered by extended warranties
options.D: Products furnished with extra stock materials
options.E: Exterior envelope and roofing assemblies
options.F: Owner-furnished, owner-installed items

questions.explanation: Construction contract documents frequently require O&M manuals, particularly for complex equipment or systems, and the manuals may matter even more for purchased goods. Finishes, envelope assemblies, warranted products, owner-installed items, and items with extra stock may carry maintenance or warranty information, but they are not what is singled out for the O&M manual requirement.

questions.question: For most purchasing contracts, industry guidance says payment procedures are based on payments at three stages. Which set lists those stages?

options.A: Contract award, delivery to the site, and installation
options.B: Completion of fabrication, shipment, and start-up
options.C: Approval of submittals, shipment, and installation
options.D: Approval of submittals, delivery, and final acceptance
options.E: Contract award, completion of fabrication, and delivery
options.F: Approval of submittals, delivery, and start-up

questions.explanation: Apart from cases needing partial deliveries or progress payments during fabrication, payment is usually made at three points: approval of submittals, delivery to the designated location, and final acceptance. The other sets substitute contract award, fabrication, shipment, installation, or start-up, none of which is one of the three standard payment stages.

questions.question: Owner-purchased chillers were delivered on schedule, but the separate installation contract has slipped by eight months, and the goods contractor is still awaiting final payment because acceptance depends on testing after installation. What provision should the purchasing documents have included?

options.A: Final payment withheld until installation and testing, however long it takes
options.B: Final payment at delivery for all equipment, with no later acceptance test
options.C: A reasonable time limit after delivery, then final payment regardless
options.D: Final payment released only at substantial completion of the installation
options.E: Liquidated damages assessed against the goods contractor for the delay
options.F: Final payment held until the installer's warranty period ends

questions.explanation: Final acceptance of equipment may wait until it is installed or placed in service and proven acceptable, but in fairness to the goods contractor a reasonable time limit should be set between delivery and installation, after which final payment is made even if the item has not been installed and tested. Open-ended holds, or payment tied to the installation contract or its warranty, ignore that limit; paying in full at delivery skips the equipment test; and the goods contractor did not cause the delay.

questions.question: An owner agrees to make progress payments on a large custom switchgear lineup while it is being manufactured and remains under the goods contractor's control. What should the purchasing documents include, and who should furnish the language?

options.A: Protection of the owner's stake in unfinished goods; owner's legal counsel
options.B: Transfer of title to the goods at each payment; the A/E's master specification
options.C: A payment bond securing each progress payment; the goods contractor's surety
options.D: Transit insurance on goods still in fabrication; the owner's insurance adviser
options.E: A retainage percentage on each payment; the A/E's Division 01 section
options.F: Owner inspection before each payment; the owner's purchasing agent

questions.explanation: When progress payments are made while goods are still being manufactured under the goods contractor's control, the purchasing documents need provisions that protect the owner's interest in the partially completed goods, and the contract language should come from the owner's legal counsel. Title transfer, bonds, retainage, inspections, and transit insurance are not the mechanism described, and the A/E, a surety, a purchasing agent, or an insurance adviser is not the named source.

questions.question: Which UCC article governs contracts for the sale of goods between buyers and sellers, and which state has not adopted it?

options.A: Article 9; Louisiana
options.B: Article 2; Louisiana
options.C: Article 2; Delaware
options.D: Article 9; Delaware
options.E: Article 3; Louisiana
options.F: Article 2; New York

questions.explanation: Article 2 of the UCC, the sales article, governs contracts for transactions in goods between buyers and sellers. It has been adopted in 49 states, with Louisiana the exception. Other UCC articles cover matters such as negotiable instruments and security interests, and states such as Delaware and New York have adopted Article 2.

questions.question: Separately from an earlier equipment purchase, an owner contracts with the manufacturer solely for on-site technical assistance and an installation check. Does UCC Article 2 govern this contract?

options.A: Yes, because the services relate to goods sold under a prior contract
options.B: Yes, because Article 2 covers any agreement with a goods contractor
options.C: Only if the contract states a quantity and is signed by the manufacturer
options.D: No, because Article 2 is limited to sales of movable goods, not services
options.E: Yes, because the manufacturer is a merchant that deals in such goods
options.F: Only if the services are worth over $500 and the contract is written

questions.explanation: Article 2 covers only sales of movable goods and excludes contracts primarily for services, and technical assistance and installation checks count as services. A link to an earlier sale, the provider being a goods merchant, or meeting the written-contract and $500 rules that apply to sales does not bring a services-only contract under Article 2.

questions.question: A purchasing contract drafted by the A/E is silent on several commercial terms, and the owner assumes the UCC applies only if the contract incorporates it by reference. Which statement is accurate?

options.A: The UCC applies only to public owners that advertise their purchases
options.B: The written contract always prevails over any conflicting UCC provision
options.C: UCC provisions fill gaps and may sometimes override written terms
options.D: The UCC applies only where the parties adopt it by express reference
options.E: The UCC applies only to contracts that exceed $500 in value
options.F: The UCC is a federal statute that displaces state contract law

questions.explanation: The A/E should know the UCC's basic provisions because they take effect when the written contract does not address a matter and may sometimes override written provisions. Each state adopts the UCC and publishes it with its statutes, so it is state law rather than a federal statute, does not depend on incorporation by reference, is not limited to public owners, and does not always yield to contract language. Its $500 figure concerns when a sale must be in writing.

questions.question: After delivery, an owner learns that the goods contractor's lender holds a security interest in the delivered goods that was never disclosed to the owner. The purchase order contains no warranty language. Under the UCC, which statement applies?

options.A: The seller generally warrants clear title, free of security interests unknown to the buyer
options.B: No title warranty exists, because the purchase order is silent on warranties
options.C: Title warranties arise only after the goods are installed, tested, and accepted
options.D: The seller warrants title only against those security interests recorded after the delivery
options.E: The title warranty applies only if the buyer inspected the goods at the plant
options.F: Only the implied warranty of merchantability applies, not one of title

questions.explanation: The UCC attaches express and implied warranties to sales, and a seller generally warrants transfer of clear title, free of any security interest the buyer did not know about. Because this warranty comes from the UCC, it does not depend on warranty language in the purchase order, on inspection, installation, or acceptance, or on when the interest was recorded. The implied warranty of merchantability concerns quality and does not replace the title warranty.

questions.question: A signed purchase agreement for lighting fixtures leaves several commercial terms open for later agreement or for reasonable commercial practice. Which term must the parties generally settle themselves, rather than rely on the UCC to supply it?

options.A: Price of the fixtures
options.B: Delivery arrangements
options.C: Payment details
options.D: Quantity of fixtures
options.E: Risk of loss during shipment
options.F: Warranties of title and quality

questions.explanation: The UCC recognizes the practice of leaving terms for later agreement and may supply payment, delivery, and even price when the written contract is silent; it also allocates risk of loss and attaches implied warranties unless the parties agree otherwise. Quantity, however, generally must be agreed by the parties themselves, and a written contract for goods must state it.

questions.question: A purchase order specifies delivery "FOB destination." According to industry guidance, where are FOB, CIF, and similar shorthand mercantile terms defined, and what do they allocate?

options.A: In the UCC; title, warranty obligations, and final acceptance
options.B: In the UCC; transportation costs, insurance, and risk of loss
options.C: In Division 01; transportation costs, insurance, and risk of loss
options.D: In the general conditions; payment terms, delivery dates, and price
options.E: In the UCC; delivery dates, quantity, and price
options.F: In the supplementary conditions; freight, title, and acceptance

questions.explanation: FOB, CIF, and comparable mercantile shorthand terms are defined in the UCC, and they assign responsibility for transportation costs, insurance, and risk of loss. Division 01, the general conditions, and the supplementary conditions are not where these terms are defined, and title, warranty, acceptance, dates, quantity, or price are not what the terms allocate.

questions.question: A purchase contract for goods is signed by both parties, but its terms are grossly unfair to the goods contractor. How should the A/E view the contract's enforceability under the UCC?

options.A: Enforceable, since the UCC defers to whatever terms the parties sign
options.B: Enforceable, as long as the A/E reviewed and approved the terms before signing
options.C: Unenforceable, because the UCC requires the parties to act in good faith
options.D: Unenforceable, because the UCC requires every contract to state a price
options.E: Enforceable, since the price exceeds $500 and the contract is in writing
options.F: Unenforceable, because the UCC requires goods to be competitively bid

questions.explanation: Agreements governed by the UCC carry a requirement that the parties act in good faith, so unfair or unconscionable contracts are not enforceable. Signatures, A/E approval, or meeting the writing rule for sales over $500 do not cure grossly unfair terms. The UCC does not require a stated price, since it can supply price when the contract is silent, and it sets no competitive bidding requirement.

questions.question: The goods contractor fails to deliver custom air-handling units as specified. Under the UCC, which remedies are available to the owner as buyer?

options.A: Cancel the contract, purchase substitute goods, and recover damages
options.B: Stop delivery, reclaim the goods, and recover the contract price
options.C: Terminate for convenience and pay only for goods already delivered
options.D: Cancel the contract, stop delivery, and recover liquidated damages only
options.E: Revoke acceptance only, with no recovery of damages
options.F: Reclaim payments made, but recover no incidental damages

questions.explanation: When the seller fails to deliver goods as specified, the buyer may cancel the contract, buy substitute goods, and recover damages, including incidental and consequential damages where appropriate. Stopping delivery, reclaiming the goods, and recovering the price are the seller's remedies, termination for convenience is a construction-contract provision rather than a UCC breach remedy, and nothing limits the buyer to liquidated damages or a refund.

questions.question: Midway through a purchasing contract, the owner becomes insolvent while a shipment of goods is in transit. Which set of options does the UCC give the goods contractor as seller?

options.A: Cancel the contract, purchase substitute goods, or recover damages
options.B: Revoke acceptance, cancel the contract, or recover incidental damages
options.C: Stop delivery, purchase substitute goods, or recover damages
options.D: Stop delivery, reclaim the goods, or recover the price or damages
options.E: Purchase substitute goods, reclaim the goods, or recover damages
options.F: Stop delivery, cancel the contract, or claim liquidated damages only

questions.explanation: When the buyer becomes insolvent or breaches, the UCC lets the seller stop delivery, reclaim the goods, or recover either the price or damages. Cancelling the contract and buying substitute goods are the buyer's remedies, and revoking acceptance is a buyer action that counts among buyer breaches rather than seller remedies. Liquidated damages come from a contract clause, enforceable only when reasonable, not from the seller's statutory remedies.

questions.question: An owner wants the purchasing contract for custom fabricated stair assemblies to include a liquidated damages amount far exceeding any delay cost the owner can document. What is the most likely result under the UCC?

options.A: The clause is enforceable because the UCC allows consequential damages
options.B: The clause is unenforceable because the amount is excessive and unsupported
options.C: The clause is enforceable because both parties agreed to the stated amount
options.D: The clause is unenforceable because the UCC bars liquidated damages in sales
options.E: The clause is enforceable because the UCC caps damages at the price
options.F: The clause is enforceable once the contract is signed and over $500

questions.explanation: The UCC enforces a liquidated damages clause when the amount is reasonable and verifiable but not when it is excessive and unsubstantiated, as here. The UCC does permit liquidated damages in sales, so a flat prohibition is wrong, and neither mutual agreement, a signed writing, nor the availability of consequential damages rescues an unsupported amount. The UCC sets no cap at the contract price.

questions.question: MasterFormat, SectionFormat, PageFormat, and similar organizational tools can greatly benefit purchasing documents under what assumption?

options.A: The goods contractor will also install the goods
options.B: The goods will be bought from a single negotiated source
options.C: The goods are to be procured by competitive bidding
options.D: The owner is a public agency purchasing under the UCC
options.E: The goods will be delivered to the owner's own warehouse
options.F: The purchasing contract will be assigned to the construction contractor

questions.explanation: Standard organizational tools such as MasterFormat, SectionFormat, and PageFormat are valuable for purchasing documents on the assumption that the goods will be competitively bid; documents that look like the ones construction-industry suppliers already know help avoid confusion. Installation by the goods contractor, a single negotiated source, public ownership, the delivery point, and assignment of the contract are not the stated condition.

questions.question: An owner will award a purchasing contract for laboratory fume hoods and, at the same time, a construction contract that includes installing them. How should the two project manuals relate?

options.A: They should be similar to each other and carefully coordinated
options.B: They should be merged into one manual under a single contract
options.C: They should use different formats to keep the contracts distinct
options.D: They should be kept independent to avoid conflicting obligations
options.E: They should share one set of general conditions for both contracts
options.F: They should be issued in sequence, the construction manual after delivery

questions.explanation: A purchasing contract for goods and a construction contract to install them can be in force at the same time, and when they are, the two project manuals should resemble each other and be coordinated with care. Merging them, using deliberately different formats, keeping them independent, or issuing one only after delivery defeats that coordination, and purchasing conditions differ from construction conditions, so one shared set does not fit both.

questions.question: A specifier proposes organizing an owner's purchasing documents in the standard construction-industry formats, such as MasterFormat and SectionFormat. Which rationale supports this approach?

options.A: Construction-contract definitions can then be reused without change
options.B: Formats familiar to goods contractors and suppliers help avoid confusion
options.C: MasterFormat titles were written specifically for purchasing contracts
options.D: Standard formats eliminate the need to coordinate with a construction contract
options.E: The UCC requires these formats for contracts for the sale of goods
options.F: Using them lets the purchasing manual omit the conditions of the contract

questions.explanation: Documents that resemble the ones construction-industry goods contractors and suppliers already know help avoid confusion, and the organization, concepts, subject-matter locations, and language of the standard formats can be adapted to purchasing. Construction definitions cannot simply be carried over, since inapplicable ones must be avoided; many MasterFormat titles deal only with construction; coordination with a simultaneous construction contract is still required; and nothing removes the need for conditions of the contract.

questions.question: A specifier is assembling a purchasing project manual for owner-procured laboratory casework and is sorting documents into their groups. Which document does industry guidance list among the procurement requirements rather than with the agreement and conditions?

options.A: Performance bond
options.B: Supplementary conditions
options.C: Bid security form
options.D: Agreement form
options.E: General conditions
options.F: Technical specifications

questions.explanation: Instructions to bidders, bid forms, bid security forms, pre-bid information, and information available to bidders make up the procurement requirements of a purchasing project manual. The performance bond, agreement form, and general and supplementary conditions are named separately as further elements of the manual, and the technical specifications are a category of their own.

questions.question: An owner's purchasing manager drafts a purchasing project manual for owner-furnished switchgear containing instructions to bidders, a bid form, a bid security form, and technical specifications. Which additional elements should the manual include?

options.A: An agreement form, a performance bond, and general and supplementary conditions
options.B: A payment bond, a maintenance bond, and the seller's standard terms of sale
options.C: A schedule of values, a notice to proceed form, and a closeout certificate
options.D: A labor and material bond, an insurance certificate, and a lien waiver form
options.E: A purchase order form, a delivery receipt, and the text of the UCC
options.F: A subcontractor list, a payment bond, and temporary facilities provisions

questions.explanation: Beyond the procurement requirements, a purchasing project manual should also carry an agreement form, a performance bond, and both general and supplementary conditions. Payment, maintenance, and labor and material bonds, lien waivers, insurance certificates, schedules of values, and delivery receipts are not among the named elements; subcontractors are rarely involved in purchasing, and temporary facilities relate to on-site work.

questions.question: A specifier is outlining the contents of a purchasing project manual for owner-bought FF&E. Which four categories of documents does a purchasing project manual customarily contain?

options.A: Bidding requirements, contract forms, general requirements, and contract drawings
options.B: Procurement requirements, agreement forms, Division 01 sections, and record documents
options.C: Solicitation documents, purchase order forms, UCC provisions, and product data
options.D: Procurement requirements, contracting forms, the conditions of the contract, and specifications
options.E: Procurement requirements, contracting forms, specifications, and drawings
options.F: Procurement requirements, the conditions of the contract, specifications, and O&M manuals

questions.explanation: A purchasing project manual customarily holds four groups: procurement requirements, contracting forms, the conditions of the contract, and specifications. They parallel the construction project manual while reflecting purchasing differences. Drawings, product data, O&M manuals, UCC provisions, and record documents are not among the four groups, and leaving out the contracting forms or the conditions breaks the set.

questions.question: A specifier is editing Division 01 for a purchasing contract for factory-finished casework delivered to the owner's warehouse. Which Level 2 section does industry guidance place in the category generally applicable to all purchasing contracts?

options.A: Section 01 20 00—Price and Payment Procedures
options.B: Section 01 40 00—Quality Requirements
options.C: Section 01 70 00—Execution and Closeout Requirements
options.D: Section 01 80 00—Performance Requirements
options.E: Section 01 50 00—Temporary Facilities and Controls
options.F: Section 01 92 00—Facility Operation

questions.explanation: Four Level 2 sections apply to essentially every purchasing contract: Summary (01 10 00), Administrative Requirements (01 30 00), Quality Requirements (01 40 00), and Product Requirements (01 60 00). Price and payment, execution and closeout, and performance requirements are only sometimes included, depending on the goods contractor's activity and the project, while temporary facilities and facility operation generally do not apply because they concern on-site work.

questions.question: A reviewer notices that the Division 01 for a purchasing contract for emergency generators includes Section 01 92 00—Facility Operation. How is that section classified for purchasing contracts?

options.A: Generally applicable to all purchasing contracts, like product requirements
options.B: Sometimes applicable, depending on the goods contractor's level of activity
options.C: Required whenever the goods are furnished by the owner for installation by others
options.D: Generally not applicable, because it relates to on-site activities
options.E: Required whenever the goods contractor performs start-up at the site
options.F: Sometimes applicable, depending on the price and payment terms

questions.explanation: Section 01 50 00 Temporary Facilities and Controls, 01 92 00 Facility Operation, and 01 94 00 Facility Decommissioning usually do not apply to purchasing contracts, since they concern on-site activities. Facility Operation is therefore not in the always-applicable group with product requirements or in the sometimes-applicable group tied to the goods contractor's activity, and neither start-up services, payment terms, nor the disposition method moves it into another group.

questions.question: For a purchasing contract under which the seller will deliver, start up, and demonstrate packaged boilers, a specifier is deciding whether to include Section 01 70 00—Execution and Closeout Requirements. What governs that decision?

options.A: The goods contractor's required level of activity and the project's particular aspects
options.B: Its classification as generally applicable, so it is included in every purchasing contract
options.C: Its classification as generally inapplicable, so it is omitted because it covers site work
options.D: Whether the section is written as a proprietary, descriptive, or performance specification
options.E: Whether the owner's legal counsel has approved the UCC provisions
options.F: Whether the goods will be shipped FOB destination or FOB origin

questions.explanation: Section 01 70 00 Execution and Closeout Requirements is in the group of sections only sometimes applicable to purchasing contracts. Inclusion turns on how much activity the goods contractor must perform and on the particular aspects of the project, so the section is neither automatically included nor automatically excluded. The specifying method, legal review of UCC terms, and shipping terms are not the deciding factors.

questions.question: A specifier is writing a section for owner-purchased commercial kitchen equipment. The goods contractor must give technical assistance while another contractor installs the equipment, then field-test it after installation. In SectionFormat, where does industry guidance say such special services would typically be stated?

options.A: PART 1—GENERAL, because the services are administrative in nature
options.B: PART 2—PRODUCTS, because the services accompany the goods supplied
options.C: PART 3—EXECUTION, because that part deals with on-site activities
options.D: Division 01 only, because SectionFormat parts address the goods alone
options.E: A separate services section, apart from the section for the goods
options.F: The supplementary conditions, since services change the contract terms

questions.explanation: PART 3—EXECUTION covers on-site activities and is the part used least in purchasing, yet items about disposition of the goods and any special services the goods contractor must provide would typically be stated there. Neither PART 1 nor PART 2 is the place for those items, and moving them out of the section into Division 01, a separate section, or the supplementary conditions is not the approach described.

questions.question: A purchasing section for loose furniture has no on-site requirements at all. How should the specifier handle PART 3—EXECUTION?

options.A: Delete PART 3 entirely so the section ends after PART 2—PRODUCTS
options.B: Retain the part and simply note “Not Used” under its heading
options.C: Move the delivery and storage articles from PART 1 into PART 3
options.D: Replace PART 3 with a reference to the Division 01 closeout section
options.E: Fill PART 3 with the installer's requirements from the construction manual
options.F: Combine PART 2 and PART 3 under a single PRODUCTS heading

questions.explanation: When a purchasing section has nothing to state in PART 3, the specifier can simply note “Not Used” there, so the part stays in place with that notation. Deleting the part, shifting PART 1 articles into it, combining it with PART 2, borrowing the installer's requirements, or substituting a Division 01 reference are not what is recommended.

questions.question: A specifier prepares two purchasing sections for identical rooftop units. One owner will stockpile the units for its own later use; the other owner will furnish them to a construction contractor for installation. Why might the articles developed in the two sections differ?

options.A: The eventual disposition of the goods is one factor that shapes article development
options.B: MasterFormat assigns a different section number whenever goods go to an installer
options.C: SectionFormat requires a PART 3 only when the owner retains goods for its own use
options.D: Reference standard specifying is not permitted when goods are furnished to an installer
options.E: UCC Article 2 applies only when the goods are furnished to an installer
options.F: Goods kept for the owner's own use need no specification section at all

questions.explanation: Five factors shape the articles under each part of a purchasing section: the basic purchasing procedures, the nature of the goods, the specifying method, the required level of contractor activity, and the eventual disposition of the goods. Stockpiling versus furnishing to an installer is a difference in disposition. Section numbering, PART 3, the UCC, and specifying methods do not turn on owner retention, and stockpiled goods still need a section.

questions.question: An owner purchased lockers and kept them in its own warehouse before handing them to the general contractor for installation. At transfer, several units are missing hardware kits. Who is responsible to the construction contractor for the completeness and condition of the goods at transfer?

options.A: The goods contractor, as the original seller of the lockers
options.B: The A/E, as coordinator of the purchasing and construction contracts
options.C: The construction contractor, once it signs for delivery of the units
options.D: The owner, as the party furnishing the goods to the installer
options.E: The goods contractor and the owner jointly, as parties to the sale
options.F: The construction contractor's surety, under its performance bond

questions.explanation: When goods are furnished by the owner for installation by others, the owner is answerable to the construction contractor for their suitability, completeness, and condition at the moment of transfer. Only after transfer does the construction contractor take over storage, handling, and installation. The duty is not placed on the goods contractor, shared with it, given to the A/E, or covered by the installer's surety.

questions.question: Owner-purchased rooftop units were furnished to the mechanical contractor, who installed them. A compressor fails during the manufacturer's warranty period, and the owner expects the mechanical contractor to pursue the manufacturer. What does industry guidance suggest about warranties under this method of disposition?

options.A: They transfer automatically to the installer when it accepts the goods at transfer
options.B: They may not transfer to the installer, so the owner may need to retain and enforce them
options.C: They lapse unless the goods contractor itself installs the goods at the project site
options.D: They are best held by the A/E, who may enforce them for the owner until final payment
options.E: They are replaced by the installer's one-year correction period
options.F: They are void because the goods were bought outside the construction contract

questions.explanation: Under the furnished-by-owner method, passing the goods' warranties to the construction contractor might be doubtful, so the owner, as original purchaser, may have to keep and enforce them. Warranties do not transfer automatically, lapse or become void because the goods were bought separately or installed by someone else, or pass to the A/E, and the installer's correction period is a separate, shorter obligation.

questions.question: An owner plans to assign its purchasing contract for long-lead switchgear to the electrical contractor. Which statement describes this method of disposition?

options.A: The owner still pays the goods contractor while the electrical contractor handles installation
options.B: The owner stays responsible to the installer for the goods' suitability and condition at transfer
options.C: The owner may lose part of the cost benefit of buying direct but keeps other inherent advantages
options.D: The A/E and goods contractor drop out after final payment except for warranty obligations
options.E: The electrical contractor receives the goods, but the owner administers the contract
options.F: The goods contractor takes over installation once the contract is assigned

questions.explanation: With assignment, the construction contractor accepts the purchasing contract, much like a purchase order, and takes on receipt, payment, administration, and installation; the owner may lose some of the cost advantage of buying direct but keeps its other inherent advantages. The owner no longer pays or administers, and the goods contractor does not install. Owner responsibility at transfer describes the furnished-by-owner method, and the A/E dropping out after final payment describes owner retention.

questions.question: An A/E's purchasing documents for laboratory fume hoods state that the hoods will be furnished by the owner for installation by others. The separate construction contract, issued at the same time, is silent on the arrangement. What is the best action?

options.A: Also state the method in the construction contract and define what each contract furnishes
options.B: Rely on the purchasing documents alone, since stating the method once is sufficient
options.C: Leave the goods contractor and construction contractor to work out the interface after award
options.D: Address the disposition method by field order once the construction contract is awarded
options.E: List the hoods only in Section 01 64 00 of the purchasing manual
options.F: Have the goods contractor send installation instructions to the installer

questions.explanation: The disposition method must be clearly stated in the purchasing documents and, when a construction contract is involved, in that contract too, with procedures set with both contractors. The documents must say which items, appurtenances, and accessories each contract furnishes and assign responsibility for the rest. Relying on one set of documents, a field order, a section in the wrong manual, the goods contractor's instructions, or the contractors' own negotiation leaves the interface undefined.

questions.question: An owner is buying boxed task chairs to be delivered to its facility, with no assembly or installation by the vendor. Which AIA document is appropriate?

options.A: A151, the agreement between owner and vendor for FF&E
options.B: A751, Invitation and Instructions to Vendors for Quotations for FF&E
options.C: A151 used with A751, since the vendor must inspect the premises
options.D: A152, Purchase Order, with its companion A152 Terms and Conditions
options.E: A101 and A201, the standard owner-contractor construction forms
options.F: The A152 Terms and Conditions alone, as the complete purchase document

questions.explanation: When FF&E is only being bought, with no assembly or installation, AIA A152, Purchase Order, should be used together with its companion A152 Terms and Conditions. A151 and A751 both require the vendor to inspect the premises and assemble or install the FF&E, so they suit purchases that include that work. A101 and A201 are construction forms, and the terms and conditions accompany the purchase order rather than standing alone.

questions.question: Owner's counsel asks how two AIA FF&E documents handle a conflict between the document's terms and the UCC. Which statement is accurate?

options.A: A152 says its terms and conditions prevail; A151 does not state which prevails
options.B: A151 says the agreement prevails over the UCC; A152 does not state which prevails
options.C: Both documents state that the UCC prevails over any conflicting contract terms
options.D: Neither document cites the UCC; the law of the project's location governs both
options.E: Both documents state that the agreement prevails over the UCC
options.F: A151 says the UCC prevails; A152 says its own terms prevail

questions.explanation: A151 refers to the UCC and provides that the agreement takes precedence if the two conflict. A152 also refers to the UCC but does not say whether its terms and conditions prevail, which rules out the reversed, both-prevail, and UCC-prevails statements. Relying on the law of the project's location without citing the UCC describes the ConsensusDocs purchasing documents, not AIA.

questions.question: A specifier converting a purchasing project manual to the EJCDC document family notices a terminology difference. Which term does EJCDC use where AIA documents and general practice speak of purchasing or the sale of goods?

options.A: Acquisition
options.B: Supply
options.C: Procurement
options.D: Furnishing
options.E: Buyout
options.F: Disposition

questions.explanation: EJCDC uses procurement where AIA documents and general practice speak of purchasing or the sale of goods, which is why its titles read, for example, Agreement Between Buyer and Seller for Procurement. Acquisition is the federal FAR term, buyout is the contractor's process of letting subcontracts and purchase orders, disposition describes what happens to purchased goods, and supply and furnishing are not the label EJCDC adopts.

questions.question: An engineer is assembling the four primary EJCDC purchasing documents for an owner buying pumps for an engineer-designed treatment plant. Which set does industry guidance list?
questions.explanation: The four primary EJCDC purchasing documents are P-200 (instructions to bidders), P-520 (agreement), P-700 (general conditions), and P-800 (guide to procurement supplementary conditions). P-400, the bid form, is used alongside them but is not one of the four; P-001 is the commentary; N-122 covers uniform location of subject matter; and C-prefixed numbers belong to EJCDC's construction series.

questions.question: A water utility is buying large vertical turbine pumps directly from a manufacturer for an engineer-designed pump station. The manufacturer insists on using its own standard sales order form. What is the best approach for the owner?

options.A: Accept the supplier form and attach the engineer's specifications to it
options.B: Use the EJCDC construction series, since the goods are engineered equipment
options.C: Accept the supplier form, relying on the UCC to fill any gaps in its commercial terms
options.D: Use the EJCDC procurement documents, which avoid the shortcomings of supplier forms
options.E: Use AIA A152, since EJCDC publishes no form for buying goods
options.F: Have the engineer issue a field order adopting the supplier's terms

questions.explanation: The EJCDC procurement documents, meant for an owner buying goods directly for an engineer-designed project, are an alternative to accepting manufacturers' and suppliers' standard purchase order forms; they avoid those forms' inadequacies and the trouble of adapting them to the owner's and project's needs. Accepting the supplier's form, with attachments, UCC gap-filling, or a field order, is what they replace; the construction series is not the purchasing set; and EJCDC does publish procurement forms.

questions.question: An engineer editing EJCDC P-200 for a procurement wants to confirm the meaning of a capitalized term used throughout the bid package. Where are the terms used in all four primary EJCDC purchasing documents defined?

options.A: In the agreement, EJCDC P-520
options.B: In the general conditions, EJCDC P-700
options.C: In the instructions to bidders, EJCDC P-200
options.D: In the supplementary conditions guide, EJCDC P-800
options.E: In the bid form for procurement, EJCDC P-400
options.F: In the procurement commentary, EJCDC P-001

questions.explanation: The terms used across all four primary EJCDC purchasing documents are defined in the general conditions, which for the procurement set is P-700, Standard General Conditions for Procurement Contracts. The agreement, instructions to bidders, supplementary conditions guide, bid form, and commentary are not where those definitions sit.

questions.question: Late in document preparation, an engineer revises the EJCDC P-520 agreement to change the payment terms. What else should the engineer consider?

options.A: Whether P-001, the procurement commentary, must be revised and issued with the bid documents
options.B: Whether bidders must countersign the revised agreement form before bids are opened
options.C: Whether the other primary documents need matching changes, since they are closely integrated
options.D: Whether EJCDC must approve the edit, since P-520 is a copyrighted standard form
options.E: Whether the change must wait for a change order issued after award
options.F: Whether the seller's standard terms of sale should replace the agreement

questions.explanation: The EJCDC purchasing documents are closely integrated, with shared terms defined in the general conditions, so changing any one of them may require changes in the others. Nothing calls for reissuing the P-001 commentary to bidders, having bidders countersign the agreement, obtaining EJCDC approval of edits, or waiting for a change order, and the EJCDC set exists to replace sellers' standard forms, not to yield to them.

questions.question: Which document should users of the EJCDC purchasing documents consult for its discussion of the comparable construction contract forms?

options.A: EJCDC C-001, the commentary on the 2018 construction series
options.B: EJCDC P-001, the commentary on the 2019 procurement documents
options.C: EJCDC C-700, the general conditions for construction contracts
options.D: EJCDC P-800, the guide to procurement supplementary conditions
options.E: EJCDC N-122, the guide to uniform location of subject matter
options.F: EJCDC P-700, the general conditions for procurement contracts

questions.explanation: Users of the EJCDC purchasing documents are advised to read the relevant parts of EJCDC C-001, the commentary on the 2018 construction series, which covers the comparable construction forms. P-001 is the procurement commentary, C-700 and P-700 are general conditions rather than commentaries, P-800 is the supplementary conditions guide, and N-122 deals with where subject matter is located.

questions.question: How does EJCDC P-400, Bid Form for Procurement, relate to the four primary EJCDC purchasing documents?

options.A: It is one of the four, taking the place of the instructions to bidders
options.B: It is a commentary explaining how the four documents should be used
options.C: It is the guide used to draft the procurement supplementary conditions
options.D: It is used in conjunction with them but is not one of the four
options.E: It is the uniform location guide the four documents follow
options.F: It replaces the agreement, P-520, on small procurements

questions.explanation: EJCDC P-400, Bid Form for Procurement, is used together with EJCDC's other procurement documents, while the four primary documents are P-200, P-520, P-700, and P-800. P-400 does not replace the instructions to bidders or the agreement, is not a commentary, is not the supplementary conditions guide, and is not the uniform location of subject matter guide, which is N-122.

questions.question: An owner wants a manufacturer to furnish and also install a specialized conveyor system, and its attorney proposes using the EJCDC purchasing documents unchanged. What is the better course?

options.A: Use the purchasing documents unchanged, treating installation as one of the seller's special services
options.B: Use standard construction contract forms, or modify the purchasing documents to add installation
options.C: Accept the manufacturer's standard sales order, since EJCDC forms cannot address installation
options.D: Use the purchasing documents and have the engineer define installation later by field order
options.E: Use ConsensusDocs 702 with 702.1, since they cover commodity goods
options.F: Use the purchasing documents, with installation stated in PART 3 of the section

questions.explanation: The EJCDC purchasing documents are not meant for cases where the manufacturer or supplier must take part in installation. When installation is included, the job resembles a traditional construction contract, so standard construction forms should be used or the primary purchasing documents modified to include installation. Seller special services only assist the installing entity, a PART 3 note or field order does not change the documents' scope, and ConsensusDocs 702 covers goods needing no installation.
questions.source: intended use of EJCDC procurement documents

questions.question: An owner will use the EJCDC purchasing documents to buy identical valve actuators to be shipped in several separate deliveries over two years. How should the needed changes to the primary procurement documents be made?

options.A: Through direct edits to the general conditions text
options.B: Through revisions to the bid form for procurement
options.C: Through the supplementary conditions
options.D: Through a change order issued after the first delivery
options.E: Through a separate agreement for each delivery
options.F: Through addenda issued after each delivery

questions.explanation: When the same item is to be delivered in several shipments, the changes needed in the primary EJCDC procurement documents belong in the supplementary conditions. Editing the standard general conditions text directly, revising the bid form, signing a separate agreement for each delivery, or issuing change orders or addenda as deliveries occur is not the method recommended.
questions.source: intended use of EJCDC procurement documents

questions.question: An engineer is adapting a technical specification section for use with the EJCDC purchasing documents and finds a paragraph reading 'Seller shall perform the Work in accordance with the drawings.' What terminology problem does this create?

options.A: Work is a construction-contract term that the EJCDC procurement set does not use
options.B: Seller should read Contractor, the term EJCDC uses for the party furnishing Goods
options.C: Seller should read Vendor, the term EJCDC uses for the furnishing party
options.D: Work should read Special Services, the term EJCDC uses for all seller duties
options.E: Seller should read Buyer, the term EJCDC uses for the furnishing party
options.F: Seller should read Manufacturer, the term EJCDC uses for the furnishing party

questions.explanation: Work is a term defined for construction contract documents, and the EJCDC purchasing documents do not use it, so a section written for them should avoid it. Seller is the correct EJCDC term for the party furnishing the goods and Buyer is the owner; a manufacturer, vendor, or contractor is someone else. Special services cover only site assistance such as instruction or start-up help, not every seller duty.

questions.question: In the EJCDC purchasing documents, how should a reader interpret a reference to a fabricator or a distributor?

options.A: As another name for the Seller, which has entered into the agreement directly with the Buyer
options.B: As a party under subcontract to a prime construction contractor or to a site subcontractor
options.C: As the Buyer's agent that receives, stores, and later transfers the Goods to the installer
options.D: As a lower-tier supplier to the Seller whose obligations also run directly to the Buyer
options.E: As the Buyer's own forces that install the Goods at the site
options.F: As the Engineer's consultant that inspects the Goods at the plant

questions.explanation: In the EJCDC purchasing documents, anyone called a manufacturer, supplier, fabricator, distributor, or vendor is a party subcontracted to one of the prime construction contractors, or sub-subcontracted to a subcontractor working at the site. The party contracting with the Buyer to furnish the Goods is the Seller, so these labels do not mean the Seller, a Buyer's agent or installer, an inspector, or a supplier owing duties directly to the Buyer.

questions.question: A construction firm needs to purchase a complex automated storage system, including its installation, for a building project. Which ConsensusDocs purchasing document is intended for this purchase?

options.A: ConsensusDocs 702 alone
options.B: ConsensusDocs 702.1 alone
options.C: ConsensusDocs 702 used with 702.1
options.D: ConsensusDocs 703
options.E: ConsensusDocs 760, the bid or proposal form
options.F: ConsensusDocs 200, the owner-constructor agreement

questions.explanation: ConsensusDocs 703, the purchase agreement for non-commodity goods bought by a contractor, is meant for complex goods and, like AIA A151, covers installation. ConsensusDocs 702 and its companion 702.1 are for goods that need no installation, so neither alone nor together do they fit. ConsensusDocs 760 is a bid or proposal form, and ConsensusDocs 200 is the owner-constructor agreement, not a purchasing document.

questions.question: An owner's counsel reviewing a ConsensusDocs 702.1 purchase order asks which law governs it. What do the ConsensusDocs purchasing documents provide?

options.A: The UCC governs, because the documents expressly incorporate it throughout by reference
options.B: The agreement governs and takes precedence over any conflicting provision of the UCC
options.C: Laws at the project's location govern, so an adopting state's UCC applies by default
options.D: The law of the seller's home state governs, regardless of where the project is located
options.E: The general conditions of the prime construction contract govern
options.F: Federal law governs, since the FAR applies to every purchase of goods

questions.explanation: Unlike the EJCDC and AIA documents, the ConsensusDocs purchasing documents do not reference the UCC directly; 702.1 and 703 instead provide that the law where the project is located governs, so the UCC controls by default in a state that has adopted it. Express UCC incorporation, an agreement-over-UCC clause, the seller's home state, the prime contract's conditions, and the FAR are not what the documents provide.

questions.question: ConsensusDocs 702 and 703 are organized very similarly. Why does 703 contain additional insurance, safety, and indemnity provisions?

options.A: It is used only for public-sector buyers
options.B: It also covers installation of the goods
options.C: It directly references the UCC throughout
options.D: It is always paired with the 702.1 terms
options.E: It is meant for low-value commodity goods
options.F: It is issued by the owner, not a contractor

questions.explanation: ConsensusDocs 702 (used with 702.1) and 703 are organized much alike, but because 703 also includes installation of the goods, it carries extra insurance, safety, and indemnity provisions. 703 is not limited to public buyers, the ConsensusDocs purchasing documents do not directly reference the UCC, 702.1 pairs with 702 rather than 703, and 703 is for complex, non-commodity goods bought by a contractor.

questions.question: A specifier on a federal agency project finds that the agency has issued its own acquisition regulation. How does that regulation relate to the FAR?

options.A: It implements or supplements the FAR, which remains the primary document
options.B: It supersedes the FAR for that agency's acquisitions once it is published
options.C: It stands outside the FAR system and governs only internal agency staff
options.D: It replaces the FAR's uniform policies for all other executive agencies
options.E: It must be adopted by each state before it takes effect
options.F: It is advisory guidance that contracting officers may disregard

questions.explanation: The Federal Acquisition Regulations System is made up of the FAR itself, which is the primary document, plus the regulations that individual agencies write to implement or supplement it. An agency regulation therefore works within the FAR system rather than superseding it, standing outside it, replacing the uniform policies for all executive agencies, or serving as optional advice; state-by-state adoption describes the UCC, not federal acquisition rules.

questions.question: The vision of the Federal Acquisition Regulations System is to deliver which of the following to the customer?

options.A: The lowest-priced product or service obtained through full and open competition
options.B: The highest-quality product or service at the minimum administrative operating cost
options.C: The lowest-priced product or service at the minimum administrative operating cost
options.D: The best value product or service on a timely basis while maintaining the public's trust
options.E: The best value product or service at the minimum administrative operating cost
options.F: The lowest-priced product or service from contractors with good past performance

questions.explanation: The FAR System's vision is to provide the customer with the best value product or service, delivered in a timely way, while keeping the public's trust and meeting public policy objectives. Lowest price, highest quality, and minimum administrative cost are not the vision's terms; minimizing administrative operating costs, using contractors with good past performance, and promoting competition appear among the guiding principles instead.

questions.question: Under the FAR guiding principles, customer satisfaction is measured in terms of which three attributes of the delivered product or service?

options.A: Cost, scope, and risk
options.B: Quality, safety, and durability
options.C: Cost, quality, and timeliness
options.D: Scope, safety, and availability
options.E: Cost, quality, and openness
options.F: Quality, timeliness, and integrity

questions.explanation: The first FAR guiding principle is customer satisfaction, judged by the cost, quality, and timeliness of what is delivered. Integrity and openness belong to a different principle about how business is conducted, and scope, risk, safety, durability, and availability are not named for this principle.

questions.question: A federal acquisition team is weighing options for furnishing a new office building. Which practice does industry guidance cite as an example of how the FAR System satisfies the customer?

options.A: Requiring custom-designed products tailored to each agency's needs
options.B: Maximizing the use of commercial products and services
options.C: Awarding contracts primarily on the basis of lowest offered price
options.D: Favoring design-build delivery for facility acquisitions
options.E: Restricting competition to a short list of incumbent vendors
options.F: Using the agency's own staff in place of outside contractors

questions.explanation: Examples of how the FAR System satisfies the customer include making the most of commercial products and services, choosing contractors with a record of successful past performance or a current superior ability to perform, and promoting competition. Custom-designed products, award chiefly on lowest price, a preference for design-build, restricted competition, and replacing contractors with agency staff are not among those examples.

questions.question: One guiding principle of the Federal Acquisition Regulations System is to conduct business with which three qualities?

options.A: Integrity, fairness, and openness
options.B: Integrity, efficiency, and economy
options.C: Fairness, accountability, and economy
options.D: Efficiency, accountability, and openness
options.E: Integrity, fairness, and timeliness
options.F: Openness, quality, and accountability

questions.explanation: One FAR guiding principle is to conduct business with integrity, fairness, and openness. The other combinations swap in efficiency, accountability, economy, timeliness, or quality; timeliness and quality belong to the customer-satisfaction principle, and efficiency, accountability, and economy are not named in this one.

questions.question: The FAR is prepared, issued, and maintained jointly by which parties?

options.A: The Secretary of Defense, the Office of Management and Budget, and the Department of Energy
options.B: NASA, the Department of Energy, and the Army Corps of Engineers
options.C: The GSA administrators, the Office of Management and Budget, and the Army Corps of Engineers
options.D: The Secretary of Defense, the GSA administrators, and NASA
options.E: The GSA administrators, NASA, and the Department of Energy
options.F: The Secretary of Defense, NASA, and the Office of Management and Budget

questions.explanation: Three parties jointly prepare, issue, and maintain the FAR: the Secretary of Defense, the GSA administrators, and NASA. Each wrong set drops at least one of the three or adds a body that is not named, such as the Office of Management and Budget, the Department of Energy, or the Army Corps of Engineers.

questions.question: A new agency project manager assumes that the roles of government contracting personnel are fixed separately in each contract. Where is the responsibility of each such position described?

options.A: In each contract's general conditions and special clauses
options.B: In the solicitation issued for each individual federal acquisition
options.C: In the FAR, which defines what each of these positions must do
options.D: In the agency's annual procurement plan for each program
options.E: In the A/E's Division 01 project management section
options.F: In each agency's own supplement, which replaces the FAR

questions.explanation: The FAR System includes government personnel assigned to manage and administer federal contracting, and every one of those positions has a defined responsibility set out in the FAR itself. Those responsibilities do not come from individual contract clauses, solicitations, program plans, or the A/E's Division 01, and agency supplements implement or add to the FAR rather than replacing it.

questions.question: At a kickoff meeting, a federal program manager describes the acquisition team as only the government's technical, supply, and procurement representatives. Which participants does this description leave out?

options.A: State and local building officials with jurisdiction over the site
options.B: The customers they serve and the contractors providing products and services
options.C: The private sureties and lenders that finance the contractors' operations
options.D: Congressional oversight staff and the agency's office of inspector general
options.E: Members of the public who attend the bid opening
options.F: Local utility companies that serve the project site

questions.explanation: The acquisition team takes in every government participant in the acquisition, such as technical, supply, and procurement representatives, along with the customers they serve and the contractors that furnish the products and services. Limiting the team to government representatives therefore leaves out customers and contractors; building officials, sureties and lenders, oversight staff, the public, and utilities are not named as team members.

questions.question: A head of the contracting activity (HCA) needs to sign a contract personally. What is the HCA's standing with respect to contracting officer authority?

options.A: The HCA must first obtain a separate contracting officer warrant
options.B: The HCA manages the activity but may not sign any contracts
options.C: The HCA is a contracting officer by virtue of the position
options.D: The HCA may sign only after a contracting officer concurs
options.E: The HCA may sign only contracts below the simplified acquisition threshold
options.F: The HCA must delegate signing to the agency's program manager

questions.explanation: The head of the contracting activity is the official responsible for managing the contracting activity and is a contracting officer by virtue of holding that position. Because the status comes with the position, no separate warrant or concurrence is needed, no dollar limit is described, and the HCA is not barred from signing. Only contracting officers may sign for the government, so a program manager could not take the HCA's place.

questions.question: On a federal courthouse project, the contracting officer is on leave when bids are opened. The agency's facilities director, a senior executive who manages the building program but is not a contracting officer, offers to sign the construction contract so award is not delayed. What is the correct position?

options.A: The director may sign if the contract is below the simplified acquisition threshold.
options.B: The director may not sign; only a contracting officer can sign for the government.
options.C: The director may sign because the director manages the agency's building program.
options.D: The director may not sign, but a contracting specialist on the officer's staff may.
options.E: The director may sign if the agency head approves the award in writing.
options.F: The director may not sign, but the A/E of record may sign for the agency.

questions.explanation: Only contracting officers may enter into and sign contracts on behalf of the United States, and then only within their delegated authority. A facilities director who is not a contracting officer cannot bind the government, and neither a dollar threshold, a management role, written approval by the agency head, a staff specialist who is not a contracting officer, nor the A/E changes who may sign.

questions.question: A contractor on a federal project wants to confirm that the contracting officer who will sign a large modification can bind the government for that amount. Which statement about a contracting officer's authority is consistent with industry guidance?

options.A: It is unlimited once the officer is appointed, and the appointment is public.
options.B: It is set case by case in each contract and stated only in that contract's terms.
options.C: It extends only as far as delegated, and the limits are kept confidential in the agency.
options.D: It extends only as far as delegated, and the written limits are available to the public.
options.E: It extends to any amount once the HCA has signed the solicitation.
options.F: It extends only as far as delegated, and the limits are given verbally at each award.

questions.explanation: Contracting officers can bind the government only to the extent of their delegated authority; the appointing authority gives them clear written instructions on those limits, and that information is readily available to the public as well as to agency personnel. The authority is therefore neither unlimited, unlocked by another official's signature, nor set verbally or contract by contract, and its limits are not kept inside the agency.

questions.question: A federal contracting officer has a responsive low bid within the government estimate, but a clearance required by agency procedures has not yet been issued, and the construction season is short. What should the officer do?

options.A: Withhold execution until the clearance and all other approvals are in place.
options.B: Execute now, since latitude for business judgment lets the officer waive the clearance.
options.C: Execute now and incorporate the clearance later through a bilateral modification.
options.D: Withhold execution only until the head of the contracting activity concurs verbally.
options.E: Execute now, provided the contractor posts an additional performance bond.
options.F: Execute now and make the clearance a condition of the notice to proceed.

questions.explanation: No contract may be executed until the contracting officer ensures that all legal, regulatory, and procedural requirements, including clearances and approvals, have been met. The officer's wide latitude for business judgment serves those responsibilities and does not excuse the precondition. A later modification, verbal concurrence from the head of the contracting activity, extra bonding, or a condition on the notice to proceed does not substitute for the missing clearance.

questions.question: On a federal acquisition for construction, a requirement in the FAR part devoted to construction conflicts with a requirement in another FAR part. Which part takes precedence?

options.A: FAR Part 36
options.B: FAR Part 43
options.C: FAR Part 46
options.D: FAR Part 49
options.E: FAR Part 25
options.F: FAR Part 52

questions.explanation: FAR Part 36 holds the construction contract requirements, and when one of them conflicts with a requirement in another part, Part 36 takes precedence for construction acquisitions. Part 43 covers modifications, Part 46 quality assurance, Part 49 termination, Part 25 includes the Buy American rules, and Part 52 holds contract clauses such as the Changes clause; none carries that precedence.

questions.question: A single, undivided federal contract covers building a vehicle maintenance facility and supplying some shop equipment; the building work is by far the largest portion. How are the contract clauses selected?

options.A: Use the supply clauses, since equipment is a distinct deliverable.
options.B: Use construction clauses for the building and supply clauses for the equipment.
options.C: Use the clauses applicable to the predominant part of the work.
options.D: Use the clauses for the part with the earliest delivery date.
options.E: Use the clauses the contractor selects in its bid.
options.F: Use construction clauses only for work above the simplified acquisition threshold.

questions.explanation: A contract combining construction with supplies or services includes the clauses applicable to the predominant part of the work. Applying clauses to each portion is the rule only when a contract is divided into parts; because this contract is undivided and building work dominates, construction clauses govern. Choosing by deliverable, schedule, dollar threshold, or the contractor's preference has no basis in the rule.

questions.question: A federal contract for construction and related services is structured in several separately identified parts, one for building construction and one for post-occupancy services. How do the contract clauses apply?

options.A: Only the predominant part's clauses apply throughout the contract.
options.B: Each part carries the clauses applicable to that part's own work.
options.C: The construction clauses apply to all parts because Part 36 governs.
options.D: The services clauses apply to all parts because services occur last.
options.E: The contractor chooses the clauses for each part at award.
options.F: The A/E selects the clauses for each part in Division 01.

questions.explanation: When a contract is split into several separately identified parts, each portion carries the clauses that apply to its own work rather than one set covering the whole. The predominant-part rule is for contracts that are not divided, and Part 36 precedence resolves conflicting FAR requirements rather than selecting clauses across portions. The government's contract, not the contractor's choice or the A/E's Division 01, carries the clauses.

questions.question: On a federal building contract, a proposed modification is expected to exceed the simplified acquisition threshold. What must be prepared and furnished to the contracting officer for this modification?

options.A: A contractor-certified schedule of values for the change
options.B: A determination signed by the head of the contracting activity
options.C: A value analysis report prepared by the design A/E of record
options.D: An independent government estimate of construction cost
options.E: An audit of the contractor's cost accounting system
options.F: A Buy American compliance certificate for the materials

questions.explanation: The contracting officer must receive an independent government estimate of construction cost for every proposed contract and for every modification expected to exceed the simplified acquisition threshold. Contractor pricing is not independent, and an HCA determination, an A/E value analysis, an accounting-system audit, or a Buy American certificate is not the document required here.

questions.question: The A/E firm that designed a new federal laboratory has a construction affiliate that wants to submit a sealed bid for the construction contract. As a general rule, the affiliate:

options.A: should generally not be awarded the contract, given its tie to the designer
options.B: may be awarded the contract if it submits the lowest responsive bid
options.C: may be awarded the contract once the design contract is closed out
options.D: is barred only if the A/E will also provide construction-phase services
options.E: may be awarded the contract if the A/E discloses the affiliation in the bid
options.F: is barred only on projects above the simplified acquisition threshold

questions.explanation: As a general rule, a federal construction contract is not awarded to the project's designer, or to that firm's subsidiaries or affiliates. Low bidding, disclosure, or closing out the design contract does not remove the affiliation, no dollar threshold limits the rule, and it is not confined to designers who stay on for construction-phase services.

questions.question: A federal installation has a fixed-price contract underway for a new barracks. The agency proposes a cost-reimbursement contract for utility work on the same site during the same period. This arrangement is:

options.A: generally acceptable, provided both contracts were procured using sealed bids
options.B: generally acceptable, provided the independent estimate shows a cost savings
options.C: generally prohibited, because the two contracts would run concurrently on one site
options.D: generally prohibited, because federal utility work must always be awarded fixed-price
options.E: generally acceptable, provided the HCA signs both contracts
options.F: generally prohibited, because cost-reimbursement contracts are barred in construction

questions.explanation: Running cost-reimbursement contracts concurrently with fixed-price contracts on the same site is generally prohibited; the concern is concurrency on one site, not the kind of work or the contract type alone. Sealed bidding, the independent government estimate, and the HCA's signature are separate matters that do not authorize the combination, and there is no rule that utility work must be fixed-price.

questions.question: Under FAR Part 43, which of the following actions is accomplished by a bilateral contract modification?

options.A: Issuing a change order under the Changes clause of the contract
options.B: Making a negotiated equitable adjustment resulting from a change order
options.C: Issuing a notice of termination to the contractor for default
options.D: Making an administrative change to the contract's provisions
options.E: Making a change authorized by a clause other than the Changes clause
options.F: Issuing a notice of termination for the government's convenience

questions.explanation: Bilateral modifications are used for negotiated equitable adjustments that follow a change order, for definitizing letter contracts, and for recording other agreements that modify the terms and conditions. Issuing change orders, making changes authorized by clauses other than the Changes clause, issuing termination notices of either kind, and making administrative changes are all unilateral actions.

questions.question: During construction of a federal facility, the agency's field inspector tells the contractor to add drainage work not shown in the contract documents and says the paperwork will follow. How should this direction be viewed?

options.A: It is binding; the contractor has an obligation to proceed with directed changes.
options.B: It is binding; once the inspector's daily report records the direction, it stands.
options.C: It is improper; only the A/E of record can direct the contractor to add work.
options.D: It is improper; only a contracting officer can execute a modification for it.
options.E: It is binding once the inspector confirms the direction in writing.
options.F: It is binding, because inspectors are authorities having jurisdiction.

questions.explanation: Only contracting officers acting within their authority can execute contract modifications, and other government personnel must not direct or encourage work that should be the subject of a modification. The obligation to proceed attaches to change orders from the contracting officer. An inspector's written confirmation or daily report, an inspector's role in code enforcement, or the A/E does not supply that authority.

questions.question: A contractor on a fixed-price federal construction contract receives a change order from the contracting officer but believes the government's proposed price for it is far too low. What course of action does industry guidance support?

options.A: Proceed with the changed work and, if no price is agreed, consider a claim.
options.B: Stop the affected work until a bilateral equitable adjustment has been agreed.
options.C: Proceed only up to the amount allowed by the Limitation of Funds clause.
options.D: Decline the change, since unilateral changes require the contractor's consent.
options.E: Proceed only after the TCO determines the price of the change.
options.F: Proceed only for the part covered by the independent government estimate.

questions.explanation: On receipt of a change order the contractor may not stop work and must comply; if the parties cannot agree on an equitable adjustment, the contractor may consider a claim. The Limitation of Cost and Limitation of Funds exceptions apply to cost-reimbursement or incrementally funded contracts, the Changes clause allows unilateral changes within scope, the TCO settles terminations rather than change pricing, and the estimate does not cap the duty to proceed.

questions.question: For a federal project's quality requirements, the contractor proposes language making its accredited third-party testing agency the sole inspecting party and stating that the government will not perform inspections of its own. This language is:

options.A: acceptable, provided the testing agency is independent and nationally accredited
options.B: acceptable, provided another federal agency approves the selected testing agency
options.C: unacceptable, because no contract may bar the government's own inspections
options.D: unacceptable, because only the A/E may perform inspections for the government
options.E: acceptable, provided warranty clauses cover the tested work
options.F: unacceptable, because only another federal agency may test the work

questions.explanation: One FAR Part 46 obligation is that no contract precludes the government from performing inspections. The testing agency's independence, another agency's approval, or warranty coverage cannot remove that right. Government inspection is not confined to the A/E, and using another agency's quality assurance services is an option when economical, not a requirement.

questions.question: Under FAR Part 46, when and under whose direction must contract quality assurance for a federal agency be conducted?

options.A: Before acceptance, by or under the direction of the A/E of record
options.B: Before acceptance, by or under the direction of government personnel
options.C: After acceptance, by or under the direction of the contractor's QC staff
options.D: After acceptance, during the warranty period, by the contracting officer
options.E: Before acceptance, by or under the direction of the testing agency
options.F: After acceptance, by or under the direction of the HCA

questions.explanation: Government contract quality assurance takes place before acceptance and is performed by or under the direction of government personnel. Handing it to the A/E, a testing agency, or the contractor's quality control staff, or deferring it until after acceptance, conflicts with that requirement.

questions.question: A federal agency has no quality assurance staff near a remote project site, but another federal agency keeps qualified inspectors nearby. Under FAR Part 46, the owner agency may:

options.A: delegate acceptance to the contractor's quality control manager if the agency certifies that manager
options.B: waive quality assurance if warranty clauses will cover the work after acceptance
options.C: defer quality assurance until after acceptance if its own staff cannot travel sooner
options.D: use the other agency's quality assurance and acceptance services if that is economical
options.E: leave acceptance to the local building official as the authority having jurisdiction
options.F: accept the work on the contractor's certification of compliance alone

questions.explanation: Agencies are to use other agencies' quality assurance and acceptance services when that is effective, economical, or otherwise in the government's interest. Quality assurance must still happen before acceptance, by or under the direction of government personnel, so shifting acceptance to the contractor or a local building official, relying on a certification or warranties, or deferring it is not supported.

questions.question: A specifier drafting a federal guide specification asks whether every federal contract must include a warranty. Under FAR 46.7, which statement is correct?

options.A: Warranty use is not mandatory; benefits must be commensurate with its cost.
options.B: Warranty use is mandatory for all construction contracts under FAR Part 36.
options.C: Warranty use is mandatory above the simplified acquisition threshold amount.
options.D: Warranty use is not mandatory; the contractor elects whether to provide one.
options.E: Warranty use is mandatory for supply contracts but not construction.
options.F: Warranty use is mandatory whenever the contract has a Changes clause.

questions.explanation: A warranty is not mandatory, and the benefits derived from it must be commensurate with its cost to the government. There is no Part 36, dollar-threshold, contract-type, or Changes-clause mandate, and the decision rests on the government's cost-benefit judgment rather than the contractor's election.

questions.question: A federal warranty clause cannot limit the government's rights under an inspection clause with respect to which of the following?

options.A: Patent defects, fraud, or negligent workmanship at acceptance
options.B: Latent defects, abuse, or damage from improper maintenance
options.C: Latent defects, fraud, or gross mistakes amounting to fraud
options.D: Patent defects, gross negligence, or mistakes found at acceptance
options.E: Latent defects, abuse, or gross mistakes amounting to fraud
