options.F: Patent defects, fraud, or gross mistakes amounting to fraud

questions.explanation: A federal warranty clause may not cut back the government's inspection-clause rights for latent defects, for fraud, or for gross mistakes amounting to fraud. Patent defects, negligent workmanship, and gross negligence are not on that list, and abuse or poor maintenance are conditions warranties commonly exclude rather than rights the rule preserves.

questions.question: A federal agency's specifier is editing warranty clauses for a construction contract and for a separate supply contract. Regarding the requirement that a warranty apply notwithstanding inspection and acceptance, industry guidance states that:

options.A: only the warranty clauses found in construction contracts must include it
options.B: warranty clauses must include it, except those in construction contracts
options.C: warranty clauses in every type of contract, without exception, must include it
options.D: no warranty clause may extend beyond acceptance by the agency
options.E: only warranty clauses in contracts above the simplified acquisition threshold must include it
options.F: only warranty clauses for services, not supplies or construction, must include it

questions.explanation: Warranty clauses must state that the warranty applies notwithstanding inspection, acceptance, or other contract terms, except for warranty clauses in construction contracts. The rule is therefore neither limited to construction nor universal, and it has no dollar threshold or services-only scope. Warranties also run past acceptance, for a stated period of time or use or until a specified event.

questions.question: A federal construction contractor has fallen so far behind that the contracting officer anticipates it will fail to perform, and partially terminates the contract for default. With respect to the undelivered work, the government:

options.A: owes the contractor's costs for services rendered up to the termination date
options.B: owes the contractor's costs once the TCO determines the amount that is due
options.C: may not terminate yet, since default requires actual rather than anticipated failure
options.D: owes none of the contractor's costs and may recover advance and progress payments
options.E: owes the contractor's costs once settlement is costed out on SF 1034
options.F: owes the contractor's costs but may keep the retainage on that work

questions.explanation: In a default termination, the government owes nothing toward what the contractor spent on undelivered work, and it can recover the advance and progress payments made for that work. Payment for services up to the effective date describes termination for convenience, settlement methods such as a TCO determination or SF 1034 do not create liability in default, and default may rest on anticipated as well as actual failure.

questions.question: A contracting officer determines that ending part of a federal construction contract is in the government's best interest, with no fault by the contractor. How is the termination effected and what does the government owe?

options.A: Notice of Termination with extent and effective date; services rendered until then
options.B: Notice of Termination stating extent and effective date; all work through completion
options.C: Bilateral modification signed by both parties; costs plus profit on terminated work
options.D: Unilateral change order deleting the work; full contract value of the deleted portion
options.E: Notice of Termination with extent and effective date; profit expected on the unperformed work
options.F: Notice of Termination for Default; nothing for the costs of undelivered work

questions.explanation: A termination for convenience is made by the contracting officer's Notice of Termination, which states how much of the work is ended and the effective date; the government then pays only for services rendered up to that date. It owes nothing for work through completion or for profit on unperformed work. A default termination applies only when the contractor fails to perform, which this stem rules out.

questions.question: After a termination for convenience on a federal construction contract, the termination contracting officer (TCO) must reach a settlement. Which approach does industry guidance say the TCO should take whenever possible?

options.A: Issue a unilateral determination of the amount owed the contractor
options.B: Negotiate a fair and prompt settlement with the contractor
options.C: Cost out the settlement on the prescribed standard form alone
options.D: Refer the settlement to the agency's board of contract appeals
options.E: Use a combination of all the listed settlement methods in every case
options.F: Have the A/E certify the amount owed to the contractor

questions.explanation: A federal termination may be settled by negotiated agreement, a TCO determination, costing out under SF 1034, or a combination, but the preferred course, whenever it can be done, is for the TCO to negotiate a prompt and fair settlement. A unilateral determination, costing out, or a combination are available but not the stated preference. An appeals board is not a settlement method, and the A/E has no part because a contracting officer administers federal contracts.

questions.question: Industry guidance lists costing out as one of the methods generally used to settle a federal contract termination. Under which standard form is this costing out performed?

options.A: Standard Form 25
options.B: Standard Form 30
options.C: Standard Form 1034
options.D: Standard Form 1442
options.E: Standard Form 24
options.F: Standard Form 25A

questions.explanation: Costing out under Standard Form (SF) 1034 is one of the termination settlement methods, alongside negotiated agreement, a TCO determination, or a combination of these. SF 1034 is the only form named for termination settlement; the other numbers are federal forms used for other purposes, not for settling a termination.

questions.question: Final payment on a federal construction contract was made in March 2023, but a related claim stayed open until June 2025. Under the federal access-to-records clause, what is the earliest date the contractor may dispose of the records required under the contract?

options.A: March 2026
options.B: June 2026
options.C: June 2028
options.D: March 2030
options.E: June 2025
options.F: March 2028

questions.explanation: The contractor must keep the required books, records, and reports for at least three years after final payment and after all pending matters are closed, so the clock starts at the later event. The claim closed in June 2025, so the period runs to June 2028. Counting from final payment gives March 2026, the records may not be discarded the moment the claim closes, and the other dates use the wrong start or period.

questions.question: Under the federal access-to-records clause, the contractor agrees to give access to its pertinent books and records to which group?

options.A: The owner, the A/E, the surety, or any of their duly authorized representatives
options.B: The contracting officer, the A/E, and the local building official only
options.C: The Comptroller General only, and only after a formal audit is opened
options.D: The owner, federal agencies, Comptroller General, or their authorized agents
options.E: The contracting officer and the contractor's surety only
options.F: The owner and the local authority having jurisdiction only

questions.explanation: The clause opens the contractor's books and records that bear directly on the contract to the owner, to the federal agencies, to the Comptroller General, and to any of their authorized representatives. The A/E, the surety, and local code officials are not given that right, and access is neither limited to the Comptroller General nor delayed until a formal audit opens.

questions.question: A federal auditor reviewing a contractor's records on a federal project asks to copy extracts of cost records and also requests records of the contractor's unrelated private-sector projects. The access clause:

options.A: covers only records directly pertinent to this contract, which may be excerpted
options.B: covers all of the contractor's business records, which may be excerpted
options.C: covers only records directly pertinent to this contract, examined but not copied
options.D: covers only the cost accounting system itself, examined but not transcribed
options.E: covers records of all the contractor's federal contracts, which may be excerpted
options.F: covers all of the contractor's business records, examined but not copied

questions.explanation: The contractor must give access to the books, documents, papers, and records directly pertinent to the specific contract so the government can audit and examine them and take excerpts or transcriptions. Records of the contractor's other work, federal or private, fall outside that scope, and the clause expressly allows excerpting and transcribing, not just examination.

questions.question: A U.S.-manufactured steel stair assembly is predominantly steel. Imported steel accounts for 7 percent of the assembly's cost, and domestic components make up 80 percent of total component cost. Under the Buy American test, the assembly:

options.A: passes, because domestic components exceed 55 percent of component cost
options.B: fails, because foreign iron and steel must be under 5 percent of its cost
options.C: passes, because U.S. manufacture is the only test for steel materials
options.D: fails, because iron and steel materials must be 100 percent domestic
options.E: passes, because foreign iron and steel stay under 10 percent of its cost
options.F: passes, because the Buy American test covers supplies, not construction materials

questions.explanation: A material that is wholly or predominantly iron or steel must be made in the United States, and its foreign iron and steel content must stay under 5 percent of its cost, so 7 percent fails. The 55 percent domestic-component test applies only to materials that are not predominantly iron or steel, the rule does not demand 100 percent domestic content, and it expressly restricts construction materials.

questions.question: A contractor on a federal project proposes a U.S.-manufactured light fixture that fails the domestic-component cost test. The fixture sells in large volumes commercially, but it would have to be altered to meet the project's requirements. Regarding the commercially available off-the-shelf (COTS) exception, industry guidance indicates that the fixture:

options.A: qualifies, because substantial commercial sales alone establish COTS status
options.B: qualifies, provided alteration costs stay below 55 percent of the item's cost
options.C: does not qualify, because COTS status is granted only on a contractor request
options.D: does not qualify, because the government must be able to buy it unmodified
options.E: qualifies, because U.S. manufacture alone satisfies the COTS exception
options.F: does not qualify, because large commercial sales rule out COTS status

questions.explanation: A COTS item must sell in large volumes on the commercial market and be available to the government without changes from its commercial form, so a fixture that must be altered fails. Sales volume or U.S. manufacture alone does not make an item COTS, and large commercial sales are a requirement, not a bar. The 55 percent figure belongs to the domestic-component test, and the request-and-review process covers foreign material.

questions.question: An A/E editing a federal agency guide specification finds paragraphs numbered 1.1, 1.1.1, 1.1.2, and 1.1.2.1. This legal-style numbering departs from which standard convention?

options.A: The PageFormat preferred alphanumeric paragraph arrangement
options.B: The SectionFormat three-part arrangement of section content
options.C: The MasterFormat numbers and titles of the current edition
options.D: The UniFormat elemental arrangement of project descriptions
options.E: The OmniClass table arrangement of construction information
options.F: The Uniform Drawing System arrangement of drawing sheets

questions.explanation: Most government guide specifications follow SectionFormat, but some agencies number paragraphs in a legal Arabic-numeral style instead of PageFormat's preferred alphanumeric arrangement. Paragraph numbering is a PageFormat matter; SectionFormat governs the parts of a section, MasterFormat governs section numbers and titles, and OmniClass and the Uniform Drawing System do not deal with specification paragraphs at all.

questions.question: A specifier moving from private-sector work to a federal agency project plans to state all shop drawing and maintenance information procedures only in Division 01. What agency requirement may conflict with that plan?

options.A: Placing those procedural requirements in agency contract clauses only
options.B: Placing those procedural requirements in drawing general notes sheets
options.C: Placing those procedural requirements in each technical section
options.D: Placing those procedural requirements in a separate Division 00 form
options.E: Placing those procedural requirements in the agreement form
options.F: Placing those procedural requirements in the supplementary conditions

questions.explanation: Some federal agencies want the procedures for shop drawings and maintenance information written into every technical section rather than stated once in Division 01. That is the requirement that may clash with the plan; nothing suggests the agency moves these procedures into contract clauses, the agreement, supplementary conditions, drawing notes, or a Division 00 form.

questions.question: While editing a federal agency's guide specifications, a specifier notices that several section numbers and titles do not match the current MasterFormat edition. Which explanation is consistent with industry guidance?

options.A: The agency's guide specifications are organized by UniFormat, not MasterFormat.
options.B: The agency's numbers can differ from the current edition, at times deliberately.
options.C: The agency's guide specifications must be renumbered to match the current edition.
options.D: The agency's numbers follow SectionFormat, which assigns its own section numbers.
options.E: The agency's guide specifications are organized by OmniClass, not MasterFormat.
options.F: The agency's numbers follow PageFormat, which lets each agency set section numbers.

questions.explanation: Most government agencies organize guide specifications by MasterFormat, but their numbers and titles may differ from the current edition, and agencies sometimes depart from it on purpose to meet unique requirements. Renumbering is not required; the A/E normally uses the agency's numbers. UniFormat and OmniClass are not the organizing system, and SectionFormat and PageFormat govern a section's arrangement and page layout, not section numbers.

questions.question: A federal agency retains an A/E for a new clinic but does not have the A/E prepare the entire solicitation package. Which split of preparation work does industry guidance describe for such cases?

options.A: A/E: procurement requirements and technical sections; agency: general requirements
options.B: A/E: contracting requirements and general requirements; agency: technical sections
options.C: A/E: procurement and contracting requirements; agency: Division 01 and technical
options.D: A/E: general requirements and technical sections; agency: procurement and contracting
options.E: A/E: contracting requirements and technical sections; agency: procurement and Division 01
options.F: A/E: procurement requirements and general requirements; agency: contracting and technical

questions.explanation: Federal agencies usually do not have the A/E prepare the whole solicitation package. A common split gives the A/E the general requirements (Division 01) and the technical sections, while the agency furnishes the procurement and contracting requirements. That is why the A/E must learn the agency's procedures and expect its Division 01 to differ from private-sector practice. The other splits hand front-end documents to the A/E or technical work to the agency.

questions.question: A specifier on a federal project looks for the document that serves the role AIA A201 serves on private-sector work. Under which title might that federal document appear?

options.A: Supplementary Conditions
options.B: Instructions to Bidders
options.C: Contract Clauses
options.D: Agreement Form
options.E: General Requirements
options.F: Procurement Requirements

questions.explanation: Federal contract conditions, the counterpart of A201 or EJCDC C-700, may carry titles such as Contract Clauses, General Provisions, General Standards, or Special Provisions, all based on the FAR. Supplementary Conditions modify general conditions, Instructions to Bidders and the other procurement requirements govern bidding, General Requirements is Division 01, and the agreement is a separate contract form.

questions.question: An A/E experienced with AIA-based private work assumes it will administer the construction phase of a federal project, including decisions on change orders. What does industry guidance indicate instead?

options.A: A contracting officer administers the procurement and construction phases.
options.B: The A/E administers construction, while the agency administers procurement.
options.C: The local authority having jurisdiction administers the construction phase.
options.D: The A/E administers both phases, subject to concurrence by the agency.
options.E: The A/E administers construction once the contracting officer awards the contract.
options.F: The agency's design reviewers administer construction, with the A/E advising.

questions.explanation: On federal projects a contracting officer, either a military officer or a civilian government employee, administers both the procurement and construction phases, so the A/E lacks its usual private-sector authority over matters such as change orders. Handing construction to the A/E after award or with agency concurrence, or to a local AHJ or the agency's reviewers, misstates that difference.

questions.question: A federal agency leases floor space in a privately owned office building, and an A/E is designing the tenant improvements. Which statement about building code jurisdiction is correct?

options.A: Only the federal agency has jurisdiction, as both owner and primary regulator.
options.B: Local authorities having jurisdiction have authority over the leased space.
options.C: Local authorities have authority only if the lease expressly names them.
options.D: Only other federal agencies have authority, since local codes never reach federal work.
options.E: Local authorities have authority only over the building's common areas.
options.F: The General Services Administration has sole authority over leased space.

questions.explanation: Local building code authorities lack jurisdiction on federal property, where other federal agencies may have authority instead. On private property leased by a federal agency, however, local AHJs do have jurisdiction over the space, with no condition tied to the lease terms and no limit to common areas. Answers giving the agency, the GSA, or other federal agencies sole authority misapply the federal-property rule.

questions.question: Federal guide specifications may impose stricter fire protection, security, and durability requirements than typical private-sector specifications. What condition helps explain this?

options.A: Federal agencies adopt local building codes as their maximum requirements.
options.B: Contractors' commercial insurers demand stricter criteria on federal work.
options.C: The FAR requires every federal building to exceed the local building code.
options.D: The federal government self-insures and buys no commercial property insurance.
options.E: Federal buildings are insured by the GSA, which sets stricter criteria.
options.F: Local building officials enforce stricter codes on federal property.

questions.explanation: The more stringent fire protection, safety, security, and durability provisions are tied to the government being self-insuring: it buys no commercial insurance for its buildings or their contents. Local codes are not a federal ceiling, local officials have no jurisdiction on federal property, no insurer drives the criteria, and federal specifications may exceed local codes without a FAR rule requiring it.

questions.question: Federal construction contracts may include provisions such as wage rates, affirmative action, and accessibility standards. What collective term does industry guidance use for this category of provisions?

options.A: Social value regulations
options.B: Special provisions
options.C: Public interest clauses
options.D: Equal opportunity clauses
options.E: Labor standards
options.F: Buy American provisions

questions.explanation: Requirements such as wage rates, affirmative action, small and minority- or women-owned business utilization, and accessibility standards are grouped as social value regulations. Labor standards and the Buy American provision are individual examples within that group, not its name, Special Provisions is one possible title for federal contract conditions, and the other two labels are not the term used.

questions.question: Which of the following does industry guidance cite as an example of a social value regulation in federal contracts?

options.A: Termination for convenience
options.B: Independent government estimates
options.C: Preference for American shipping
options.D: Access to records and reports
options.E: Sealed bid procedures
options.F: Warranty clauses

questions.explanation: Preference for American shipping is one of the social value examples, together with wage rates, environmental regulations, affirmative action, small and minority- or women-owned business utilization, labor standards, and accessibility standards. Termination for convenience, independent government estimates, sealed bidding, warranty clauses, and records access are FAR contracting mechanisms, not social value provisions.

questions.question: A specifier reviewing a federal project manual finds requirements for labor standards, use of small businesses, and domestically produced construction materials. What common purpose links these requirements?

options.A: Protecting the government's rights regarding defective work
options.B: Assisting particular industries and other special interest groups
options.C: Ensuring the government can audit the contractor's own costs
options.D: Preventing conflicts among the separate parts of the FAR
options.E: Fostering quality performance through warranties and inspection
options.F: Maximizing competition among standard products and current models

questions.explanation: Social value regulations, which include labor standards, small business utilization, and the Buy American provision, are meant to help particular industries and other special interest groups. Protecting against defective work, fostering quality, auditing costs, maximizing competition, and resolving FAR conflicts are the purposes of the warranty, inspection, records-access, brand-name, and Part 36 precedence provisions instead.

questions.question: A federal agency is adding a wing to a facility, and the new building automation components must match the existing system's manufacturer. How is the single brand procured?

options.A: The agency prepares a justification and approval document, with technical input from the A/E as needed.
options.B: The A/E names at least three acceptable products and adds a statement that other products are permitted.
options.C: The contractor proposes the matching brand later through the agency's substitution request procedures.
options.D: The A/E specifies performance only, and the contracting officer selects the brand after the contract award.
options.E: The A/E adds a salient-characteristics statement so that products of equal quality are permitted.
options.F: The A/E names the brand in Part 2 without any justification, since the match is required.

questions.explanation: Extending or connecting to an existing system is a stated exception to the federal ban on brand names: the agency documents the one-brand purchase with a justification and approval, and the A/E may have to supply technical input for it. Listing three products or describing salient characteristics belongs to other exceptions that admit nonmatching products, and naming the brand with no justification, or leaving it to substitutions or post-award selection, skips that procedure.

questions.question: A specifier writing a federal resilient flooring section names two manufacturers' products and adds a statement that products of other manufacturers may also be used. Which change would bring this listing within one of the federal exceptions that permit brand names?

options.A: Delete the statement allowing other manufacturers, since two named products are sufficient.
options.B: Keep both names and attach a justification and approval document supporting the two choices.
options.C: Name a third acceptable product and keep the statement permitting other products.
options.D: Reduce the listing to one brand and identify it by model number as a proprietary requirement.
options.E: Keep both names and require the contractor to propose a third product after award.
options.F: Keep both names and add the model number of each listed product to the listing.

questions.explanation: Named products are allowed in federal specifications when at least three acceptable products are listed and the text states that other manufacturers' products are permitted, so adding a third name while keeping the open statement meets that exception. Deleting the open statement, adding model numbers, or leaving the third name to the contractor does not; a justification and approval belongs to matching an existing system, and a single-product requirement is reserved for when no other product can do the job.

questions.question: A federal agency buys a particular manufacturer's brand-name lighting fixture from a multiple-award contract that offers products from many sources. When is the justification for the brand-name item required?

options.A: Before the multiple-award contract is awarded
options.B: When the order for the item is placed
options.C: When the item is first listed on the contract
options.D: When the contract's next option period begins
options.E: When the requirements contract is awarded
options.F: When the item is delivered and accepted

questions.explanation: On a multiple-award contract, the need for one manufacturer's item is decided at the time of the order, so the justification comes at order placement. Completing it before award is the rule for a single-source requirements contract, whose brand need is known before that contract is let. A brand-name item's presence on a multiple-award contract does not make it the only such item available, so its listing is not the trigger, and option periods and delivery play no part.

questions.question: An A/E concludes that only one manufacturer's fire alarm control unit, identified by brand name and model number, can perform a required function on a federal project. How is this proprietary requirement handled?

options.A: The agency's contracting authority writes the justification, and the A/E approves its inclusion.
options.B: The A/E includes the unit without any justification as long as the phrase "or equal" is added.
options.C: The contractor justifies the unit in a submittal, and the A/E accepts or rejects the request.
options.D: The A/E provides a technical justification, and the agency approves or disapproves its inclusion.
options.E: The A/E lists the unit with two other acceptable products, and no justification is needed.
options.F: The A/E states only the unit's salient characteristics, and the agency need not review them.

questions.explanation: A single-product proprietary specification is an exception on federal work, used only when no other product can do the task: the A/E must furnish a technical justification, and the agency decides whether the requirement goes into the specifications. The A/E does not approve its own requirement; an or-equal phrase, a three-product list, or a salient-characteristics statement would admit other products; and the decision is not left to contractor submittals.

questions.question: Which list puts the four classifications of reference standards for government construction in their order of preferred usage, most preferred first?

options.A: Private-sector standards, CIDs, federal specifications, military specifications
options.B: Federal specifications, CIDs, private-sector standards, military specifications
options.C: Private-sector standards, federal specifications, CIDs, military specifications
options.D: CIDs, private-sector standards, military specifications, federal specifications
options.E: Private-sector standards, military specifications, CIDs, federal specifications
options.F: CIDs, federal specifications, private-sector standards, military specifications

questions.explanation: Government construction ranks reference standards in this order of preference: private-sector standards first, then commercial item descriptions (CIDs), then federal specifications, with military specifications last. Swapping CIDs and federal specifications is the most tempting slip; the current policy of replacing federal specifications with private-sector standards or with CIDs fits that ranking.

questions.question: A specifier cites a federal specification in PART 2 of a section by its document designation only. What additional information is usually necessary in that citation?

options.A: The issue date of the GSA Federal Supply Service index that lists it
options.B: The particular class or grade of the product within that specification
options.C: The equivalent military specification type and quality designation
options.D: The commercial item description that the specification will replace
options.E: The Defense Department office that issued the federal specification
options.F: The salient characteristics of an acceptable brand-name product

questions.explanation: Most federal specifications are classification documents that grade products by their physical and functional characteristics, so a reference usually must state which class or grade is wanted. An equivalent MIL-SPEC, a replacement CID, an index date, an issuing office, or brand-name characteristics does not tell the contractor which level of the referenced product is required; federal specifications come from the GSA in any case, not the Defense Department.

questions.question: Which pairing of a government reference document with the body that issues it is correct?

options.A: Military specifications, issued by the GSA Federal Supply Service
options.B: Federal specifications, issued by the US Department of Defense
options.C: Federal standards (FED-STD), issued by ANSI for federal agencies
options.D: Commercial item descriptions, issued and controlled by the GSA
options.E: Military specifications, issued by NIST for the defense agencies
options.F: Commercial item descriptions, issued by ASTM International

questions.explanation: The GSA issues and controls CIDs, the GSA Federal Supply Service issues federal specifications and standards, and the Department of Defense issues military specifications. The distractors swap those issuers: ANSI and ASTM are private-sector standards developers rather than sources of federal documents, and NIST supplies voluntary product standards, not military specifications.

questions.question: While editing an agency guide section, an A/E finds a referenced federal specification that has not been updated in years; a current ASTM standard covers the same product and meets the agency's needs. What is the best course?

options.A: Keep the federal specification, because agency guide text always takes precedence.
options.B: Cite both documents and let the contractor choose which one will govern the work.
options.C: Use the ASTM reference instead, provided the owner has no objection.
options.D: Replace it with a military specification that covers the same type of product.
options.E: Replace it with a commercial item description, since CIDs rank first in preference.
options.F: Delete the reference and identify the product by brand name and model instead.

questions.explanation: Government policy favors private-sector standards when they exist and meet the agency's needs, and outdated federal specifications should not be used when a more current standard is available, provided the owner has no objection. Keeping the stale document ignores that policy, letting the contractor pick creates ambiguity, CIDs rank second rather than first, military specifications rank last, and federal agencies generally prohibit brand names.

questions.question: On a federal project, the A/E's mechanical and electrical consultants will produce their sections from separate software with different fonts. Why should the A/E raise this when negotiating its fee?

options.A: The agency may require one typeface for all sections and reject a mixed set.
options.B: The agency may require each consultant to submit its sections under a separate contract.
options.C: The agency may require SpecsIntact, which will not accept sections from other software.
options.D: The agency may limit each discipline to a fixed number of copies for each review.
options.E: The agency may require its contract number to appear in each section.
options.F: The agency may require redlining on electronic media rather than paper.

questions.explanation: One fee-negotiation item is whether the agency will insist on a single typeface for every section, because printing produced by different disciplines may be refused as a mixture. Separate contracts and SpecsIntact rejecting outside sources are not described, and copy counts, contract-number placement, and electronic redlining are separate matters that have nothing to do with mixed fonts.

questions.question: A federal project's guide sections cite dozens of criteria manuals and industry standards that the A/E's library lacks. Which fee-negotiation question addresses this?

options.A: Whether the contractor must furnish copies of the standards at the preconstruction meeting
options.B: Whether the references can be deleted from each section to avoid any acquisition cost
options.C: Whether the agency will furnish copies or reimburse the cost of acquiring them
options.D: Whether the A/E may cite older editions already on hand to avoid purchasing new ones
options.E: Whether the agency's page format will require additional formatting work
options.F: Who develops the sections that are not included in the agency's guides

questions.explanation: One fee-negotiation item asks whether reference documents will have to be obtained and, if so, whether the agency will supply copies or reimburse their cost. Page format and who writes missing sections are separate items that do not address the library gap, and shifting the burden to the contractor, deleting references, or relying on outdated editions are not listed and would weaken the specifications.

questions.question: During fee negotiation, an A/E asks a federal agency whether the agency will furnish the front-end documents or the A/E must write them. What related question should the A/E also consider?

options.A: Whether the agency's legal counsel will sign the front-end documents before bidding
options.B: What effect the answer will have on preparing the rest of the contract documents
options.C: How many bidders the agency expects will obtain the front-end documents
options.D: Whether the front-end documents will follow the AIA or the EJCDC document family
options.E: Whether the agency will reimburse printing of the bid sets for bidders
options.F: Whether the front-end documents will be bound as a separate volume

questions.explanation: The question of who writes the front-end documents comes paired with a follow-up: what effect that answer will have on preparing the rest of the contract documents, since the split of that work changes the A/E's effort. Legal sign-off, bidder counts, bid-set printing, binding, and the choice of document family are not items on the fee-negotiation list.

questions.question: Under typical federal agency policies, how is work on the construction documents divided between the A/E and the agency?

options.A: The agency tailors the guide specifications for Divisions 01-49; the A/E adds procurement and contracting requirements.
options.B: The A/E tailors only Division 01; the agency tailors Divisions 02-49 and adds procurement and contracting requirements.
options.C: The agency's contracting officer tailors Division 01; the A/E tailors Divisions 02-49 and prepares the procurement forms.
options.D: The A/E tailors the guide specifications for Divisions 01-49; the agency adds procurement and contracting requirements.
options.E: The A/E tailors Divisions 01-49 and also writes the procurement and contracting requirements for agency review.
options.F: The agency tailors Divisions 01-49 and adds procurement and contracting requirements; the A/E prepares drawings only.

questions.explanation: Typically the A/E tailors the federal guide specifications for Divisions 01 through 49 to the project, and the agency then incorporates its procurement and contracting requirements before issuing the project for procurement. Reversing those roles, giving the A/E the front-end documents too, or leaving it only the drawings contradicts that pattern, and Division 01 is not split off for the contracting officer. Individual agencies vary, but this is the general pattern.

questions.question: An A/E new to federal work asks where the procurement and contracting documents and forms for an agency project originate. Which answer is accurate?

options.A: Each agency publishes its own, or joins other agencies to publish common ones.
options.B: The FAR prescribes one set of forms that every agency must use without change.
options.C: The A/E adapts its standard AIA or EJCDC forms to suit each agency's policies.
options.D: The GSA publishes a single standard set that all construction agencies must use.
options.E: The contracting officer drafts new ones for each project directly from the FAR.
options.F: NIBS publishes one set through the WBDG that all agencies must use.

questions.explanation: Every federal agency that builds has its own policies and procedures, and each issues its own procurement and contracting documents and forms or joins other agencies to publish shared ones. A single mandatory FAR, GSA, or WBDG form set, fresh drafting by the contracting officer for each project, and the A/E's own commercial forms do not match that practice.

questions.question: The A/E has finished tailoring the federal guide specifications for Divisions 01-49. When are the procurement and contracting requirements incorporated into the construction documents?

options.A: After bids are opened and before the contract is awarded
options.B: At the 30 percent review, before the A/E edits Division 01
options.C: Before the agency issues the project for procurement
options.D: After procurement closes, when the conformed set is assembled
options.E: At the preconstruction conference after award
options.F: When the notice to proceed is issued

questions.explanation: After the A/E tailors the guide specifications, the agency incorporates the procurement and contracting requirements into the construction documents before it issues the project for procurement. Waiting until bids are opened, until award, or until the preconstruction conference or notice to proceed would leave bidders without those requirements, and the step is not tied to an early design review.

questions.question: What reason have various groups given for recommending uniform development of federal master guide specifications?

options.A: To eliminate the need for A/Es to edit guide specifications for each project
options.B: To cut duplicated effort and costs for contractors, A/Es, and manufacturers
options.C: To replace private-sector reference standards with uniform federal standards
options.D: To require every agency to adopt a single commercial master guide system
options.E: To let each agency meet its own unique needs independently
options.F: To keep section numbers matched to the current MasterFormat

questions.explanation: Agencies first built master guide specifications independently to meet their own needs, and uniform development was urged to minimize duplicated effort and make doing business with the government easier and cheaper for contractors, A/Es, manufacturers, and others. Independent development is the problem it answers, guide specifications still must be edited for each project, government policy favors private-sector standards, and no single commercial system or MasterFormat match is mandated.

questions.question: A specifier asks why most federal agency specifications can now be obtained online. What development made this possible?

options.A: The GSA Federal Supply Service's online specifications catalog
options.B: NASA's free SpecsIntact download from the Kennedy Space Center
options.C: A FAR requirement that agencies post all their guide specifications
options.D: The advent of NIBS and the WBDG Federal Facility Criteria
options.E: The Unified Facilities Criteria issued by the Department of Defense
options.F: The 1995 act requiring agencies to use private-sector standards

questions.explanation: The arrival of the National Institute of Building Sciences and the WBDG Federal Facility Criteria put most agency specifications online. SpecsIntact is editing software rather than the clearinghouse, the Unified Facilities Criteria are one set of documents reached through the WBDG, the GSA Federal Supply Service does not host agency guides, and neither a FAR rule nor the 1995 standards act made them available online.

questions.question: Which federal agency uses a commercially available master guide specification system for its projects?

options.A: General Services Administration (GSA)
options.B: Naval Facilities Engineering Command (NAVFAC)
options.C: National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)
options.D: Department of the Army, Corps of Engineers (COE)
options.E: Veterans Administration (VA)
options.F: Federal Highway Administration (FHWA)

questions.explanation: Among the federal agencies, the GSA is the one that relies on a commercially available master guide specification system. The Corps of Engineers and NAVFAC publish the Unified Facilities Guide Specifications jointly with other agencies, and NASA created SpecsIntact; neither they nor the VA or the highway administration are the agency noted for using a commercial product.

questions.question: What was the origin of the WBDG Federal Facility Criteria?

options.A: It began as the Unified Facilities Criteria, prompted by conflicts among Defense Department design manuals.
options.B: It began as the SpecsIntact system, prompted by a NASA study of errors in editing project specifications.
options.C: It began as the Construction Criteria Base, prompted by problems publishing federal guide specifications.
options.D: It began as a GSA Federal Supply Service catalog, prompted by a study of outdated federal standards.
options.E: It began as the EPA's Federal Green Construction Guide, prompted by sustainability mandates.
options.F: It began as the UFGS master list, prompted by a USACE review of district guide specifications.

questions.explanation: The WBDG Federal Facility Criteria started as the Construction Criteria Base, which grew out of a study of difficulties in publishing federal master guide specifications for construction. The Unified Facilities Criteria, the UFGS, and the EPA's green guide are documents reached through it, SpecsIntact is NASA's editing software, and the GSA Federal Supply Service issues federal specifications, so none of these is its origin.

questions.question: Which organization joins USACE, NAVFAC, and NASA in jointly publishing the Unified Facilities Guide Specifications (UFGS)?

options.A: General Services Administration (GSA)
options.B: Air Force Civil Engineer Center (AFCEC)
options.C: National Institute of Building Sciences (NIBS)
options.D: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
options.E: US Access Board
options.F: Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)

questions.explanation: The US Army Corps of Engineers, NAVFAC, the Air Force Civil Engineer Center, and NASA jointly publish the UFGS included in the WBDG Federal Facility Criteria. GSA, NIBS, NIST, the Access Board, and the EPA have other roles (NIST supplies voluntary product standards, the Access Board guidelines, and the EPA a green construction guide through the WBDG), but none is a UFGS publisher.

questions.question: Which pairing of an agency with a document it makes available through the WBDG Federal Facility Criteria is correct?

options.A: NIST: Standards for the Treatment of Historic Properties
options.B: NPS: Energy Star manuals for federal buildings
options.C: US Access Board: Unified Facilities Criteria and handbooks
options.D: EPA: Federal Green Construction Guide for Specifiers
options.E: NIST: Federal Green Construction Guide for Specifiers
options.F: DHS: Unified Facilities Criteria and design guidance

questions.explanation: The EPA's Federal Green Construction Guide for Specifiers is among the documents available through the WBDG Federal Facility Criteria. The other pairings are scrambled: historic-treatment standards come from the National Park Service, Energy Star manuals from the EPA, the Unified Facilities Criteria from DOD, and FEMA guides from DHS, while NIST supplies voluntary product standards and the US Access Board guidelines and standards.

questions.question: A small A/E firm with its first UFGS-based project asks how to obtain SpecsIntact. Which statement is accurate?

options.A: It is licensed by USACE to firms holding a federal design contract.
options.B: It is sold through the GSA Federal Supply Service with UFGS updates.
options.C: It is a free download from NASA's Kennedy Space Center website.
options.D: It is issued by NIBS only to registered WBDG Federal Facility users.
options.E: It is bundled with NAVFAC design contracts at no extra cost.
options.F: It is a licensed module of the GSA's commercial master system.

questions.explanation: NASA created SpecsIntact, and it can be downloaded free from the NASA Kennedy Space Center website. It is not a USACE license, a NAVFAC contract item, a GSA product or module, or a NIBS registration benefit, even though UFGS sections are formatted for editing within it.

questions.question: How does SpecsIntact handle the editor's notes in a UFGS section?

options.A: It embeds the notes in the section body and can delete them during printing.
options.B: It keeps the notes in a separate companion file linked to each paragraph number.
options.C: It shows the notes only in its online help, never in the section text.
options.D: It requires the user to delete the notes manually before final processing.
options.E: It converts the notes into a separate submittal list for reviewers.
options.F: It moves the notes to a closing article at the end of each section.

questions.explanation: SpecsIntact places notes within the body of the specification section and includes a feature that removes them when the section is printed. Notes are therefore not stored in a separate file, moved to the end, confined to help screens, or turned into a submittal list, and manual deletion is unnecessary because note deletion is one of the program's listed features.

questions.question: An A/E evaluating SpecsIntact for a UFGS project wants to know what the software does. Which pair of capabilities is among SpecsIntact's features?

options.A: Automatic MasterFormat section renumbering and cost reports
options.B: Reference verification and testing requirement reports
options.C: Spell checking and product substitution request tracking
options.D: Drawing cross-referencing and keynote list generation
options.E: Bid tabulation and contract award tracking
options.F: Product data sheet libraries and cost estimating

questions.explanation: SpecsIntact's features include verification that the references at the front of each section are cited and generation of testing requirement reports, along with submittal lists, paragraph renumbering, and note deletion. Cost reports and estimating, MasterFormat section renumbering, substitution tracking, bid tabulation, product libraries, and drawing keynote lists are not among them.

questions.question: An A/E is about to sign its first design contract with a federal agency. Which three determinations about the agency's master guide specifications should the A/E make before entering into the contract?

options.A: Whether they follow MasterFormat, whether they cite current standards, and who maintains them
options.B: Whether they are proprietary, whether reviewers accept edits, and when they were last revised
options.C: Whether they cover renovation work, how long they run, and whether the A/E may reformat them
options.D: Whether they exist, whether their use is required, and whether editable copies are free
options.E: Whether they are online, whether they use SpecsIntact, and whether reviews are required
options.F: Whether they use SectionFormat, whether they need editing, and who writes the front end

questions.explanation: Before contracting, the A/E should find out whether the agency has master guide specifications, whether using them is mandatory, and whether editable copies come at no charge. The other combinations raise matters that come up later in fee negotiation, editing, or review, or not at all, and none matches those three threshold determinations.

questions.question: Which variable is chief among those affecting how long it takes an A/E to produce project specifications from a federal agency's guide specifications?

options.A: The number of review submittals the agency requires during design
options.B: The number of drawing sheets in the agency's construction documents
options.C: The A/E's familiarity with the agency's required methods of specifying
options.D: Whether the agency distributes its guide specifications electronically
options.E: The page format and typeface the agency's written instructions require
options.F: The number of guide sections longer than 100 pages in the agency's master

questions.explanation: The chief variable is the A/E's degree of familiarity with the agency's prescribed specifying methods, such as heavy reliance on reference standards and generic descriptions instead of brand names. The number of reviews, page format and typeface, and the form of the guide specifications are fee-negotiation or editing considerations, and section length and drawing count are not named, so none of these is the chief factor.

questions.question: An agency's guide specifications assign section numbers and titles that depart widely from the latest MasterFormat edition. What is the A/E usually expected to do?

options.A: Renumber every section to the current MasterFormat edition
options.B: Follow the numbering and titling the agency defines
options.C: Use the numbering from the A/E's own office master guide
options.D: Use MasterFormat for new sections and agency numbers for others
options.E: Ask the contracting officer to renumber the sections for the project
options.F: Use UniFormat element numbers in place of the section numbers

questions.explanation: Agency guide specifications may depart from standard practice and the current MasterFormat, and when they do, the A/E is usually expected to use the agency's numbers and titles. Converting to MasterFormat, substituting the office master's scheme or UniFormat, mixing systems, or handing renumbering to the contracting officer departs from what the agency requires.

questions.question: After finishing edits to an agency guide section, the A/E notices the index at the front of the section. Unless the agency requires otherwise, what does industry guidance say to do with it?

options.A: Keep it and update its page references
options.B: Move it into the project manual's table of contents
options.C: Convert it into a list of the section's editing notes
options.D: Delete it from the section
options.E: Replace it with the section's list of references
options.F: Move it to the end of the section

questions.explanation: The index at the front of each section should be deleted once editing is finished, unless the agency instructs otherwise; SpecsIntact can generate an index electronically if one is wanted. Keeping and updating it, moving it to the end or into the table of contents, or turning it into notes or a references list is not the practice.

questions.question: An agency requires paper submittal of marked-up guide sections, and a junior specifier plans to mark retained text with a highlighter. Why should this be avoided?

options.A: Some highlighting reproduces as solid black on photocopies.
options.B: Agency reviewers reserve highlighting for their own comments.
options.C: Highlighted text is read as deleted text by most agency reviewers.
options.D: Highlighting is reserved for bracketed choices the A/E must make.
options.E: SpecsIntact strips highlighted text when it prints the section.
options.F: Agency reviewers accept markups made only in red ink.

questions.explanation: A highlighter should not be used on review copies because some highlighting photocopies as solid black and hides the text. The other reasons are invented; the related guidance is that handwritten changes be dark enough to scan clearly and that the agency's rules on electronic markup or redlining be followed.

questions.question: When editing the list of references at the beginning of an agency guide section, which approach follows industry guidance?

options.A: Keep every standard on the master list so that the agency's reference record stays complete
options.B: Keep all listed standards but label the ones no longer cited as for information only
options.C: List only standards still cited, each with its current issue date unless told otherwise
options.D: List only standards still cited, omitting dates so that the latest edition always governs
options.E: List every standard cited anywhere in the project manual in each section
options.F: Move the references list to Division 01 and delete it from each section

questions.explanation: Trim the references list to the standards that remain in the edited text, and date each one with its current issue or revision unless an older edition is needed for a specific reason or the agency says otherwise. Keeping uncited standards, with or without labels, listing the whole manual's standards, or moving the list out of the section contradicts that instruction, and dropping dates removes edition control.

questions.question: A federal project needs a section for which the agency has no guide specification, and the A/E's office master version names a single manufacturer. What is the best course?

options.A: Insert the office master section unchanged, keeping the A/E's own format, numbering, and named product
options.B: Prepare a new section in agency format and numbering, open to competition among current standard products
options.C: Ask the agency to write the section, because agencies are obligated to furnish all of the technical sections
options.D: Omit the section and describe the work in general notes on the drawings to avoid naming any product
options.E: Borrow another agency's guide section, keeping that agency's format, numbering, and product names
options.F: Keep the named manufacturer and have the agency prepare a justification and approval for it

questions.explanation: When no agency guide specification exists, the A/E prepares the section from other resources, conforming to the agency's format and numbering, avoiding proprietary or restrictive requirements, and basing it on standard products and current models. Reusing the single-manufacturer office section or another agency's format violates those requirements, a justification and approval is for matching an existing system, shifting the work to the agency contradicts the A/E's responsibility, and dropping the section leaves work unspecified.

questions.question: At which design-phase milestones does a federal agency often want reviews of the A/E's documents?

options.A: 30, 60, and 90 percent, plus final completion
options.B: 35, 65, and 95 percent, plus final completion
options.C: 25, 50, and 75 percent, plus final completion
options.D: 30, 50, and 90 percent, plus final completion
options.E: 30, 60, and 95 percent, plus final completion
options.F: 50, 75, and 90 percent, plus final completion

questions.explanation: Agencies commonly want design reviews at 30, 50, and 90 percent, followed by a final completion review, with specific specification content expected at each stage. The other sequences are plausible-sounding intervals that do not match that common pattern.

questions.question: For the 30 percent design review on a federal project, which submittal matches one of the options industry guidance describes for that stage?

options.A: A marked-up copy of the agency guide specifications with unneeded pages deleted
options.B: One section completed in final form to show what the finished set will look like
options.C: A list of sections generated from the agency's master list of section titles
options.D: A typed rough draft of every specification section needed for the project
options.E: A processed copy of all the specifications in final draft form
options.F: A typed copy of the specifications in final form in electronic format

questions.explanation: At 30 percent, the A/E provides either a list of sections drawn from the agency's master list of section titles or outline specifications identifying the products. A marked-up guide specification and a typed rough draft are 50 percent options, a processed final draft or a single section finished as a model are 90 percent options, and a typed final copy in electronic form is for the final review.

questions.question: At the 90 percent review, an A/E will resubmit its marked-up copy of the agency guide specification. What should this resubmittal contain?

options.A: Every page of the guide, even pages that may be deleted later
options.B: The pages being kept, with any deleted pages removed from the set
options.C: The paragraphs revised in response to 50 percent comments
options.D: The sections reviewers flagged, with the written responses
options.E: The kept pages retyped in final form, with the markups removed
options.F: A list of the deleted pages in place of the pages themselves

questions.explanation: A 90 percent resubmittal of the marked-up guide specification covers the complete document with all of its pages, even those that may eventually be dropped. Removing or merely listing deleted pages, retyping only the kept pages, sending only revised paragraphs, or limiting the set to flagged sections would not give reviewers the complete marked-up document expected at that milestone.

questions.question: Reviewers return no comments on the final typed electronic copy of a federal project's specifications. What happens next?

options.A: The A/E advertises the project for bids.
options.B: The agency advertises the project for bids.
options.C: The A/E makes a compliance-check submittal.
options.D: The agency schedules another 90 percent review.
options.E: The A/E schedules a preconstruction conference.
options.F: The contracting officer issues a notice to proceed.

questions.explanation: If reviewers have no comments on the final electronic copy, the agency then advertises the project for bids. Advertising is the agency's act rather than the A/E's, a compliance check follows significant changes rather than a clean final review, an earlier milestone need not be repeated, and a preconstruction conference and notice to proceed come only after a contract is awarded.

questions.question: On a federal project, the fire protection reviewer and the HVAC reviewer issue comments that conflict with each other. Who should resolve the conflict?

options.A: The A/E's project specifier
options.B: The agency's contracting officer
options.C: The agency's project manager
options.D: The lead architectural reviewer
options.E: The A/E's fire protection consultant
options.F: The local fire marshal as the AHJ

questions.explanation: Separate discipline reviewers can produce conflicting requirements, and the agency's project manager should resolve them. The A/E and its consultants must respond to comments but do not arbitrate between agency reviewers, the contracting officer and any one discipline's reviewer are not given that role, and local officials have no jurisdiction on federal property.

questions.question: A plumbing reviewer's comment on a federal project is minor, and the A/E has already made the requested change. How should the A/E respond to the comment?

options.A: Not at all, since the revised documents show the change
options.B: Orally, at the next scheduled review meeting
options.C: In writing, but only if the A/E disagrees with it
options.D: In writing, usually on a form the agency provides
options.E: By noting the change in the next submittal's cover letter
options.F: In writing, but only if the agency marks the comment as critical

questions.explanation: Every reviewer comment needs a written response, usually on a form the agency provides, however minor the comment is and whether or not the A/E agrees. Relying on the revised documents or a cover letter, answering orally, or responding only to disputed or critical comments falls short of that requirement.

questions.question: After incorporating review comments, the A/E has made significant changes to a federal project's drawings and specifications. What is usually required?

options.A: A compliance-check submittal
options.B: A repeat of the 30 percent review
options.C: A new A/E fee negotiation
options.D: A justification and approval document
options.E: A new set of 50 percent review copies
options.F: A contract modification by the contracting officer

questions.explanation: A compliance-check submittal is usually required after significant changes. Restarting the review cycle at 30 or 50 percent is not called for, fee renegotiation is not automatic, a contract modification belongs to the construction contract, and a justification and approval document relates to brand-name procurement rather than design review.

questions.question: A federal agency requires printed review copies of the contract documents to go to several reviewing offices. How is responsibility for distributing them determined?

options.A: By the agency alone, because review copies become government records
options.B: By the terms of the agreement, so it should be addressed in negotiation
options.C: By the A/E alone, because it produces and prints the review documents
options.D: By the FAR, which assigns review distribution to the contracting officer
options.E: By the contracting officer, after the design contract is signed
options.F: By the agency's project manager at each review milestone

questions.explanation: Depending on the terms of their agreement, the job of sending out review copies may fall to the A/E or to the agency, and because the task affects time and expense it should be settled during negotiation. Assigning it automatically to one party, to the contracting officer under the FAR or otherwise, or to the project manager is not supported.

questions.question: A local military facility contracts directly with a local A/E for a building project that is not subject to USACE district jurisdiction. Which specifications might the A/E use?

options.A: The installation's own guide specification version, or the A/E's office master
options.B: The USACE Washington, DC, guide specifications, used without any local modification
options.C: The USACE district office's supplemented and modified guide specifications
options.D: The WBDG Federal Facility Criteria masters, used in place of agency guides
options.E: The NAVFAC guide specifications, required on all military work
options.F: A commercial master system chosen by the contracting officer

questions.explanation: When a local military facility hires a local A/E directly for work outside USACE district control, the facility may use its own version of the guide specifications or let the A/E use its office masters. The Washington-published guides and the district-supplemented versions describe the normal USACE route, not this direct-contract case, no other agency's guides or commercial system is mandated, and the WBDG distributes jointly published guides rather than replacing them.

questions.question: An A/E accustomed to private-sector work plans to adapt its office masters, which list three named manufacturers per product, for its first federal agency project. Given the policies most federal agencies share, what should the A/E expect?

options.A: Three named manufacturers plus an "or equal" clause are the norm
options.B: Named manufacturers are acceptable in Part 2 if they are listed alphabetically
options.C: Naming manufacturers or brands is barred except in special circumstances
options.D: Named manufacturers are required wherever the agency guide is silent
options.E: Named manufacturers are acceptable if each is identified by model number
options.F: Named manufacturers are allowed if the A/E signs its own justification

questions.explanation: Most federal agencies share the policy that the A/E may not name manufacturers or brands for products except in special circumstances. The private-sector habit of three named products with an or-equal clause does not carry over by default, and alphabetical order, model numbers, or a justification the A/E approves itself do not lift the ban. Nothing makes naming mandatory where a guide is silent.

questions.question: An A/E is preparing the project manual for a federal agency. Given the policies most federal agencies share, how are procurement and contracting requirements most often handled?

options.A: The A/E drafts them from its office masters for agency review
options.B: The agency issues them separately and keeps them out of the manual
options.C: The A/E adapts AIA or EJCDC forms to meet federal requirements
options.D: The agency issues its own and requires them in the manual
options.E: The contracting officer drafts them after the A/E's final review
options.F: The A/E prepares them from FAR clauses for each project

questions.explanation: Most federal agencies issue their own procurement and contracting requirements and require that they be included in the project manual. The A/E therefore does not draft them from office masters or FAR clauses or adapt private-sector AIA or EJCDC forms, they are not drafted after the final review, and they are not kept outside the manual.

questions.question: At a kickoff meeting, an owner suggests that a performance bond and the contractor's insurance are interchangeable, since each shields the owner from occurrences beyond its control. How should the A/E characterize the two?

options.A: Seemingly similar purposes, and essentially the same protection method
options.B: Seemingly similar purposes, but very different protection methods
options.C: Clearly different purposes, but essentially the same protection method
options.D: Clearly different purposes, and very different protection methods
options.E: Identical purposes and methods, so either may replace the other
options.F: Unrelated purposes, since bonds protect only the contractor

questions.explanation: Bonds and insurance may look as if they serve similar purposes, since both protect a party against acts and events largely outside its control, but their methods of protection are very different, so they are not interchangeable. Calling the methods the same or the purposes clearly different contradicts that view, and construction bonds protect the owner, not only the contractor.

questions.question: A specifier is sorting bond requirements within a project manual. How are the three basic construction bond types classified?

options.A: Bid bond as a procurement requirement; performance and payment bonds as contract documents
options.B: Bid and performance bonds as procurement requirements; payment bond as a contract document
options.C: Bid bond as a contract document; performance and payment bonds as procurement requirements
options.D: All three as procurement requirements until the owner-contractor agreement is executed
options.E: All three as contract documents once the bids have been received
options.F: Bid and payment bonds as procurement requirements; performance bond as a contract document

questions.explanation: The bid bond, when used, is a procurement requirement, while performance and payment bonds are classified as contract documents. The bid bond secures the bid itself, whereas performance and payment bonds back the contractor's obligations under the contract. The other choices move one or more of the bonds into the wrong category or tie the classification to the timing of bids.

questions.question: An owner wants a two-year maintenance bond on a new roofing system, in addition to the standard bonds for the project. Where are bonds of this kind generally called for?

options.A: In the instructions for procurement, alongside the bid bond
options.B: In the supplementary conditions, with the performance bond
options.C: In the individual specification section covering that work
options.D: In the owner-contractor agreement, with the payment bond
options.E: In the general conditions, with the warranty provisions
options.F: In the bid form, listed as a bid alternate

questions.explanation: Other bonds, such as warranty or maintenance bonds, are generally called for by the individual specification sections for the work they cover, unlike the three basic bonds. The procurement instructions address bid bonds and the supplementary conditions address performance and payment bonds, so neither is the usual home for a work-specific maintenance bond, nor are the general conditions, the agreement, or the bid form.

questions.question: A surety's premium for performance and payment bonds is based on the bonded contract amount and generally falls within what range?

options.A: Between 1 and 5 percent
options.B: Between 2 and 10 percent
options.C: Between 0.1 and 0.5 percent
options.D: Between 0.3 and 2 percent
options.E: Between 2 and 4 percent
options.F: Between 5 and 8 percent

questions.explanation: The typical premium is roughly 0.3 to 2 percent of the bonded contract amount, varying with the type of risk, the financial strength of the principal and any indemnitors, past claims history, and the extent of the project. The higher ranges overstate typical bond cost, and 0.1 to 0.5 percent understates the upper end.

questions.question: A contractor seeking performance and payment bonds is a closely held corporation. With whom does the surety typically have a separate indemnity agreement?

options.A: The obligee, which agrees to share any losses with the surety
options.B: The principal and its individual owners, officers, or operators
options.C: The principal only, since its owners are shielded from liability
options.D: The first-tier subcontractors that the principal intends to use
options.E: The A/E, which reviewed the contractor's qualifications
options.F: The owner's lender, which finances the bonded contract

questions.explanation: The surety usually holds a separate indemnity agreement with the principal and, when the principal is a closely held corporation, with its individual owners, officers, or operators as well. The corporate form does not shield those individuals under that arrangement. The obligee is the owner being protected, not an indemnitor, and subcontractors, the A/E, and lenders are not parties to it.

questions.question: Comparing a surety bond with an insurance policy, which statement correctly describes the surety's position?

options.A: The surety accepts primary responsibility to pay valid claims, as insurers do
options.B: The surety absorbs losses as a priced risk, recovering them through premiums
options.C: The surety is liable only secondarily and expects reimbursement from indemnitors
options.D: The surety shares liability equally with the principal from the very outset of work
options.E: The surety pays claims first, then seeks repayment from the owner
options.F: The surety is primarily liable, and the principal only secondarily

questions.explanation: A surety is like a cosigner on a note: the principal stays primarily liable, and the surety is only secondarily liable after the principal defaults. In theory the surety should not pay out of its own pocket, because the principal and individual indemnitors must reimburse it, not the owner. Primary responsibility for claims is the insurer's model, which contrasts with suretyship.

questions.question: With its bid, a contractor proposes to furnish performance and payment bonds through a wealthy private individual instead of a bonding company. How is such an offer generally handled?

options.A: Reject it; the surety should hold a license in the project's state
options.B: Accept it if the individual's net worth exceeds the penal amount
options.C: Accept it if the individual is licensed in the contractor's home state
options.D: Reject it unless the A/E verifies the individual's AM Best rating
options.E: Accept it if the individual pledges cash equal to the penal amount
options.F: Accept it if the individual appears on the Treasury's annual listing

questions.explanation: The surety should be licensed by the insurance department of the state where the project is located, and offers to bond through an individual or an unlicensed company should generally be rejected. Personal net worth or pledged cash does not substitute for that licensing, the contractor's home state is not the test, the Treasury listing certifies surety companies, and AM Best rates insurance companies, not individuals.

questions.question: An owner's insurance advisor wants sureties whose Best's Key Rating Guide classification suggests that the carrier is financially excellent. Which minimum rating fits that description?

options.A: B+ or better
options.B: B or better
options.C: C- or better
options.D: A- or better
options.E: B- or better
options.F: C or better

questions.explanation: An A- or better rating in Best's Key Rating Guide suggests a financially excellent carrier. The guide's classes run from A for superior down to C- for fair, so the B-level and C-level ratings fall below the level associated with excellent financial strength.

questions.question: An A/E is preparing bidding documents for a federal agency project and must identify which sureties are acceptable to the government. Which source applies?

options.A: Best's Key Rating Guide, limited to sureties holding A- or better ratings
options.B: The Treasury's Bureau of the Fiscal Service annual certified listing
options.C: The Standard & Poor's and Fitch annual ratings of surety companies
options.D: The approved surety roster kept by each USACE district office
options.E: The surety list kept by the GSA Federal Supply Service
options.F: The NIBS listing of sureties posted on the WBDG website

questions.explanation: The federal government applies its own surety criteria: each year the Treasury Department's Bureau of the Fiscal Service issues a list of certified sureties acceptable for federal work. Best's, Standard & Poor's, and Fitch ratings are private rating services useful on other projects but are not the federal acceptance list, and no USACE, GSA, or WBDG surety roster serves that purpose.

questions.question: The federal government's annual list of sureties acceptable for federal projects is published in which document?

options.A: The January 1 Federal Register
options.B: The July 1 Federal Register
options.C: Best's Key Rating Guide
options.D: The WBDG Federal Facility Criteria
options.E: The October 1 Federal Register
options.F: Standard & Poor's annual ratings

questions.explanation: The Treasury Department's Bureau of the Fiscal Service lists the certified sureties acceptable for federal projects each year in the July 1 Federal Register, and the list is also on the Treasury website. January 1 and October 1 are near-miss dates. Best's Key Rating Guide and Standard & Poor's ratings are private publications, and the WBDG distributes federal guide specifications, not surety listings.

questions.question: A specifier is placing bond requirements in the project manual. Where do bid bond information and performance and payment bond requirements belong, respectively?

options.A: Supplementary conditions; procurement requirements
options.B: Procurement requirements; Division 01 general requirements
options.C: General conditions; supplementary conditions
options.D: Procurement requirements; supplementary conditions
options.E: Division 01 general requirements; general conditions
options.F: General conditions; procurement requirements

questions.explanation: Bid bond information goes in the procurement requirements because it governs bidding, and performance and payment bond requirements go in the supplementary conditions. Division 01 and the general conditions are not the locations for either item, and putting the bid bond in the supplementary conditions or the performance and payment bonds in the procurement requirements reverses the correct pairing.

questions.question: An A/E is designing its fourth branch library for the same municipal owner and plans to copy the bond requirements from the previous library's documents into the new manual. What is the best course of action?

options.A: Request this project's bond information early enough to include it
options.B: Reuse the prior requirements unless the owner objects in writing
options.C: Ask the low bidder's surety to set the requirements after bid opening
options.D: Issue the prior requirements now and correct them later by addendum
options.E: Reuse the prior requirements, since the owner and building type match
options.F: Set the bond amounts itself, based on the prior library's figures

questions.explanation: Bond information has to be requested from the owner for every project, even for a repeat client or an owner building several projects, and early enough for the owner to answer before the project manual is completed. Reusing old requirements, setting the amounts itself (bonding is the owner's decision), deferring to a bidder's surety, or planning to fix them by addendum all skip that owner request.

questions.question: An architect uses AIA Document G612, Owner's Instructions to the Architect, to collect the owner's bonding requirements. Which description of the form is accurate?

options.A: Part A: bidding procedures, including bid bond information
options.B: Part B: construction contract, including insurance requirements
options.C: Part B: bidding procedures, including bid bond information
options.D: Part A: construction contract, including bid bond information
options.E: Part A: bidding procedures, including insurance requirements
options.F: Part B: construction contract, including bid bond information
