questions.explanation: G612 is a two-part form: Part A relates to the construction contract and asks for the project's insurance and bond requirements, while Part B relates to bidding procedures and includes bid bond information. Any description that puts bidding procedures in Part A, the construction contract in Part B, or bid bond information in Part A reverses that structure.

questions.question: A bond requirement on a small commercial project drew only two bids, and several capable local contractors chose not to bid at all. What is the most likely explanation?

options.A: Bid bonds were billed separately, making bidding too costly for them
options.B: Bond premiums had to be paid by the bidders before bids were opened
options.C: Bidders lacking established surety relationships were discouraged
options.D: Bonds exposed bidders personally to mechanic's liens on the project
options.E: Surety rules barred closely held firms from obtaining bonds
options.F: Bonds may be required only on publicly funded projects

questions.explanation: On residential and small commercial work, some capable contractors have no established surety relationship, so a bond requirement may keep them from bidding; screening out contractors who cannot qualify for bonding is one function of the requirement. The premium is carried in the bid price rather than paid before opening, bid bonds are usually not billed separately, closely held firms can be bonded with personal indemnity, and private owners may require bonds too.

questions.question: Among the advantages of a fully bonded project, which one comes from the indemnity agreement?

options.A: Added incentive for the contractor's principals to perform properly
options.B: Protection of the owner against mechanic's liens on the project
options.C: Protection of the owner against withdrawal of a favorable bid
options.D: Satisfaction of statutory requirements for publicly funded work
options.E: Assurance that the surety pays if the contractor fails
options.F: Protection of suppliers against non-payment of amounts due

questions.explanation: The indemnity agreement motivates the contractor's principals to perform, because they may be personally liable to the surety for amounts it pays on the project. Lien protection and protection of suppliers come from the payment bond, protection against bid withdrawal comes from the bid bond, the surety's guarantee to pay comes from the bond itself, and meeting statutory requirements is an advantage of bonding generally.

questions.question: An owner with no separate legal counsel or insurance adviser follows the A/E's informal comment that bonds are unnecessary, and the contractor later defaults. What exposure does this create for the A/E?

options.A: The A/E becomes the obligee under any replacement performance bond
options.B: The A/E takes on the surety's duty to complete the defaulted work
options.C: The A/E must refund the fees it earned for bidding-phase services
options.D: The owner may claim the A/E's advice on bonding was insufficient
options.E: The A/E becomes the indemnitor for the defaulted contractor
options.F: The A/E must pay any mechanic's liens filed on the project

questions.explanation: Unless the owner is expressly cautioned, it may rely on the A/E's statements without further investigation, especially without its own counsel, and may later argue that the A/E's bonding advice was inadequate if an unbonded contractor defaults. That is why the owner should always be told to get an attorney's or surety adviser's counsel. The A/E does not become an obligee, surety, or indemnitor, or take on liens.

questions.question: Under a traditional bid bond with a penal amount of 5 percent of the bid, the selected bidder at $2,000,000 refuses without justification to sign the contract. The next-lowest bid is $2,150,000. The most the owner can recover from the surety is:
questions.explanation: Under a traditional bid bond the owner may seek the difference between the principal's bid and the next-lowest bid, but only up to the bond's penal amount. The difference here is $150,000, while the penal amount is 5 percent of $2,000,000, or $100,000, so recovery is capped at $100,000. The other figures ignore the cap, apply the percentage to the wrong bid or rate, or combine the numbers incorrectly.

questions.question: The selected bidder declines to sign the contract. In which situation would the bid bond most likely be discharged, leaving the surety with no liability?

options.A: The bidder finds its price far below the others but proves no mistake
options.B: The owner accepted the bid after the stated acceptance period expired
options.C: The other bidders have withdrawn, so the owner must rebid the work
options.D: The owner tenders an agreement at the exact price and terms bid
options.E: The owner accepted the bid well within the stated acceptance period
options.F: The bidder's surety has asked the owner to release the bond

questions.explanation: Late acceptance beyond the time set in the procurement documents can discharge the bid bond, along with a proven mistake or a unilateral change of terms by the owner. A low price without a provable mistake is exactly the reluctance the bond guards against, timely acceptance and a tender on the bid terms do not justify refusal, other bidders' withdrawal increases the surety's exposure, and the surety cannot simply ask to be released.

questions.question: Under a traditional bid bond, the selected bidder refuses without justification to sign, and every other bidder has already withdrawn, so the owner must rebid the work. For what may the surety be responsible?

options.A: The cost of rebidding only, with no liability for any price difference
options.B: Nothing, because no next-lowest bid remains to set the owner's damages
options.C: The full penal amount, regardless of the outcome of the reprocurement
options.D: The difference to the low rebid price, and possibly the rebid's cost
options.E: Only the premium that was charged for the bid bond
options.F: The full cost of building the work under the new contract

questions.explanation: When the owner must rebid, the surety answers for the difference between the principal's bid and the low bid on the reprocurement and may also owe the cost of the reprocurement. The absence of a remaining next bidder does not end liability, the traditional bid bond pays actual damages rather than an automatic full penal amount, and the surety does not pay the whole cost of the new contract or merely refund a premium.

questions.question: A $5,000,000 contract with a 100 percent performance bond goes into default after $3,200,000 has been properly paid. Completing the work costs $2,300,000. The surety's liability is limited to:
questions.explanation: Whatever completion method is used, the surety receives credit for the unpaid contract balance at default and owes only the excess cost to complete. The balance is $1,800,000, so the excess is $2,300,000 minus $1,800,000, or $500,000. The full completion cost, the balance itself, the penal sum, the total project cost, and the contract sum less the completion cost all ignore that credit.

questions.question: The owner's payments to the contractor were proper, but during construction the owner materially expanded the bonded work's scope without the surety's consent, and the contractor then defaulted. What relief may the surety claim on the owner's performance bond claim?

options.A: None, because the bond covers any changes the owner directs
options.B: Relief limited to any amount the owner overpaid the contractor
options.C: Relief for the increase in the contract sum over the original
options.D: A demand that the owner first pursue the A/E over the scope change
options.E: A refund of the bond premium paid on the original contract sum
options.F: Relief only if the contractor had objected to the scope change

questions.explanation: The performance bond protects against the contractor's default, not the owner's, and a material scope increase without the surety's consent lets the surety claim relief for the amount by which the contract sum grew over the original. Relief for overpayment is the other example, but the owner's payments here were proper. The bond does not absorb unconsented owner changes, the contractor's objection is irrelevant, and a premium refund is not the remedy.

questions.question: After a valid default claim, the surety's investigation finds the contractor's work fully satisfactory and its problems purely financial. Which course is suited to this situation?

options.A: Pay the owner the full penal amount and close out the bond
options.B: Have the owner finish the work and pay the full cost to complete
options.C: Arrange a completion contractor to work directly for the A/E
options.D: Finance the contractor, under careful supervision, to finish
options.E: Deny the claim, since satisfactory work means no default occurred
options.F: Fund the contractor directly, with no oversight of the money

questions.explanation: When the work is satisfactory and the trouble is only financial, the surety may finance the contractor to pay subcontractors, suppliers, and payroll so it can finish, doing so only under careful supervision. The claim here is already valid, and a completion contractor would work for the owner, not the A/E. The surety gets credit for the contract balance and owes only the excess cost to complete, not a full penal payout or the full completion cost.

questions.question: A sub-subcontractor on a bonded project has not been paid by the first-tier subcontractor. What notice do most payment bonds require of such a remote claimant?

options.A: Written notice to the contractor within 90 days of its last furnishing
options.B: Written notice to the owner within 90 days of substantial completion
options.C: Written notice to the surety within 30 days of its last furnishing
options.D: Written notice to the contractor within 90 days of final payment
options.E: Written notice to the surety within 90 days of final completion
options.F: Written notice to the first-tier subcontractor within 60 days

questions.explanation: Most payment bonds require a remote claimant to give the contractor written notice that it is unpaid within 90 days after the last day it furnished labor or material to the project. The notice protects a contractor that has already paid the first-tier subcontractor. The other choices change the recipient, the period, or the event that starts the clock.

questions.question: A supplier makes a payment bond claim for the unpaid purchase price of a crane that a subcontractor bought and now rotates among several of its jobs. How is the claim generally treated?

options.A: Covered, since the supplier furnished equipment to a bonded subcontractor
options.B: Covered, provided the supplier gave notice within the bond's time limit
options.C: Not covered; capital goods used across projects are outside the bond
options.D: Not covered, since payment bonds protect only first-tier subcontractors
options.E: Covered only for the share of time the crane spent on this project
options.F: Not covered, since payment bonds exclude all equipment suppliers

questions.explanation: Payment bond coverage is limited to labor and material on the bonded project, and the purchase price of capital goods or inventory usable on several projects is generally not a bond obligation, so there is no prorated share. Timely notice does not make an excluded item covered. Equipment furnished to the project is covered in general, and coverage reaches beyond first-tier parties to sub-subcontractors and suppliers to subcontractors.

questions.question: An owner wants a bid bond form that pays it the bond's full face amount whenever the selected bidder does not sign the agreement, even if that exceeds the gap to the next-lowest bid. Which form provides this?

options.A: EJCDC C-435, Bid Bond (Damages)
options.B: EJCDC C-430, Bid Bond (Penal Sum)
options.C: AIA Document A310, Bid Bond
options.D: ConsensusDocs 262, Bid Bond
options.E: EJCDC C-610, Performance Bond
options.F: AIA Document A312, Performance and Payment Bond

questions.explanation: EJCDC C-430 is the penal-sum form: it pays the owner the bond's face amount when the selected bidder fails to execute the agreement, which can exceed the actual bid difference. EJCDC C-435 pays actual damages up to the bond sum, AIA A310 and ConsensusDocs 262 follow that same traditional damages structure, and C-610 and A312 are performance and payment bond forms, not bid bonds.

questions.question: A specifier wants evidence that the agent who signs a bond on the surety's behalf has authority to bind the surety. What should be required, and where?

options.A: A power of attorney filed with the bond, required in the instructions for procurement
options.B: A certificate of authority filed with the bid, required in the supplementary conditions
options.C: A surety rating letter filed with the bond, required in Division 01 general requirements
options.D: A notarized agent license filed at contract signing, required by the agreement form
options.E: A surety indemnity agreement filed with the bid, required in the bid form
options.F: A Treasury surety listing filed with the bond, required in the general conditions

questions.explanation: Authority to bind the surety is usually shown by a power of attorney naming the authorized agent, and the instructions for procurement should require a copy to be filed with the signed bond. A rating letter, certificate, indemnity agreement, or Treasury listing does not prove an agent's signing authority, and the requirement does not belong in the supplementary or general conditions, Division 01, the bid form, or the agreement.

questions.question: The bidding package for a project calls for performance and payment bonds but includes no bond form. What is the likely consequence, and how could it have been avoided?

options.A: The surety's standard form governs; specify a surety rated A- or better
options.B: The A/E must draft a form; add bond language to the general conditions
options.C: AIA forms apply by default; reference them in Division 01 requirements
options.D: The form becomes negotiable; include the forms in procurement documents
options.E: The bond requirement lapses; restate it in the agreement form
options.F: EJCDC forms apply by default; cite them in the supplementary conditions

questions.explanation: When no form is included, the bond form can become a matter for negotiation among the owner, contractor, and surety, and including the required bond forms in the procurement documents avoids this. No AIA or EJCDC form applies by default, the requirement does not lapse, and drafting does not shift to the A/E; bond form choices carry significant legal consequences for the owner and its counsel.

questions.question: A first-time client asks the A/E to recommend the commercial general liability limits the contractor should carry. Who should be the source of that recommendation?

options.A: The A/E, drawing on limits used on similar past projects
options.B: The contractor's insurance broker, confirmed at bid time
options.C: The owner's legal counsel and the owner's insurance advisor
options.D: The specifier, using defaults stated in the general conditions
options.E: The surety, as part of its bond underwriting
options.F: The A/E's own professional liability insurer

questions.explanation: All recommendations on construction insurance should come from the owner's legal counsel and insurance advisor, and the A/E should neither act as an insurance advisor nor set or recommend limits. The contractor's broker serves the contractor rather than the owner, the specifier is part of the A/E team, the general conditions contain no dollar amounts, and neither the surety nor the A/E's insurer advises the owner on limits.

questions.question: The A/E gives the owner AIA Document G612 or EJCDC C-052 to obtain the owner's insurance instructions. Where are the resulting insurance requirements incorporated?

options.A: The instructions for procurement
options.B: The supplementary conditions
options.C: Division 01 general requirements
options.D: The general conditions
options.E: The bid form
options.F: The certificates of insurance

questions.explanation: G612 and C-052 are insurance information request forms used to get the owner's instructions for incorporating insurance requirements into the supplementary conditions, because amounts vary from project to project. The general conditions contain no dollar amounts, procurement instructions, the bid form, and Division 01 do not set contract insurance requirements, and certificates of insurance are the contractor's later proof of coverage.

questions.question: What is the owner's first line of financial defense on a construction project?

options.A: A fully bonded contractor
options.B: An adequately insured contractor
options.C: The owner's builder's risk policy
options.D: Retainage held from progress payments
options.E: An owner's protective liability policy
options.F: Additional insured status for the owner

questions.explanation: An adequately insured contractor is the owner's first line of financial defense, and the owner is protected partly by requiring the contractor to carry specific coverages at adequate limits. Bonds, owner-purchased policies such as builder's risk or protective liability, additional insured status, and retainage are other protections, but none carries that label.

questions.question: An owner assumes that the coverages it will require the contractor to carry make any insurance of its own unnecessary. How should the A/E respond?

options.A: Agree; required contractor coverage fully protects the owner
options.B: Agree, provided the owner is named on each certificate
options.C: Caution that contractor coverage may not meet all owner needs
options.D: Caution that contractor coverage protects only the contractor
options.E: Agree, provided the contractor also carries an umbrella policy
options.F: Caution that the owner must buy all of its own coverage instead

questions.explanation: The contractor's required coverage supplies most of the protection both parties need, but it may not cover everything the owner needs, and several policies exist for owners who want coverage beyond it. An umbrella or certificate naming the owner does not close that gap, contractor coverage does protect the owner and third parties to a degree, and the owner need not replace it with its own policies.

questions.question: The insurance that provides most of the protection both the owner and the contractor need during construction is the coverage required by which part of the documents?

options.A: Division 01 general requirements
options.B: The instructions for procurement
options.C: The individual specification sections
options.D: The conditions of the contract
options.E: The performance and payment bonds
options.F: The owner's insurance instructions form

questions.explanation: The coverage required by the conditions of the contract supplies most of the protection the owner and contractor need during construction. Insurance requirements are contractual matters set in the general and supplementary conditions, not in Division 01, procurement instructions, or technical sections. Bonds are a separate kind of protection, and the owner's instructions form only collects the information the A/E puts into the conditions.

questions.question: The contractor's own excavator is damaged at the site, and the contractor submits the loss under its liability policy. How is the claim treated?

options.A: Not covered; it does not insure the insured's own equipment
options.B: Covered, because the loss occurred at the project site
options.C: Covered, because the contractor is the named insured
options.D: Not covered, because the policy applies only away from the site
options.E: Covered, because the excavator was being used for the insured's work
options.F: Not covered unless another party's negligence caused the damage

questions.explanation: Liability policies protect the named insured against legal liability to others and do not cover damage to or loss of the insured's own products, machinery, or equipment, whoever caused it. Being the named insured, using the machine for the work, or having the loss occur on site does not change that. The off-site rationale is also wrong, since liability coverage is described as effective only at the project site.

questions.question: The AIA, EJCDC, and ConsensusDocs general conditions assign the duty to provide liability insurance to which party, and why?

options.A: The owner, because it holds title to the project property
options.B: The A/E, because it administers the construction contract
options.C: The contractor, because owners cannot purchase liability coverage
options.D: The contractor, because it is responsible for site activities
options.E: The owner, because it is the party most exposed to third-party suits
options.F: The subcontractors, because they perform most of the site work

questions.explanation: All three families of general conditions make the contractor furnish liability insurance, because the contractor is responsible for what happens on the project site. The requirement rests on that control of site activities, not on any inability of owners to buy coverage or on the owner's exposure to suits. The A/E's administration role does not make it the provider, and subcontractors' own coverage does not replace the contractor's.

questions.question: As industry guidance describes liability policies, which statement about their scope is accurate?

options.A: They pay the insured's own losses at the site, regardless of fault
options.B: They cover the insured's activities at any location it operates
options.C: They respond to others' claims arising from the insured's site work
options.D: They compensate for damage to covered property from insured perils
options.E: They cover the A/E's errors and omissions as an additional insured
options.F: They pay to repair the insured's own defective work at the site

questions.explanation: Liability policies protect the named insured against losses from its legal liability to others caused by its activities, and the coverage is described as effective only at the project site. They do not pay the insured's own first-party losses or repair its defective work, an additional insured's own errors are not covered, and compensating for damage to covered property from insured perils describes property insurance.

questions.question: A specifier is editing the supplementary conditions for a project on which one small subcontractor is exempt from the state's workers' compensation law. What should the contract documents require of that subcontractor?

options.A: A copy of its state exemption certificate in lieu of any coverage
options.B: Additional insured status under the contractor's compensation policy
options.C: Voluntary workers' compensation insurance having the statutory effect
options.D: Employer's liability coverage only, without workers' compensation
options.E: A certificate of insurance showing general liability coverage only
options.F: Coverage under the owner's own workers' compensation policy instead

questions.explanation: A contractor that the statute exempts should still be made to buy voluntary workers' compensation insurance, which works the same way as legally mandated coverage and keeps the owner protected from employee injury suits. An exemption certificate or general liability alone leaves that protection missing, employer's liability fills gaps in non-comprehensive statutes rather than replacing compensation, and the coverage is not extended through additional insured status or the owner's policy.

questions.question: The state where a project is located has a compensation statute that does not reach every injury or every category of recoverable damages. Which policy covers the resulting immunity gap?

options.A: Employer's liability insurance
options.B: Umbrella excess liability insurance
options.C: Owner's protective liability insurance
options.D: Other states coverage
options.E: Voluntary workers' compensation insurance
options.F: Commercial general liability insurance

questions.explanation: When a state's compensation law leaves some injuries or categories of damages outside its reach, the resulting immunity gap is covered by employer's liability insurance, which the AIA, EJCDC, and ConsensusDocs general conditions require the contractor to carry. Voluntary compensation is for contractors exempt from the statute, umbrella coverage adds limits above other policies, owner's protective coverage addresses the owner's liability, and other states coverage extends compensation to more states.

questions.question: A contractor's employees will fabricate subassemblies at its shop in one state and install them at a project site in another. Which term describes workers' compensation coverage that extends to every jurisdiction named in the policy's endorsement schedule?

options.A: Monopolistic fund coverage
options.B: Difference-in-conditions coverage
options.C: Broad form coverage
options.D: Other states coverage
options.E: Longshore and harbor workers coverage
options.F: Employer's liability coverage

questions.explanation: Compliance with state workers' compensation laws reaches subassemblies fabricated outside the project's state, and coverage should be arranged wherever employees work; coverage reaching all states in the endorsement schedule is called other states coverage. Monopolistic fund states require a state fund, difference-in-conditions fills builder's risk gaps, broad form is a hold-harmless type, employer's liability fills gaps in the statute, and longshore coverage applies to navigable-water work.

questions.question: Site work for a new hospital requires rock blasting and deep excavation with temporary shoring next to an occupied building. To cover claims from the blasting and from structural failure when shoring is pulled, what change to the contractor's commercial general liability coverage should the owner require?

options.A: Conversion of the policy from an occurrence form to a claims-made form
options.B: Removal of the exclusion for explosion, collapse, and underground damage
options.C: Addition of an installation floater endorsement covering the temporary shoring
options.D: Modification of the general aggregate so that it applies only to this project
options.E: Addition of the owner and the A/E as additional insureds on the policy
options.F: Purchase of equipment breakdown insurance covering the shoring system

questions.explanation: The basic CGL form carries the XCU exclusion (explosion, collapse, underground property damage), which must be removed to cover blasting, collapse from excavation or removal of shoring, and underground damage from excavation. A claims-made form weakens the owner's protection, additional insured status does not widen what the policy covers, an installation floater or equipment breakdown policy insures property, and a per-project aggregate does not restore excluded perils.

questions.question: During construction of an addition, a subcontractor's incorrectly installed through-wall flashing lets water into the adjoining occupied building and damages a tenant's furnishings. How would the contractor's general liability policy typically respond?

options.A: It would cover the tenant's damaged furnishings but not the cost to redo the flashing
options.B: It would cover the cost to redo the flashing but not the tenant's damaged furnishings
options.C: It would cover both the flashing rework and the tenant's damaged furnishings in full
options.D: It would cover neither, since faulty workmanship is excluded from such policies
options.E: It would cover the furnishings only if the owner had named the tenant as an insured
options.F: It would cover the furnishings only if the claim is made during the policy period

questions.explanation: A general liability policy pays for damage that results from defective work but not for repairing the defective work itself, so the tenant's furnishings are the covered loss while redoing the flashing stays the contractor's cost. Paying for the rework reverses or ignores that rule, refusing everything overstates the exclusion, and most such policies are occurrence-based, so the claim need not fall in the policy period and the tenant need not be named.

questions.question: An owner learns that its contractor carries one CGL policy for all of its jobs, so claims paid on other jobs during the policy year could erode the coverage shown on the certificate furnished for this work. What should the owner require?

options.A: A claims-made policy form so that each claim is tied to its own policy period
options.B: AIA Document G715 attached to the ACORD 25 certificate of liability insurance
options.C: A higher products and completed operations aggregate stated in Division 01
options.D: A per-project general aggregate, required in the supplementary conditions
options.E: A higher each occurrence limit shown on the certificate of insurance
options.F: Additional insured status for the owner under the existing policy

questions.explanation: The general aggregate caps everything the policy pays except products and completed operations claims, so claims paid on other jobs can leave less than the certificate shows; the fix is a general aggregate that applies to each project, identified in the supplementary conditions. A higher each occurrence limit still draws on the same aggregate, additional insured status does not add limits, claims-made forms weaken the owner's position, and G715 adds subjects such as pollution liability.

questions.question: The contractor's superintendent uses a personal pickup to run to a supplier for fasteners and causes an accident on the way. Which coverage should the specifications have required to address the contractor's liability exposure?

options.A: Owned-vehicle coverage under the contractor's general property and equipment policy
options.B: Non-owned, rented, or hired vehicle coverage within the contractor's auto insurance
options.C: Products and completed operations coverage under the contractor's general liability
options.D: Employer's liability coverage under the contractor's workers' compensation policy
options.E: Owner's and contractor's protective liability coverage for the project
options.F: Commercial general liability coverage under the contractor's policy

questions.explanation: An employee running an errand in a personal car is the standard example of non-owned vehicle exposure, so the contractor's automobile insurance, written on a business auto coverage form, should include non-owned, rented, or hired vehicle coverage. General property and equipment insurance covers tools and mobile equipment, completed operations relates to finished work, employer's liability concerns employee injuries, and neither OCP nor general liability is the vehicle coverage.

questions.question: The contractor plans to use a leased helicopter to set rooftop skylights that are too heavy for the available crane. What should the owner require?

options.A: Nothing added, since hired vehicles fall under the business auto coverage form
options.B: Coverage under the contractor's general property and equipment insurance
options.C: Appropriate liability coverage for both owned and non-owned aircraft
options.D: Removal of the XCU exclusion from the contractor's general liability policy
options.E: An installation floater covering the skylights while they are lifted
options.F: Equipment breakdown insurance on the leased helicopter

questions.explanation: Automobile liability policies uniformly exclude aircraft and powerboats beyond set size and horsepower limits, so when a project needs aircraft, such as a helicopter erecting skylights, the owner should require suitable liability coverage for both owned and non-owned aircraft. Relying on the auto form leaves the exclusion in place, property coverages such as floaters, equipment breakdown, or general property and equipment insurance protect property rather than liability to others, and the XCU exclusion concerns explosion, collapse, and underground damage.

questions.question: A specifier is coordinating automobile liability requirements with the general conditions. On what basis do the AIA, EJCDC, and ConsensusDocs documents require that coverage to be written?

options.A: Per-occurrence (per-accident) basis
options.B: Claims-made basis
options.C: Reporting form basis tied to pay applications
options.D: Named-peril basis listing covered hazards
options.E: Completed value basis for the construction period
options.F: All-risk basis covering every peril not excluded

questions.explanation: The AIA, EJCDC, and ConsensusDocs documents call for automobile coverage written on a per-occurrence (accident) basis for bodily injury or property damage arising from use of covered vehicles. Claims-made is a liability form seldom used for construction, and the reporting form, completed value form, named-peril coverage, and all-risk coverage all describe property or builder's risk insurance.

questions.question: An owner's attorney notes that the supplementary conditions already name the owner as an additional insured on the contractor's liability policy and asks whether anything better is available. What is the correct response?

options.A: No; additional insured status is the most protection an owner can obtain
options.B: Yes; a broad form hold-harmless from the contractor offers stronger protection
options.C: Yes; an umbrella policy naming the owner supersedes additional insured status
options.D: Yes; owner's and contractor's protective insurance offers greater protection
options.E: Yes; a waiver of subrogation gives the owner its own direct coverage
options.F: No; OCP insurance would only duplicate the contractor's liability policy

questions.explanation: Additional insured status under the supplementary conditions gives the owner better protection, but not the best; an OCP policy covering the same hazards as the contractor's liability insurance serves the owner's interests better, and it is not duplicate coverage. A broad form hold-harmless is a contract clause, not insurance, and is unenforceable in some states, an umbrella adds limits rather than replacing protective coverage, and a waiver of subrogation provides no coverage.

questions.question: An owner on a ConsensusDocs 200 project selects the option for OCP insurance. Which party should obtain the policy, and why?

options.A: The owner, so that it can select a carrier already familiar with its risks
options.B: The contractor, to avoid conflict with the owner's existing liability policy
options.C: The A/E, because the coverage extends to its own design errors and omissions
options.D: The owner, since the policy insures the owner's role in the construction
options.E: The owner's insurance advisor, since it determines the coverage limits
options.F: The contractor, because OCP is an endorsement to its general liability policy

questions.explanation: The contractor typically obtains OCP insurance, which is the ConsensusDocs 200 default when that option is chosen, and the contractor should provide it so that it does not conflict with the owner's existing liability policy. OCP is a stand-alone policy, not an endorsement, the owner's legal liability for its role explains why OCP is not duplicate coverage rather than who buys it, advisors do not buy policies, and OCP does not cover the A/E's errors.

questions.question: An owner's risk manager objects that requiring OCP insurance would merely duplicate the contractor's own liability coverage. What is the basis for rejecting that objection?

options.A: OCP insures the contractor's tools and equipment, which liability coverage does not
options.B: OCP replaces builder's risk insurance, so total premiums stay about the same
options.C: The owner bears its own legal liability for its role in the construction process
options.D: OCP covers the owner's ordinary business operations away from the site
options.E: OCP pays to repair the contractor's defective work, which its CGL excludes
options.F: OCP covers the A/E's design errors that the contractor's policy excludes

questions.explanation: OCP insurance is not duplicate coverage because the owner carries its own legal liability for the part it plays in the construction process, even though OCP addresses the same hazards as the contractor's liability insurance. OCP is liability coverage tied to the construction work, so it neither insures the contractor's equipment or defective work, substitutes for builder's risk, covers the A/E's professional errors, nor covers the owner's unrelated operations.

questions.question: Which pair of reasons supports specifying a relatively high-limit umbrella excess liability policy for the contractor?

options.A: It replaces the primary policies and removes their standard exclusions
options.B: It covers the owner's own acts and the A/E's errors and omissions
options.C: It converts claims-made forms and fixes a per-project general aggregate
options.D: It economically raises limits and can broaden the underlying coverage
options.E: It replaces OCP insurance and names the owner as the insured
options.F: It covers the contractor's own equipment and builder's risk losses

questions.explanation: An umbrella serves two purposes: it is the most economical way to buy limits higher than general liability and automobile policies usually provide, and it can broaden the coverage of those policies. It sits as a layer above the primary policies rather than replacing them or OCP, it does not cover the owner's or A/E's own acts or the contractor's property, and aggregate or policy-form changes are made to the CGL itself.

questions.question: A specifier is comparing how standard documents handle umbrella liability. What does the Insurance and Bonds attachment to AIA Document A101 require?

options.A: Primary plus umbrella coverage at least equal to the stipulated primary coverage
options.B: Specific umbrella dollar limits entered in the supplementary conditions
options.C: An umbrella limit at least equal to the initial Contract Sum plus subsequent Modifications
options.D: Umbrella coverage written on a claims-made form with a stated extended reporting period
options.E: An umbrella limit equal to the Work's full insurable replacement cost
options.F: Umbrella coverage only if the owner elects it, at the owner's option

questions.explanation: The A101 insurance attachment addresses umbrella insurance only by requiring that the primary and umbrella policies together equal or exceed the coverage stipulated for the primary policies. Specific umbrella dollar amounts in the supplementary conditions are the EJCDC C-800 approach, the Contract Sum plus Modifications and full insurable replacement cost measures size property insurance, and owner's-option coverage describes delayed completion insurance.

questions.question: On a project using EJCDC documents, the owner's insurance advisor has set umbrella limits. Which two umbrella values does EJCDC C-800 call for in the supplementary conditions?

options.A: Each occurrence limit and medical expense limit
options.B: Products-completed operations and personal injury limits
options.C: General aggregate and damage-to-rented-premises limits
options.D: General aggregate limit and each occurrence limit
options.E: Each occurrence and personal and advertising injury limits
options.F: General aggregate and products-completed operations limits

questions.explanation: EJCDC C-800 handles umbrella liability by having the supplementary conditions state dollar amounts for both the general aggregate and each occurrence. The other pairs mix in medical expense, products-completed operations, personal and advertising injury, and damage-to-rented-premises limits, which are separate CGL limits not tied to the umbrella requirement.

questions.question: A specifier is distinguishing liability coverage from property insurance, which compensates insureds for damage to covered property caused by insured perils. Which policy is the cornerstone of a project's property insurance?

options.A: Equipment breakdown insurance
options.B: Builder's risk insurance
options.C: Installation floater
options.D: General property and equipment insurance
options.E: Owner's and contractor's protective insurance
options.F: Business interruption insurance

questions.explanation: Property insurance compensates insureds for damage to covered property from insured perils, and builder's risk insurance is the cornerstone of a project's property insurance. Equipment breakdown, installation floaters, the contractor's general property and equipment insurance, and business interruption are narrower or related coverages that supplement it, and OCP is liability insurance, not property insurance.

questions.question: A university with several concurrent capital projects is starting a large, multiyear lab building whose insured value will climb steeply during the final phases. Which builder's risk form is likely most advantageous?

options.A: Completed value form, written for the anticipated completed value
options.B: Named peril form, limited to the perils listed in the policy
options.C: Difference-in-conditions form, maintained by the contractor
options.D: Reporting form, with premiums based on values at each update
options.E: Installation floater form, covering equipment as it is installed
options.F: Delayed completion form, covering income lost to a late opening

questions.explanation: The reporting form bases premiums on insured values at a given time, is most advantageous when values rise sharply late in construction, and suits large projects with long schedules and owners with many projects at once, provided the owner keeps up the value reports. The completed value form fits inexperienced owners or a single project, while named peril, difference-in-conditions, floaters, and delayed completion are not the two builder's risk forms.

questions.question: On an addition that ties into an existing building, the owner wants the builder's risk amount to equal what it would cost to replace the property when a loss occurs, existing structures included. That measure comes from which standard document?

options.A: AIA A101 Insurance and Bonds attachment
options.B: EJCDC C-700
options.C: ConsensusDocs 200
options.D: AIA A201
options.E: EJCDC C-800
options.F: AIA G612

questions.explanation: The A101 insurance attachment sets property insurance at no less than the initial Contract Sum plus later Modifications and work supplied by others; EJCDC C-700 uses the Work's full insurable replacement cost, subject to deductibles; and ConsensusDocs 200 uses full replacement cost at the time of loss, existing structures included. A201, the EJCDC C-800 supplementary conditions, and the G612 request form are not the documents that state that measure.

questions.question: A transit authority will award three prime contracts for one station and will not purchase builder's risk insurance itself. What should the supplementary conditions do?

options.A: Name one prime contractor to insure the work, including the other primes' contract values
options.B: Require each prime contractor to carry a separate all-risk policy for its own contract
options.C: Require each prime contractor's subcontractors to purchase installation floaters instead
options.D: Require the primes to form a contractor-controlled insurance program for the station
options.E: Name one prime contractor to insure the work, covering only its own contract value
options.F: Rely on each prime contractor's general property and equipment insurance instead

questions.explanation: When the owner does not furnish builder's risk on multiple-prime work, the supplementary conditions should name the prime contractor that provides it; that contractor must include the value of the other prime contracts and give the other primes proof of coverage. Separate policies for each prime duplicate premiums, and all-risk coverage may not be available. Floaters and property and equipment insurance supplement builder's risk rather than replace it, and a CIP would require significant changes to the standard forms.

questions.question: A mechanical subcontractor will install two large chillers. The project's builder's risk policy lists the subcontractor by name and broadly covers equipment once it is installed. Is a separate installation floater normally needed?

options.A: Yes; a floater is always required for generators, chillers, and similar items
options.B: No; that builder's risk coverage generally makes a floater unnecessary
options.C: Yes; builder's risk policies exclude equipment until the owner accepts the work
options.D: No; the contractor's property and equipment coverage protects the chillers instead
options.E: Yes; builder's risk policies exclude tools and equipment, so a floater is needed
options.F: No; the subcontractor's general liability policy covers the installed chillers

questions.explanation: Installation floaters insure a subcontractor's materials and work until the owner accepts the project and are generally required for expensive items such as generators or chillers, but are usually not required when the builder's risk policy names the subcontractor and broadly covers installed equipment. The usual tools-and-equipment exclusion concerns construction equipment, not installed systems; liability policies do not insure the insured's own property, and property and equipment coverage protects tools and mobile equipment.

questions.question: An owner wants to move staff into the completed first floor of a building while upper floors are still under construction. What must happen first regarding property insurance?

options.A: The A/E must certify the floor complete and notify the builder's risk carrier
options.B: The carrier must permit it and, under AIA A101 terms, give written notice of changes
options.C: The contractor must cancel builder's risk for that floor and add an OCP policy
options.D: The owner must purchase an installation floater covering the occupied area
options.E: The owner must add delayed completion coverage for the occupied floor
options.F: The contractor must obtain its surety's consent to the early occupancy

questions.explanation: Partial occupancy changes the insurer's risk, so it should not begin without the property carrier's permission, and the A101 insurance attachment requires that the carrier be contacted before occupancy and written notice be received from it confirming the needed coverage changes. An A/E certification, cancelling coverage, buying a floater or delayed completion coverage, or asking the surety does not meet that requirement, and floaters cover materials only during installation.

questions.question: A specifier who usually works with EJCDC documents takes on a project using AIA documents. How does responsibility for purchasing builder's risk insurance differ between the two families by default?

options.A: AIA: the contractor; EJCDC: the owner, transferable by agreement
options.B: Both: the contractor, with the owner named as an additional insured
options.C: Both: the owner, because it holds the insurable interest
options.D: AIA: the owner; EJCDC: the contractor, transferable to the owner
options.E: AIA: the owner; EJCDC: the owner, transferable to the contractor
options.F: AIA: the contractor; EJCDC: the contractor, with no transfer allowed

questions.explanation: AIA documents place builder's risk on the owner because of its insurable interest, with the A101 insurance attachment allowing transfer to the contractor, while EJCDC, like ConsensusDocs, places it on the contractor and allows transfer to the owner through the supplementary conditions. Answers that reverse the two families, give both the same default, or forbid any transfer miss that difference.

questions.question: While updating an older office master, a specifier finds a requirement for boiler and machinery insurance. What is this coverage now called?

options.A: Equipment breakdown insurance
options.B: Installation floater insurance
options.C: Inland marine insurance
options.D: Difference-in-conditions insurance
options.E: General property and equipment insurance
options.F: Business interruption insurance

questions.explanation: Equipment breakdown insurance is the coverage formerly called boiler and machinery insurance, insuring against accidents to boilers, pressure vessels, machinery, electrical and HVAC equipment, and listed computer and communications equipment. An installation floater covers a subcontractor's equipment during installation, difference-in-conditions coverage fills gaps in an owner's builder's risk program, general property and equipment insurance covers tools and mobile equipment, and business interruption covers lost income.

questions.question: A specifier's master supplementary conditions still list a separate equipment breakdown policy as mandatory. How do the current AIA and EJCDC documents treat this coverage?

options.A: Both require it as a separate policy issued apart from builder's risk
options.B: AIA requires it in A101's insurance attachment, but EJCDC has dropped it
options.C: Both required it previously but no longer list it as a required type
options.D: EJCDC requires it in C-700, but AIA leaves it to the owner's option
options.E: Both require it, but as an endorsement to builder's risk instead
options.F: Neither ever listed it, leaving the coverage entirely to the owner

questions.explanation: AIA and EJCDC documents once required equipment breakdown coverage (formerly called boiler and machinery insurance), but their current editions no longer name it as a required type of insurance. Builder's risk policies now usually cover equipment, so a separate policy is seldom needed. The other options either keep it as a requirement in one or both document families or deny that it was ever required.

questions.question: During construction, which loss falls within the scope of equipment breakdown insurance as industry guidance describes it?

options.A: A rented forklift damaged when it tips over in the laydown yard
options.B: A delivery truck damaged in a collision on the way to the site
options.C: A transformer that is damaged in an electrical accident
options.D: Owner-furnished casework stolen from an off-site warehouse
options.E: A worker injured while unloading pipe at the material hoist
options.F: A neighbor's foundation cracked by the contractor's blasting

questions.explanation: Equipment breakdown insurance covers losses from accidents to boilers and pressure vessels, machinery, electrical equipment such as transformers and generators, HVAC equipment, and listed computer and communications equipment. A tipped forklift falls under the contractor's general property and equipment insurance, a delivery truck under automobile coverage, stolen stored materials under property insurance, an injured worker under workers' compensation, and blasting damage to a neighbor under liability insurance.

questions.question: A contractor's crawler crane is damaged in a work accident on the site. Which insurance is intended to cover this asset?

options.A: Contractor's general property and equipment insurance
options.B: Contractor's business automobile liability coverage form
options.C: Project builder's risk insurance, all-risk form
options.D: Equipment breakdown insurance on the project
options.E: Commercial general liability, completed operations coverage
options.F: Owner's and contractor's protective liability policy

questions.explanation: Builder's risk covers the value of the construction, not the tools and equipment used to build it, and mobile equipment such as cranes, bulldozers, backhoes and forklifts falls outside the contractor's automobile insurance, so general property and equipment insurance covers these assets. Equipment breakdown insurance addresses accidents to boilers, transformers and HVAC units, and liability coverages such as CGL or OCP pay for harm to others, not damage to the insured's own equipment.
questions.source: contractor's general property and equipment insurance

questions.question: Which of these losses would the contractor's general property and equipment insurance typically cover?

options.A: Wages for a crew left idle while a broken excavator was repaired
options.B: A backhoe on the site damaged by vandals over a weekend
options.C: A forklift drive train worn out from normal heavy use
options.D: Chillers installed in the project damaged by a fire
options.E: A dump truck damaged in a collision on the highway
options.F: A neighbor's parked car dented by the contractor's backhoe

questions.explanation: This coverage pays for physical damage to the contractor's own tools and equipment, such as a backhoe vandalized on site, but not for wear and tear or for the wages of a crew idled while equipment is repaired. Installed chillers are part of the work under builder's risk, a highway collision is an automobile claim, and damage the backhoe does to a neighbor's car is a liability claim.
questions.source: contractor's general property and equipment insurance

questions.question: A well-capitalized contractor objects to buying insurance on its construction tools and equipment. What alternative may the owner accept, and why does the owner care?

options.A: Adding the tools to builder's risk, since equipment losses raise the owner's premiums
options.B: Naming the owner an additional insured, since the owner could be sued for losses
options.C: A waiver of subrogation, since the owner's insurer might otherwise pursue the contractor
options.D: Proof of ability to replace them, since such losses can affect progress and quality
options.E: A larger performance bond, since the surety would pay for lost tools
options.F: An umbrella excess policy, since tool losses create liability to others

questions.explanation: The owner should require either insurance on the contractor's construction tools and equipment or proof that the contractor can afford to replace them, because losing them can slow the work and may hurt its quality. Builder's risk does not cover the contractor's tools; additional insured status, subrogation waivers and umbrella coverage deal with liability among parties, and a performance bond guarantees completion of the work, not replacement of equipment.
questions.source: contractor's general property and equipment insurance

questions.question: A lightning-caused fire during construction pushes back the opening of a new retail center, and the owner loses projected rental income. Which coverage is designed for this loss, and how is it typically provided?

options.A: Loss-of-use coverage, purchased as a separate residential policy
options.B: Delayed completion coverage, as an endorsement to builder's risk
options.C: Business interruption coverage, under the owner's existing CGL policy
options.D: Equipment breakdown coverage, as an extension of the boiler policy
options.E: Property damage coverage, under the contractor's CGL policy
options.F: Owner's and contractor's protective coverage, as a stand-alone policy

questions.explanation: Delayed completion coverage gives the same kind of protection as loss-of-use and business interruption but is limited to construction delays from perils insured under builder's risk, so it is usually added to that policy as an endorsement. Loss-of-use is tied to residences, business interruption to an operating business that cannot run, equipment breakdown to equipment accidents, and liability coverages such as CGL and OCP to harm the insured causes others.

questions.question: A fire in an occupied apartment building undergoing renovation forces tenants out of their units for several weeks. Which coverage is typically associated with the tenants' temporary housing, food, and moving costs?

options.A: Loss-of-use coverage
options.B: Business interruption coverage
options.C: Delayed completion coverage
options.D: Equipment breakdown coverage
options.E: Builder's risk coverage
options.F: Reporting form coverage

questions.explanation: Loss-of-use coverage is tied to residential buildings such as homes and leased apartments and pays living expenses like temporary housing, food and moving costs when a residence becomes uninhabitable from a covered event. Business interruption pays a business for lost income, delayed completion is limited to construction delays, equipment breakdown covers equipment, builder's risk covers the work itself, and reporting form coverage handles fluctuating property values.

questions.question: An owner's project uses AIA Document A101 with its insurance and bonds attachment, and the owner is weighing delayed completion insurance that would continue after the new facility opens. Which statement is accurate?

options.A: The contractor must buy it, and it may run past completion only by Change Order
options.B: The owner must buy it, and coverage must end at substantial completion
options.C: The owner may buy it at its option and may extend it past construction
options.D: The owner may buy it at its option, but it must end when construction ends
options.E: The contractor may buy it at its option and may extend it past construction
options.F: The owner must buy it, but it may continue for a period after construction

questions.explanation: The insurance attachment to A101 lets the owner purchase and maintain delayed completion insurance at its option, and the owner may carry it through construction and extend it for a period afterward because a new facility's performance is untested. It is the owner's coverage, not the contractor's, nothing makes it mandatory for either party, and nothing limits it to the construction period.

questions.question: After paying the owner's fire loss in full, the owner's property insurer finds that the electrical contractor installed the transformer contrary to the manufacturer's instructions and sues the contractor. In what role is the insurer acting?

options.A: Indemnitee
options.B: Subrogee
options.C: Additional insured
options.D: Indemnitor
options.E: Obligee
options.F: Named insured

questions.explanation: Once the insurer pays the loss, subrogation transfers the owner's rights against other parties to the insurer, which becomes a subrogee able to sue the contractor or engineer. An indemnitee is the party held harmless under a contract and an indemnitor the party giving that protection; an additional insured or named insured is covered by a policy, and an obligee is the party a bond protects.

questions.question: To keep one party's insurance settlement from becoming another party's lawsuit midway through a project, what does current contract practice suggest?

options.A: All parties waive their claims against each other wherever insurance covers them
options.B: All parties waive all claims against one another regardless of insurance coverage
options.C: Each party names every other party as a named insured on its liability policies
options.D: The contractor gives the owner and A/E a broad form hold-harmless agreement
options.E: Each party carries an umbrella excess policy above its primary liability limits
options.F: All parties agree to send any insurer's recovery claim to binding arbitration

questions.explanation: Current contract practice is for all parties to waive claims against each other to the extent insurance covers those claims, so a right of subrogation never arises. A waiver regardless of insurance goes further than that practice, cross-naming parties as named insureds is not the suggested approach, a hold-harmless shifts liability rather than stopping an insurer's suit, and higher limits or arbitration still leave the insurer free to pursue recovery.

questions.question: The owner proposes a mutual waiver of subrogation among the owner, contractor, and A/E. What should each party do before accepting it?

options.A: Name the other two parties as additional insureds on its own policies
options.B: Obtain the surety's written consent, since the waiver affects the bonds
options.C: Confirm the waiver does not violate any term of its own insurance policies
options.D: Have the owner's insurance advisor certify the waiver in the supplementary conditions
options.E: Raise its own liability limits to absorb the claims it is giving up
options.F: Obtain a hold-harmless agreement from each of the other parties

questions.explanation: Each party to the construction contract should check whether the waiver violates any term or condition of its own insurance policies, since the waiver keeps the right of subrogation from ever arising. Naming additional insureds, getting surety consent, certifying the waiver, raising limits and trading hold-harmless agreements are not the check industry guidance calls for.

questions.question: An owner using AIA contract forms decides to implement an owner-controlled insurance program (OCIP) for a large commercial project. What must happen to the standard forms?

options.A: Nothing; A101's insurance attachment already includes an optional OCIP provision
options.B: They must be significantly modified with insurance and legal advice
options.C: Only the insurance amounts in the supplementary conditions change
options.D: They must be replaced with ConsensusDocs forms, which include CIPs
options.E: Only an OCIP enrollment form needs adding to the bid documents
options.F: They must be replaced with EJCDC forms, which include an OCIP option

questions.explanation: None of the standard AIA, EJCDC or ConsensusDocs forms include controlled insurance programs, so an OCIP requires the forms to be modified substantially, with guidance from an insurance advisor and an attorney. No standard family, including A101's insurance attachment, offers a built-in CIP option, and the change goes far beyond filling in insurance amounts or adding an enrollment form.

questions.question: A health system plans a series of clinic projects that will start and finish at staggered times over several years and wants a single consolidated insurance program. Which arrangement fits this situation?

options.A: A contractor-controlled program purchased for each clinic
options.B: A reporting form builder's risk policy for each clinic
options.C: A difference-in-conditions policy held by each contractor
options.D: A rolling wrap-up that clinics move into and out of
options.E: An owner's protective liability policy for each clinic
options.F: An umbrella excess liability policy held by each contractor

questions.explanation: A rolling wrap-up is a controlled insurance program for an owner with several construction projects: each project is rolled into the program when it starts and out when it is complete. A separate contractor-controlled program per clinic defeats the single program, a reporting form is a builder's risk valuation method, difference-in-conditions coverage fills gaps in a builder's risk program, and OCP and umbrella policies are separate liability coverages, not a consolidated program.

questions.question: An owner of a small project is considering a controlled insurance program. What is the principal benefit for a project of that size, as distinct from the main advantage on large commercial projects?

options.A: Significant premium savings from consolidating coverage
options.B: Elimination of builder's risk from the project's coverage
options.C: Simplicity and a streamlined process for handling claims
options.D: Use of standard contract forms without any modification
options.E: No further need for the owner to use an insurance advisor
options.F: Lower rates as each subcontractor buys its own coverage

questions.explanation: Cost savings are the most significant CIP advantage on large commercial projects, while smaller projects gain from the program's simplicity and streamlined claims process. A CIP consolidates most required coverage into one policy rather than eliminating builder's risk or leaving each subcontractor to buy its own, and setting one up still calls for an insurance advisor, legal counsel and significant changes to the standard forms.

questions.question: The A/E was named an additional insured on the contractor's CGL coverage. Later, the A/E is sued over a detailing error in its drawings. How does that coverage respond?

options.A: It defends the A/E, since additional insureds share the named insured's rights
options.B: It excludes the error; the A/E's own professional liability policy responds
options.C: It covers the error up to the each occurrence limit, after the A/E's deductible
options.D: It covers the error only if the owner is also named as an additional insured
options.E: It covers the error under the products-completed operations aggregate
options.F: It covers the error only if the claim is made during the policy period

questions.explanation: Industry guidance explains that naming the A/E as an additional insured does not expand the contractor's policy; it extends benefits only for the contractor's operations, and the acts, errors, or omissions of the owner or A/E are not covered. Errors and omissions coverage must come from the A/E firm's own professional liability policy, so any option in which the contractor's CGL defends or pays for the design error is wrong.

questions.question: The 'shotgun lawsuit' phenomenon, in which injury from construction operations draws the owner and A/E into litigation, is the rationale for which contract requirement?

options.A: Naming the owner and A/E additional insureds under the contractor's liability coverage
options.B: Requiring the contractor to purchase a claims-made general liability policy for the owner
options.C: Requiring a mutual waiver of subrogation among the owner, the A/E, and the contractor
options.D: Requiring the owner to provide builder's risk insurance covering all parties' interests
options.E: Requiring the contractor to carry general property and equipment insurance
options.F: Requiring the owner to purchase delayed completion insurance for the project

questions.explanation: Injury from the contractor's operations can pull the owner and A/E into costly litigation even when they are not at fault, so the contract documents should make both of them additional insureds on the contractor's liability policy. Subrogation waivers deal with an insurer's recovery after a paid loss, and a claims-made form, builder's risk, equipment insurance and delayed completion coverage do nothing about third-party injury suits.

questions.question: When a liability policy designates a firm by name as an insured, what does industry guidance say that firm becomes entitled to for a covered occurrence?

options.A: Reimbursement of its own repair costs for defective work it performed
options.B: Coverage for its own professional errors and omissions in design
options.C: Payment of its own property losses, including tools and equipment
options.D: Legal defense of such claims and payment of damages on its behalf
options.E: Replacement of its own income lost while its operations are interrupted
options.F: Benefits for its own employees who are injured on the job

questions.explanation: A named insured on a liability policy is entitled to a legal defense of covered claims and to the policy's payment of damages on its behalf for legal liability arising from a covered occurrence. Liability insurance does not repair the insured's own defective work, cover its professional errors, or insure its own property; lost business income and injured employees are handled by business interruption and workers' compensation coverage.

questions.question: On a project using AIA documents, where does industry guidance say the project-specific insurance dollar amounts are entered?

options.A: In the supplementary conditions, as modifications to A201
options.B: In Division 01, in a section on contract requirements
options.C: In the instructions to bidders, with bid security amounts
options.D: In the insurance attachment to the owner-contractor agreement
options.E: In the bid form, as limits each bidder proposes
options.F: In the general conditions, in A201's insurance article

questions.explanation: The standard general conditions contain no insurance dollar amounts, and because the amounts vary by project they normally belong in the supplementary conditions. AIA documents are the exception: the amounts are entered in the insurance and bonds attachment to A101, the owner-contractor agreement. A201 itself, Division 01, the bid form and the instructions to bidders are not where coverage amounts go.

questions.question: The owner returns a completed EJCDC C-052 to the A/E, but the umbrella liability limits are left blank and one auto limit looks inconsistent with the rest. What should the A/E do?

options.A: Insert the limits used on the owner's previous project
options.B: Ask the A/E's own insurance carrier to recommend limits
options.C: Return the form to the owner for completion or clarification
options.D: Fill in the limits suggested in the EJCDC guidance documents
options.E: Leave the blanks for the contractor's insurer to fill in
options.F: Copy the limits from the general conditions' insurance article

questions.explanation: An incomplete or apparently incorrect form goes back to the owner for completion or clarification; the A/E should not guess the owner's intent. The A/E is not the owner's insurance advisor and its liability insurance does not cover specifying insurance information, so supplying amounts from a prior job, its own carrier or published guidance is inappropriate, the contractor's insurer does not set the owner's requirements, and the general conditions contain no amounts to copy.

questions.question: A specifier wants the owner's bonds and insurance decisions, made with its insurance advisor, recorded on a standard form for transfer to the A/E. Which EJCDC document is recommended for this purpose?

options.A: C-051, Letter to Owner on Bonds and Insurance
options.B: C-052, Owner's Instructions Concerning Bonds and Insurance
options.C: C-800, Supplementary Conditions of the Construction Contract
options.D: C-700, Standard General Conditions of the Construction Contract
options.E: G612, Owner's Instructions to the Architect
options.F: C-520, Agreement Between Owner and Contractor (Stipulated Price)

questions.explanation: EJCDC C-052, Owner's Instructions Concerning Bonds and Insurance, is the recommended EJCDC form for recording the owner's insurance decisions for the A/E, and C-051 is a prototype letter the A/E can send to ask for that information. C-700, C-800 and C-520 are the general conditions, supplementary conditions and agreement where the information ends up, and G612 is the comparable AIA form, not an EJCDC document.

questions.question: A draft owner-contractor agreement requires the contractor to hold the owner harmless even for suits based solely on the owner's own negligence. What type of clause is this, and what caution applies?

options.A: Broad form; such clauses are unenforceable in a number of states
options.B: Limited form; it protects the owner only when vicariously liable
options.C: Intermediate form; it applies only where both parties are negligent
options.D: Contractual liability form; it requires an owner's protective policy
options.E: Waiver of subrogation; it applies only to losses covered by insurance
options.F: Additional insured endorsement; it does not expand the policy's coverage

questions.explanation: A broad form hold-harmless makes one party hold the other harmless even for suits based on the other party's sole negligence, and broad form agreements are unenforceable in a number of states. The limited form covers only the indemnitor's sole negligence and the intermediate form adds joint negligence, while subrogation waivers and additional insured endorsements are insurance provisions, not hold-harmless clauses.

questions.question: The owner will carry its own builder's risk program, and the general contractor wants protection against coverage gaps that program may leave. What policy does the contractor maintain for this purpose?

options.A: Owner's and contractor's protective policy
options.B: Installation floater on contractor property
options.C: All risks, difference-in-conditions policy
options.D: Reporting form builder's risk coverage
options.E: Umbrella excess liability policy
options.F: Named perils builder's risk policy

questions.explanation: An all risks, difference-in-conditions policy is one a general contractor or subcontractor maintains to fill coverage gaps when the owner, or the general contractor, carries its own builder's risk program. OCP covers the owner's liability for a contractor's work, an installation floater covers property being installed, a reporting form suits fluctuating values, umbrella coverage adds liability limits, and named perils coverage is narrower than all-risk.

questions.question: A contractor with employees working on a project in Ohio must provide workers' compensation coverage. How is that coverage obtained in Ohio?

options.A: From the compulsory state fund, or as a self-insurer where allowed
options.B: From any licensed private carrier, using an other states endorsement
options.C: Through an owner-controlled program that wraps all project workers
options.D: Through the federal Longshore and Harbor Workers program
options.E: From the contractor's home-state carrier, since coverage follows the employer
options.F: Through employer's liability coverage alone, without a statutory policy

questions.explanation: Ohio is one of the monopolistic fund states, with North Dakota, Washington and Wyoming, where workers' compensation must come from the state's compulsory fund unless the employer qualifies to self-insure, which two of those states allow. Private or home-state carriers, wrap-up programs and employer's liability coverage alone are not how coverage is obtained there, and the Longshore and Harbor Workers' Act covers maritime employment.

questions.question: Industry guidance names fire sprinkler systems, curtain walls, and sophisticated exterior claddings as building components the A/E often does not fully design or engineer. What primary reason does it give for delegating their design?

options.A: Their design is usually reserved to the authority having jurisdiction under a separate building permit
options.B: Their unique requirements are known mainly to the manufacturer, which routinely engineers the attachment
options.C: Their design typically falls outside the coverage of most A/E professional liability insurance policies
options.D: Their design must be completed by a separate prime contractor whom the owner retains directly
options.E: Their performance is fixed by reference standards, so no project-specific criteria are needed
options.F: Their design is normally left to the owner's commissioning authority during construction

questions.explanation: These components are delegated because only the manufacturer knows their unique design requirements, or because designing and engineering their attachment to the building is part of the manufacturer's normal service. Delegation is not tied to AHJ permits, insurance exclusions, separate prime contracts or the commissioning authority, and it still needs project-specific performance and design criteria; the specification section assigns the design responsibility to the contractor.

questions.question: A specifier is writing a glazed aluminum curtain wall section in which anchorage design is delegated to the contractor's licensed professional. Under SectionFormat, where should the loads and other design parameters that professional must satisfy be specified?

options.A: In PART 1, within the Delegated Design Submittals article that describes the submittal
options.B: In PART 1, within the Quality Assurance article that lists the professional's qualifications
options.C: In PART 2, within the appropriate product articles such as Performance/Design Criteria
options.D: In PART 3, within the Installation article that governs the anchorage work itself
options.E: In PART 1, within the Administrative Requirements article on coordination
options.F: In PART 1, within the Field Conditions article on existing conditions

questions.explanation: Under SectionFormat, the Delegated Design Submittals article describes only what is to be submitted and does not repeat the requirements the submittal must show. The design criteria belong in the appropriate PART 2 product articles, such as Performance/Design Criteria, and the professional's qualifications go under Quality Assurance. Coordination, field conditions and PART 3 installation articles cover administration, site conditions and execution, not design criteria.

questions.question: Under a delegated-design requirement, the curtain wall supplier's engineer prepares anchorage drawings and engineering calculations. How are these documents handled?

options.A: Sent through the contractor and reviewed by the contractor and A/E as a normal submittal
options.B: Sent by the supplier directly to the A/E's structural consultant, who seals them for permit
options.C: Filed with the authority having jurisdiction, with a copy sent to the A/E for its records
options.D: Delivered to the owner, who forwards them to the A/E along with the closeout documents
options.E: Reviewed only by the contractor, since the design was delegated away from the A/E
options.F: Made part of the contract documents by a change order before fabrication

questions.explanation: The manufacturer or subcontractor answers a delegated-design requirement with drawings and engineering calculations or certifications sent as submittals through the contractor, and the contractor and the A/E review them as they would any other submittal. Delegation does not remove the A/E's review, the submittals do not become contract documents, and bypassing the contractor, filing only with the AHJ or waiting for closeout breaks the submittal chain.

questions.question: An owner has just conceived the project parameters for a new fire station. The A/E's work of researching the products, materials, and systems the project needs is expected to result in which set of outcomes?

options.A: Define the owner's program, set the construction budget, and choose the project delivery method
options.B: Choose products from suppliers, determine product requirements, and design to incorporate them
options.C: Prequalify suppliers, establish allowances for unselected products, and write substitution procedures
options.D: Evaluate proposed equivalents, approve contractor substitutions, and review product submittals
options.E: Prepare the bid form, prequalify bidders, and award the construction contract
options.F: Commission the systems, train the owner's staff, and assemble O&M manuals

questions.explanation: Product research follows the owner's conception of the project; it ends with products and suppliers chosen, the product-related requirements set, and a design developed around the chosen products. Program, budget and delivery method are part of the owner's project conception, while bidding, allowances, substitution and submittal review, commissioning and closeout belong to later procurement and construction stages.

questions.question: A specifier is recording who shaped product choices on a laboratory project. Which pairing of participant and basis of influence correctly describes input to product selection?

options.A: Owner or contractor: system products, based on applicable code requirements
