options.B: MEP designers: aesthetic products, based on successful previous projects
options.C: A/E: aesthetic products and manufacturers, from past projects and research
options.D: Product representative: the final selection, based on design team discussions
options.E: Contractor: the final selection, based on its own bid pricing
options.F: Owner or contractor: aesthetic products, based on product research

questions.explanation: The A/E usually shapes the choice of aesthetic products and their manufacturers, drawing on product research and on products that worked on earlier projects. Owners and contractors contribute preferences for suppliers they have worked with, and MEP designers influence products for their own systems based on codes and experience. Neither the contractor nor a product representative makes the final call; the A/E does, alone or after discussion with the team.

questions.question: A courthouse's contract documents require the contractor to list the products and manufacturers its bid is based on. When is this list furnished, and how complete is it typically?

options.A: With each bid; often covering only key products
options.B: With each bid; covering every product to be furnished
options.C: After award; often covering only key products
options.D: After award; covering every product to be furnished
options.E: With the first application for payment; often covering only key products
options.F: With the first product submittals; covering every product to be furnished

questions.explanation: When the contract requires bidders to name the products and manufacturers their bid is based on, the list is submitted with the bid, and it often covers only key products rather than everything. It is not deferred until after award, tied to the first payment application or first submittals, or meant to be a complete inventory of every product.

questions.question: A school was bid on performance-based specifications listing several acceptable HVAC products, and the documents did not require bidders to list their products. Before award, the owner asks which HVAC units the apparent low bidder priced. How can the A/E find out?

options.A: Require the bidder to file substitution requests for the HVAC units it priced
options.B: Issue an addendum requiring all bidders to identify the HVAC units they priced
options.C: Tell the owner this cannot be learned until construction-phase product submittals
options.D: Ask the bidder in a post-bid interview which units its bid was based on
options.E: Require the bidder to submit HVAC shop drawings before the contract is awarded
options.F: Request the bidder's schedule of values, which lists each product it priced

questions.explanation: When bidders were not required to list their products, the A/E may ask the bidder in a post-bid interview which products its bid was based on, so the owner need not wait for construction submittals. The units priced are among the acceptable products, so no substitution request applies; addenda change the documents before bids are received; shop drawings come after award; and a schedule of values breaks down costs, not products.

questions.question: A specialty resin terrazzo system meets every performance criterion for a rural county courthouse, but the nearest stock of the manufacturer's repair materials and its nearest factory service technicians are 900 miles away. In evaluating the product, this finding bears most directly on:

options.A: The availability of workers skilled in that installation technique locally
options.B: The product's availability months later, when the project is under construction
options.C: The availability and cost of maintenance supplies and maintenance services
options.D: Whether standard colors meet aesthetic standards or custom colors are needed
options.E: The manufacturer's financial stability and track record
options.F: The product's compliance with federal, state, and local codes

questions.explanation: During product evaluation the A/E should weigh the availability and cost of maintenance supplies and of the maintenance services the manufacturer offers; distant repair stock and service technicians are exactly that concern. Skilled local labor, availability once construction starts, standard versus custom colors, code compliance and the manufacturer's financial health are separate evaluation factors that the facts in this scenario do not raise.

questions.question: A specifier is choosing between a domestic and an imported manufacturer of chlorine feed equipment for a water treatment plant. Country of origin is a sourcing consideration because it can affect:

options.A: Delivery time, manufacturer longevity, financial stability, and track record
options.B: Testing, distribution network, local representatives, and sustainability certifications
options.C: Availability of parts, installed cost, operating cost, and maintenance cost
options.D: Delivery time, testing, the availability of parts, and warranty service
options.E: Delivery time, distribution network, manufacturer longevity, and warranty service
options.F: Testing, availability of parts, financial stability, and local representatives

questions.explanation: Whether a product is domestic or imported is a sourcing factor because it can change the delivery time, the testing, how readily parts can be had, and warranty service. Manufacturer longevity, financial stability and track record, the distribution network, local representatives and sustainability certifications are separate items on the sourcing list, not effects of country of origin, and installed, operating and maintenance costs are economic factors.

questions.question: After selecting a roof membrane, the A/E turns to the research gathered during product evaluation. That research is used to develop which written documents detailing the product's technical aspects?

options.A: Shop drawings, product data, and samples submitted for the A/E's review
options.B: Preliminary project descriptions, design narratives, or specifications
options.C: Manufacturer datasheets, product drawings, and budgetary quotes
options.D: Life-cycle cost analyses, value analysis reports, or bid forms
options.E: Requests for information, field reports, and change orders
options.F: Operation and maintenance manuals and warranty documents

questions.explanation: Once a product is chosen, the A/E turns the evaluation research into written documents that set out its technical aspects: preliminary project descriptions, design narratives or specifications. Datasheets, drawings and quotes are research inputs; shop drawings, product data and samples are construction submittals; RFIs, field reports and change orders are construction administration records; and O&M manuals and warranties are closeout documents.

questions.question: A specifier is evaluating a proposed rainscreen cladding system. Beyond the design intent, industry guidance names several criteria against which proposed systems are evaluated. Which group consists entirely of criteria from that list?

options.A: Code requirements, contractor means and methods, quality, and cost
options.B: Climate conditions, warranty length, reference standards, and cost
options.C: Code requirements, climate conditions, constructability, and quality
options.D: Constructability, installer availability, reference standards, and quality
options.E: Climate conditions, constructability, aesthetics, and reference standards
options.F: Code requirements, climate conditions, product availability, and cost

questions.explanation: Besides the design intent, proposed systems are judged against six criteria: code requirements, reference standards, climate conditions, constructability, quality and cost. Only the keyed group uses nothing but those. Every other group slips in something outside that list, such as contractor means and methods, warranty length, installer availability, aesthetics or product availability.

questions.question: A specifier on a wastewater treatment upgrade has limited time to analyze the products proposed for the project. Which kinds of products does industry guidance single out as especially needing the specifier's analysis to confirm they suit the project?

options.A: Finish materials chosen mainly for their appearance
options.B: Products specified solely by reference standard
options.C: Owner-furnished items installed by the contractor
options.D: Complex equipment and new technologies
options.E: Commodity items available from many suppliers
options.F: Products the owner has used on earlier projects

questions.explanation: The specifier analyzes proposed products to confirm they suit the project, and complex equipment and new technologies are singled out as needing that scrutiny most. Finishes chosen for appearance, products specified by reference standard, owner-furnished items, commodity items and products the owner already knows are not the categories singled out for extra analysis.

questions.question: In summarizing the specifier's role in product evaluation, industry guidance states that the evaluation of systems, assemblies, and materials is driven primarily by which of the following?

options.A: The owner's needs and requirements
options.B: The contractor's preferred installation methods
options.C: The manufacturers' published performance data
options.D: The A/E firm's office master specifications
options.E: The product representatives' recommendations
options.F: The plan review comments of the code official

questions.explanation: In short, the specifier judges proposed systems, assemblies and materials by the owner's needs and requirements for the project. Manufacturer data, office masters and representatives' advice are tools in that process, code review is one of the checks, and the contractor's preferred methods do not drive design-phase evaluation.

questions.question: An A/E must select a building's HVAC system as well as the diffusers, dampers, and controls that connect to it. How should the A/E order these evaluations to make the selection process efficient?

options.A: Evaluate the components first, then fit a system around them
options.B: Evaluate the major system first, then the components for compatibility
options.C: Evaluate system and components together, resolving conflicts at submittals
options.D: Evaluate the system only, leaving components to contractor submittals
options.E: Evaluate system and components separately, each on its own merits
options.F: Evaluate whichever item has the longest lead time first

questions.explanation: Because some products affect the performance of others and later selections, the A/E should start with the major systems and subsystems and only then judge smaller components on quality, performance and compatibility with the choices already made. Starting with components or with lead times reverses that logic, judging items separately ignores compatibility, and deferring components or conflicts to contractor submittals abandons the A/E's evaluation role.

questions.question: What is the primary goal of evaluating systems, assemblies, and materials during design?

options.A: To identify the least costly product that still satisfies minimum code
options.B: To establish a list of acceptable manufacturers before bidding begins
options.C: To determine product applicability and compatibility for the project
options.D: To confirm that installers hold the required trade qualifications
options.E: To confirm that product warranties meet the owner's terms
options.F: To choose the products the contractor can install fastest

questions.explanation: The primary goal is to determine whether available products are applicable and whether different products and systems are compatible in meeting the project requirements. Cost savings are mentioned only as a possible side benefit of competition. Manufacturer lists, installer qualifications, warranty terms and installation speed are not what the evaluation is for.

questions.question: An A/E's checklist for a proposed curtain wall covers three of the four standard product evaluation components: requirements and design intent, code requirements, and constructability and construction sequence. Which component is missing from the checklist?

options.A: Availability from multiple local suppliers
options.B: Conformance with the schedule of values
options.C: Consistency with the project drawings
options.D: Acceptance by the owner's maintenance staff
options.E: Agreement with the manufacturer's warranty terms
options.F: Approval by the owner's commissioning authority

questions.explanation: Systems, assemblies and materials are checked four ways: do they meet the project requirements and design intent, are they consistent with the drawings, do they comply with code, and do they suit the desired constructability and construction sequence. The missing one is consistency with the drawings. Supplier availability, the schedule of values, maintenance staff acceptance, warranty terms and commissioning approval are not on the list.

questions.question: An owner asks when the A/E will begin evaluating products for a new clinic. Under the progressive evaluation industry guidance describes, in which phase does product evaluation begin?

options.A: Schematic design
options.B: Design development
options.C: Construction documents
options.D: Procurement
options.E: Project conception
options.F: Construction

questions.explanation: Product evaluation is progressive: it begins in schematic design, when the A/E or owner makes conceptual decisions on the primary products to define the functional requirements, and detailed product information is gathered and reviewed in design development. Project conception sets the owner's requirements before evaluation starts, and construction documents, procurement and construction come after products have been evaluated.

questions.question: Which pairing correctly describes the roles in establishing and checking the requirements that drive product selection?

options.A: The A/E sets the requirements; the owner checks products against them
options.B: The owner sets the requirements; the A/E evaluates products for compliance
options.C: The A/E sets the requirements; the contractor verifies them during submittals
options.D: The owner sets the requirements; the contractor evaluates products for compliance
options.E: The contractor sets the requirements; the A/E checks submittals against them
options.F: The owner and A/E set them jointly; the contractor verifies them at closeout

questions.explanation: The owner establishes the requirements for the project's details and design, and those requirements shape product selection; the A/E then evaluates products for compliance with them. Reversing the roles, giving the contractor the job of setting or checking requirements at submittals or closeout, or making the owner the evaluator misstates who does what during design.

questions.question: During design development, an A/E collects detailed manufacturer data on three candidate roofing systems. Under a progressive evaluation approach, what must be established before the A/E prepares the drawings and specifications covering the roofing products?

options.A: That contractor pricing has been obtained for each candidate system
options.B: That the owner has signed an acceptance of each listed manufacturer
options.C: That the installing subcontractor has completed a constructability review
options.D: That the selected items comply with the project's requirements
options.E: That the roofing manufacturer has issued a project-specific warranty
options.F: That the building official has issued the building permit

questions.explanation: The A/E prepares specifications and drawings for selected products only after determining that those products comply with the project requirements. Contractor pricing, a subcontractor's constructability review, owner sign-off on each manufacturer, a manufacturer's warranty and a building permit are not the gate for this step; the gate is the A/E's compliance determination.

questions.question: While reviewing regulatory requirements, an A/E finds that two different standards each define functional requirements for the same type of product, and their requirements differ substantially. What does this redundancy make especially important?

options.A: Specifying whichever of the two standards was published most recently
options.B: Knowing what the compliance evaluation covers and which standard is cited
options.C: Leaving the choice of governing standard to the AHJ at plan review
options.D: Citing both standards and letting the contractor choose either one
options.E: Writing a new performance standard specific to the project
options.F: Adopting the less stringent standard to widen competition

questions.explanation: Overlapping codes and standards can set very different requirements for the same product, so it is critical to know which aspects of the product the code compliance evaluation covers and which standard the specifications reference. Picking the newest edition, deferring to the AHJ, writing a new standard or adopting the weaker one does not address that, and letting the contractor choose would invite the lesser requirement.

questions.question: Late in design development, an A/E finds that a light fixture the owner favors for its appearance fails to comply with a safety standard specified for the project. What is the best course of action?

options.A: Include it, provided the owner accepts the risk in writing
options.B: Include it and require the contractor to seek an AHJ variance
options.C: Exclude it from the products selected for the work
options.D: List it as an approved substitution for the specified fixture
options.E: Include it as an owner-furnished item outside the contract
options.F: Include it if the manufacturer will warrant its performance

questions.explanation: A product that fails an applicable code, safety rule or other specified standard should be kept out of the project; code compliance is the screen that removes products creating unreasonable hazards. Owner acceptance of risk, a contractor-sought variance, listing it as a substitution, furnishing it outside the contract or relying on a warranty would all still put a noncompliant product into the work.

questions.question: In the recommended approach to evaluating products for constructability and sequencing, which two inputs does the constructability evaluation use to develop the dates and milestones that feed the sequence evaluation?

options.A: The schedule of values and the submittal register
options.B: The bid tabulation and the list of proposed subcontractors
options.C: The drawing index and the project manual table of contents
options.D: The overall project schedule and the major equipment list
options.E: The geotechnical report and the site survey
options.F: The cost estimate and the list of allowances

questions.explanation: The constructability evaluation uses the overall project schedule together with the major equipment list to set the dates and milestones that feed the sequence evaluation; product procurement dates and supplier delivery needs are then checked against that sequence. The schedule of values, bid tabulation, drawing index, site data and cost estimate are not the inputs this evaluation relies on.

questions.question: A pump station design includes six identical pumps that each require factory start-up and testing. When evaluating design and construction sequencing, which approach does industry guidance direct the A/E to take?

options.A: Group the similar pump work and integrate commissioning into the schedule
options.B: Stagger each pump installation across separate phases to level the workforce
options.C: Defer commissioning considerations until the work reaches substantial completion
options.D: Assign each pump to a separate subcontractor so the work proceeds in parallel
options.E: Specify a different pump manufacturer for each unit to spread risk
options.F: Have the owner's staff perform start-up after occupancy to save cost

questions.explanation: On projects with several pieces of the same equipment, similar activities should be sequenced together to gain the efficiency of repetition, and the A/E should evaluate commissioning and start-up needs so the overall schedule integrates them with design and construction sequencing. Staggering, splitting or mixing manufacturers loses those efficiencies, and deferring commissioning or start-up defeats the integration.

questions.question: A school renovation must be completed over one summer, and the specified switchgear has a long manufacturing lead time. Which action does industry guidance identify as a way to reduce the schedule impact of such materials?

options.A: Procure the long-lead item early in the project schedule
options.B: Wait to order it until the contractor's schedule is approved
options.C: Replace it with field-assembled equipment built on site
options.D: Extend the contract time by change order after award
options.E: Add liquidated damages to push the supplier to deliver faster
options.F: Carry the switchgear as an allowance to be selected after award

questions.explanation: Ordering long-lead materials early in the schedule limits their effect on the overall project schedule, and the schedule must leave enough time to procure what is specified. Waiting for the contractor's schedule or deferring selection through an allowance pushes the order later, and field assembly, liquidated damages or a time extension do not shorten the lead time.

questions.question: An owner's project has a very short construction timeframe, and the lowest-cost source of a key product cannot deliver in time. Which trade-off may be appropriate?

options.A: Splitting the order among several lower-cost suppliers
options.B: Employing a more expensive manufacturer to save time
options.C: Relaxing the reference standards to widen product availability
options.D: Replacing the manufactured product with site-built construction
options.E: Extending the construction timeframe to suit the cheapest supplier
options.F: Covering the product with a cash allowance to be selected later

questions.explanation: On projects with short schedules, a more expensive manufacturer may be used to save time in the product's schedule and lessen the effect on the overall schedule. Splitting the order, relaxing reference standards or switching to site-built work are not that trade-off, and relaxing standards would sacrifice quality; stretching the timeframe ignores the owner's requirement, and an allowance only postpones the decision.

questions.question: An A/E is comparing a factory-built pump skid with field assembly of the same components. Industry guidance notes that using a shop-fabricated item, where working conditions can be better controlled, is often beneficial to the owner on what assumption?

options.A: That the fabricator is located in the same state as the site
options.B: That the AHJ inspects the work at the fabrication facility
options.C: That the contractor waives the right to propose substitutions
options.D: That the fabricated product can be transported to the site
options.E: That the item is purchased by the owner and furnished to the contractor
options.F: That the shop holds a third-party quality management certification

questions.explanation: Shop work under better-controlled conditions is often to the owner's benefit as long as the finished product can actually be shipped to the site, and project conditions decide whether off-site assembly saves cost or time. Fabricator location, off-site AHJ inspection, substitution waivers, owner purchase and shop certification are not the condition attached to that benefit.

questions.question: When selecting products for interior conditions, which group consists entirely of components that industry guidance lists for evaluation?

options.A: Building air quality, ventilation, lighting, and noise
options.B: Heating, ventilation, lighting, and occupant security
options.C: Air quality, noise, lighting, and fire separation
options.D: Heating, noise, ventilation, and space planning
options.E: Air quality, heating, noise, and accessibility
options.F: Ventilation, lighting, noise, and wayfinding

questions.explanation: The interior components to evaluate when selecting products are building air quality, heating, ventilation, lighting and noise. Occupant security, fire separation, space planning, accessibility and wayfinding are not on that list, so only the keyed group stays entirely within it.

questions.question: To keep interior materials in a busy school from needing frequent replacement and becoming costly maintenance items, industry guidance directs particular attention to durability for which materials?

options.A: Materials concealed within wall and ceiling cavities
options.B: Materials selected for appearance, such as wall coverings
options.C: Materials subject to heavy wear, such as flooring
options.D: Materials with long lead times, such as custom casework
options.E: Materials exposed to exterior weather, such as roofing
options.F: Materials chosen to control sound, such as acoustical panels

questions.explanation: To keep interior materials from needing frequent replacement and becoming costly maintenance items, the A/E should evaluate durability within the interior conditions, especially for materials that take a lot of wear, such as flooring. Concealed materials, appearance-driven finishes, long-lead items and acoustical products are not the emphasis, and roofing is an exterior-conditions concern.

questions.question: An A/E evaluates products for their effect on a building's interior conditions and on its energy efficiency. This is mainly accomplished by efficiently reducing the energy needed for which uses?

options.A: Cooling, plumbing, and vertical transportation
options.B: Heating, ventilation, and stormwater pumping
options.C: Heating, lighting, and equipment operation
options.D: Lighting, elevators, and domestic hot water
options.E: Heating, cooling, and domestic water heating
options.F: Lighting, ventilation, and vertical transportation

questions.explanation: Energy-efficient product selection for interior conditions mainly targets the energy used for heating, lighting and equipment operation. Ventilation is one of the interior components to evaluate, not part of this energy statement, and stormwater pumping is a site concern. Cooling, plumbing, elevators and hot water are not the uses named.

questions.question: A national developer wants to build its southwestern stucco-wall, flat-roof house prototype unchanged in a Midwest subdivision. Besides the colder climate, what does industry guidance say materials and methods must also be compatible with?

options.A: The developer's national brand and marketing standards
options.B: Regional and local cultural and aesthetic conditions
options.C: The original prototype's referenced standard editions
options.D: Nationally available manufacturer warranty programs
options.E: The developer's preferred national supplier contracts
options.F: The lowest first cost available in the region

questions.explanation: Materials and methods must suit regional and local cultural and aesthetic conditions as well as the climate: southwestern stucco and flat roofs are not typical in the Midwest, where homes usually have wood framing, vinyl siding and pitched roofs. National brand standards, supplier contracts or warranty programs do not override local conditions, carrying over the prototype's standard editions does not address regional fit, and first cost is a separate economic question.

questions.question: For a site that experiences frequent wet weather events and intense storms, which design response does industry guidance identify as becoming more important?

options.A: Specifying products suited to mild climates with humidity swings
options.B: Assembling components off-site under controlled shop conditions
options.C: Selecting stucco walls and flat roofs typical of arid regions
options.D: Directing stormwater away from the site and controlling its release
options.E: Matching materials to regional cultural and aesthetic conditions
options.F: Selecting floor finishes for durability under heavy wear

questions.explanation: Where wet weather and intense storms are frequent, moving stormwater off the site and controlling its release matter more, as does choosing products suited to wetter climates. Products for mild, humid climates answer a different condition, off-site assembly is about shop control and schedule, stucco and flat roofs illustrate an arid regional style, and regional aesthetics and floor durability are separate evaluation concerns.

questions.question: Among the types of reference standards, ASTM E2112, the standard practice covering how exterior windows, doors and skylights are installed, is given as an example of which type?

options.A: Basic material standard
options.B: Performance standard
options.C: Workmanship standard
options.D: Test method standard
options.E: Design standard
options.F: Product standard

questions.explanation: ASTM E2112 is the usual example of a workmanship standard, even though its title is about installation: it sets out how the work is to be done. Basic material standards cover raw materials such as aluminum bar, ASTM F1487 illustrates performance standards, ASTM E119 test method standards, ACI 318 design standards and APA PS-1 product standards.

questions.question: Reference standards are commonly sorted into types. Under which type is ACI 318, Building Code Requirements for Structural Concrete, usually listed?

options.A: Code
options.B: Product standard
options.C: Basic material standard
options.D: Design standard
options.E: Installation standard
options.F: Test method standard

questions.explanation: Although its title mentions building code requirements, ACI 318 is the standard example of a design standard. The usual code example is ANSI/ASME A17.1 for elevators and escalators, APA PS-1 illustrates product standards, ASTM B211 basic material standards, NFPA 13 installation standards and ASTM E119 test method standards.

questions.question: A specification section cites a referenced standard only by its designation and title. The contractor argues that the standard's provisions are not binding because their text does not appear in the project manual. How do the referenced provisions apply?

options.A: Only provisions restated in Part 2 of the section are binding
options.B: They become binding only when the local AHJ adopts the standard
options.C: They become part of the specifications as if included in full
options.D: They serve as guidance unless repeated in Division 01 sections
options.E: They apply only where the drawings note the standard by name
options.F: They bind only if a copy of the standard is bound into the manual

questions.explanation: A standard cited by number, title or other designation becomes part of the specifications just as though its full text were included, which is what saves the A/E from writing lengthy text. Restating provisions in PART 2 or Division 01, noting the standard on the drawings, or binding a copy into the project manual is not required, and AHJ adoption governs code status, not whether a cited standard binds the contract.

questions.question: An A/E is choosing between two reference standards for a fire-resistive joint system and wants to ensure acceptance by the authority having jurisdiction. Where applicable, what does industry guidance recommend?

options.A: Use the standards listed in the model or local codes
options.B: Use the more recent of the two standards' editions
options.C: Use whichever standard the manufacturer certifies to
options.D: Use the standard with the most demanding requirements
options.E: Use the standard with the broadest product availability
options.F: Use whichever standard the installer is trained under

questions.explanation: Where applicable, the A/E should pick standards that the model or local codes list, so that the AHJ will accept them; depending on how a code lists it, the standard may act as a code requirement or as a guideline for acceptance. Edition date, manufacturer certification, stringency, product availability and installer training do not by themselves establish AHJ acceptance.

questions.question: While reviewing a reference standard before citing it, an A/E finds that several of its provisions conflict with other parts of the project. What choice must the A/E make?

options.A: Cite it with a precedence clause, or let the AHJ resolve the conflicts
options.B: Cite it with stated exceptions, or write original requirements instead
options.C: Omit it and let the contractor propose an equivalent standard instead
options.D: Cite it unchanged and resolve the conflicts through submittal review
options.E: Cite it and rely on a more-stringent-governs clause for every conflict
options.F: Cite it and list the conflicts in a general note on the drawings

questions.explanation: When a standard is not compatible with other project requirements or contains duplications and contradictions, the A/E must either reference it and define exceptions or write original requirements into the specifications. Precedence or more-stringent-governs clauses cannot handle every conflict, and AHJ resolution, contractor-proposed equivalents, submittal review and drawing notes all leave the contradiction in the documents.

questions.question: A small A/E firm finds that keeping a current library of every reference standard it might cite is expensive and difficult. What does industry guidance advise as the minimum?

options.A: Rely on manufacturers' summaries of the cited standards
options.B: Obtain each standard only when a contractor requests it
options.C: Cite only standards that the AHJ keeps on file locally
options.D: Obtain at least the commonly referenced standards
options.E: Cite standards only by title, so no copies are needed
options.F: Require the contractor to keep the cited standards at the site

questions.explanation: The A/E should have access to the standards it proposes to cite; a complete current library is costly, but at a minimum the commonly referenced standards should be obtained. Manufacturer summaries are not the standard itself, citing by title does not tell the A/E what it is requiring, and waiting for contractor requests, relying on the AHJ's files or putting copies at the site does not give the A/E access during design.

questions.question: A specifier intends to cite a newly revised ASTM standard that she has not yet read, planning to check its content during submittal review. What is wrong with this plan?

options.A: It should be reviewed and understood in full before it is incorporated
options.B: Revised standards may not be cited until the AHJ formally adopts them
options.C: Submittal review of standards is the responsibility of the contractor
options.D: Newly revised standards must be referenced by title without a date
options.E: A revised standard must be restated in full within the section
options.F: Only the manufacturer can confirm what a revised standard requires

questions.explanation: The A/E must read a reference standard and fully understand what it says and why before writing it into the specifications, because other requirements must be compatible with it and it must be free of duplications and contradictions. Submittal review is too late to catch those problems. There is no AHJ-adoption prerequisite, citation by reference avoids restating the text, and omitting the date weakens a citation rather than fixing it.

questions.question: To deal with overlaps between referenced standards, a specifier adds a statement that the more stringent requirement governs whenever a standard conflicts with the specifications or another standard. How should this statement be viewed?

options.A: It resolves every conflict, so duplications need not be identified
options.B: It cannot cover every conflict; duplications must still be resolved
options.C: It is improper because it shifts design responsibility to the contractor
options.D: It belongs in the owner-contractor agreement, not in Division 01
options.E: It is improper, since specifications may never modify a cited standard
options.F: It is valid only if repeated in every section that cites a standard

questions.explanation: The A/E may state that the more stringent requirement applies when a standard conflicts with the specifications or another standard, but such a statement cannot be relied on for every possible conflict. The A/E still has to identify duplications and modify the references in the specifications to remove contradictions. The statement is not prohibited, does not belong in the agreement, and need not be repeated in every section.

questions.question: One reference standard is often cited because it covers numerous contractor-owner and contractor-subcontractor relationships and uses the terms owner and contract documents in a different sense than the general conditions do. Which standard is it?

options.A: AISC Code of Standard Practice
options.B: AISC Specification for Structural Steel Buildings
options.C: NFPA 13 Standard for Installation of Sprinkler Systems
options.D: ACI 318 Building Code Requirements for Structural Concrete
options.E: ASTM C150 Standard Specification for Portland Cement
options.F: ASME A17.1 Safety Code for Elevators and Escalators

questions.explanation: The AISC Code of Standard Practice is the usual example of a standard whose relationship provisions, and whose use of the terms owner and contract documents, differ from the general conditions and invite misunderstandings. The AISC structural steel specification illustrates nested references to other standards, ASTM C150 embedded options, and ACI 318, NFPA 13 and A17.1 the design, installation and code types of standard.

questions.question: A specifier cites a standard because one of its provisions appears to be a mandatory, permanent part of the standard, and does not restate that provision in the section. What risk does this create?

options.A: A footnote or later paragraph may void it unless the specs state it
options.B: The provision binds only the subcontractor that the standard names
options.C: The provision lapses once the related submittals have been approved
options.D: The general conditions automatically override the cited provision
options.E: The provision binds the manufacturer but not the installer
options.F: The provision takes effect only once the AHJ enforces it

questions.explanation: Some provisions look like a permanent part of a standard, yet a footnote or later paragraph can void them unless the specifications state them explicitly. References to particular subcontractors are a separate problem to avoid, submittal approval does not cancel a provision, the general conditions do not automatically override it, and a cited provision does not split between manufacturer and installer or wait for AHJ enforcement.

questions.question: Which situation in a draft specification illustrates what industry guidance calls an embedded option in a reference standard?

options.A: A cited standard that refers in turn to several other standards
options.B: A cited standard whose minimums nearly any product can meet
options.C: A cited standard that assigns work to a particular trade
options.D: A cited standard offering several classes that must be selected
options.E: A cited standard repeating statements found in Division 01
options.F: A cited standard enforced in different editions by different AHJs

questions.explanation: Embedded options are the categories, classes or groups within a standard from which the applicable properties must be chosen; ASTM C150, for example, covers ten cement types, and if the A/E does not choose, the contractor will likely pick the cheapest. A standard citing other standards is the multiple-standards problem, very liberal minimums concern the level of requirements, and trade references, duplicated Division 01 statements and differing enforced editions are separate issues.

questions.question: The problem of multiple standards is often illustrated with a structural steel document that refers to several ASTM standards, which in turn refer to still other ASTM standards. Which document is it?

options.A: AISC Code of Standard Practice for Steel Buildings and Bridges
options.B: AISC Specifications for Design, Fabrication, and Erection of Structural Steel
options.C: AWS D1.1, Structural Welding Code, Steel
options.D: ACI 318, Building Code Requirements for Structural Concrete
options.E: ASTM A615, Specification for Deformed Steel Bars for Concrete Reinforcement
options.F: ASTM C150, Standard Specification for Portland Cement

questions.explanation: The AISC document on design, fabrication and erection of structural steel for buildings is the example: it cites ASTM standards that cite still others, so the A/E must know the added material. The AISC Code of Standard Practice illustrates conflicting contractual terms, ASTM C150 illustrates embedded options, ACI 318 is a design standard, and AWS D1.1 and ASTM A615 are not the example used.

questions.question: A section cites a primary standard that in turn lists several secondary standards. How do these nested standards affect the specification?

options.A: They take precedence over the primary standard wherever they differ
options.B: They can create conflicts and multiple choices, as a single reference can
options.C: They eliminate any embedded options found in the primary standard
options.D: They apply to the fabricator but not to the prime contractor
options.E: They have no effect unless the section also cites each one by name
options.F: They resolve any conflicts between the primary standard and the section

questions.explanation: Standards cited inside another standard create conflicting information and multiple choices just as a single reference standard does, so the A/E must know what they contain. They do not take precedence over the primary standard, they add embedded options rather than removing them, and they come in through the primary citation without being named again. Far from resolving conflicts with the specifications, they are a source of them, and nothing limits them to the fabricator.

questions.question: An A/E is concerned that standards nested within a cited AISC document may carry qualifications that contradict the project specifications. What does industry guidance identify as the only real solution?

options.A: Adding a clause stating that the latest edition of each standard governs
options.B: Deleting every secondary reference contained in the cited primary standard
options.C: Knowing and understanding what each additional referenced standard contains
options.D: Requiring the contractor to certify compliance with each nested standard listed
options.E: Adding a clause to Division 01 that the more stringent requirement governs
options.F: Leaving conflicts among the nested standards for the AHJ to resolve at plan review

questions.explanation: Standards cited within a primary standard must not carry qualifications that contradict other referenced standards or the project specifications, and the only real safeguard is for the A/E to know and understand that added material. Latest-edition and more-stringent-governs clauses cannot catch every contradiction, contractor certification and AHJ rulings leave the conflicts in the documents, and a specifier cannot delete references from a published standard.

questions.question: A referenced roofing standard states that the roofing subcontractor shall perform certain field tests. Why should such a subcontractor reference be avoided in the project specifications?

options.A: MasterFormat sections are organized to assign work to specific trades
options.B: Construction contracts are usually written for one contractor
options.C: The owner normally selects and contracts with each subcontractor
options.D: Subcontractor duties may be defined only in Division 01 sections
options.E: The A/E assigns the work among the subcontractors in the specifications
options.F: Reference standards bind the contract only once the AHJ adopts them

questions.explanation: Construction contracts are usually written with one contractor, so a specification should not make a subcontractor responsible for work even when a reference standard does; how the work is divided among subcontractors is the contractor's decision, not the A/E's. MasterFormat sections are not meant to assign work to trades, the owner does not normally contract with subcontractors, no rule confines subcontractor duties to Division 01, and a cited standard binds the contract without AHJ adoption.

questions.question: A specifier finds that the minimum requirements in a reference standard are so liberal that nearly any product on the market can meet them. What is the appropriate response?

options.A: Cite the standard unchanged because its minimums govern
options.B: Leave the quality level to the contractor's product submittals
options.C: Ask the AHJ to amend the standard before it is cited
options.D: Make exceptions to the standard within the specifications
options.E: Rely on an extended warranty to make up for the low bar
options.F: Add a clause stating that the more stringent requirement governs

questions.explanation: Reference standards often set minimums that are either so strict they rule out most available materials or so loose that almost anything passes, and the A/E may write exceptions to the standard into the specifications to avoid either extreme. Citing it unchanged accepts the low bar, submittals and the AHJ cannot raise a requirement the specifications never state, a more-stringent-governs clause has nothing stricter to compare against, and a warranty is no substitute for investigating the product.

questions.question: A specifier is sorting the warranty requirements in a project manual using the two basic warranty types that industry guidance identifies. Which pair matches those categories?

options.A: Construction warranties covering products and workmanship, and product-only warranties
options.B: Express warranties stated in writing, and implied warranties arising from a sale
options.C: Full warranties with all UCC remedies, and limited warranties with reduced remedies
options.D: Contractor correction-period obligations, and manufacturer extended warranties
options.E: Two-party warranties from the contractor, and three-party guaranties through a surety
options.F: Prorated warranties that decline each year, and no-dollar-limit warranties

questions.explanation: The two basic types used in construction are construction warranties or guaranties, which cover products and workmanship and are usually extended warranties specified in individual sections, and warranties that cover products only. Express versus implied and full versus limited are UCC distinctions, the correction period is a contract obligation, a surety-backed guaranty describes a three-party relationship, and prorated and no-dollar-limit describe how a warranty pays.

questions.question: An owner building identical facilities in two states asks why its counsel warns that the same manufacturer's product warranty might be interpreted differently at each site. Which explanation is consistent with industry guidance?

options.A: The UCC is a federal statute, but each state's building code modifies its warranty terms
options.B: Each state separately adopted the UCC as its own law, and the enactments vary somewhat by state
options.C: Product warranties are governed by the general conditions, which each state amends by statute
options.D: The UCC applies only to consumer goods, so state common law governs construction products
options.E: The FAR governs product warranties, and each state applies it differently
options.F: Product warranties are governed only by the warranty's own written terms

questions.explanation: Warranties on goods arise from a sale and are governed by the UCC, other applicable state law and the warranty's own terms. Each state enacted the UCC as its own law, so the law is largely uniform nationally but varies somewhat from state to state. The UCC is not a federal statute and is not limited to consumer goods, the FAR governs federal contracts rather than state law, and building codes and general conditions do not rewrite the UCC.

questions.question: Construction warranties, which cover both products and workmanship, are usually which of the following?

options.A: Third-party guaranties furnished through a surety company
options.B: One-year warranties set by the standard general conditions
options.C: Implied warranties attached by law to the sale of goods
options.D: Extended warranties specified in various specification sections
options.E: Purchase warranties covering the products alone
options.F: Warranties of title given by the seller of the goods

questions.explanation: Construction warranties, which cover both products and workmanship, are usually extended warranties written into the individual specification sections. The one-year obligation in standard general conditions is a correction period, implied warranties and warranties of title come from the UCC with a sale of goods, purchase warranties cover products only, and a surety-backed guaranty is a separate three-party arrangement.

questions.question: Industry guidance cites Black's Law Dictionary to explain that guaranty and warranty are etymologically the same word. What basis does it give?

options.A: The Old German letter w was rendered as g in Middle English law
options.B: Both derive from a Latin legal term for a promise made under seal
options.C: Both entered American usage through the drafters of the UCC
options.D: The Norman French letter g is interchangeable with the English w
options.E: Both come from an Anglo-Saxon term for a pledge of quality
options.F: Both were coined in English insurance law of the 1700s

questions.explanation: Black's Law Dictionary traces both words to one root: the g of Norman French corresponds to the English w, so guaranty and warranty are etymologically the same word. Old German, Latin, Anglo-Saxon, UCC and insurance-law origins are not the basis given. Despite the shared root, the law gives the two words slightly different meanings.

questions.question: A surety company signs a separate contract agreeing to step in if a roofing contractor does not perform its obligations to the owner. Using the legal meanings industry guidance gives, this arrangement is best described as a:

options.A: Warranty, because it assures stipulated responsibilities for completed work
options.B: Guaranty, because a third party assumes responsibility if the principal defaults
options.C: Warranty, because the surety becomes the principal for the roofing work
options.D: Guaranty, because the principal itself assures performance of its own completed work
options.E: Express warranty, because the surety's promise is made in writing
options.F: Implied warranty, because the law attaches it to the roofing contract

questions.explanation: In its strict legal sense, a guaranty is a separate agreement in which a third party, much like a surety on a bond, takes on responsibility if the principal fails to perform. A warranty is the principal's own promise to carry stipulated responsibilities for its completed work, so calling the surety's promise a warranty misapplies the terms, and a principal assuring its own work describes a warranty, not a guaranty. Express and implied warranties are UCC sales concepts, not third-party commitments.

questions.question: A contractor installs a manufacturer's storefront system. Using the strict legal meanings industry guidance assigns to guaranty and warranty, which statement correctly describes the parties' assurances for the storefront?

options.A: The manufacturer warrants the material; the contractor warrants both that material and its installation
options.B: The manufacturer guarantees the material; the contractor warrants both that material and its installation
options.C: The manufacturer warrants the material; the contractor guarantees that material and warrants its installation
options.D: The manufacturer guarantees the material; the contractor guarantees both that material and its own installation
options.E: The manufacturer warrants the material; the contractor guarantees both that material and its installation
options.F: The manufacturer warrants the material; the contractor warrants its installation and gives no assurance on the material

questions.explanation: In the strict legal sense, the manufacturer is the principal for its product, so it warrants the material rather than guaranteeing it. The contractor is a third party as to that product, so it gives a guaranty for the material, and it warrants its own installation work. Choices in which the manufacturer guarantees, the contractor warrants the material or guarantees its own installation, or the contractor gives no assurance on the material miss that split, even though everyday contracts often say the contractor warrants materials.

questions.question: A pump section requires a five-year manufacturer's warranty. At closeout, the contractor states that this warranty begins only when the one-year correction period expires. How do specified warranties relate to the contractor's general warranty and correction period?

options.A: They replace the general warranty for the specified equipment
options.B: They follow the correction period and begin when it expires
options.C: They are in addition to them and run concurrently with them
options.D: They govern over the general warranty when durations conflict
options.E: They expire when the contractor's correction period expires
options.F: They cover only defects that the correction period excludes

questions.explanation: Warranties specified for materials and equipment are in addition to the contractor's general warranty and the correction period and run concurrently with them, so the five-year term neither waits for the one-year period to end nor stops when it does. A specified warranty does not replace or override the general warranty, and it is not limited to defects the correction period leaves out; both apply at the same time.

questions.question: Industry guidance cautions that warranties are as technical and confusing as another subject, one that it says most A/Es have learned to avoid specifying. Which subject?

options.A: Project insurance requirements
options.B: Performance and payment bonds
options.C: Testing and inspection services
options.D: Product substitution procedures
options.E: Quality control requirements
options.F: Commissioning requirements

questions.explanation: Warranties are compared to insurance: most A/Es have learned not to write insurance requirements, yet specifying warranties is still common, so those who do must know warranties as well as they know product properties. Bonds are a related risk topic but not the comparison made, and testing, substitution procedures, quality requirements and commissioning are routinely specified by A/Es rather than avoided.

questions.question: A specifier routinely copies warranty durations from manufacturers' literature into PART 1 without reviewing the warranty terms, reasoning that product research is the real job. Which course of action reflects recommended practice?

options.A: Stop specifying warranties and rely on the general conditions' correction period
options.B: Keep the durations and require submittal of each manufacturer's standard warranty
options.C: Transfer warranty review to the contractor through the closeout submittal process
options.D: Understand warranty terms as thoroughly as the products' physical properties
options.E: Specify only the duration, since it is the main basis for comparing warranties
options.F: Specify the longest warranty offered, since its length reflects service life

questions.explanation: Anyone specifying warranties for the owner must understand them as thoroughly as the physical properties and materials of the products specified. Copying durations or asking only for the standard warranty lets the manufacturer limit its responsibility, duration may be one of the least important terms, and a longer term does not mean a longer service life. Shifting review to the contractor drops the A/E's evaluation, and the advice is to learn warranties, not to stop specifying them.

questions.question: A roofing manufacturer's warranty states adequate maintenance by the owner as a condition rather than an exclusion. The owner skips the required inspections, and the membrane later fails from a manufacturing defect unrelated to maintenance. What is the likely result?

options.A: Only damage traceable to the missed maintenance is removed from the warranty coverage
options.B: The warranty still applies, because the failure is unrelated to the missed maintenance
options.C: Liability may be disclaimed, since the unmet requirement voids the warranty
options.D: The contractor's correction-period obligations shift the claim to the roofing installer
options.E: Coverage becomes prorated from the date of the first missed inspection
options.F: The manufacturer must still pay, since conditions apply only to installation

questions.explanation: An exclusion narrows what a warranty covers, but a condition must be met for the warranty to take effect at all; if it is not met, the warranty is void. A roofing manufacturer that states adequate maintenance as a condition may refuse liability even for a failure unrelated to the missed inspections. Removing only maintenance-related damage is how an exclusion works, and nothing here makes coverage prorated, limits conditions to installation, or shifts the claim to the installer.

questions.question: A firm's master specifications include a one-year warranty article in every section, and its project manuals place the 20-year roofing warranty in Division 01. The project uses AIA general conditions. Which revision aligns with industry guidance?

options.A: Keep the one-year articles and move the roofing warranty into the supplementary conditions
options.B: Delete the one-year articles and specify the roofing warranty in PART 1 of the roofing section
options.C: Delete the one-year articles and specify the roofing warranty in PART 3 of the roofing section
options.D: Keep the one-year articles and leave the roofing warranty in Division 01 for coordination
options.E: Keep the one-year articles and add the roofing warranty to the general conditions
options.F: Delete the one-year articles and put the roofing warranty in the owner-contractor agreement

questions.explanation: With AIA, EJCDC or similar standard general conditions, one-year warranty articles in each section are unnecessary. Those general conditions do not provide extended warranties, so the 20-year roofing warranty must be specified in PART 1, General, of the roofing section. PART 3 covers execution, and neither Division 01, the general or supplementary conditions nor the agreement is where an extended product warranty is specified.

questions.question: Industry guidance notes that the general warranty and the one-year correction period are not always distinguished, and that some contracts actually cap the contractor's warranty obligations at one year. Which contracts does it cite as the most notable example?

options.A: Public works contracts using EJCDC general conditions
options.B: Private contracts using ConsensusDocs general conditions
options.C: Design-build contracts using AIA general conditions
options.D: Federal contracts written using language from the FAR
options.E: Negotiated contracts using the contractor's own general conditions
options.F: Multiple-prime contracts using the construction manager's forms

questions.explanation: The one-year correction period in standard general conditions is a specific contractor obligation and owner remedy, not a limit on warranties, but the two are not always kept apart. The most notable contracts that actually cap the contractor's warranty obligations at one year are federal construction contracts using warranty language from the Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR). The warranties in AIA, EJCDC and ConsensusDocs general conditions carry no time limit, and the other contract types are not the example given.

questions.question: An owner's main concern on a hospital project is being able to pursue the insulating glass fabricator directly if seals fail; the fabricator was engaged by the glazing subcontractor, not by the owner. Which purpose of construction warranties listed in industry guidance addresses this concern?

options.A: Extending the manufacturer's obligations past the close of the correction period
options.B: Protecting the owner against failures despite technical compliance with the contract
options.C: Giving the owner recourse against parties outside a direct contractual relationship
options.D: Allowing the owner a remedy beyond the normal statute of limitations
options.E: Providing a remedy for nonconformance found after completion and acceptance
options.F: Transferring design responsibility for the glazing to the fabricator

questions.explanation: One purpose of construction warranties is to give the owner recourse against manufacturers, subcontractors and suppliers that have no direct contract with the owner, which is exactly the concern with a fabricator hired by the glazing subcontractor. Protecting against failures in compliant work, giving a remedy after acceptance, and reaching past the correction period or the statute of limitations are also purposes of warranties, but they address latent defects or timing, and a warranty does not transfer design responsibility.

questions.question: An owner insists on 10-year extended warranties for all rooftop compressors after a bad experience on a prior project. What should guide the A/E's decision whether to specify them?

options.A: Whether the general conditions already include a correction period
options.B: Whether competing manufacturers offer warranties of equal duration
options.C: Whether the warranty duration matches the expected service life
options.D: Whether the benefit to the owner justifies the warranty's cost
options.E: Whether a warranty can stand in for investigating the compressors
options.F: Whether the warranty would shorten the contractor's correction period

questions.explanation: Owners often insist on extended warranties for products like compressors, roofing and insulating glass because their performance and replacement cost are hard to predict, but the A/E should decide based on the cost-benefit to the owner. Matching competitors' durations or the expected service life is not the test, a warranty is no substitute for investigating the product, and an extended warranty runs alongside the correction period rather than depending on it or shortening it.

questions.question: Industry guidance recounts that the built-up roofing industry once offered a third-party roof bond that was considered of little value. What led that industry to begin offering extended warranties instead?

options.A: Single-ply systems entered the market with extended warranties
options.B: Model building codes began requiring extended warranties on roof systems
options.C: Owners began rejecting the one-year correction period as insufficient
options.D: Federal agencies began requiring roof warranties under the FAR
options.E: Manufacturers used warranties as an incentive to introduce new built-up products
options.F: Strict product liability concerns made roof bonds too costly to offer

questions.explanation: Built-up roofing shows warranties driven by market conditions: when single-ply systems arrived with extended warranties, built-up roofing manufacturers began offering similar warranties to stay competitive. No code mandate, rejection of the correction period or federal rule was involved, and new-product incentives and product liability concerns explain other warranty practices, not this change. When two products perform similarly, the available warranty may decide the purchase.

questions.question: Two roofing manufacturers offer identical 20-year extended warranties. Which of the following is a prerequisite for anyone to benefit from either warranty?

options.A: The installer must be certified by the manufacturer before bidding
options.B: The manufacturer must have the financial strength to pay its warranty liabilities
options.C: The owner must register and sign the warranty at substantial completion
options.D: The warranty term must equal the roof system's expected service life
options.E: The warranty must be backed by a third-party roof bond for its full term
options.F: The warranty must be a no-dollar-limit warranty with no proration

questions.explanation: No one benefits from an extended warranty unless the manufacturer is financially able to cover its liabilities, so its financial backing should always be considered. Manufacturer qualification of the installer is one of the benefits a sound warranty brings, not a precondition; a signing requirement is a warning sign, warranty length does not equal service life, and bonds or no-dollar-limit terms are options rather than prerequisites.

questions.question: Industry guidance identifies immediate benefits that an equitable extended warranty can provide, which could make it worth the owner's cost. Which set matches its list?

options.A: Installer qualification by the manufacturer, manufacturer involvement in construction, and insurance against failure
options.B: Installer qualification by the manufacturer, longer system service life, and reduced owner maintenance costs
options.C: Manufacturer involvement in construction, longer system service life, and transfer of design liability to the manufacturer
options.D: Insurance against failure, reduced owner maintenance costs, and transfer of design liability to the manufacturer
options.E: Insurance against failure, installer qualification by the manufacturer, and coverage of consequential damages
options.F: Manufacturer involvement in construction, insurance against failure, and full replacement without proration

questions.explanation: The immediate benefits of an equitable extended warranty are that the manufacturer qualifies the installer, the manufacturer takes part in construction, and the warranty acts as insurance against failure. Every other set includes at least one item not on that list, such as longer service life, lower maintenance costs, transfer of design liability, coverage of consequential damages or replacement without proration. Warranty length should also not be read as service life.

questions.question: On a prior project, an A/E specified a built-up roof with a short warranty and learned the roofer had become an approved installer with a single phone call. To obtain manufacturer prequalification of the installer and involvement during construction, what does industry guidance recommend?

options.A: Extend the contractor's correction period to match the manufacturer's warranty term
options.B: Keep the shorter warranty but require a third-party roof bond from the installer
options.C: Require the owner to register the warranty with the manufacturer before installation
options.D: Specify the manufacturer's best system, often a 20-year system with full warranty
options.E: Require installation by the manufacturer's own field crews instead of a roofer
options.F: Accept the manufacturer's standard warranty of whatever length it offers

questions.explanation: Specifying and buying the manufacturer's best system, often a 20-year built-up roof carrying a full workmanship and materials warranty, leads most manufacturers to prequalify the installer and take part in construction, because they now have a stake in long-term performance. A roof bond, early registration, a longer correction period, factory crews or the standard warranty does not create that manufacturer involvement.

questions.question: A below-grade waterproofing membrane sold with no stipulated warranty limitations fails, flooding finished spaces below. Under the full warranty that the UCC provides, what may the remedy include?

options.A: Refund or replacement plus labor, but excluding any damage to furnishings or adjacent construction
options.B: Refund or replacement of the product only, prorated for the years of service already provided
options.C: Refund or replacement, labor to repair or replace, and consequential and incidental damages
options.D: Labor to repair the product only, capped at the original installed cost of the waterproofing
options.E: Repair costs only, after the owner pays a deductible on each claim
options.F: A refund of the purchase price only, as the owner's sole and exclusive remedy

questions.explanation: When no limitations are stated, materials are sold under a full warranty, and under the UCC that means refund or replacement, the labor to repair or replace, and consequential and incidental damages such as harm to furnishings and adjacent work. Excluding labor or consequential damages, prorating, capping repairs at the original cost, deductibles and sole-remedy refunds are limitations found in limited warranties, not features of a full one.

questions.question: An A/E is concerned that manufacturers will submit warranties with exclusions that strip the owner's protection. Which specification approach does industry guidance recommend for controlling unwanted exclusions?

options.A: List acceptable exclusions and make A/E approval of others a condition of acceptance
options.B: Require the manufacturer's standard warranty and rely on the UCC to void unfair exclusions
options.C: Specify only the warranty duration so that exclusions can be negotiated during submittals
options.D: Require the owner to sign each warranty so that exclusions are enforceable only by consent
options.E: Accept any exclusion the manufacturer states conspicuously in its product literature
options.F: Specify a longer warranty term so that the exclusions matter less to the owner

questions.explanation: The A/E should list the exclusions it will accept and make its approval of any other exclusion a condition of accepting the product or its warranty. Accepting the standard warranty or conspicuous disclaimers lets the manufacturer limit its responsibility, specifying only duration or a longer term leaves no basis to reject a deficient warranty, and requiring the owner to sign the warranty is itself a warning sign of limiting language.

questions.question: Six years into a 15-year roofing warranty, the owner sells the building. The warranty expressly prohibits assignment. What is the new owner's position?

options.A: Covered for the remaining term, but only for materials and not for labor
options.B: Covered, because the law assumes a warranty transfers with the facility
options.C: Not covered, because the warranty's terms bar its transfer to a buyer
options.D: Not covered, because warranties never transfer when a facility is sold
options.E: Covered, but only after paying a transfer fee to the manufacturer
options.F: Covered for the rest of the term, but prorated from the date of sale

questions.explanation: The law generally presumes a warranty transfers when a facility is sold before the warranty expires, which makes the transfer-by-law choice tempting. When the warranty specifically prohibits assignment, however, the new owner is not covered at all, so partial, prorated or fee-based coverage does not apply. Saying warranties never transfer overstates the rule, since transfer is the default when no such prohibition exists.

questions.question: A sealant manufacturer's 10-year warranty begins on the date the contractor installs the product, about 14 months before the project is complete. What effect does this start date have on the owner's protection?

options.A: More protection, because coverage begins earlier in the construction project
options.B: Less protection than a warranty starting at substantial completion
options.C: Equal protection, because the warranty term is the same length
options.D: No effect, because the term restarts automatically at substantial completion
options.E: Equal protection, provided the owner registers the warranty at closeout
options.F: No effect, because the correction period covers the first year anyway

questions.explanation: A product warranty that starts when the contractor buys or installs the product gives the owner less protection than one starting at substantial completion, because part of the term is used up before the owner takes over. An equal term length does not mean equal coverage, the one-year correction period runs separately rather than replacing the lost months, and nothing restarts the term automatically; the A/E has to study when each warranty begins.

questions.question: A manufacturer offers a no-dollar-limit roof warranty that eliminates prorated coverage. What specific requirement does the manufacturer impose in exchange for paying full replacement costs?

options.A: Owner acceptance of the warranty as the sole and exclusive remedy
options.B: Installation exclusively by the manufacturer's own field crews and inspectors
options.C: A performance bond from the installer covering the full warranty term
options.D: Use of all or almost all of its own products within the warranted system
options.E: A deductible paid by the owner on each claim
options.F: Registration of the warranty for an extra fee

questions.explanation: Manufacturers that drop exclusions usually add other costs or conditions to protect themselves. A no-dollar-limit roof warranty removes proration and pays full replacement cost, but in exchange the system must use all or nearly all of the manufacturer's own products. Exclusive-remedy clauses, factory crews, installer bonds, deductibles and registration fees are other warranty terms, not the trade-off made for this warranty type.

questions.question: Two extended warranties for a waterproofing system are being compared. Which of their features are the most essential?

options.A: Its duration and the start date of its term
options.B: The nature of its remedies and their limitations
options.C: The registration fee and the claim procedure
options.D: The products and components it lists as being covered
options.E: The identity of the warrantor and its address for claims
options.F: The format of the warranty form and who must sign it

questions.explanation: The UCC lets a manufacturer disclaim implied warranties in writing and limit both how long it is responsible and what remedies the buyer has, so the nature of the remedies and their limits are the most essential features of a warranty. Duration is the term most often compared but may be among the least important, and covered components, the warrantor's identity, claim procedures and the form itself matter less.

questions.question: A specification section states only: Submit manufacturer's standard warranty. What risk does this create for the owner?

options.A: The manufacturer may limit its responsibility to an unreasonable level
options.B: The correction period is shortened to match the manufacturer's warranty term
options.C: The implied warranties are automatically converted into express warranties
options.D: The A/E becomes liable for gaps between the warranty and UCC remedies
options.E: The contractor's general warranty is replaced by the manufacturer's warranty
options.F: The warranty term begins only when the A/E accepts the warranty submittal

questions.explanation: Asking only for the manufacturer's standard warranty lets the manufacturer set limits that may be unreasonable from the owner's standpoint, and the owner could be better off with no warranty at all. A specified warranty runs alongside the correction period and the contractor's general warranty rather than shortening or replacing them, extended warranties typically begin at substantial completion, and the requirement neither converts implied warranties nor shifts liability to the A/E.

questions.question: A roof leaks at a large owner's facility, and the firm that installed the roof makes repairs immediately, before obtaining the manufacturer's approval under its warranty claim procedure. What is the risk?

options.A: The A/E must certify the repairs before the manufacturer can reimburse them
options.B: The owner forfeits the rest of the warranty because the repair was unauthorized
options.C: The repairs restart the warranty term as of the date the repair work was done
options.D: The manufacturer may decline to pay for those repairs
options.E: The manufacturer's liability shifts to the owner's property insurer
options.F: The repair converts the warranty into a prorated warranty

questions.explanation: Most manufacturers have a procedure contractors must follow to be paid for warranty repairs, and repairs made before the manufacturer approves them may go unpaid. That puts the contractor in a bind, because a slow response can harm its relationship with a large owner. Since the original installer did the work, the risk of voiding the warranty through repairs by others does not arise, and nothing restarts, prorates or shifts the coverage.

questions.question: An air barrier assembly includes membrane, transition flashing, and sealant from three manufacturers, each offering its own warranty. To keep the owner from having to resort to litigation to sort out who is at fault after a failure, what does industry guidance recommend?

options.A: Require separate warranties from each manufacturer with matching durations
options.B: Specify a warranted system whose manufacturer accepts system responsibility
options.C: Require the contractor to extend its correction period to cover all components
options.D: Specify prorated component warranties that run concurrently with one another
options.E: Require each manufacturer to name the other two as additional insureds
options.F: Specify a no-dollar-limit warranty from each of the three manufacturers

questions.explanation: For a multicomponent system, the A/E should make the warranting manufacturer accept responsibility for the whole system and specify a warranted system rather than separately warranted components, so the owner need not go to court to find out who is at fault. Matching durations, concurrent or no-dollar-limit component warranties and cross-insurance still leave three separate promises, and a longer correction period does not create single-source manufacturer responsibility.

questions.question: A sealant section says only: Provide 15-year manufacturer's warranty. The submitted warranty runs 15 years but excludes labor and limits remedies to replacement material. What is the A/E's position?

options.A: The A/E may reject it, since a limited warranty violates the implied full warranty
options.B: The A/E has no basis to reject it, since the specified duration was met
options.C: The A/E may reject it, since the UCC requires labor in every product warranty
options.D: The A/E has no basis to reject it, since warranties are outside the A/E's review
options.E: The A/E may reject it, since a warranty must cover consequential damages
options.F: The A/E may reject it, since the correction period requires labor for 15 years

questions.explanation: When a specification states only a duration, the A/E has no basis to reject a warranty that meets that duration but is unacceptable in other ways.
