Deferring the work, patching it with a cross-reference table, reusing identical Level 2 numbers, numbering by order of issue or leaving numbering to the CM would leave the merged manual disorganized.

questions.question: Under the construction manager as advisor/agent option, why might the separate bid packages be merged into combined documents, and how should the drawings be handled?

options.A: For convenience; the drawings should follow a logical numbering system from the start
options.B: For permit review; the drawings should be reissued with new numbers at combination
options.C: For legal precedence; the drawings should be bound behind the combined project manual
options.D: For record documents; the drawings should be renumbered after substantial completion
options.E: For bonding; the drawings should be grouped by prime contract
options.F: For bid comparison; the drawings should go out only in the final package

questions.explanation: The owner or CM might combine the packages simply for convenience, so the A/E should give the drawings a logical numbering system from the start so they fit together. Permit review, precedence, bonding, bid comparison and record documents are not the reasons given, and later renumbering is what early planning is meant to avoid.

questions.question: On an integrated project delivery project, the owner, A/E, and contractor form a limited liability company and become its members. Which contractual arrangement is this?

options.A: Multi-party agreement
options.B: Standard tripartite arrangement
options.C: Single-purpose entity (SPE) agreement
options.D: Joint venture agreement between the A/E and the contractor
options.E: Teaming agreement among the companies
options.F: Construction manager at risk agreement

questions.explanation: IPD uses one of three arrangements, and the one in which the owner, A/E and contractor become members of a limited liability company is the single-purpose entity agreement. A multi-party agreement binds them in one contract without forming a company, the tripartite arrangement uses separate owner agreements, a joint venture of only the A/E and contractor leaves out the owner, and teaming or CMAR agreements create no shared company.

questions.question: An owner wants integrated project delivery but insists on keeping one agreement with the A/E and a separate agreement with the contractor. Can this still be an IPD project?

options.A: No; integrated delivery forbids separate agreements and requires one multi-party agreement
options.B: No; integrated delivery requires the three parties to form a single-purpose entity
options.C: Yes; but only if the contractor also serves as construction manager as agent
options.D: Yes; this standard tripartite arrangement is one of the recognized IPD options
options.E: No; integrated delivery requires the contractor to hold the design contract
options.F: Yes; but only if the construction contract is awarded by competitive bidding

questions.explanation: A standard tripartite arrangement, with separate owner-A/E and owner-contractor agreements, is one of the three recognized IPD contractual arrangements. Multi-party and single-purpose entity agreements are alternatives, not requirements, and IPD is not conditioned on a CM as agent role, on competitive bidding, or on the contractor holding the design contract, which would describe design-build.

questions.question: Regardless of the contractual arrangement chosen, industry guidance says integrated project delivery works in practice much like which approach?

options.A: Design-bid-build using competitive bidding and a single set
options.B: CM as advisor using multiple-prime contracts and full sets
options.C: CMAR using fast-track scheduling and multiple work packages
options.D: Design-build using bridging documents and a single package
options.E: Owner-build using in-house staff and a single set
options.F: Negotiated design-bid-build using a GMP and one set

questions.explanation: Whatever its contractual arrangement, IPD works in practice much like construction manager at risk with fast-track scheduling and multiple work packages: documentation is staggered by package, and the A/E's preparation time usually grows even as the overall schedule shrinks. The other combinations describe different methods, each issued differently, that are not equated with IPD.

questions.question: On an integrated project delivery project, the A/E's specifier finds that decisions normally made by the A/E, such as product selections, are being made jointly with other stakeholders. How does industry guidance characterize this?

options.A: As improper, because the A/E alone makes such decisions for the project manual
options.B: As expected, because IPD is a collaborative process in which decisions are shared
options.C: As expected only under a single-purpose entity agreement, in which the parties share one company
options.D: As expected for Divisions 00 and 01, though technical section decisions stay with the A/E
options.E: As expected only after the parties agree on a guaranteed maximum price
options.F: As improper unless the owner's attorney approves each joint decision

questions.explanation: IPD is a collaborative process, so the A/E may not be the only decision-maker on items that would usually be its responsibility; those decisions are often shared with other stakeholders. Shared decisions are not tied to one IPD agreement, a price agreement or legal approval, technical sections are not exempt, and sharing is not improper.

questions.question: How much Division 00 preparation effort does industry guidance expect from the A/E on an integrated project delivery project?

options.A: Little, although owner-provided documents and some standard forms may be included
options.B: Little, since Division 00 is omitted from the project manual under IPD
options.C: Moderate, since the A/E drafts the multi-party agreement for the parties
options.D: Extensive, since the A/E prepares procurement requirements for every work package
options.E: Extensive, since the A/E drafts the conditions for every work package
options.F: Moderate, since the A/E prepares the contractor's subcontract forms

questions.explanation: The A/E expects little Division 00 effort under IPD, but the division is not dropped: it may hold owner-provided documents, a few procurement and contract forms, and contractor-supplied subcontract documents. The contractor may prepare procurement requirements for work packages and its own subcontract forms, the conditions are already established, and drafting the agreement is not the A/E's job.

questions.question: A specifier is assembling the project manual for an integrated project delivery project. Which group of items does industry guidance list as possibly included in Division 00?

options.A: Multiple contract summary, allowances, alternates, and testing laboratory services for each package
options.B: Warranties, operation and maintenance data, project record documents, and final cleaning requirements
options.C: Shop drawings, product data, samples, and the submittal procedures for each package
options.D: Geotechnical data, hazardous material information, wage rates, and substitution request and RFI forms
options.E: Temporary utilities, field offices, project signs, and the temporary facilities for each package
options.F: Construction progress schedules, network analysis, long-lead items, and milestone dates

questions.explanation: Division 00 on an IPD project may contain owner-provided items such as geotechnical data and existing hazardous material information, procurement forms such as wage rates, and contract forms such as substitution request and RFI forms. The other groups are Division 01 topics (contract summary, allowances, temporary facilities, progress schedules, closeout) or submittals, not Division 00 content.

questions.question: On an integrated project delivery project, the contractor adds its own forms and documents for subcontractors to Division 00. What does industry guidance say the project manual should do?

options.A: List the added forms and documents in the table of contents
options.B: Relocate the added forms and documents to Division 01
options.C: Have the A/E rewrite the added forms to match its own forms
options.D: Bind the added forms separately and omit them from the contents
options.E: Have the owner execute the added forms before the manual is issued
options.F: Replace the added forms with the owner's standard legal forms

questions.explanation: The contractor may supplement Division 00 with forms and documents that apply to subcontractors, and when they are included the table of contents should list them. Nothing calls for moving them to Division 01, having the A/E rewrite them, replacing them with owner forms, having the owner execute them first, or leaving them out of the contents.

questions.question: On an integrated project delivery project, who may prepare the procurement requirements for individual work packages, and what is the A/E's role?

options.A: The contractor may; the A/E works with it on drawings and specifications for each package
options.B: The construction manager may; the A/E reviews the work packages only after they have been issued
options.C: The A/E must; the contractor reviews each package for constructability before issue
options.D: The owner must; the A/E furnishes drawings but not specifications for each package
options.E: The design-builder may; the A/E furnishes only the performance specifications
options.F: The subcontractors may; the A/E has no role in assembling the work packages

questions.explanation: Under IPD the contractor may prepare the procurement requirements for work packages, and whoever prepares them, the A/E works with that party on the drawings and specifications so each package has the needed information. The construction manager version comes from CMAR, the design-builder from design-build, and neither the A/E, the owner nor the subcontractors are the required preparer.

questions.question: On an integrated project delivery project, how does industry guidance describe the agreement forms included in the project manual?

options.A: Usually prepared by the construction manager, using its standard subcontract forms
options.B: Usually prepared by the A/E, using standard owner-contractor agreement forms
options.C: Usually prepared by the construction manager, compatible with the owner-CM agreement
options.D: Usually prepared by the contractor, using its standard subcontract forms
options.E: Usually prepared by the owner's attorney, using the owner's in-house forms
options.F: Usually prepared by the design-builder, with its own general conditions built in

questions.explanation: Under IPD the contractor usually prepares the agreement forms, which are usually its standard subcontract forms. The CM's standard subcontract forms describe CMAR, CM-prepared forms compatible with the owner-CM agreement describe the CM as advisor/agent option, owner-attorney forms fit owner-build, and design-builder forms belong to design-build.

questions.question: A specifier preparing the project manual for an integrated project delivery project asks whether to draft new general conditions for it. What does industry guidance indicate?

options.A: Yes; new conditions are drafted for each work package because packages are issued at different times
options.B: No; they are already set, and a copy is included since subcontractors are bound by them
options.C: No; the conditions are omitted because subcontractors are bound only by their subcontract forms
options.D: Yes; separate supplementary conditions are drafted to fit each subcontractor's scope of work
options.E: Yes; the A/E drafts them because the multi-party agreement omits them
options.F: No; Division 01 restates them, so no copy of the conditions is needed

questions.explanation: Under IPD the conditions of the contract are already set before the project manual is prepared, and because subcontractors are held to the same provisions as the contractor, a copy belongs in the manual. Drafting new or package-specific conditions, leaving them out, or relying on Division 01 to restate them conflicts with that.

questions.question: An IPD team issued Division 01 as a stand-alone package that its later work packages reference. The fourth work package, for the building envelope, needs a change to a Division 01 closeout requirement. How can that change be handled?

options.A: Republish the complete Division 01 in every remaining package
options.B: Issue the Division 01 revision along with that work package
options.C: Place the revised requirement in Part 1 of each envelope section
options.D: Defer the change until the integrated agreement is amended
options.E: Hold the revision for the conformed set after the last package
options.F: Send the revision to the envelope subcontractor as a field order

questions.explanation: A Division 01 revision that a later work package needs can be issued along with that package, so the stand-alone Division 01 stays the common reference. Republishing all of Division 01 in each package defeats issuing it once, and scattering the change into product sections, waiting for an agreement amendment or the conformed set, or sending a field order to one trade does not keep the common requirements current.

questions.question: A specifier new to IPD asks how the IPD method affects the general requirements portion of the project manual. What does industry guidance say about Division 01 on an IPD project?

options.A: It is largely superseded by the multiparty agreement and kept minimal
options.B: It is limited to Division 01 temporary facility and closeout requirements
options.C: It is written separately by each team member for its own scope
options.D: It follows the same Division 01 requirements as most other methods
options.E: It is written by the owner as part of its project description
options.F: It is replaced by the contractor's standard subcontract forms

questions.explanation: IPD specifications are subject to the same Division 01 requirements that apply to most other delivery methods. The collaborative agreement does not replace Division 01, it is not narrowed to temporary facilities and closeout, it is not the owner's project description or the contractor's subcontract forms, and it is one shared document rather than one authored piecemeal by each participant.

questions.question: An IPD team will issue Division 01 once as a stand-alone package that later work packages reference, issuing any Division 01 revisions with those later packages. Which document-management practice does this approach depend on?

options.A: Version control of previously issued and developing documents
options.B: Addenda procedures during each package's procurement
options.C: Conformed documents prepared after each package's award
options.D: Change order procedures during each package's construction
options.E: Substitution request logs kept for each package
options.F: Record document markups kept at the project site

questions.explanation: With Division 01 issued once and revised in later packages, documents already issued exist alongside documents still being developed, so the team needs version control that shows which requirements are current. Addenda, conformed documents, change orders, substitution logs and record markups are other document tools, but none of them tracks versions across work packages.

questions.question: On an IPD project, besides the owner's project requirements, which party does industry guidance identify as possibly influencing the level of detail in the Divisions 02 through 49 specifications?

options.A: The construction manager
options.B: The design-builder
options.C: The contractor
options.D: The building official
options.E: The owner's legal counsel
options.F: The bonding surety

questions.explanation: Under IPD, the level of specification detail may be shaped by the contractor as well as by the owner's project requirements. The construction manager fills that role in CMAR and the design-builder in design-build, while the building official, legal counsel and the surety are not named as influences on specification detail.

questions.question: An owner is starting a design-build project. Which set of documents would the owner, rather than the design-builder, typically prepare or issue?

options.A: The construction drawings, specifications, and their later modifications
options.B: Subcontract procurement documents and instructions to bidders
options.C: The RFP, conditions of the contract, and performance specifications
options.D: Shop drawings, product data, and samples for approval
options.E: Requests for information and substitution requests from the trades
options.F: The subcontract agreements, bonds, and certificates for each trade

questions.explanation: In design-build, the owner develops its project requirements or description and may issue an RFP, owner-design-builder conditions, technical or performance specifications and design requirements. The construction drawings, specifications and later modifications come from the design-builder after it negotiates its agreement, and subcontract procurement, subcontract agreements, RFIs, substitution requests and submittals all originate on the design-builder's side.

questions.question: On a design-build project, which statement best describes the construction documents prepared by the design-builder's A/E?

options.A: Contract status depends on the arrangements; usually sent to the owner for approval
options.B: Contract status depends on the arrangements; usually withheld from the owner until closeout
options.C: Always part of the contract; usually sent to the owner for approval
options.D: Never part of the contract; usually withheld from the owner until closeout
options.E: Never part of the contract; usually sent to the owner for approval
options.F: Always part of the contract; usually withheld from the owner until closeout

questions.explanation: Whether the design-builder's construction documents form part of the owner-design-builder contract depends on the contract arrangements, and they are usually submitted to the owner for approval. Saying they are always or never part of the contract ignores that conditional answer, and they are not withheld from the owner until closeout.

questions.question: An architect is retained by a design-builder to produce the drawings and specifications for a design-build office building. How does industry guidance characterize the architect's basic services?

options.A: Performed as the owner's agent rather than for the design-builder
options.B: Limited to preparing the owner's performance specifications and RFP
options.C: Exempt from the documentation principles that govern traditional project documents
options.D: Like a traditional contract's, though performed in the design-builder's interest
options.E: Limited to reviewing the design-builder's shop drawings for the owner
options.F: Performed under a multi-party agreement that includes the owner

questions.explanation: The A/E working for the design-builder prepares the construction documents, and its basic services may resemble those under a traditional contract even though they serve the design-builder's interest. The owner prepares its own RFP and performance requirements, the A/E is neither the owner's agent nor a party with the owner to a multi-party agreement, its work goes well beyond submittal review, and the same documentation principles still apply.

questions.question: A county is procuring a design-build courthouse, and the selected design-builder will then obtain proposals from trade subcontractors. How does industry guidance allocate preparation of the procurement and contracting requirements?

options.A: Design-builder for both the design-build contract and the subcontracts
options.B: Owner for the design-build contract; design-builder for subcontracts
options.C: Owner for both the design-build contract and the subcontracts
options.D: Owner's A/E for subcontracts; design-builder for the design-build contract
options.E: Owner's A/E for both the design-build contract and the subcontracts
options.F: Design-builder for the design-build contract; owner for subcontracts

questions.explanation: The owner prepares the procurement and contracting requirements used to obtain the design-build contract itself, while the design-builder prepares the requirements it uses to get bids or proposals from its subcontractors. Answers that give both sets to one party, reverse the split, or bring the owner's A/E into subcontract procurement do not match.

questions.question: In developer-led design-build, the design-builder hires a separate contractor to perform the construction. Which statement about procuring that construction contract matches industry guidance?

options.A: Any of the three design-bid-build options may be used; negotiation is most likely
options.B: Any of the three design-bid-build options may be used; competitive bidding is most likely
options.C: Only the negotiated option may be used, since design-builders use known contractors
options.D: Only competitive bidding may be used, since it protects the owner's budget
options.E: Any of the three design-bid-build options may be used; competitive proposals are most likely
options.F: Only the competitive proposal option may be used, since qualifications matter

questions.explanation: When a design-builder contracts out the construction, as in developer-led design-build, any of the three design-bid-build options may be used, but negotiation is the most likely because design-builders tend to work with contractors they already know. Competitive bidding and competitive proposals are allowed but not described as the usual choice, and the design-builder is not restricted to a single option.

questions.question: During which stage does a design-builder prepare its subcontract procurement requirements, including instructions to bidders?

options.A: The project delivery stage
options.B: The procurement stage
options.C: The design stage
options.D: The construction documents stage
options.E: The construction stage
options.F: The facility management stage

questions.explanation: The design-builder prepares its subcontract procurement documents, such as instructions to bidders, during the construction documents stage. The project delivery stage is when the owner may already have selected the design-builder, and the design, procurement, construction and facility management stages are not where this task falls.

questions.question: How does industry guidance say the contract between an owner and a design-builder may be formed?

options.A: As a stipulated-sum contract from bids on complete construction documents
options.B: As a negotiated contract that results from the owner's RFP
options.C: As a cost-plus contract awarded by the owner's independent A/E
options.D: As a multiparty agreement among the owner, A/E, and contractor
options.E: As separate prime contracts for design and for construction
options.F: As a construction manager at risk agreement with a GMP

questions.explanation: The owner-design-builder contract may be a negotiated contract that results from an RFP issued by the owner, with the selection possibly made during the project delivery stage. Bidding on complete documents does not fit because the design-builder produces the construction documents, the owner's A/E does not award the contract, and design-build gives the owner one agreement with the design-builder rather than separate, multiparty or CMAR contracts.

questions.question: A specifier consulting to a design-builder is assembling bid packages for the mechanical and electrical subcontracts. The owner's representative asks whether these bid packages will need a fundamentally different format. What does industry guidance indicate?

options.A: They must be written entirely as performance specifications
options.B: They should omit instructions to bidders because terms are negotiated
options.C: They may closely resemble documents for other delivery methods
options.D: They must be reviewed by the owner's attorney before issue
options.E: They must follow the owner's RFP format word for word
options.F: They must be issued as one package covering all the trades

questions.explanation: Subcontract procurement requirements and construction documents in design-build might not vary significantly from those prepared for design-bid-build or other methods. Instructions to bidders are among the documents the design-builder prepares, and nothing imposes an all-performance format, owner-attorney review, the owner's RFP format or a single all-trades package on these subcontract bid packages.

questions.question: Most standard owner-design-builder agreements are organized around which two phases?

options.A: Preliminary design phase and documents/construction phase
options.B: Proposal phase and design-build construction phase
options.C: Schematic design phase and design development phase
options.D: Bridging documents phase and construction phase
options.E: Study and report phase and construction phase
options.F: Programming phase and construction administration phase

questions.explanation: Most standard design-build agreements are written for two phases: a preliminary design phase and a documents/construction phase. Proposal, schematic design, design development, bridging, study and report, and programming phases are not the pair these agreements use, and most of them also build the conditions of the contract into the agreement form.

questions.question: Which group of organizations does industry guidance list as sources of standard agreements and conditions of the contract between an owner and a design-builder?

options.A: AIA, EJCDC, DBIA, and NIBS
options.B: AIA, DBIA, ICC, and ConsensusDocs Coalition
options.C: EJCDC, DBIA, ASTM, and ConsensusDocs Coalition
options.D: AIA, EJCDC, DBIA, and ConsensusDocs Coalition
options.E: AIA, EJCDC, CMAA, and ConsensusDocs Coalition
options.F: AIA, CMAA, DBIA, and ConsensusDocs Coalition

questions.explanation: Standard owner-design-builder agreements and conditions come from four publishers: the AIA, EJCDC, DBIA (Design-Build Institute of America) and the ConsensusDocs Coalition. CMAA's forms address construction management, NIBS is known for building science resources, the ICC publishes model codes, and ASTM publishes material and testing standards, not design-build contract forms.

questions.question: During negotiation of a design-build agreement for a data center, the design-builder proposes using its own general conditions developed for that building type instead of a standard form. What does industry guidance indicate?

options.A: Only standard AIA, EJCDC, DBIA, or ConsensusDocs forms may be used
options.B: Only conditions prepared by the owner's attorney may be used
options.C: It may use its own conditions tailored to a project type
options.D: Its general conditions must be bound as a separate section within Division 01
options.E: It must first get the authority having jurisdiction to approve them
options.F: It may do so only if the owner's A/E rewrites them as supplementary conditions

questions.explanation: Standard AIA, EJCDC, DBIA and ConsensusDocs forms are available, but a design-builder may also use general conditions of its own, written for a particular type of project. The parties are not limited to standard forms or owner-attorney documents, building officials do not approve contract terms, the owner's A/E need not rewrite them, and they are not bound in Division 01; most design-build agreements build the conditions into the agreement form.

questions.question: On a design-build project, a roofing subcontractor submits shop drawings. Under the submittal procedure industry guidance describes for design-build, what happens next?

options.A: The A/E checks them first, then forwards them to the design-builder for distribution
options.B: The design-builder checks them, then sends them to the A/E or back to the subcontractor
options.C: The owner checks them, then returns them to the subcontractor through the design-builder
options.D: The A/E receives them directly from the subcontractor and sends a copy to the owner
options.E: The design-builder approves them for construction without A/E review
options.F: The owner's construction manager checks them before the A/E sees them

questions.explanation: In design-build, the design-builder receives and checks the shop drawings, samples and product data, then either distributes them to the A/E or returns them to the subcontractor for resubmittal. The A/E does not receive them first or directly, the design-builder's check does not replace A/E review, there is no owner's CM in the chain, and the owner receives a set of approved shop drawings rather than doing the first check.

questions.question: Section 01 21 00 Allowances can be used on a design-build project to postpone some design decisions. Why does industry guidance advise keeping such unknowns to a minimum?

options.A: Design-build is selected partly because requirements are predictable
options.B: Allowances undermine the design-builder's ability to control cost
options.C: Allowances must be priced by the owner before the RFP is issued
options.D: Allowances prevent the owner from tracking substitutions
options.E: Allowances shift design responsibility back to the owner
options.F: Allowances must be bid separately by each subcontractor

questions.explanation: Allowances actually help the design-builder keep accurate cost control when some products are unknown, but unknowns should be kept few because one reason for choosing design-build is that the project requirements are reasonably predictable. Allowances do not undermine cost control, shift design responsibility to the owner, require RFP pricing or separate subcontractor bids, or interfere with substitution tracking.

questions.question: A design-build clinic is nearing completion. Under Section 01 70 00 for design-build, how is substantial completion handled?

options.A: The owner's A/E inspects and certifies the date to the design-builder
options.B: The owner inspects and gives the results to the design-builder to evaluate
options.C: The building official inspects and issues the certificate to the owner
options.D: The design-builder inspects and gives the results to the owner to evaluate
options.E: The design-builder's surety inspects and reports to the owner
options.F: The subcontractors inspect and certify the date to the owner

questions.explanation: Under the design-build closeout requirements, the design-builder performs the substantial completion inspection and presents the results to the owner for evaluation. Reversing those roles, having an owner's A/E, the surety or the subcontractors certify the date, or relying on a building official's certificate is not how design-build closeout is described.

questions.question: What two purposes should the Divisions 02 through 49 specifications serve on a design-build project?

options.A: Establish the owner's performance criteria and support the owner's RFP package
options.B: Secure accurate subcontract pricing and define each subcontractor's duties
options.C: Set the design-builder's guaranteed price and record owner approvals
options.D: Obtain building permits and document products for facility management
options.E: Define the owner's project description and approve substitutions
options.F: Fix the owner's budget and replace the design-builder's warranties

questions.explanation: Design-build specifications should secure accurate subcontract bids or proposals and clearly define the responsibilities of the various subcontractors. Performance criteria, the RFP and the project description are owner documents developed before the design-builder is engaged, and guaranteed pricing, budgets, warranties, permits and facility records are not the purposes named here.

questions.question: The design-builder tells its specifier to keep specifications brief and leave wide latitude in product selection, but the owner's project description sets stringent requirements for interior finishes. What should govern how detailed those finish sections are?

options.A: The owner's requirements, which can dictate the detail needed
options.B: The design-builder's preference, as it engaged the specifier
options.C: The subcontractors' requirements, gathered during bidding
options.D: The specifier's office standard for that building type
options.E: The construction manager's preference, as it manages the cost
options.F: The manufacturers' standard literature for those finishes

questions.explanation: A design-builder may want brief specifications with wide product latitude, but an owner's stringent project requirements may dictate the specification detail required. The design-builder's preference does not override those requirements, and the decision does not pass to subcontractors, an office standard, manufacturers' literature or a construction manager, who has no role here.

questions.question: Who does industry guidance say should prepare the Divisions 02 through 49 specifications on a design-build project?

options.A: The owner's in-house A/E as part of the RFP package
options.B: Each design-build subcontractor for its portion of the work
options.C: The design-builder or a specifier consulting to it
options.D: The owner's construction manager acting as an advisor
options.E: The owner's attorney as part of the conditions of the contract
options.F: The authority having jurisdiction during permit review

questions.explanation: Design-build specifications are prepared by the design-builder or a specifier working as its consultant, aiming at accurate subcontract pricing and clear subcontractor responsibilities. The owner's in-house A/E develops owner requirements rather than these specifications, subcontractors do not write what they price, and the task does not belong to a construction manager, the owner's attorney or the building official.

questions.question: A hospital's facilities department will use its own forces to build a new central plant addition, with documents produced by an outside A/E. The construction documents may concentrate mainly on what?

options.A: The information needed to obtain competitive bids
options.B: The information needed to establish a guaranteed price
options.C: The information needed for the owner's financing
options.D: The information needed to obtain permits
options.E: The information needed to price change orders
options.F: The information needed for the contractor's surety

questions.explanation: When the owner builds with its own forces, the construction documents may concentrate on what is needed to obtain permits, because no outside contractor is pricing the work. Competitive bids, a guaranteed price, change order pricing and a surety's review all assume buying construction from a contractor, and the owner's financing is not what these documents serve.

questions.question: Within an owner-build program, industry guidance notes that an owner might consider which delivery approach for a pre-engineered structure?

options.A: A construction manager at-risk arrangement
options.B: A simple design-build arrangement
options.C: An integrated project delivery arrangement
options.D: A multiple-prime arrangement with a CM advisor
options.E: A cost-plus negotiated arrangement
options.F: A single-purpose entity arrangement

questions.explanation: An owner that builds for itself might use a simple design-build approach for a pre-engineered structure, buying the design and the building from one source. CMAR, IPD, multiple-prime with a CM advisor, cost-plus negotiation and single-purpose entities are separate arrangements that are not tied to pre-engineered structures in owner-build work.

questions.question: An owner with an in-house facilities group plans a simple owner-build renovation that it will not fully self-perform. Which procurement approaches does industry guidance name for such a simple project?

options.A: Through a CMAR agreement or an IPD multiparty agreement
options.B: Through a job order contract or an indefinite-quantity contract
options.C: As design-bid-build, or split into multiple contracts
options.D: Through one negotiated GMP contract or a cost-plus contract
options.E: Through a CM as agent or a single-purpose entity
options.F: Through a teaming agreement or a joint venture

questions.explanation: A simple owner-build project can be procured just like a design-bid-build project, or divided into several contracts. CMAR, IPD, CM as agent, single-purpose entities, job order, indefinite-quantity, GMP, cost-plus, teaming and joint venture arrangements are not the approaches named for a simple owner-build project.

questions.question: A state agency acting as its own builder will award separate prime contracts for sitework, structure, and building systems. What does industry guidance indicate about project manual preparation?

options.A: It is similar to other methods, and several project manuals may be needed
options.B: A single project manual is required regardless of the number of contracts
options.C: No project manual is needed because the owner self-performs the work
options.D: The permit drawings take the place of a project manual for owner-build
options.E: Each prime contractor writes its own project manual for its scope
options.F: One manual is issued only after all of the contracts are awarded

questions.explanation: Project manual preparation for owner-build work resembles that of other delivery methods, and multiple-prime contracts may call for several project manuals rather than one. Acting as its own builder does not eliminate the project manual, permit drawings do not replace it, the primes do not write their own manuals, and the documents must be issued before the contracts are awarded, not after.

questions.question: For an owner-build project, what does industry guidance say determines which procurement and contracting requirements are included in the project manual?

options.A: Whether the owner's attorney has prepared standard forms
options.B: The total construction cost relative to the owner's budget
options.C: Whether the authority having jurisdiction requires them
options.D: What the owner will do in-house versus what contractors will do
options.E: Whether the project is a renovation or an entirely new facility
options.F: Whether the owner's facility manager has approved the project

questions.explanation: Owner-build procurement and contracting requirements vary considerably, and which ones are included depends on the work the owner performs in-house and the work contractors perform. Owner-prepared forms, project cost, regulatory demands, project type and internal approvals are not the deciding factor.

questions.question: On an owner-build project, the owner needs specialty contractors for elevators and roofing. Who might prepare the procurement requirements for those subcontract packages?

options.A: The construction manager
options.B: The owner
options.C: The design-builder
options.D: The specialty contractors
options.E: The general contractor
options.F: The product manufacturers

questions.explanation: On an owner-build project, the owner might write the procurement requirements itself for the packages it lets to specialty contractors. A construction manager prepares package procurement in CMAR and the design-builder in design-build, there is no general contractor in this arrangement, and the specialty contractors and manufacturers are being procured or supplying products rather than writing the requirements.

questions.question: The procurement requirements for an owner-build project depend on the project's nature and on what other factor?

options.A: Whether the work is to be bid, negotiated, or purchased
options.B: Whether the owner's A/E is an in-house department or independent
options.C: Whether the owner has an in-house legal department
options.D: Whether the owner also holds a design-build agreement
options.E: Whether the facility is new construction or maintenance work
options.F: Whether the work packages will be issued on a fast track

questions.explanation: Owner-build procurement requirements are developed much as in other methods and hinge on the project's nature and on whether the work will be bid, negotiated or purchased. The A/E's employment status, in-house counsel, a design-build agreement and fast-track packaging are not the factors named, and new versus maintenance work is part of the project's nature rather than a second factor.

questions.question: An A/E in independent practice is asked to bind an owner's in-house owner-contractor agreement into the project manual for an owner-build project. What should the A/E specifically check in that form?

options.A: Whether the agreement includes liquidated damages for late completion
options.B: Whether the form follows the article numbering of AIA standard forms
options.C: Any A/E responsibilities beyond those in the owner-A/E agreement
options.D: Whether the form is enforceable under the governing state statutes
options.E: Whether the form includes the owner's insurance limits
options.F: Whether the contractor has signed the form before binding

questions.explanation: An independently practicing A/E reviews owner-prepared agreement forms to confirm they do not assign the A/E responsibilities beyond its owner-A/E agreement. Checking liquidated damages, insurance limits, AIA numbering, signatures or legal enforceability is not that review; the forms come from the owner's own legal staff, who answer for their legal content.

questions.question: Why should the A/E on an owner-build project have access to a copy of the owner-contractor agreement form?

options.A: To verify the contractor's insurance and bonding requirements before award
options.B: To confirm the contract sum against the A/E's cost estimate
options.C: To let the A/E negotiate the agreement terms for the owner
options.D: To avoid conflicts with the conditions of the contract and Division 01
options.E: To check the contract time against the design schedule
options.F: To prepare the bid form from the agreement's terms

questions.explanation: Having the agreement form lets the A/E confirm that the agreement does not clash with the conditions of the contract or with Division 01. Insurance checks, price or schedule checks, bid form preparation and negotiating for the owner are not the reasons, and the A/E may not even take part in preparing the agreement.

questions.question: While reviewing an owner-build project manual, the A/E notices that the owner's proposed owner-contractor agreement does not obligate the contractor to respond to the A/E's responsibilities, such as submittal reviews. What is the A/E's best course of action?

options.A: Rewrite the agreement to add the missing contractor obligations
options.B: Inform the owner that the agreement lacks those obligations
options.C: State in Division 01 that its provisions override the agreement
options.D: Leave the agreement as is, since the A/E did not negotiate it
options.E: Ask the contractor to add the obligations by letter
options.F: Delete the A/E's submittal review duties from Division 01

questions.explanation: When a proposed agreement does not make the contractor respond to the A/E's duties, the A/E should tell the owner. The agreement is the owner's document, often from its legal staff, so the A/E should not rewrite it or arrange fixes with the contractor; a Division 01 override or deleting the A/E's duties would create conflicts, and silence ignores the duty to notify.

questions.question: On an owner-build project, the owner's in-house legal department provides nonstandard conditions of the contract that assign the A/E and contractor roles unlike those in AIA or ConsensusDocs documents. What does industry guidance require of the A/E?

options.A: Replace them with industry-standard conditions before issuing
options.B: Accept them as written, since the owner's attorney is responsible
options.C: Review them carefully to understand the variations and reconcile them
options.D: Add a Division 01 article that restores the standard role definitions
options.E: Return them to the legal department to be rewritten in standard form
options.F: Omit them and rely on the owner-contractor agreement alone

questions.explanation: When conditions of the contract are not industry standard, the A/E must review them carefully to understand how they vary from standard documents, and differing A/E and contractor roles must be reconciled. Swapping in or demanding standard forms, or using Division 01 to restore standard roles, oversteps the owner's documents, accepting them unread ignores the variations, and omitting them removes the basis for Division 01.

questions.question: The owner-contractor agreement for an owner-build project already sets out procedures for payments and changes. How should the specifier handle those topics in Division 01?

options.A: Avoid repeating requirements the agreement covers
options.B: Restate them in full so all requirements appear in one place
options.C: Move them out of the agreement and into Division 01 sections
options.D: Repeat them in the conditions of the contract instead
options.E: Restate them in the instructions to bidders
options.F: Summarize them in each Divisions 02-49 section

questions.explanation: Payment and change requirements that the owner-contractor agreement already covers should not be repeated in Division 01. Restating, summarizing or relocating them invites duplication and conflict among the documents, the conditions of the contract are not the place to repeat them either, and instructions to bidders are procurement documents rather than contract requirements.

questions.question: Why should the project manual for an owner-build project contain the conditions of the contract?

options.A: They replace the owner-contractor agreement on owner-build work
options.B: Building officials require them to be submitted with the permit set
options.C: They serve as procurement instructions for specialty contractors
options.D: They are the basis of Division 01 and provide continuity
options.E: They set the owner's internal budget approvals
options.F: They define each product's warranty terms

questions.explanation: The conditions of the contract form the basis of the Division 01 requirements, and including them in the project manual gives those requirements continuity. They do not replace the agreement, are not a permit submission item, are not instructions to bidders, and do not set internal budget approvals or the warranty terms of individual products, which belong in the specification sections.

questions.question: An owner-build renovation will occur inside an operating research campus. In preparing Division 01, which group of issues does industry guidance specifically associate with operations at existing facilities?

options.A: Payment procedures, progress schedules, submittals, and substitutions
options.B: Use of the site, security, identification of personnel, and access to the work
options.C: Warranties, maintenance materials, record documents, and final cleaning
options.D: Parking, staging areas, storage sheds, hoists, and temporary utilities
options.E: Allowances, alternates, unit prices, and testing laboratory services
options.F: Multiple contract summary, long-lead items, and construction document packages

questions.explanation: For owner-build work at an operating facility, Division 01 should address how the site is used, security, how personnel are identified and access to the work. Payment, scheduling, submittal and substitution procedures form a separate group of procedures, and the closeout, temporary facility, price and multiple-contract items come from other Division 01 discussions.

questions.question: On an owner-build project, the owner's legal department is still revising its conditions of the contract, and the specifier wants to finalize Division 01 now to stay on schedule. What approach does industry guidance support?

options.A: Finalize Division 01 now and have the contract conditions conform to it later
options.B: Finalize Division 01 now and state that it governs over the conditions
options.C: Wait for the final conditions, then restate their provisions in Division 01
options.D: Prepare Division 01 in conjunction with the conditions of the contract
options.E: Finalize Division 01 now and omit any topic the conditions might cover
options.F: Issue Division 01 as a draft and let the contractor reconcile it later

questions.explanation: Division 01 should be developed together with the conditions of the contract, since conflicts among the agreement, the conditions and Division 01 can arise. Locking Division 01 first, declaring that it overrides the conditions, restating their provisions, dropping topics or leaving reconciliation to the contractor would create conflicts or duplication instead of coordinated requirements.

questions.question: On an owner-build project, Division 01 can end up in conflict with the agreement or the conditions of the contract. What does the likelihood of such conflicts depend on?

options.A: The outcomes of negotiations with the contractor
options.B: The scope assigned to each separate prime contract
options.C: Their source and the particular project requirements
options.D: The procurement option chosen for the contract
options.E: The number of in-house trades the owner employs
options.F: The delivery schedule for owner-furnished products

questions.explanation: On owner-build projects, potential conflicts among these documents depend on where the documents come from and on the project's particular requirements. Negotiation outcomes are the driver for the negotiated design-bid-build option and contract-by-contract scope is the concern in multiple-prime work, so neither answers the owner-build question, and staffing or delivery schedules are not named.

questions.question: A restaurant chain building its own stores requires the same exterior signage lighting system on every location. How might the specifier write that section?

options.A: As a proprietary specification, eliminating a level of detail
options.B: As a performance specification with stated design criteria
options.C: As a descriptive specification listing physical properties
options.D: As a reference standard specification citing industry tests
options.E: As a multiple-name specification inviting substitutions
options.F: As an outline specification for later completion

questions.explanation: When an owner requires specific products, the specification might be written as proprietary, which removes a level of detail. Performance, descriptive and reference standard methods describe requirements instead of naming the owner's chosen product, a multiple-name specification with substitutions opens the choice the owner has closed, and an outline specification is a design-phase document, not the final section.

questions.question: In an owner-build project, why might the owner insist on specific products?

options.A: They were selected through prior negotiations or value analysis
options.B: They have become standard in the owner's identity or operations
options.C: They were the lowest-priced products in competitive bids
options.D: They are mandated by the authority having jurisdiction
options.E: They carry the longest manufacturer warranties available
options.F: They were recommended by the contractor's suppliers

questions.explanation: Some owners that build for themselves have product requirements that have become standard in their identity or operations. Choices driven by prior negotiations or value analysis belong to the negotiated design-bid-build option, and low bid prices, code mandates, warranty length or supplier recommendations are not the reason given here.

questions.question: When the specifier decides to use a particular product the owner has adopted on its other facilities in an owner-build project, what might that decision require?

options.A: A substitution request from the contractor
options.B: A value analysis by the construction manager
options.C: A variance from the authority having jurisdiction
options.D: The owner's specific approval
options.E: A product data submittal approved by the A/E
options.F: A competitive bid from at least three suppliers

questions.explanation: Decisions to use specific products on owner-build work might require the owner's specific approval, since the owner sets its own product standards. A substitution request, value analysis by a construction manager, a regulatory variance, a submittal or competitive supplier bids is not the step needed for an owner-standard product choice.

questions.question: During design development, a specifier evaluates a proposed rainscreen cladding system. She has confirmed it complies with the project requirements and design intent, is consistent with the drawings, and meets code requirements. Which remaining project component should she evaluate it against?

options.A: Conformance with the project's sustainability certification targets
options.B: Availability from at least three manufacturers to keep bidding competitive
options.C: Coverage by a manufacturer's warranty longer than the correction period
options.D: Compatibility with the desired constructability and construction sequence
options.E: Successful use of the system on the firm's earlier projects of this type
options.F: Inclusion of the system in the firm's office master guide specification

questions.explanation: Systems, assemblies and materials are evaluated against four project components: meeting the project requirements and design intent, consistency with the drawings, compliance with code requirements, and compatibility with the desired constructability and construction sequence. Sustainability targets, the number of manufacturers and warranty length can matter elsewhere in product selection, and past use or an office master entry may suggest a product, but none of them is one of the four components.

questions.question: A specification section cites a reference standard by its number and title but restates none of the standard's text. What is the status of that standard's provisions on the project?

options.A: They serve as guidance only, unless the AHJ has adopted that standard by code
options.B: They apply only to the extent the section restates them in its own language
options.C: They are part of the specifications as fully as if their text were included
options.D: They govern only where they are more stringent than the section's own text
options.E: They apply only if a copy of the standard is bound into the project manual
options.F: They cover products only, while installation follows the manufacturer's instructions

questions.explanation: Citing a standard by its number, title or other designation incorporates it by reference: its provisions become part of the specifications just as if the full text were included, which spares the A/E from writing lengthy text. Restating is not needed for enforceability, AHJ adoption is not a precondition, the standard need not be bound into the project manual, its workmanship and installation provisions apply along with its product ones, and no automatic stringency rule limits where it applies.

questions.question: Two published test standards could each verify the fire performance a specifier needs, but only one is listed in the model building code the jurisdiction has adopted. Which choice is preferred and why?

options.A: The code-cited standard, because using it helps ensure the AHJ will accept it
options.B: The other standard, because codes refer only to minimum and outdated editions
options.C: Either one, because any standard cited in the specifications becomes a code requirement
options.D: Both together, because the stricter requirement automatically governs any conflict
options.E: Either one, provided the specification states the edition the AHJ enforces
options.F: Whichever is newer, because the latest edition of a standard always governs

questions.explanation: Where applicable, specifiers should choose standards that the model or local codes list, so the work will be acceptable to the authority having jurisdiction. Citing a standard in the specifications does not make it a code requirement, and naming an edition does not erase that preference. AHJs may not enforce the latest edition and standards set minimums, but those are liabilities to manage, not reasons to avoid the code-listed standard. Citing both invites duplication and conflict that a blanket stringency clause cannot fully resolve.

questions.question: A project requires the below-slab vapor retarder to be placed directly on the granular fill, which differs from the installation practice in the reference standard the specifier intends to cite. The rest of the standard suits the project. Which approach is appropriate?

options.A: Cite the standard and add a general clause that the more stringent requirement governs
options.B: Cite the standard and show the different placement only on the drawing details
options.C: Cite the standard and let the manufacturer's installation instructions set the placement
options.D: Cite the standard and state the different placement as a defined exception to it
options.E: Cite the standard and leave the placement to be settled later by an RFI
options.F: Cite the standard and price the different placement as a bid alternate

questions.explanation: When a project requirement is incompatible with a reference standard, the A/E either cites the standard and defines exceptions to it or writes original requirements; since the rest of this standard suits the project, citing it with a stated exception fits. A general more-stringent clause cannot resolve every conflict, and placement is not a matter of stringency. Showing the change only on drawings, deferring to manufacturer's instructions or an RFI, or making it an alternate the owner may reject leaves the conflict in place.

questions.question: Reviewing a consultant's section, the specifier finds a product described only as complying with a cited ASTM standard that contains several types and classes, none of which is selected. What should be done?

options.A: Leave it open so the contractor's choice can be judged during submittal review
options.B: Specify the highest type and class listed, since standards set only minimum levels
options.C: Evaluate each available type and class, then specify the one the project needs
options.D: Add a clause stating that the most stringent type and class always governs
options.E: Specify the lowest type and class listed, since every one meets the standard
options.F: Repeat the type and class chosen in a previous project's section for consistency

questions.explanation: Standards with categories, classes or groups contain embedded options that the A/E must identify, evaluate and resolve by specifying the one the project needs. Left open, the choice passes to the contractor, who can be expected to pick the least expensive option, so submittal review does not protect the owner. Defaulting to the highest or lowest class, or copying a previous project's choice, skips the evaluation, and a blanket stringency clause cannot be relied on to settle choices like these.

questions.question: A roofing specification requires a 20-year warranty covering both the membrane materials and the installer's workmanship. Under the two basic warranty types used on building projects, this warranty is a:

options.A: Products-only warranty, because the roofing manufacturer is the party that issues it
options.B: Construction warranty or guaranty, usually an extended warranty specified in a section
options.C: Purchasing warranty that arises from the sale and is governed by the Uniform Commercial Code
options.D: Implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose arising from the installer's skill
options.E: General warranty in the general conditions, since it covers the contractor's work
options.F: Roof bond, because a third party backs the roofing system for its full term

questions.explanation: Construction-project warranties come in two basic types: construction warranties or guaranties, which cover products and workmanship and are usually extended warranties specified in individual sections, and warranties covering products only. Because this one also covers workmanship, it is a construction warranty whoever issues it. Purchasing and implied warranties are UCC concepts tied to sales, the contractor's general warranty in the general conditions has no specified term, and a roof bond is a separate third-party instrument.

questions.question: An owner asks why the specifications should require a 15-year manufacturer warranty on insulating glass units when the general conditions already require the contractor to correct defective work found within one year. Which reason given in industry guidance best answers the owner?

options.A: It shifts responsibility for the glazing design from the A/E to the manufacturer
options.B: It replaces the need to investigate the product's performance history before selection
options.C: It converts the manufacturer's limited warranty into a full warranty under the UCC
options.D: It keeps the manufacturer responsible after the correction period has ended
options.E: It relieves the contractor of correcting defective glass during the first year
options.F: It guarantees the units will remain serviceable for the full warranty term

questions.explanation: A specified extended warranty is chiefly a way to keep the manufacturer responsible after the one-year correction period ends; it adds to the contractor's warranty and correction obligations rather than replacing them. A warranty is a remedy, not a promise of service life, and it is no substitute for investigating the product's performance history. It does not move design responsibility to the manufacturer, and manufacturers typically issue limited rather than full warranties.

questions.question: An owner intends to sell a new office building within five years. While comparing two manufacturers' 20-year roofing warranties, which clause should the A/E flag as most directly threatening the coverage the buyer would receive?

options.A: A deductible whose starting point is not defined in the warranty
options.B: A prohibition on assigning the warranty to a subsequent owner
options.C: A provision allowing the warrantor to recover its legal costs
options.D: A clause limiting the time allowed to take legal action for breach
options.E: Language making the warranty the owner's exclusive remedy
options.F: A clause excluding installation of the replacement product

questions.explanation: The law generally presumes that a warranty transfers when a facility is sold before the warranty runs out, but a clause specifically prohibiting assignment leaves the new owner without coverage. Deductibles, legal-cost recovery, limits on the time to sue, exclusive-remedy language and exclusion of replacement installation are also limitations of concern, but they reduce the value of the coverage rather than remove it for a purchaser.

questions.question: An A/E is concerned that roofing manufacturers will attach broad exclusions to the special warranty the specifications require. What is the recommended way to address unwanted exclusions in the specification?

options.A: List the acceptable exclusions and require A/E approval of any additional exclusions
options.B: Prohibit all exclusions and require a full warranty covering consequential damages
options.C: Accept the manufacturer's standard warranty and rely on the UCC's implied warranties
options.D: Specify only the warranty duration so that manufacturers can compete on their terms
options.E: Require a no-dollar-limit warranty, which removes all exclusions and conditions
options.F: Leave the exclusions for the owner to negotiate after the contract is awarded

questions.explanation: The recommended approach is to list the exclusions that are acceptable and make the A/E's approval of any others a condition of accepting the product or its warranty. Manufacturers rarely accept full-warranty risk without raising cost, and even no-dollar-limit warranties trade exclusions for other terms; standard warranties often strip away UCC implied warranties; warranty terms are seldom truly negotiated; and specifying only duration leaves no basis to reject an otherwise unacceptable warranty.

questions.question: An A/E firm is reorganizing how it produces specifications. Which pairing of firm size and specifications arrangement is typical?

options.A: Small firm: employs a full-time specifier for all work
options.B: Large firm: a principal prepares the specifications
options.C: Firm of 20 to 70 people: employs a full-time specifier
options.D: Firm of 20 to 70 people: keeps a specifications department
options.E: Firm of 20 to 70 people: a principal prepares the specifications
options.F: Small firm: maintains a specifications department

questions.explanation: Typical practice ties the arrangement to firm size: in a small firm a principal takes responsibility for the specifications, a mid-sized firm of about 20 to 70 people might have one full-time specifier, and a large firm may keep a specifications department staffed by several people. The other pairings mismatch these arrangements, since a principal belongs with small firms and a full department with large ones.

questions.question: In the typical project manual arrangement, where does 00 43 13 Bid Security Form fall?

options.A: Contracting requirements, under 00 60 00 Project Forms with the bond forms
options.B: Procurement requirements, under 00 40 00 Procurement Forms and Supplements
options.C: Contracting requirements, under 00 50 00 Contracting Forms and Supplements
options.D: Procurement requirements, under 00 20 00 Instructions for Procurement
options.E: Procurement requirements, under 00 30 00 Available Information
options.F: Contracting requirements, under 00 70 00 Conditions of the Contract

questions.explanation: In the typical arrangement, 00 43 13 Bid Security Form falls under 00 43 00 Procurement Form Supplements, within 00 40 00 Procurement Forms and Supplements in the procurement requirements. Bond forms (00 61 00) sit under 00 60 00 Project Forms, agreement forms under 00 50 00 and the general and supplementary conditions under 00 70 00, all in the contracting requirements; 00 20 00 holds instructions and 00 30 00 holds available information such as geotechnical data.

questions.question: For a state university project, a project architect downloads an elevator manufacturer's guide specification and plans to issue it with only project-name edits. What concern does industry guidance raise?

options.A: The specification is copyrighted and cannot be reproduced in a project manual
options.B: The specification omits PART 3, which the installer must then supply
options.C: The specification must first be accepted by the authority having jurisdiction
options.D: The specification likely contains proprietary text that public rules may bar
options.E: The specification shifts responsibility for its content to the manufacturer
options.F: The specification must be issued unedited to keep the product warranty valid

questions.explanation: Manufacturers' guide specifications must be reviewed carefully for bias and accuracy and edited to remove embedded proprietary content; text that fits only one manufacturer may be barred by public procurement rules on a state project, or by the owner on a private one. The A/E cannot hand responsibility for that review to the manufacturer, the guidance calls for editing rather than issuing the text unchanged, and no copyright, missing-PART 3 or AHJ pre-acceptance issue is raised.

questions.question: Specification sections are usually produced using which two techniques?

options.A: Developing from product reference material and editing master guides
options.B: Copying previous project sections and updating their references
options.C: Editing manufacturer guide specifications and adding drawing notes
options.D: Expanding the outline specifications and the project description
options.E: Writing performance criteria and citing reference standards
options.F: Transcribing the designer's checklist and the cost estimate

questions.explanation: Sections are usually produced in one of two ways: built up from product reference material, or edited down from a master guide specification. Performance criteria and reference standards are methods of specifying within a section, while previous project specifications, manufacturer guide specifications, drawing notes, outline specifications, project descriptions, checklists and cost estimates are sources of information or reference, not the two techniques.

questions.question: A mechanical consultant edits its HVAC sections from a widely used commercial master and argues that product research and coordination with the drawings are therefore unnecessary. The consultant is:

options.A: Correct; commercial master text has already been researched and coordinated
options.B: Correct; only the specifier's own sections need that coordination
options.C: Incorrect; the steps apply no matter who writes a section or how
options.D: Incorrect; consultant sections must be written from product literature
options.E: Correct; submittal review will catch any coordination gaps later
options.F: Incorrect; commercial masters may be edited only by the specifier

questions.explanation: Product research, selection, evaluation, coordination with other products and the drawings, and clear, consistent specifying are required no matter who writes a section or how it is produced. Starting from a commercial master does not waive these steps, they are not confined to the specifier's own sections, and they belong to producing the section rather than to later submittal review. Editing a master is an accepted technique for anyone, so consultants need not write from product literature and are not barred from masters.

questions.question: Industry guidance lists what must happen to products regardless of how specification sections are developed. Which of the following is NOT on that list?

options.A: Evaluated and coordinated with other products
options.B: Specified consistently and clearly
options.C: Approved by the owner in writing
options.D: Researched and selected for the project
options.E: Coordinated with applicable code requirements
options.F: Coordinated with the drawings

questions.explanation: No matter who writes the sections, the products in them must be researched, chosen, and evaluated; coordinated with other products, with the drawings, and with code requirements; and specified clearly and consistently. Written owner approval is not one of those steps. Every other choice restates an item on the list, so none of them can be the answer.

questions.question: Industry guidance divides the information a specifier needs into project-specific requirements and reference materials about products and methods. Which item is a source of project-specific requirements?

options.A: Reference standards published by national standards associations
options.B: The detailed cost estimate prepared for the project
options.C: Commercial master guide specifications for the section
options.D: Specifications from a similar, previously built project
options.E: Manufacturers' product data and guide specifications
options.F: Handbooks published by manufacturers' trade associations

questions.explanation: Project-specific requirements come from the owner's requirements, the drawings, the specification notebook or checklist, the PPD or outline specification, the detailed cost estimate, any government RFP, and the applicable codes. Reference standards, commercial master guides, specifications from similar projects, manufacturers' data, and trade association handbooks are the other kind: reference materials about products and construction methods.

questions.question: Early in construction documents, the owner states it intends to insure the new structure through FM Global. How does industry guidance say this information affects the specifications?

options.A: It drives mandatory use of FM Global standards on the project
options.B: It makes FM Global the authority having jurisdiction for code review
options.C: It replaces the owner's green building rating system target goal
options.D: It requires the contractor to name FM Global on all of the bond forms
options.E: It affects only the insurance articles of the supplementary conditions
options.F: It shifts the duty to buy property insurance from the owner to the contractor

questions.explanation: An owner's decision to insure the building with FM Global is one of the project-specific requirements a specifier gathers, because it makes FM Global's standards mandatory and they must show up in the technical sections. The insurer does not become the authority having jurisdiction, the green building target is a separate owner requirement, and the choice neither stays in the supplementary conditions nor moves property insurance to the contractor.

questions.question: Many design and contractor team members help select and purchase products. Which participant is most likely to request comprehensive technical assistance from product representatives?

options.A: The contractor's purchasing agent
options.B: The owner's facility manager
options.C: The design architect during schematic design
options.D: The person producing the specifications
options.E: The general contractor's project manager
options.F: The owner's construction manager

questions.explanation: Many people on the design and construction teams help choose and buy products, but industry guidance singles out whoever prepares the project specifications as the one most likely to ask product representatives for comprehensive technical help. Purchasing agents, facility managers, designers, project managers, and construction managers may also call on representatives, but none of them is the participant named.

questions.question: A specifier is lining up help from a roofing manufacturer's representative. Which request matches a task industry guidance says product representatives should be able to perform?

options.A: Perform the field quality-control testing for the installed roof
options.B: Certify that the roof section complies with the building code
options.C: Provide generic descriptions of the products and systems
options.D: Select the roof system and accessories for the project
options.E: Review and approve the roofing contractor's shop drawings
options.F: Evaluate substitution requests for competing roof systems

questions.explanation: Providing generic descriptions of products and systems is on the list of tasks a product representative should be able to perform for the specifier. The other choices overstate or misplace the role: representatives discuss field quality control, supply code information, and help determine options and accessories, but they do not test, certify, or select, and reviewing shop drawings and evaluating substitutions is the A/E's work.

questions.question: A hospital addition will be bid in three work packages. Before drafting, the specifier wants to set a planned order for preparing the sections. Which Division 00 document does industry guidance point to for this purpose?

options.A: 00 31 32 Geotechnical Data
options.B: 00 72 00 General Conditions
options.C: 00 22 13 Supplementary Instructions to Bidders
options.D: 00 31 13 Preliminary Schedules
options.E: 00 41 00 Bid Forms
options.F: 00 73 00 Supplementary Conditions

questions.explanation: 00 31 13 Preliminary Schedules may show how the project is phased into work packages, which lets the specifier plan the order in which sections are prepared. Geotechnical data supports sections such as waterproofing, earthwork, and pavements, and the conditions of the contract, general and supplementary, chiefly shape Division 01. Bid forms and supplementary instructions to bidders do not set the order of preparing sections.
questions.source: reviewing the procurement and contracting requirements

questions.question: Among the procurement and contracting documents industry guidance says to review before writing, which one has the most influence on preparing Division 01 sections?

options.A: 00 31 13 Preliminary Schedules
options.B: 00 70 00 Conditions of the Contract
options.C: 00 52 00 Agreement Forms
options.D: 00 20 00 Instructions for Procurement
options.E: 00 31 32 Geotechnical Data
options.F: 00 61 00 Bond Forms

questions.explanation: Of the Division 00 documents to review before writing, 00 70 00 Conditions of the Contract has the greatest influence on the Division 01 sections. Preliminary schedules help set the order of preparing sections, geotechnical data informs sections such as earthwork and pavements, and agreement forms, bond forms, and procurement instructions are not named as drivers of Division 01.
questions.source: reviewing the procurement and contracting requirements

questions.question: Beyond Division 01, industry guidance notes that the conditions of the contract may also influence provisions within which Parts of some specification sections?

options.A: PART 1—GENERAL and PART 3—EXECUTION
options.B: PART 1—GENERAL and PART 2—PRODUCTS
options.C: PART 2—PRODUCTS and PART 3—EXECUTION
options.D: PART 2—PRODUCTS only
options.E: PART 1—GENERAL only
options.F: PART 3—EXECUTION only

questions.explanation: The conditions of the contract chiefly shape Division 01, but they can also affect provisions in some sections' PART 1—GENERAL and PART 3—EXECUTION. PART 2—PRODUCTS is not named, so any choice that includes it is wrong, and a choice naming only PART 1 or only PART 3 leaves out the other Part that is affected.
questions.source: reviewing the procurement and contracting requirements

questions.question: Industry guidance cites 00 31 32 Geotechnical Data as providing information necessary to specify several sections. Which examples does it give?

options.A: Earthwork, foundations, and site utilities
options.B: Shoring, dewatering, and driven piles
options.C: Waterproofing, earthwork, and pavements
options.D: Earthwork, landscaping, and irrigation
options.E: Waterproofing, foundations, and retaining walls
options.F: Pavements, landscaping, and site drainage

questions.explanation: Geotechnical data gives the specifier information needed for several sections, and the examples industry guidance names are waterproofing, earthwork, and pavements. Each other trio swaps in soil-related work such as foundations, shoring, piles, landscaping, or drainage, so none of them is the set of examples given.
questions.source: reviewing the procurement and contracting requirements

questions.question: The project architect emails the specifier that paneling in the executive offices will be bookmatched walnut veneer, a typical specification memorandum item. How should this email be filed?

options.A: Under the appropriate MasterFormat section of the specifications
options.B: Chronologically within the project's general correspondence file
options.C: With the drawing sheet on which the paneling is detailed
options.D: In the meeting-minutes file for the next design review
options.E: In the submittal log kept for the paneling installer
options.F: In the owner's project requirements binder
