options.D: The current revision number and the name of the person who last edited it
options.E: The date of initial preparation and the number of projects using it
options.F: The date of the latest revision and the MasterFormat edition it follows

questions.explanation: A section's current status on the master list means the date it was first prepared and the date it was last revised. The wrong choices substitute last project use, number of uses, an approving principal, a revision number, an editor's name, or a MasterFormat edition; naming the party responsible for each section is a separate item on the list.

questions.question: A firm's draft shortform master guide uses four levels of paragraphs under several articles. What paragraph-level limit should its standard shortform format apply?

options.A: No more than three paragraph levels under each article; a fourth only for schedules
options.B: A single paragraph level under each article; subparagraphs replaced by streamlined lists
options.C: No more than two article levels under each PART; paragraphs limited to a single level
options.D: No more than two paragraph levels under each article; a third only occasionally for lists
options.E: No limit on paragraph levels, as long as PageFormat indentation is followed
options.F: Up to four paragraph levels under each article; a fifth only for schedules

questions.explanation: A standard shortform format uses the three-part SectionFormat with no more than two levels of paragraphs under any article. A third level is acceptable now and then for listing items, but should be avoided where possible. Three, four, or unlimited levels go past that limit, a single level is stricter than required, and the rule counts paragraph levels under articles, not article levels.

questions.question: A specifier proposes dropping the PART 1, PART 2, and PART 3 headings from the firm's shortform master guide because the sections are so brief. What reasons does industry guidance give for keeping the three-part headings?

options.A: They are needed for each shortform section to be enforceable as part of the contract documents
options.B: They let bidders price each part separately, which supports preparation of the schedule of values
options.C: They serve as organizational markers for finding and coordinating information and as consistency reminders
options.D: They let the A/E omit Division 01, since each part restates the project's procedural and administrative requirements
options.E: They are needed so specification software can read, sort, and number each shortform section
options.F: They mark where each subcontractor's scope of work begins and ends within the section

questions.explanation: The three-part headings are recommended because they work as organizational markers that help people find and coordinate information quickly, and they remind the writer to keep the project manual consistent. Enforceability, pricing, software, and subcontract scopes do not depend on them, the organization of the specifications does not divide work among subcontractors, and shortform sections are not meant to repeat Division 01.

questions.question: A specifier is drafting the selected sections of a new shortform master guide specification. Which writing method should be used for them, and what does it do?

options.A: Indicative mood, which states each requirement as a full sentence built around 'shall'
options.B: Streamlining, which puts the subject first and gives keywords for quick reference
options.C: Narrative description, which explains each installation sequence in full paragraphs
options.D: Performance specifying, which states required results in place of listing products
options.E: Outline style, which keeps only the decisions that have a cost impact
options.F: Reference standard specifying, which cites standards in place of written text

questions.explanation: The sections of a shortform master guide are written with the streamlining method, which lists items with the subject first and keywords that make them quick to find. Full 'shall' sentences and narrative paragraphs add the words streamlining removes, keeping only cost-related content is the outline master technique, and performance and reference standard specifying are methods of specifying, not this writing method.

questions.question: A firm is developing the Division 01 sections of a shortform master guide specification for its building renovation work. How should these Division 01 sections be developed?

options.A: Include every article of the firm's full-length Division 01 master guide so that no requirement is omitted
options.B: Omit Division 01 and specify cutting and patching within each affected section in Divisions 02 to 49
options.C: Use the new-construction Division 01 articles unchanged and cover renovation conditions on drawings
options.D: Use only articles that apply to renovation, adding others it usually needs, such as cutting and patching
options.E: Fold the Division 01 requirements into the supplementary conditions so the technical sections stay brief
options.F: Write a separate Division 01 for each phase of the renovation so the articles match the work

questions.explanation: Division 01 sections for a shortform master use only the articles that apply to the project type, plus others needed for situations that type usually meets, such as cutting and patching for renovation. Including every full-length article defeats the shortform purpose, and pushing the requirement into technical sections, drawings, or the supplementary conditions, or splitting Division 01 by phase, works against using Division 01 for these items.

questions.question: When writing a shortform master guide specification, where does industry guidance direct the specifier to specify coordination and quality assurance items?

options.A: In PART 1 of each section in Divisions 02 through 49
options.B: In the supplementary conditions to the general conditions
options.C: In Division 01—General Requirements
options.D: In the instructions for procurement issued to bidders
options.E: In the agreement between the owner and the contractor
options.F: In the general notes on the drawings for each discipline

questions.explanation: Coordination and quality assurance items are specified in Division 01. PART 1 of sections in Divisions 02 through 49 should not repeat Division 01 and includes quality assurance articles only to elaborate on it. The supplementary conditions, the agreement, procurement instructions, and drawing notes are not where these items are placed.

questions.question: For a project whose requirements allow less complexity, a specifier combines all Division 01 sections into one section. How is that combined section numbered and organized?

options.A: Section 01 00 00 General Requirements; all articles in PART 1, with PARTS 2 and 3 Not Used
options.B: Section 01 10 00 Summary; procedural articles in PART 1, with temporary facilities in PART 2
options.C: Section 01 00 00 General Requirements; articles distributed among PARTS 1, 2, and 3 by subject
options.D: Section 01 70 00 Execution and Closeout; all articles in PART 1, with PARTS 2 and 3 Not Used
options.E: Section 01 00 00 General Requirements; all articles in PART 3, with PARTS 1 and 2 Not Used
options.F: Section 01 40 00 Quality Requirements; all articles in PART 1, with PARTS 2 and 3 Not Used

questions.explanation: When a project's requirements are simple enough, all of Division 01 may be merged into one section. A typical combined section is 01 00 00 General Requirements, with articles from Summary of Work through Closeout Submittals all in PART 1, and with PART 2 and PART 3 marked Not Used. 01 10 00, 01 40 00, and 01 70 00 are Level 2 titles the single section absorbs, and the articles are not spread across Parts or placed in PART 3.

questions.question: A firm revises its full-length master guide sections for a new energy code but schedules the matching shortform master guide revisions for next year. Its project manuals routinely mix sections from both masters. What does industry guidance recommend?

options.A: Use only full-length sections on every project until the shortform revisions are complete
options.B: Revise the shortform master at the same time as the full-length master
options.C: Add a Division 01 statement that full-length sections govern over conflicting shortform text
options.D: Correct the shortform sections on each project as they are edited from the master guide
options.E: Freeze the full-length master until the shortform revisions catch up
options.F: Issue the revised full-length sections and fix conflicts by addendum

questions.explanation: The shortform master must be updated together with the full-length master, so that project specifications combining sections from both avoid coordination and consistency errors. Dropping shortform sections, adding a precedence clause, patching each project, freezing the full-length master, or repairing conflicts by addendum leaves the two masters out of step.

questions.question: As a general rule for shortform project specifications, what should be done with sections that carry MasterFormat Level 3 and Level 4 numbers and titles?

options.A: Keep each Level 3 and Level 4 title as a separate section so the content stays focused
options.B: Combine them under the Level 1 title so that each division becomes a single section
options.C: Convert them into article headings within PART 2 of the related Division 01 section
options.D: Combine them under a Level 2 title when possible, as the A/E judges efficient
options.E: Convert them into Level 5 UniFormat designations for each system
options.F: Assign each one to a separate subcontract package for bidding

questions.explanation: Level 3 and Level 4 titles should be combined under a Level 2 title whenever possible, with the A/E judging whether each combination is convenient or efficient; broad Level 2 titles shorten specifications by combining similar paragraphs. A single division-level section is the limited-scope option, keeping every lower title separate works against shortening, and Division 01, UniFormat, and subcontract packages are not where technical titles go.

questions.question: Reviewing a shortform gypsum board section, the specifier finds PART 1 repeats the general submittal procedures and quality assurance requirements already stated in Division 01. What should PART 1 of this section contain?

options.A: All submittal and quality assurance requirements, so the section can stand alone in bidding
options.B: Only a reference to Division 01, with submittal and quality assurance articles never included
options.C: Only administrative and procedural requirements that apply solely to that portion of the work
options.D: The general submittal procedures, with Division 01 limited to temporary facilities and controls
options.E: Every Division 01 requirement restated in brief, streamlined form for quick reference
options.F: Only product and installation requirements, with the administrative text moved to PART 3

questions.explanation: PART 1 of each section in Divisions 02 through 49 should hold only the administrative and procedural requirements that apply to that section's work and should not repeat Division 01. Submittal and quality assurance articles appear only when they need to elaborate on Division 01, so they are neither required in full nor banned, and restating Division 01 briefly is still repetition.

questions.question: An owner asks the A/E to trim the Division 01 sections of a shortform specification to help control construction cost. What is the best approach?

options.A: Remove Division 01 entirely and rely on the general conditions to establish all administrative requirements
options.B: Include only the administrative requirements needed, without reducing detail below project requirements
options.C: Keep the full-length Division 01 sections unchanged, since administrative requirements add little cost
options.D: Move the administrative requirements into PART 1 of each section in Divisions 02 through 49
options.E: Delete the temporary facilities requirements so the contractor may choose its own arrangements
options.F: Move the administrative requirements into the supplementary conditions to shorten Division 01

questions.explanation: Detail in Division 01 should not drop below what the project requires, but because administrative requirements are often significant cost items, include only those the project needs. Keeping everything ignores that cost, removing Division 01 or deleting needed requirements goes below the project's needs, and moving the text into PART 1 of technical sections or the supplementary conditions does not trim it.

questions.question: A specifier condensing a full-length section into shortform revises the sentence "Portland cement shall be ASTM C150, Type I." Applying the streamlining method, how should it read?

options.A: Portland Cement: ASTM C150, Type I.
options.B: Portland cement shall comply with ASTM C150, Type I.
options.C: Provide portland cement conforming to ASTM C150, Type I.
options.D: ASTM C150, Type I, shall be used for portland cement.
options.E: Portland cement—ASTM C150, Type I, shall be used.
options.F: Use ASTM C150, Type I, for all portland cement.

questions.explanation: Streamlining lists materials with the subject first and replaces 'shall be' with a colon, so the sentence becomes 'Portland Cement: ASTM C150, Type I.' The other versions keep a full sentence with 'shall', 'provide', or 'use', or put the standard ahead of the subject, which is the opposite of the streamlined form.

questions.question: A shortform concrete section reads: "Aggregates: ASTM C33, Standard Specification for Concrete Aggregates." Which condensing technique applies to this paragraph?

options.A: Delete the reference standard and describe the aggregate gradation requirements in the text instead
options.B: Move the reference into a related section and add a cross-reference to that section in this one
options.C: Spell out the standards organization's full name and keep the title so the reference is unambiguous
options.D: Delete the standard's title, since the standard is already identified by abbreviation and number
options.E: Add the standard's edition date and full title so the paragraph is complete and current
options.F: Replace the reference standard with a named manufacturer and product to remove ambiguity

questions.explanation: One condensing technique is to drop a reference standard's title when the text already identifies the standard by its abbreviation and number, as 'ASTM C33' does. Reference standards save space and set a minimum level of requirements, so replacing one with descriptive text or a named product lengthens or narrows the section, and the guidance cuts excessive cross-references rather than adding them or spelling out more.

questions.question: An A/E's door hardware schedule is generated from a spreadsheet, and the team debates whether it belongs on the drawings or in the shortform project manual. What does industry guidance report as the US National CAD Standard® position?

options.A: NCS requires all schedules to be placed in the specifications to keep drawings uncluttered
options.B: NCS recommends schedules in the drawing set and prohibits schedules in the specifications
options.C: NCS recommends schedules in the drawing set but allows database schedules in either
options.D: NCS leaves schedule placement to the owner, who decides it in the project requirements
options.E: NCS requires every schedule to appear in both the drawings and the specifications
options.F: NCS assigns schedule placement to the contractor through its shop drawings and submittals

questions.explanation: NCS recommends that schedules be part of the drawing set, but schedules produced as electronic databases or spreadsheets may go in either the drawings or the specifications. So NCS neither requires schedules in the specifications nor forbids them there, does not require both, and does not leave placement to the owner or to shop drawings.

questions.question: To condense text, a specifier rewrites the door hardware finish descriptions so that one statement covers all of them without ambiguity. Which condensing technique is this?

options.A: Combining and editing related articles or paragraphs
options.B: Combining and editing sentences within an article or paragraph
options.C: Combining and editing related sections into one section
options.D: Condensing the text by using the streamlining method
options.E: Deleting the titles of reference standards cited by number
options.F: Eliminating excessive cross-references to related sections

questions.explanation: The door example works at three scales: combining wood, plastic, and steel doors is combining related sections; combining the hardware item descriptions is combining related articles or paragraphs; and merging the hardware finish descriptions into one clear sentence is combining and editing sentences within an article or paragraph. Streamlining, deleting standard titles, and cutting cross-references are separate techniques.

questions.question: A firm licenses a commercially available shortform master guide specification and wants to use it on a project starting next month. What should the firm do before using it on a project?

options.A: Scrutinize the guide to determine what it does not cover
options.B: Confirm that a standards body has certified the guide's level of detail
options.C: Obtain the owner's written acceptance of the guide's content
options.D: Convert the guide's sections to full-length format for review
options.E: Register the guide with the authority having jurisdiction
options.F: Ask bidders to accept the guide's content when they bid

questions.explanation: Before a commercial shortform master guide is used on a project, it should be scrutinized to find out what it does not cover, along with the level of detail it represents and the project types it suits. No certification, AHJ registration, owner acceptance, or bidder acceptance step is involved, and converting the sections to full-length format would defeat the purpose of a shortform master.
questions.source: commercially available shortform master guide specifications

questions.question: While evaluating a commercial shortform master guide specification, which two determinations does industry guidance say the firm should make about it?

options.A: The publisher's update frequency and the cost of licensing it for each new project
options.B: The MasterFormat® edition it follows and whether its sections are full-length or outline
options.C: The number of sections it contains and whether it includes the Division 01 sections
options.D: The level of detail it represents and the type of project for which it is appropriate
options.E: The publisher's liability limits and the indemnity terms of its license agreement
options.F: The reference standard editions it cites and the building codes it was written to

questions.explanation: After scrutinizing what a commercial shortform guide leaves out, the firm should determine the level of detail it represents and the type of project it is appropriate for. Update frequency, licensing cost, MasterFormat edition, section count, liability terms, and cited editions may matter in other ways, but they are not the determinations named.
questions.source: commercially available shortform master guide specifications

questions.question: A firm has finished scrutinizing a commercial shortform master guide specification as recommended, including what it does not cover and which project types it suits. What should the firm then do with the guide's sections?

options.A: Use them as published, since the publisher has already edited them into condensed form
options.B: Expand each of them to full-length format so they match the firm's other master sections
options.C: Modify them as needed to fit the firm's practice and keep detail consistent
options.D: Limit them to outline specifications, where a lower level of detail is expected
options.E: Submit them to the owner for approval as the project specifications
options.F: Hold them unchanged until the publisher releases its next edition

questions.explanation: After that review, the firm modifies the guide's sections as needed to fit its own practice and to keep the level of detail consistent. Using them unchanged skips the tailoring, expanding them to full length or converting them to outline form defeats the purpose of a shortform master, and owner approval does not replace editing them.
questions.source: commercially available shortform master guide specifications

questions.question: A flooring manufacturer's literature for its broadloom product is titled "Product Specification." Per industry guidance, how does a construction specification for the project differ from such literature?

options.A: It describes the quantities and locations of the product, which the drawings cannot fully convey
options.B: It describes the work result of effort applied to products, such as carpeting rather than carpet
options.C: It restates the manufacturer's product data so that bidders can compare competing products
options.D: It is limited to administrative requirements, since product data comes from manufacturers
options.E: It lists only the manufacturer's product name and model number for each item installed
options.F: It repeats the manufacturer's warranty terms so the owner has them in one place

questions.explanation: Manufacturers' technical data is often also called a specification, but a construction specification describes the work result of effort applied to products: the product is carpet, the work result is carpeting. Specifications define qualitative requirements, not quantities and locations, and they cover products, workmanship, and administrative requirements rather than restating product data, model numbers, or warranty terms.

questions.question: An owner asks why the A/E cannot simply put everything in the drawing notes. It is not practical for notes to describe product quality and installation in detail, so specifications define the qualitative requirements for which items?

options.A: Products, materials, workmanship, and administrative requirements
options.B: Products, quantities, locations, and dimensional requirements
options.C: Materials, systems, sequencing, and allocations of the contract cost
options.D: Products, materials, means and methods, and safety programs
options.E: Products, schedules, cost allocations, and phasing requirements
options.F: Workmanship, subcontract scopes, payment terms, and bond amounts

questions.explanation: Drawing notes cannot practically describe product quality and installation methods in detail, so the specifications set the qualitative requirements for the products, materials, workmanship, and administrative requirements the project is based on. Quantities, locations, and dimensions are not qualitative requirements, and the other lists slip in items such as cost allocations, safety programs, or subcontract scopes.

questions.question: Industry organizations in the United States and Canada developed several standards, called formats, that apply from project conception through the facility's life cycle. What is the chief advantage of these formats?

options.A: A single classification that replaces the separate drawing and specification systems
options.B: A mandatory framework that building officials use in code compliance review
options.C: A uniform basis for pricing the work and preparing the schedule of values
options.D: A standardized means of organizing, storing, retrieving, and communicating data
options.E: A single method of specifying that replaces the other methods
options.F: A uniform set of contract forms for every delivery method

questions.explanation: The formats exist chiefly to give the industry a standardized way to organize, store, retrieve, and communicate the very large body of project information. They are several related standards, not one system replacing the others, and they are not a code compliance framework, a pricing basis, a specifying method, or a set of contract forms.

questions.question: A facility owner wants to use OmniClass® to manage information about its campus over the facilities' entire life cycle. How many classification tables make up OmniClass®, and how may they be used?

options.A: 15 tables, which are designed to be used together as one set
options.B: 12 tables, which can be used together or individually
options.C: 15 tables, which can be used together or individually
options.D: 12 tables, which are designed to be used together as one set
options.E: 21 tables, which can be used together or individually
options.F: 15 tables, which replace MasterFormat and UniFormat entirely

questions.explanation: OmniClass is made up of 15 classification tables, and they may be used together or one at a time to manage information about facilities over their whole life cycle. Twelve or 21 is not the count, the tables are not a set that must be used together, and OmniClass incorporates MasterFormat and UniFormat as the bases of two of its tables rather than replacing them.

questions.question: Industry guidance names two ISO standards that describe the concepts on which OmniClass® is based. Which statement about them is correct?

options.A: ISO 12006-2 frames object-oriented exchange; ISO 12006-3 frames the classification of information
options.B: ISO 12006-2 frames the classification of information; ISO 12006-3 frames object-oriented exchange
options.C: ISO 12006-2 and ISO 12006-3 were created in the United Kingdom in 1997 and published as Uniclass
options.D: ISO 12006-2 frames the classification of information; ISO 12006-3 frames the table for elements
options.E: ISO 12006-2 frames the classification of information; ISO 12006-3 frames the MasterFormat numbering
options.F: ISO 12006-2 frames object-oriented exchange; ISO 12006-3 frames the table for work results

questions.explanation: ISO 12006-2 is the framework for classification of information and ISO 12006-3 is the framework for object-oriented information exchange; together they set out the basis OmniClass follows. Uniclass, a UK system from 1997, also followed them but is not them, and UniFormat and MasterFormat, not ISO standards, are the bases of the OmniClass tables for elements and work results.

questions.question: A firm's BIM manager is mapping its specification library to OmniClass and needs the table that classifies work results. Which table number does industry guidance list for that table?

options.A: Table 21
options.B: Table 22
options.C: Table 23
options.D: Table 42
options.E: Table 31
options.F: Table 13

questions.explanation: In the list of OmniClass tables, Work Results is Table 22, and it is based on MasterFormat. Table 21 is Elements, Table 23 is Products, Table 31 is Phases, Table 13 is Spaces by Function, and Table 42 is Materials; the neighboring numbers are easy to confuse with it.

questions.question: OmniClass Tables 11 through 14 (construction entities and spaces) are numbered ahead of Table 21—Elements and Table 23—Products. What principle explains this ordering of the tables as a whole?

options.A: Tables follow the life-cycle phases from planning through facility operation
options.B: Tables are sequenced in the order in which they were first published
options.C: Tables used by owners precede tables used by design and construction teams
options.D: Tables progress from the general to the specific, wholes before parts
options.E: Tables are arranged alphabetically by their titles
options.F: Tables follow the sequence of the MasterFormat divisions

questions.explanation: Taken as a whole, the tables form an implied hierarchy that runs from the general to the specific: tables about whole construction entities come before tables that break them into their composite elements. The order is not by publication date, user type, life-cycle phase (phases have their own table, Table 31), alphabet, or MasterFormat division.

questions.question: A specifier who knows MasterFormat and UniFormat numbering is reviewing an OmniClass designation for the first time. How is the numbering of OmniClass table entries structured?

options.A: A pair of numbers for each level of hierarchy represented
options.B: Three pairs of digits, plus an optional pair for expansion
options.C: A letter for the category plus two digits for each level
options.D: A table prefix followed by a user-assigned sequential number
options.E: A single four-digit code assigned to each entry
options.F: The table number alone, with entries listed alphabetically

questions.explanation: OmniClass entries are numbered with a pair of numbers for each level of the hierarchy they represent. Three pairs of digits with an optional added pair describes MasterFormat, a category letter followed by digits describes UniFormat, and OmniClass uses neither user-assigned sequences, single four-digit codes, nor alphabetical lists.

questions.question: A small A/E office wants to organize its modest collection of manufacturers' product literature using a single OmniClass table. Which table does industry guidance cite as the example for this use?

options.A: Table 22—Work Results
options.B: Table 41—Information
options.C: Table 23—Products
options.D: Table 42—Materials
options.E: Table 21—Elements
options.F: Table 31—Phases

questions.explanation: At its simplest, OmniClass can organize a small collection of product literature using one table, and the example given is Table 23—Products. Work results is the basis MasterFormat uses for filing product literature, which makes Table 22 tempting, and Elements, Phases, Information, and Materials are not the example given.

questions.question: A firm's technical library has outgrown a single OmniClass table. What is gained by using designators from more than one table to qualify and refine entries?

options.A: New entries can be added without renumbering existing entries
options.B: Information can be recalled for user needs with greater precision
options.C: Entries can be cross-referenced directly to UniFormat Level 5 titles
options.D: Each table can be extended with user-defined designators and titles
options.E: Entries can be converted directly into MasterFormat section numbers
options.F: Fewer tables are then needed to classify the whole collection

questions.explanation: For a larger collection, designators from more than one table qualify and refine the entries, so information can be retrieved to suit the user's needs much more precisely. Adding entries without renumbering, links to UniFormat Level 5, user-defined extensions, conversion to MasterFormat numbers, and needing fewer tables are not the benefit described.

questions.question: An owner's facility information manager must classify an extensive, complex collection of information drawn from various data sources and show the conceptual relationships between entries. What is the appropriate method?

options.A: Classify each entry using only the most specific level of one table
options.B: Assign each item a user-defined Level 5 extension with a MasterFormat number
options.C: Add an optional fourth pair of digits to each entry for expansion
options.D: Combine designators from multiple tables using delimiters
options.E: Prefix each entry with a UniFormat Level 1 category letter
options.F: File each entry by its MasterFormat division number only

questions.explanation: For extensive, complex collections, designators from several OmniClass tables are joined with delimiters so the conceptual relationships between entries are defined. One table suits only a small collection of similar material, user-assigned Level 5 extensions and category letters belong to UniFormat, and the optional added pair of digits and division numbers belong to MasterFormat.

questions.question: A design-build team wants to use UniFormat as a stand-alone contracting structure. Under which Level 1 category are the bidding, proposal, and contract requirements placed?

options.A: Project Description, which has no letter designation
options.B: Z—General, which remains last in the list
options.C: A—Substructure, the first lettered category
options.D: F—Special Construction and Demolition
options.E: B—Shell, the second lettered category
options.F: G—Building Sitework, the last building category

questions.explanation: Project Description has no letter and is not a building system or assembly; it holds the bidding, proposal, and contract requirements, which lets UniFormat serve as a stand-alone contracting structure, especially for design-build. Category Z—General is lettered and kept last for expansion, and Substructure, Shell, Special Construction, and Building Sitework are building categories.

questions.question: A specifier extends the UniFormat list beyond building construction by adding new Level 1 categories for civil work. Where does Category Z—General fall in the expanded list, and why?

options.A: It moves to first position, because general information precedes elements
options.B: It is renumbered to follow G, because the letters must remain consecutive
options.C: It remains last, because it was given the last letter to allow expansion
options.D: It is merged into Project Description, because both hold general data
options.E: It becomes Category H, the first of the civil categories
options.F: It is dropped, since civil work is classified only by MasterFormat

questions.explanation: Category Z, General, was assigned the final letter, Z, to leave room for the classification to grow beyond building construction, and when the list is expanded it stays last. Because Level 1 letters and titles are fixed, Z is not relettered, merged, or dropped, and it is the unlettered Project Description, not Z, that comes first.

questions.question: At schematic design, a specifier is preparing a preliminary project description and the estimator a preliminary cost estimate for a typical building. Titles from which UniFormat levels can be applied to most such documents?

options.A: Levels 1 and 2 only
options.B: Levels 1 through 3
options.C: Levels 1 through 4
options.D: Levels 4 and 5
options.E: Levels 2 through 4
options.F: Level 5 only

questions.explanation: For most PPDs and preliminary cost estimates, the titles of UniFormat Levels 1 through 3 are enough. Levels 4 and 5 are there for detailed, complex projects, where their titles and listings act as a checklist for a thorough application of UniFormat, so a typical building at schematic design does not need them.

questions.question: A specifier needs a Level 5 entry for a concrete continuous footing under UniFormat A1010.10 Wall Foundations. Under the rules for user-assigned Level 5 numbers, which designation is properly formed?
questions.explanation: A user-assigned Level 5 number carries the parent Level 4 designation followed by added characters, such as a two-digit number, a letter code, or the matching MasterFormat number, set off by an additional decimal point: A1010.10.03 30 00. The other choices drop the Level 4 pair or Level 3 digits, omit the separating decimal point, or put the MasterFormat number ahead of or inside the UniFormat designation.

questions.question: During schematic design, the owner requests a cost estimate, but the A/E has not yet selected the roofing materials. Under the concept of the preliminary project description (PPD), how should the written description of the roof be prepared?

options.A: With enough information for cost estimating, without making final design decisions
options.B: By naming a single basis-of-design product so the estimator has a firm price
options.C: By deferring the roof description until materials are chosen in design development
options.D: By listing each candidate material under its MasterFormat section number and title
options.E: By describing the roof only by its expected installed cost per square foot
options.F: By copying the full-length roofing section from the office master guide

questions.explanation: A basic idea behind the PPD is that written descriptions let designers give enough information for cost estimating without making final design decisions. Naming one product or deferring the roof defeats that purpose, a cost figure is not a description, a full master section is construction-document text, and PPDs are organized by systems and assemblies, not MasterFormat sections.

questions.question: Beyond giving more detail for preparing PPDs, PPDFormat includes additional material responding to which industry changes?

options.A: The latest MasterFormat edition, BIM, and design-build delivery
options.B: The latest UniFormat edition, sustainable design, and design-build
options.C: The latest UniFormat edition, BIM, and Integrated Project Delivery
options.D: OmniClass coordination, BIM, and construction manager delivery
options.E: The latest UniFormat edition, the National CAD Standard, and Integrated Project Delivery
options.F: The latest SectionFormat edition, BIM, and Integrated Project Delivery

questions.explanation: PPDFormat adds material for three industry developments: alignment with the current edition of UniFormat, building information modeling (BIM), and Integrated Project Delivery (IPD). PPDs are organized by UniFormat, not MasterFormat or SectionFormat, and the National CAD Standard, sustainable design, design-build, and construction manager delivery are not among the three.

questions.question: The written descriptions in a PPD should document which kind of project requirements, matched to how far design decisions and detail have progressed?

options.A: Quantitative
options.B: Prescriptive
options.C: Proprietary
options.D: Qualitative
options.E: Procedural
options.F: Contractual

questions.explanation: A PPD's narrative records qualitative requirements, at whatever depth the design decisions made so far allow, so estimators can price the work without final decisions being made. It describes systems and assemblies before specific materials and methods are chosen, so it is not quantitative, prescriptive, or proprietary, and procedural or contractual requirements belong to Division 01 and the contract documents, not the PPD.

questions.question: An estimator receives a schematic-design PPD and must prepare a preliminary cost estimate that can be related easily to the PPD's descriptions. Which format should organize the estimate?

options.A: MasterFormat, because its numbers parallel the specifications
options.B: UniFormat, because it is organized by systems and assemblies
options.C: OmniClass Table 23, because estimates are priced by product
options.D: SectionFormat, because its parts separate labor from materials
options.E: The Uniform Drawing System, because it parallels the drawing set
options.F: MasterFormat Division 01, because it holds price and payment procedures

questions.explanation: UniFormat is the basis for organizing preliminary cost estimates, and because a PPD also describes the project by its systems and assemblies, the estimate and the PPD line up and are easy to compare. MasterFormat follows the specifications, including the payment procedures in Division 01, and the Uniform Drawing System, OmniClass Table 23 and SectionFormat are not formats for preliminary estimates.

questions.question: An office tries to file its standard drawing details under MasterFormat numbers and finds the system awkward. What is the reason?

options.A: Most details include multiple materials classified by MasterFormat
options.B: MasterFormat numbers change with each new edition of the list
options.C: MasterFormat reserves its numbers for specifications and product data
options.D: Most details show work by several trades under different subcontracts
options.E: MasterFormat is organized by systems and assemblies, not materials
options.F: Most details are drawn before the materials have been chosen

questions.explanation: A typical detail shows several materials, each classified in a different MasterFormat section, so no single MasterFormat number fits it. UniFormat suits details because it is organized by elements, systems and assemblies, which is what a detail depicts; that describes UniFormat, not MasterFormat. Edition changes, reserved numbers, and trade or subcontract divisions are not the problem; the difficulty is precisely that each detail already shows several chosen materials.

questions.question: An A/E firm files its library of standard details by UniFormat. The CAD manager proposes using those UniFormat designations as the detail identifiers on the sheets of the next project's drawings. What is the best response?

options.A: Adopt it, provided Level 4 designations identify each detail
options.B: Adopt it, provided the matching MasterFormat number is shown alongside
options.C: Decline it; the system is meant for internal filing and retrieval
options.D: Decline it; details on drawings must use MasterFormat numbers
options.E: Adopt it, provided the same designations appear in the specifications
options.F: Decline it; UniFormat is meant only for preliminary cost estimates

questions.explanation: UniFormat is meant for filing and retrieving details inside the office that creates or uses them; it is not intended as the way to identify details in a project's drawing set. Adding Level 4 designations, MasterFormat numbers, or matching references in the specifications does not change that. Declining because UniFormat is only for estimates gives the wrong reason, since UniFormat also serves PPDs and detail filing, and no rule requires MasterFormat numbers as detail identifiers.

questions.question: A specifier is adding a parapet detail (showing blocking, membrane, flashing, and coping) to the office detail library. How should the detail be filed so it can be retrieved efficiently?

options.A: Under the MasterFormat section for the predominant material shown
options.B: Under the UniFormat element or assembly that the detail depicts
options.C: Under each MasterFormat section for every material in the detail
options.D: Under the OmniClass Table 42 entry for the principal material
options.E: Under the drawing discipline of the sheet it was drawn on
options.F: Under the project and sheet number where it was first used

questions.explanation: UniFormat is organized by elements, systems and assemblies, which match what a detail depicts, so it is the recommended way to file and retrieve details. A detail like this one contains materials from several MasterFormat sections, so filing it under one material, or under every material, is the awkward approach. Discipline, project, or sheet number filing does not tell the next user what assembly the detail shows, and OmniClass Table 42 is not the method described.

questions.question: Besides its U.S. publisher, which organization jointly developed MasterFormat?

options.A: The American Institute of Architects
options.B: The Canadian Construction Association
options.C: The National Institute of Building Sciences
options.D: Construction Specifications Canada
options.E: The Canadian Standards Association
options.F: The Design-Build Institute of America

questions.explanation: MasterFormat is a joint product of the U.S. specifications institute that publishes it and Construction Specifications Canada (CSC), the same pairing that produces SectionFormat. The Canadian Standards Association is a source of reference standards, the National Institute of Building Sciences oversees the National CAD Standard, and neither they nor the AIA, the Canadian Construction Association or the Design-Build Institute of America co-developed MasterFormat.

questions.question: MasterFormat's numbers and titles cover the subject matter necessary for constructing a facility and also for which other activities?

options.A: Programming and schematic design
options.B: Financing and property acquisition
options.C: Operation and maintenance
options.D: Zoning approval and permitting
options.E: Feasibility studies and site selection
options.F: Leasing and property management

questions.explanation: MasterFormat classifies the subject matter needed to build a facility and then to operate and maintain it, which is why its Division 01 includes facility operation and maintenance titles. Programming and design, financing and acquisition, feasibility and site selection, zoning and permitting, and leasing are owner and design activities outside the scope of its numbers and titles.

questions.question: Into which two groups are the numbers and titles in MasterFormat organized?

options.A: Bidding and Contract Requirements Group and Facility Construction Group
options.B: Bidding and Contract Requirements Group and Specifications Group
options.C: Procurement and Contracting Requirements Group and Specifications Group
options.D: Procurement and Contracting Requirements Group and Facility Construction Group
options.E: Procurement and Contracting Requirements Group and Facility Services Subgroup
options.F: General Requirements Subgroup and Facility Construction Subgroup

questions.explanation: MasterFormat has two groups: the Procurement and Contracting Requirements Group (Division 00) and the Specifications Group (Divisions 01 through 49). The General Requirements, Facility Construction, and Facility Services subgroups are subdivisions inside the Specifications Group, not groups of their own, and Bidding and Contract Requirements is not the name of either group.

questions.question: The MasterFormat group that holds introductory information and procurement information is also the location for which other information?

options.A: Administrative requirements that apply to the project as a whole
options.B: Relationships, responsibilities, and processes for construction
options.C: Descriptions of the physical aspects of construction work
options.D: Performance requirements for building systems and assemblies
options.E: Product, material, and installation requirements
options.F: Commissioning and facility operation requirements

questions.explanation: The Procurement and Contracting Requirements Group holds introductory and procurement information and also the information that defines the relationships, responsibilities, and processes for construction, such as the agreement and conditions of the contract. Administrative requirements, the physical aspects of the work (products and installation), commissioning, facility operation, and elemental performance requirements are all located in the Specifications Group.

questions.question: Which pairing correctly describes what the MasterFormat Specifications Group provides locations to describe?

options.A: Administrative requirements and physical aspects of construction
options.B: Procurement information and contract relationships for construction
options.C: Introductory information and physical aspects of construction
options.D: Administrative requirements and procurement information
options.E: Contracting forms and physical aspects of construction
options.F: Administrative requirements and conditions of the contract

questions.explanation: The Specifications Group is where both administrative requirements and the physical aspects of construction are described. Introductory information, procurement information, contracting forms, and the conditions of the contract that define relationships, responsibilities, and processes all belong to the Procurement and Contracting Requirements Group, so any pairing that includes one of them is wrong.

questions.question: A firm numbers its specification sections sequentially from 1 on each new project. Which two needs does such a random designation system fail to meet?

options.A: Competitive bidding and subcontractor buyout by the contractor
options.B: Code-compliance review and permit submission by the A/E
options.C: Preliminary cost estimating and value analysis by the owner
options.D: Standardizing specifications and electronic data retrieval
options.E: Construction scheduling and progress reporting by the contractor
options.F: Life cycle cost and energy analysis by the A/E

questions.explanation: Numbering sections at random fails people who want to standardize parts of their specifications and people who rely on electronic data retrieval and automated processing, because nothing lands in the same place twice. MasterFormat's fixed order prevents those breakdowns. Bidding and buyout, permitting, cost estimating, progress scheduling, and life cycle costing are not the needs this problem affects.

questions.question: A specifier uses the MasterFormat keyword index to find where a construction product is classified. What do the index references use?

options.A: Eight-digit numbers that designate Level 1, 2, or 3 titles
options.B: Six-digit numbers that designate Level 1, 2, or 3 titles
options.C: Eight-digit numbers that designate Level 4 titles
options.D: Six-digit numbers that designate Level 4 titles
options.E: Two-digit numbers that designate Level 1 divisions only
options.F: Alphanumeric UniFormat designations for each element

questions.explanation: The alphabetical subject index in MasterFormat points to six-digit classification numbers, which designate Level 1, 2 or 3 titles. Each pair of digits is one level, so a six-digit number cannot reach Level 4, the optional eight-digit numbers are not used in the index, a two-digit division number alone is too coarse, and alphanumeric designations belong to UniFormat, not MasterFormat.

questions.question: Besides organizing project manuals, what does MasterFormat do for A/Es and for the people who use their project manuals?

options.A: Assigns each section's work to a single subcontractor
options.B: Sets the sheet order within each drawing discipline
options.C: Helps users find information in standard locations
options.D: Matches each drawing detail number to a section number
options.E: Defines the three parts used within each section
options.F: Sets the page layout and numbering of each section

questions.explanation: A/Es use MasterFormat to organize project manuals and so that readers can find information in predictable, standard locations. The three parts of a section come from SectionFormat and the page layout from PageFormat, not MasterFormat. MasterFormat sections are not meant to match a single trade or subcontractor, and it plays no role in drawing sheet order or detail numbering.

questions.question: A small A/E firm that designs only K-12 schools considers abandoning MasterFormat for its own numbering, arguing that MasterFormat suits only general-practice firms. What is the best response?

options.A: Keep MasterFormat; it is flexible enough for any company or project type
options.B: Adopt the custom system, provided it is used consistently on every project
options.C: Switch to UniFormat, which is recommended for specialized building types
options.D: Keep MasterFormat only for Division 01 and use custom numbers elsewhere
options.E: Keep MasterFormat but renumber its sections to match the trades
options.F: Adopt the custom system, provided a MasterFormat cross-reference is issued

questions.explanation: MasterFormat is flexible enough for any company, discipline or project type, and firms that specialize in one building type use it too. A custom scheme, even with a cross-reference, recreates the random designation problem that defeats standardization and electronic retrieval. Renumbering sections to match trades is wrong because sections are not meant to correspond to trades, and UniFormat is not a replacement for project manual numbering.

questions.question: A building product manufacturer reorganizes its catalog around MasterFormat numbers and titles. Manufacturers and suppliers use MasterFormat to organize and identify product literature and also to do what?

options.A: Obtain prior approval of their products from the A/E
options.B: Market their products to users of the information
options.C: Certify product compliance with reference standards
options.D: Establish unit prices for the contractor's bid forms
options.E: Assign installation of their products to specific trades
options.F: Set the warranty period for their products by section

questions.explanation: Manufacturers and suppliers use MasterFormat to organize and identify their literature and to market their products to the people who use that information, since specifiers and contractors look for products by section number. Prior approval, compliance certification, unit prices, trade assignments, and warranty terms are handled by other procedures and documents, not by numbering literature.

questions.question: A specifier is organizing requirements for a roofing system in a project manual. Which arrangement of MasterFormat sections is an accepted way to specify a system?

options.A: The system in a Level 1 division, its materials in several Level 2 sections
options.B: The system in a Level 3 section, its materials in several Level 2 sections
options.C: The system in a Level 2 section, its materials in several Level 3 sections
options.D: The system in a Level 3 section, its materials in a Level 1 division
options.E: The system in a Level 4 section, its materials in several Level 3 sections
options.F: The system in a Level 1 division, its materials in a Level 4 section

questions.explanation: A system may be specified entirely in one Level 2 section, or the overall system may go in a Level 2 section with its component materials in several Level 3 sections below it. The other arrangements put the parent at a lower level than its parts, or use a Level 1 division, which is a grouping of sections rather than a section, so none is an accepted arrangement.

questions.question: An A/E office is setting up a technical library of product literature filed by MasterFormat. What is data filing under MasterFormat primarily concerned with?

options.A: Archiving superseded literature for later dispute resolution
options.B: Tracking product approvals and substitutions on each project
options.C: Developing unit cost data for preliminary project estimates
options.D: Rapid retrieval of data on products or work being specified
options.E: Organizing literature by manufacturer name and brand
options.F: Recording warranties and maintenance data for the owner

questions.explanation: Filing product literature by MasterFormat is mainly about retrieving technical data quickly for the products or work results being specified, because the same numbers organize the specifications. Filing by manufacturer name defeats that, archiving and tracking approvals are not the purpose, warranties and maintenance data are closeout submittals for the owner, and preliminary estimates are organized by UniFormat.

questions.question: A specifier notices that much of the manufacturers' literature arriving at the office carries MasterFormat numbers. What does this practice allow?

options.A: Their products can be tied to the work result sections where used
options.B: Their products are accepted as named products without a substitution request
options.C: Their literature can be filed by UniFormat element without cross-reference
options.D: Their products are listed automatically in the MasterFormat keyword index
options.E: Their products comply with the referenced industry standards
options.F: Their product data is accepted as a submittal without review

questions.explanation: Because most manufacturers number their literature by MasterFormat, each product can be tied to the work result sections that use it. Putting a section number on literature does not show compliance with reference standards, exempt a product from substitution procedures or submittal review, change UniFormat filing, or create keyword index entries.

questions.question: A general contractor's estimating department organizes its historical cost database by MasterFormat numbers and titles. What relationship makes this organization useful?

options.A: It parallels the organization of the drawing sheets
options.B: It parallels the organization of the specifications
options.C: It follows the contractor's subcontract work packages
options.D: It follows the Level 1 categories of the PPD
options.E: It follows the UniFormat elements used in the estimate
options.F: It parallels the organization of the conditions of the contract

questions.explanation: MasterFormat numbers and titles are the basis for organizing construction costs and match the way specifications are organized, so a user can connect a section to its product information and its cost data. MasterFormat does not follow drawing sheets, subcontract packages, or the conditions of the contract, and UniFormat elements, including the Level 1 categories of a PPD, are a different system.

questions.question: MasterFormat is widely used to organize which three kinds of information under a single classification system?

options.A: Specifications, drawing details, and cost information
options.B: Product literature, drawing details, and PPDs
options.C: Specifications, product literature, and cost information
options.D: Specifications, product literature, and drawing details
options.E: Specifications, cost information, and PPDs
options.F: Product literature, cost information, and drawing sheets

questions.explanation: MasterFormat serves as one shared classification for specifications, product literature, and cost information. Drawing details are filed by UniFormat, since most details show several materials that MasterFormat would place in different sections, PPDs are organized by UniFormat as well, and the order of drawing sheets comes from the Uniform Drawing System, not MasterFormat.

questions.question: MasterFormat's single classification system for specifications, product literature, and cost information is based on work results or on what else?

options.A: Building systems and assemblies
options.B: Functional elements of a facility
options.C: Products and their constituent materials
options.D: Construction practices
options.E: Construction trades and subcontracts
options.F: Project phases and life cycle stages

questions.explanation: MasterFormat classifies information by work results or construction practices. Systems and assemblies, or functional elements, are the basis of UniFormat; products, materials, and phases each have their own OmniClass tables; and MasterFormat sections are expressly not meant to correspond to a single trade or subcontract.

questions.question: A specifier's office master contains several hundred sections. For a small tenant renovation, which sections should be included in the project manual specifications?

options.A: Every master section, with unused ones marked 'Not Used'
options.B: Only those sections needed to meet the project requirements
options.C: All sections in each division that contains any project work
options.D: Every Level 2 section, so that the numbering stays continuous
options.E: All Division 01 sections, plus those for the work involved
options.F: Only the sections for work the contractor will self-perform

questions.explanation: A project manual carries a section only when the project's requirements call for it, so a small renovation uses a small selection from the master. Keeping unused sections, whole divisions, all of Division 01, or every Level 2 section adds bulk for nothing, because MasterFormat's fixed numbers let sections be left out without renumbering. Sections do not follow who performs the work, so self-performed work is not the test.

questions.question: Under SectionFormat, a specification section is intended to cover what scope?

options.A: The work of one trade or subcontractor
options.B: All requirements of one MasterFormat division
options.C: One portion of the project requirements
options.D: The work shown on one drawing discipline
options.E: All the work in one UniFormat element
options.F: All the work under one bid package

questions.explanation: Each section is meant to address one part of the project requirements, such as a material, product, system or assembly, with its installation and the administrative requirements that go with it. Divisions group related sections, so one section does not cover a whole division, and sections are not meant to line up with a single trade, a drawing discipline, a UniFormat element, or a bid package.

questions.question: A specifier must decide where to describe site-built assemblies and site-manufactured systems within a SectionFormat section. Which part includes them?

options.A: PART 3—EXECUTION, with installation or application
options.B: PART 2—PRODUCTS, with fabrications and mixes
options.C: PART 1—GENERAL, with the section's temporary requirements
options.D: PART 2—PRODUCTS, with systems and assemblies
options.E: PART 1—GENERAL, with the section's quality assurance
options.F: Division 01, with execution and closeout requirements

questions.explanation: PART 3—EXECUTION covers installation or application, preparation, and cleaning and protection after installation, and it is also where site-built assemblies and site-manufactured products and systems go. PART 2 covers products, fabrications, mixes, systems and assemblies to be incorporated into the work, PART 1 covers administrative, procedural and temporary requirements, and Division 01 is not part of the section at all.

questions.question: To make each section 'complete,' a specifier copies the full submittal procedures from Division 01 into PART 1 of every section. What is the best course of action?

options.A: Retain the copies, since sections are meant to stand alone in bidding
options.B: Retain the copies, but add an order-of-precedence clause in Division 01
options.C: Move the procedures from Division 01 into PART 3 of each affected section
options.D: Delete the copies; add only items that supplement Division 01
options.E: Move the procedures from Division 01 into the conditions of the contract
options.F: Delete Division 01 and keep the procedures in each section

questions.explanation: Sections work together with the rest of the documents and are not meant to stand alone, so PART 1 should not repeat what Division 01 already says; it should only supplement and coordinate with it. Duplicated text invites conflicts, which an order-of-precedence clause only papers over. Deleting Division 01 multiplies the duplication, PART 3 covers execution rather than procedures, and the conditions of the contract are not the place for detailed submittal procedures.

questions.question: A specifier must address a temporary requirement that applies only to the work of one section and is not covered in Division 01. Where is it described?

options.A: PART 3—EXECUTION, with preparatory actions
options.B: PART 1—GENERAL, as an extension of Division 01
options.C: PART 2—PRODUCTS, with the materials it needs
options.D: Division 01, in the temporary facilities and controls section
options.E: The supplementary conditions, as a change to the general conditions
options.F: The drawings, in a general note on the affected sheet

questions.explanation: PART 1—GENERAL holds the administrative, procedural and temporary requirements that apply only to the section, extending the subjects Division 01 covers for the whole project. Division 01 itself is for project-wide temporary facilities and controls, PART 3 covers installation and preparation, PART 2 covers products, the supplementary conditions modify the general conditions, and drawings are not where such requirements are written.

questions.question: A specifications manager argues that adopting PageFormat in the office master is purely cosmetic because SectionFormat already governs content. Which benefit comes specifically from PageFormat's uniform arrangement of text on the page?

options.A: It eases preparation, review, and publication and saves users time searching for information
options.B: It establishes the three-part structure that organizes text consistently within each section
options.C: It assigns the numbers and titles that locate each section within the project manual
options.D: It fixes the sequence of standard article titles under PART 1, PART 2, and PART 3
options.E: It sets the writing style and grammar rules for each paragraph
options.F: It ties each section's text to the matching UniFormat element

questions.explanation: A uniform page layout makes sections easier to prepare, review and publish, and readers find information faster. The three-part structure and the order of article titles come from SectionFormat, section numbers and titles come from MasterFormat, writing style is a matter of specification language rather than page layout, and linking text to UniFormat elements is not a PageFormat function.

questions.question: A specifier requires the flooring installer to test the in-place concrete slab for moisture vapor emission and alkalinity immediately before installing sheet vinyl. Following the SectionFormat outline, where does this preinstallation testing requirement belong?

options.A: PART 1, under the Quality Assurance article with Preconstruction Testing
options.B: PART 1, under the Administrative Requirements article with Preinstallation Meetings
options.C: PART 3, under the Examination article with Verification of Conditions
options.D: PART 3, under the Preparation article with Surface Preparation
options.E: PART 2, under the Source Quality Control article with Tests and Inspections
options.F: PART 3, under the Field Quality Control article with Field Tests and Inspections

questions.explanation: SectionFormat lists Preinstallation Testing in PART 3 under EXAMINATION, beside Verification of Conditions, and its standard example is testing a slab for vapor emission and alkalinity before a non-breathable floor finish goes down. Preconstruction Testing in PART 1 qualifies products in advance, Source Quality Control covers testing at the plant, Field Quality Control tests the installed work, and Surface Preparation readies the substrate rather than testing it.

questions.question: A specification calls for concrete mixed at 4 parts coarse aggregate to 2 parts fine aggregate to 1 part cement, with a water-cement ratio of 0.5. The contractor supplies concrete exactly as proportioned, but it does not withstand a 3000 psi load. Who is responsible for the shortfall?

options.A: The contractor, because 3000 psi strength is implied by the specified mix
options.B: The A/E, because it assumes the burden of performance under this method
options.C: The concrete supplier, because it furnished the mix that failed to perform
options.D: The contractor and A/E jointly, because the strength was implied but unstated
options.E: The testing agency, because it should have tested the mix before placement
options.F: The contractor, because it is responsible for construction means and methods

questions.explanation: Specifying the mix proportions is descriptive specifying: the 3000 psi strength is only implied, never stated, so a contractor who followed the mix cannot be held to it, and the A/E carries the burden of performance. The supplier and testing agency are not bound by an unstated strength, means and methods do not cover a mix the A/E prescribed, and no joint responsibility applies.

questions.question: A state agency's enabling statute prohibits naming manufacturers in its construction specifications, and no adequate industry reference standard exists for a custom-fabricated lobby screen. Which specifying method may be the only logical choice?

options.A: Reference standard specifying, citing the nearest related industry standard
options.B: Open proprietary specifying, naming three products followed by 'or equal'
options.C: Closed proprietary specifying, naming the single product that suits the design
options.D: Descriptive specifying, detailing the required properties and workmanship
options.E: A cash allowance, leaving selection of the screen to the owner
options.F: A federal specification, citing the closest FED-STD document

questions.explanation: When the law bars naming products and no adequate reference standard exists, a descriptive specification may be the only logical choice. Both proprietary methods name products, which the statute forbids, and reference standards, including federal specifications and standards, fail because none fits the work. A cash allowance only postpones a decision; it does not specify a custom screen.

questions.question: A senior specifier notes that her firm now writes far fewer descriptive specifications than it did 30 years ago. Which explanation for this trend does industry guidance give?

options.A: Projects have become more complex, and better reference standards are now available
options.B: Public owners now prohibit descriptive text, and proprietary names are now preferred
options.C: Descriptive text shifts performance risk to contractors, who now decline to accept it
options.D: Building codes now mandate performance criteria for most products and assemblies
options.E: Manufacturers' guide specifications have replaced descriptive text
options.F: Design-build delivery has replaced most design-bid-build work

questions.explanation: Descriptive specifying, once widely preferred, is used less often now that projects are more complex and better reference standards exist; writing it is also slow and tedious. It leaves the performance burden with the A/E rather than contractors, it remains the logical choice where proprietary names are prohibited, and guide specifications, design-build, and code mandates are not the reasons given for the decline.

questions.question: While preparing a descriptive specification for a commodity shelf bracket, a specifier finds that catalog information fully describes the product and that a manufacturer's product certification covers every required property. Following the fifth step in preparing descriptive specifications, which submittal and testing requirements should the section include?

options.A: Shop drawings and a product certification, with no laboratory tests
options.B: Product data and a product certification, with no shop drawings or tests
options.C: Product data and independent laboratory tests, with no shop drawings
options.D: Shop drawings, product data, and independent laboratory tests of each property
options.E: Product data, a product certification, and a mock-up of the installed bracket
options.F: Samples and independent laboratory tests, with no product data

questions.explanation: The fifth step is to require only the submittals, tests and procedures needed to make sure acceptable products are provided: no extensive shop drawings when catalog data is adequate, and no tests when a product certification is enough. Here product data and a certification cover everything, so shop drawings, laboratory tests, samples, or a mock-up add cost without adding assurance.

questions.question: Drafting a descriptive specification for a door closer, a specifier combines the slimmest arm profile from one manufacturer, the highest cycle rating from a second, and the widest backcheck adjustment from a third. Which risk does industry guidance warn this practice creates?

options.A: The section becomes proprietary because three manufacturers are implied
options.B: The section may describe a product that does not actually exist
options.C: The A/E shifts the burden of performance onto the hardware supplier
options.D: The section may require tests where a product certification would suffice
options.E: The section turns into a performance specification by default
options.F: The section conflicts with the closer's reference standard

questions.explanation: Selecting the best features from several manufacturers' products can produce a description of a product that does not exist, which is the warning in the fourth step of preparing descriptive specifications. Implying several sources does not make the section proprietary, describing features does not make it a performance specification, the A/E keeps the burden of performance, and excess testing is a separate fifth-step issue.

questions.question: A specifier writes a descriptive specification for a shelf support assembly. Which information would be shown on the drawings rather than in the specification?

options.A: Finish of the standards and the type of mounting screws
options.B: Maximum spacing of mounting screws and slot spacing
options.C: Bracket depth at the butt and at the tip
options.D: Location, length, and spacing of the supports
options.E: Projection of the standards from the finished surface
options.F: Width of the shelves the brackets must support

questions.explanation: In a descriptive specification for shelving, the drawings show where the supports go, how long they are, and how far apart they are spaced, because the third step is deciding which features to specify and which to show. The written section covers the properties of the parts: projection and finish of the standards, screw size, type and spacing, slot spacing, shelf width, and bracket depths.

questions.question: A performance specification for an operable partition states the required sound transmission class but provides no means to measure, test, or evaluate whether the installed partition achieves it. Which element of a complete performance specification is deficient?

options.A: A statement of the required results
options.B: Freedom from unnecessary limitations on methods
options.C: Criteria for verifying compliance
options.D: A description of the means of achieving results
options.E: A list of acceptable manufacturers and products
options.F: A warranty covering the installed performance

questions.explanation: A performance specification states the required results, gives criteria for verifying that they are met, and avoids unnecessary limits on methods. The verification criteria must be measurable, testable, or otherwise assurable, and that is what is missing. The result (the STC rating) is stated and nothing limits methods; describing the means, listing products, or adding a warranty are not elements of a performance specification.

questions.question: A design-build RFP's performance specification for a building envelope omits several of the end results the owner actually expects. What is the principal risk of this incomplete statement of required results?

options.A: Requirements that no manufacturer can meet, making the work unachievable
options.B: Loss of quality control over materials, equipment, and workmanship
options.C: Transfer of the burden of performance from the contractor back to the A/E
options.D: Restriction of competition to the single product that the A/E had in mind
options.E: Excessive testing that adds cost without assurance
options.F: Duplication of requirements already in Division 01

questions.explanation: A performance specification must spell out every end result the owner wants; leaving some out can cost the owner much of its control over the quality of materials, equipment and workmanship. Unachievable criteria, burden shifting, restricted competition, over-testing and duplicated text are other drafting problems, not the consequence of omitting required results.

questions.question: A performance specification for a curtain wall requires that water penetration resistance be verified after the building has been occupied through one full rainy season. A reviewer objects that performance criteria must be verified before installation. How should the specifier respond?

options.A: Keep it; measurement and testing may occur after a period of service
options.B: Revise it; measurement and testing must occur before production
options.C: Revise it; measurement and testing must occur at the time of production
options.D: Keep it, but only if testing is also performed in place at the site
options.E: Revise it; compliance must be shown by a mock-up before installation
options.F: Keep it, but only if the warranty covers the same rainy season

questions.explanation: Performance criteria may be checked ahead of production, while the product is being made, on the site after installation, or once the work has been in service for a while, so testing after a rainy season of occupancy is acceptable as written. The revise options wrongly limit verification to one early stage, and nothing requires pairing it with site testing or with a matching warranty.

questions.question: A specifier knows exactly which ceiling-hanger wire she wants and plans to write a full set of performance criteria derived from that wire's properties so that bidders will provide it. What is the better course?

options.A: Write the criteria anyway, since performance language invites innovation
options.B: Delete the product name and list its catalog properties as the criteria
options.C: Use a systems approach and leave the hanger design to the contractor
options.D: Describe the wire directly, stating its gage, coating, and annealing
options.E: Make the hanger a delegated design submittal by the contractor
options.F: Specify the hanger only as 'non-sag' and stop there

questions.explanation: When the exact item is already known, reverse-engineering performance criteria from it takes far more effort and gets nothing better than a descriptive or proprietary specification; asking for 10-gage galvanized, annealed steel wire is much simpler. Listing catalog properties without a name is still a disguised product description, delegating the design or using a systems approach abandons the known product, and 'non-sag' alone would not get her that wire.

questions.question: An owner intends to make performance specifying the primary mode of design and contracting for a new transit maintenance facility. What should the project team anticipate?

options.A: Standard contract documents, with simpler procedures and fewer participants
options.B: Specialized contract documents, with complex procedures and many participants
options.C: Standard contract documents, with complex procedures and many participants
options.D: Specialized contract documents, with simpler procedures and fewer participants
options.E: Specialized contract documents, with complex procedures and fewer participants
options.F: Specialized contract documents, with simpler procedures and many participants

questions.explanation: When a project relies mainly on performance specifying for design and contracting, it often needs specialized contract documents, its contract procedures grow more complex, and many kinds of participants take part. Every other combination gets at least one of the three wrong: standard documents, simpler procedures, or fewer participants.

questions.question: Who should determine a project's suitability for performance specifying, and at what point?

options.A: The A/E alone, during the construction documents phase
options.B: The owner and the A/E, early in the planning process
options.C: The owner and the contractor, during the procurement phase
options.D: The A/E and the AHJ, during design development review
options.E: The owner and the CM at risk, during preconstruction services
options.F: The A/E and its consultants, during schematic design

questions.explanation: The owner and the A/E should decide together, early in planning, whether the project suits performance specifying, because the decision rests on the owner's needs and shapes the whole design and contracting approach. Waiting for construction documents, procurement, or design development is too late, and leaving out the owner, or handing the decision to a contractor, CM, or AHJ, misses who must make it.
