questions.question: An owner's main concern is speed: a data center must open within 14 months. The owner wants proposers to offer any proven, commercially available modular power system that meets stated capacities. Which recognized owner need for performance specifying does this best reflect?

options.A: To utilize technology not yet standardized within the industry
options.B: To develop new technology through the project's procurement
options.C: To expedite construction and access a wide range of existing options
options.D: To delegate technical design responsibility to industry specialists
options.E: To reduce the A/E's design effort and fees
options.F: To keep the A/E responsible for system performance

questions.explanation: One owner need that makes performance specifying feasible is speeding up construction while drawing on the broad range of options that existing technologies and systems offer, which matches a tight schedule and proven, off-the-shelf systems. Unstandardized or new technology does not fit proven products, the owner is choosing among existing systems rather than delegating design, and lower fees or keeping the performance burden on the A/E are not recognized reasons.

questions.question: A design architect tells the owner that performance specifying is all-or-nothing: either every section is performance-based or none is. Which statement corrects this?

options.A: Performance specifying is limited to complete systems and never single attributes
options.B: Performance specifying applies only where codes have adopted performance criteria
options.C: Performance specifying is reserved for projects using design-build delivery
options.D: Performance specifying can extend from a single attribute to an entire project
options.E: Performance specifying cannot be combined with descriptive sections
options.F: Performance specifying is limited to products lacking reference standards

questions.explanation: Performance specifying is scalable: it can be applied to one attribute, a product, a subsystem, or a whole project, with many levels in between. It can be combined with descriptive specifying in the same project, and it is not confined to complete systems, to code-adopted criteria, to products without standards, or to design-build delivery, even though the broadest levels are mostly used there.

questions.question: A specifier cites an industry-accepted standard for gypsum board rather than writing detailed product requirements. What does referencing the standard establish, and what does it provide?

options.A: Minimum requirements, giving greater confidence in the outcome of its use
options.B: Maximum requirements, limiting the contractor's liability to the standard
options.C: Exact requirements, eliminating the need to review related submittals
options.D: Recommended practices, which the contractor may adopt at its option
options.E: Minimum requirements, shifting design responsibility to the manufacturer
options.F: Average industry requirements, ensuring the lowest available price

questions.explanation: Citing an industry-accepted standard sets minimum requirements for the material, product or installation, which gives the specifier more confidence in how the work will turn out. A standard does not set maximums or exact limits, does not shift design responsibility or guarantee a low price, still has to be enforced through submittal review, and once cited it is mandatory, not optional.

questions.question: A specifier is deciding whether to cite an industry-accepted standard for vinyl composition tile or to write out detailed product requirements in the section. Which observation about reference standard specifying supports citing the standard?

options.A: Reference standards set maximum values, which limits the contractor's liability
options.B: Citing a standard avoids duplication and contradiction with other documents
options.C: Many manufacturers know the standards that shape their products' development
options.D: AHJs enforce the same edition of each standard, which simplifies compliance
options.E: Citing a standard transfers the burden of performance to the AHJ
options.F: Reference standards rarely change, so citations seldom need review

questions.explanation: Many manufacturers already know the standards that guide how their products are developed, so citing one gives familiar minimum requirements and more confidence in the result. Standards usually set minimums, not maximums; they must be checked to avoid duplication and contradiction; they are revised periodically, so editions matter; and AHJs may adopt different editions and do not take on the performance burden.

questions.question: A section's References article lists 'ASTM International (ASTM) C150/C150M, Standard Specification for Portland Cement,' and the entire standard applies to the work. Judged against the elements of a complete reference standard designation, what is missing?

options.A: A citation of the applicable requirements within the standard
options.B: The website address where the standard may be purchased
options.C: The mailing address of the issuing organization
options.D: The date of issue of the standard
options.E: The name of the manufacturer whose product complies
options.F: The edition of the building code that adopts it

questions.explanation: A complete designation gives the issuing organization's name, the standard's number, its title, its date of issue, and a citation of the applicable requirements when only part of the standard applies. Here the whole standard applies, so no citation is needed, and only the date of issue is missing. Websites, addresses, manufacturer names, and code editions are not elements of the designation.

questions.question: Rather than spelling out each standards-issuing organization's name at first mention in every section, a specifier wants one central place in the project manual that defines those abbreviations and can also list the organizations' addresses. Where does this belong?

options.A: Division 01, Section 01 42 00—References
options.B: Division 01, Section 01 41 00—Regulatory Requirements
options.C: Division 01, Section 01 43 00—Quality Assurance
options.D: Division 00, Document 00 21 13—Instructions to Bidders
options.E: Division 01, Section 01 33 00—Submittal Procedures
options.F: Division 00, Document 00 72 00—General Conditions

questions.explanation: Instead of spelling out each organization's name with its abbreviation at first mention in every section, a project manual can define all reference standard abbreviations once in Section 01 42 00—References, which can also list the organizations' addresses. Regulatory requirements, quality assurance, submittal procedures, the instructions to bidders, and the general conditions are not where these definitions go.

questions.question: While updating the office master, a specifier uses the standards organizations' current catalogs to replace each dated reference with the year of the latest edition. What must the A/E also do before changing these publication dates?

options.A: Obtain the contractor's agreement to cite the newer editions
options.B: Obtain the owner's written approval of each newer edition
options.C: Move the dated designations from PART 1 into Division 01
options.D: Review the changes made to each standard in the new edition
options.E: Notify the AHJ of each newer edition adopted
options.F: Issue the revised dates to bidders by addendum

questions.explanation: Standards are revised periodically, and when dates are listed it is the A/E's job to identify the right edition, so a year should not be updated until the changes in the new edition have been reviewed. Contractor agreement, owner approval, and AHJ notice play no part, an office master is not issued to bidders by addendum, and dated designations stay in the PART 1 References article.

questions.question: A project manual lists reference standards without dates. To avoid contradictions among editions, a statement in Section 01 42 00 is recommended that fixes the governing date as the one in effect as of:

options.A: The date of the owner-contractor agreement, or as adopted by the AHJs
options.B: The date of the notice to proceed, or as accepted by the A/E
options.C: The date of receipt of bids, or as adopted by the AHJs
options.D: The date the specifications were issued, or the latest edition
options.E: The date of substantial completion, or as adopted by the AHJs
options.F: The date of the building permit, or as accepted by the owner

questions.explanation: When standards are listed without dates, the recommended statement in Section 01 42 00 makes the governing edition the one in effect on the date bids are received, or the edition adopted by the authorities having jurisdiction. The agreement date, notice to proceed, permit date, issue date, and substantial completion are other milestones, and A/E or owner acceptance is not part of the statement.

questions.question: Under the two approaches to dating reference standards, who determines the applicable edition when dates are listed, and who becomes responsible for checking compliance when standards are undated and Section 01 42 00 carries the recommended statement?

options.A: The A/E when dates are listed; the contractor when undated
options.B: The contractor when dates are listed; the A/E when undated
options.C: The A/E when dates are listed; the AHJ when undated
options.D: The AHJ when dates are listed; the contractor when undated
options.E: The owner when dates are listed; the contractor when undated
options.F: The A/E when dates are listed; the owner when undated

questions.explanation: Listing dates makes the A/E responsible for identifying the applicable edition. Leaving dates out and adding the recommended Section 01 42 00 statement (the edition in effect when bids are received, or as adopted by the authorities) makes the contractor responsible for checking compliance. The owner and the AHJ take on neither duty, although an AHJ may adopt particular editions.

questions.question: A specifier wants to cite a tentative standard for a new anchor test method because it reflects the sponsoring organization's latest practice. What is the principal concern with doing so?

options.A: It has not yet been approved by the sponsoring organization
options.B: It is unofficial, and AHJs usually do not accept it
options.C: It reflects practices the final standard will likely supersede
options.D: It must be quoted in full because it is not yet published
options.E: It shifts the burden of performance to the sponsoring organization
options.F: It must be listed in Division 00 instead of in PART 1

questions.explanation: A tentative standard is unofficial, and authorities having jurisdiction usually will not accept it, so A/Es should cite one only with caution. It has already been approved by the sponsoring organization and is awaiting final approval by its members, and it usually reflects that organization's latest practice. Nothing requires quoting it in full, moving it to Division 00, or making the sponsor responsible for performance.

questions.question: A specifier references ASTM C1193 for sealant joints and is deciding how to handle the portions of that standard that matter most on this project. Which approach follows industry guidance?

options.A: Quote the clauses most pertinent to the work so bidders see them
options.B: Cite specific clauses that bidders commonly overlook, for emphasis
options.C: Cite a specific clause only where the specification modifies that clause
options.D: Reproduce pertinent clauses verbatim so bidders need not buy the standard
options.E: Cite every clause of the standard so that none is overlooked
options.F: Bind a full copy of the standard into the project manual

questions.explanation: Cite an individual clause of a referenced standard only where the specification changes what that clause requires. Quoting or reproducing selected passages risks errors and suggests that only the quoted text applies, singling out clauses for emphasis or listing every clause causes similar confusion, and binding in the full text is discouraged because standards are usually copyrighted; referencing the designation is enough.

questions.question: After reference standards are specified, conformance is usually enforced by reviewing required submittals such as shop drawings, samples, product literature, and test reports, along with periodic visits to the site by whom?

options.A: Field representatives sent by the standards-issuing organizations
options.B: Building inspectors employed by the authorities having jurisdiction
options.C: The contractor's quality control manager and independent testing agency
options.D: Construction contract administrators or knowledgeable design team members
options.E: The manufacturers' technical representatives for each product
options.F: Representatives of the surety that issued the performance bond

questions.explanation: Standards are enforced through submittal review plus periodic site observation by construction contract administrators or knowledgeable members of the design team. Standards organizations do not observe projects, AHJ inspectors enforce codes rather than the specification, and the contractor's quality control staff, testing agencies, manufacturers' representatives, and sureties are not the parties who check conformance on the owner's behalf.

questions.question: A section names three acceptable manufacturers for a fire alarm control panel and states that no other products will be considered and that bids must be based on one of those named. How does industry guidance classify this specification?

options.A: Closed proprietary, because substitutions are not allowed
options.B: Open proprietary, because more than one product is named
options.C: Non-restrictive, because at least three products are named
options.D: Open proprietary, because bidders may choose among products
options.E: Descriptive, because no single product is required
options.F: Performance, because the bidder selects the product

questions.explanation: What separates closed from open proprietary specifying is the treatment of substitutions. A closed specification may name one product or several options, but no substitutes are considered and bids must use a named product. Naming several products does not make it open or non-restrictive, and naming brands rules out descriptive and performance specifying, which do not name products.

questions.question: An owner's project manager asks why the A/E chose to proprietary-specify the curtain wall system. Which reason does industry guidance list as an advantage of proprietary specifications?

options.A: The contractor's prior experience with the named product is assured
options.B: The named product's continued availability through construction is assured
options.C: More detailed drawings can be prepared from the manufacturer's precise data
options.D: Errors in model and product designations are eliminated from the documents
options.E: Competition among manufacturers for the product is increased
options.F: No manufacturer or product is favored over the others

questions.explanation: One advantage of proprietary specifying is that the A/E can produce more detailed and complete drawings from the precise data of the selected manufacturer. The other choices contradict known drawbacks: competition is reduced, some manufacturers are favored, the contractor may have little or bad experience with the product, it may become unavailable, and model or product designations can be specified in error.

questions.question: On a closed proprietary specification naming optional products, how does industry guidance say control of products and substitutions is accomplished?

options.A: By the instructions for procurement, cross-referencing Section 01 42 00
options.B: By the instructions for procurement, cross-referencing Section 01 25 13
options.C: By the supplementary conditions, cross-referencing Section 01 25 13
options.D: By the supplementary conditions, cross-referencing Section 01 42 00
options.E: By the instructions for procurement, cross-referencing Section 01 33 00
options.F: By the agreement form, cross-referencing Section 01 25 13

questions.explanation: In a closed proprietary specification, the instructions for procurement control products and substitutions by referring bidders to Section 01 25 13, which holds the product substitution procedures. Section 01 42 00 covers references and Section 01 33 00 covers submittals, not substitutions, and the supplementary conditions or the agreement are not where this control is placed.

questions.question: A closed proprietary specification names four acceptable manufacturers for toilet compartments, and no substitutes will be considered. The A/E wants to know promptly which of the four products the successful bidder priced. What may the specifications require?

options.A: A substitution request identifying the product within 10 days of award
options.B: A product selection list at bid time or within a few days after opening
options.C: Identification of the product in the first shop drawing submittal after award
options.D: A/E selection among the named products at the preconstruction conference
options.E: Identification of the product in the schedule of values after award
options.F: Product data for all four named products before the bid opening

questions.explanation: With optional products, the specifications can require the successful contractor to submit a product selection list with the bid or within a few days after bids are opened, so the A/E knows early which product was priced. A substitution request does not fit because no substitutes are considered, and waiting for shop drawings or the schedule of values, having the A/E choose, or requiring data on every option does not answer the question promptly.

questions.question: On a project using controlled substitutions, the A/E sets the deadline for bidders' substitution requests and will issue written acceptances to all bidders by addendum. At least how much time should be allowed between that deadline and publication of the addendum?

options.A: Three days
options.B: Five days
options.C: Seven days
options.D: Ten days
options.E: Two days
options.F: Fourteen days

questions.explanation: The A/E sets the deadline for substitution requests, but at least three days should separate that deadline from publication of the addendum so each request can be properly considered and the written acceptances issued to all bidders. Two days falls short of that minimum, and five, seven, ten or fourteen days are not the stated minimum interval.

questions.question: During bidding, (1) a roofer asks to replace the specified membrane with another manufacturer's product, and (2) the bid form requests an added price for a named upgraded membrane. Using standard terminology, what are items (1) and (2)?

options.A: (1) an alternate; (2) a substitute
options.B: (1) an alternate; (2) an alternate
options.C: (1) a substitute; (2) a substitute
options.D: (1) a substitute; (2) an alternate
options.E: (1) a substitute; (2) an allowance
options.F: (1) a product option; (2) an alternate

questions.explanation: The terms are often misused. A substitute is a product someone asks to use in place of the specified one, so the roofer's request is a substitute; an alternate is named in the documents with a separate price requested on the bid form, so the priced upgrade is an alternate. An allowance is a sum carried for work not yet defined, and product options are choices the specification already allows.

questions.question: For a hospital's emergency power transfer switches, the owner values assured performance far above competitive pricing. Which proprietary approach best fits this item?

options.A: Open proprietary with controlled substitutions under Section 01 25 13
options.B: Closed proprietary that prohibits substitutions entirely
options.C: Open proprietary that invites proposed substitutions with bid prices
options.D: Three named products, each followed by 'or equal' to admit equals
options.E: Open proprietary with requested alternates priced on the bid form
options.F: Open proprietary allowing substitutions after contract award

questions.explanation: Accepting substitutions opens the project to unknown or inferior products, so for an item in a vital system a proprietary specification that prohibits substitutions entirely may be called for. Controlled or proposed substitutions, substitutions after award, requested alternates, and 'or equal' language all admit other products, which suits projects where competition and low cost matter more than assured performance.

questions.question: A firm on a compressed design schedule wants to minimize its own design and specifying effort for interior finishes. Which method is best from that standpoint, and why?

options.A: Open proprietary, because bidders carry the burden of proving comparability
options.B: Open proprietary, because A/E workload falls as bidders' choices increase
options.C: Closed proprietary, because one named product speeds the documents
options.D: Descriptive, because no product research is needed before writing
options.E: Performance, because the contractor completes the design
options.F: Reference standard, because one citation replaces product research

questions.explanation: For keeping design and specifying effort to a minimum, closed proprietary is best: with one named product per application, drawings and specifications can be finished quickly and precisely without accommodating options. Open methods add A/E work in proportion to the bidders' choices, descriptive specifying starts with product research, performance sections take considerable effort to write, and standards still need careful review.

questions.question: An owner insists that substitutions be allowed on a school project to get the lowest material costs. The A/E worries that apparent savings may be lost to high maintenance and replacement costs. What should the A/E do?

options.A: Word the procurement documents to give a definite, controllable review method
options.B: Prohibit all substitutions, since cost must never outweigh assured performance
options.C: Append 'or equal' after every product name to signal substitutions are allowed
options.D: Let the contractor approve substitutions to speed the procurement process
options.E: Have the owner approve each substitution without A/E review
options.F: Require an extended warranty to cover future maintenance costs

questions.explanation: Allowing substitutions makes competition keenest and lowers material cost, but it also lets in lesser products whose savings can vanish through later maintenance and replacement. The answer is for the A/E to write the procurement documents so that there is a clear, controllable way to review and approve what is accepted as a substitute. Prohibiting substitutions ignores the owner's goal, repeated 'or equal' is awkward, and approval should stay with the A/E rather than the contractor or owner alone.

questions.question: For a public project, a specifier deletes a manufacturer's name and lists that product's salient qualities verbatim from its literature as the requirements, giving no ranges. How does industry guidance characterize the result?

options.A: A non-restrictive performance specification, since no name appears
options.B: An open proprietary specification, since substitutions are not barred
options.C: A fully proprietary, closed specification despite the missing name
options.D: A descriptive specification that is suitable for most public work
options.E: A reference standard specification, since published data is cited
options.F: An 'or equal' specification, since omitting the name implies equals

questions.explanation: This is a proprietary specification disguised as a performance specification. Because the copied properties give no ranges of characteristics or performance, only the original product can comply, so the result is a fully proprietary, closed specification that is unsuitable for a non-restrictive project. Removing the name does not make it non-restrictive, open, or an acceptable descriptive specification, and manufacturer literature is not a reference standard.

questions.question: To convert a closed proprietary specification into a non-restrictive one for a public agency, what does industry guidance say such agencies usually require?

options.A: At least three brand names plus 'or equal,' with salient characteristics described
options.B: At least two brand names plus 'or equal,' with salient characteristics described
options.C: At least three brand names plus 'or equal,' with an applicable reference standard cited
options.D: At least two brand names plus 'or equal,' with an applicable reference standard cited
options.E: At least one brand name plus 'or equal,' with salient characteristics described
options.F: At least five brand names, with no 'or equal' wording required

questions.explanation: Public agencies usually want no fewer than three named brands followed by 'or equal,' together with a description of the item's salient characteristics so there is a basis for judging whether another product is equal. One or two names is too few, five names without 'or equal' still excludes equals, and a cited reference standard is not the basis named for judging equality.

questions.question: On a federally assisted project, a specifier writes a performance specification for laboratory casework that names no manufacturer, but only one manufacturer's product can meet the combined criteria. How should this specification be characterized?

options.A: Non-restrictive, because no proprietary name appears in it
options.B: Non-restrictive, because performance methods are inherently open
options.C: Open proprietary, because other products may still be proposed
options.D: Restrictive, even though no proprietary name appears in it
options.E: Non-restrictive, provided an 'or equal' clause is added
options.F: Descriptive, because it lists the features of one product

questions.explanation: Descriptive and performance specifications lend themselves to non-restrictive specifying, but only if several manufacturers or suppliers can meet the requirements; if only one can, the specification is restrictive even though no proprietary name appears. Leaving out names, using performance language, or adding 'or equal' does not cure that, and a section stating performance criteria is not descriptive.

questions.question: An owner's representative believes performance specifying suits only whole-building design-build procurements. What are the narrowest and broadest scales to which performance specifying can be extended?

options.A: From a single product up to a complete system or assembly
options.B: From a single attribute up to an entire project
options.C: From a single component up to one complete specification section
options.D: From one specification section up to an entire division
options.E: From a single section up to an entire project
options.F: From a single attribute up to one complete assembly

questions.explanation: Performance specifying is scalable from one attribute, such as a non-sag hanger, all the way to an entire project, with many variations in between. The other options get one or both endpoints wrong, stopping at an assembly, a section, or a division, or starting at a product, component, or section, and whole-building design-build is only the broad end of the range.

questions.question: A specifier wants bidders to be free to offer different solutions, provided each one meets the same requirements. Which feature of performance specifying provides this flexibility?

options.A: Allowing substitution requests after the contract is awarded
options.B: Naming several acceptable manufacturers for each product
options.C: Incorporating a recognized industry standard by reference
options.D: Defining the end result that the work must achieve
options.E: Requesting alternate prices on the bid form
options.F: Specifying the installation means and methods

questions.explanation: Because a performance specification states the end result rather than the means, it leaves room for different solutions as long as each meets the same requirements. Substitution procedures, multiple named manufacturers, reference standards, and bid alternates are separate devices, and prescribing means and methods is the opposite of performance specifying.

questions.question: A firm's newest specifier has read about performance specifying and is about to write a complete performance-based section. Which caution applies to this step?

options.A: Putting it into an entire section can be hard for those with little experience
options.B: Describing it is the hard part; putting it into a section is straightforward
options.C: It can be applied to individual attributes but never to an entire section
options.D: A complete performance section may be written only for a design-build contract
options.E: A full performance section is quicker to write than a descriptive one
options.F: A full performance section must also name three acceptable products

questions.explanation: Performance specifying is easy to describe but can be hard to put into an actual document, such as an entire section, for someone with little experience. The reversed statement and the claim that it is quicker than descriptive writing miss that caution; it can extend to an entire project, it is not limited to design-build, and naming products is not part of it.

questions.question: When performance specifying is used for complete construction systems and assemblies, what does industry guidance identify as a primary advantage?

options.A: Attracting research-and-development expertise and resources to create new products
options.B: Delegating final design and construction tasks to a design-builder entity
options.C: Using available products and systems for conventional project requirements
options.D: Describing emerging systems the A/E is not familiar enough with to detail
options.E: Bringing the systems under AHJ licensure and regulation
options.F: Assuring that one specific manufacturer's system is installed

questions.explanation: When performance specifying covers complete systems and assemblies, its primary advantage is putting available products and systems to work on conventional project requirements, which can speed construction and increase competition. Attracting research and development belongs to developing new technology, delegating to a design-builder to delegating responsibilities, and unfamiliar emerging systems to non-standard technologies; possible AHJ licensure is a caution, and securing one manufacturer is proprietary specifying.

questions.question: A school district planning a modest classroom addition wants to performance specify the roofing and HVAC using readily available systems, but its board believes performance specifying is reserved for large programs. Which response is consistent with industry guidance?

options.A: Relying on existing technology makes it practical even for smaller projects
options.B: It is generally limited to large public agencies with high construction volume
options.C: It is practical for a small project only when the entire project is included
options.D: It is practical for a small project only under design-build project delivery
options.E: It is practical for a small project only for a single attribute
options.F: It requires the district to fund prototype tests beforehand

questions.explanation: Because it relies on existing technology, performance specifying of available systems is practical even on smaller projects, for all or part of the work. The limitation to large, high-volume owners applies to developing new technology, where prototype tests and development costs fall on the owner. No whole-project, single-attribute, or design-build condition applies to a small project.

questions.question: A specifier intends to performance specify an entire building enclosure assembly that will require specialized engineering and performance-based criteria. What does industry guidance note about this level of performance specifying?

options.A: It must be limited to portions of a project, not complete assemblies
options.B: It requires the owner to fund prototype tests before solicitation
options.C: It is feasible only for owners with in-house engineering departments
options.D: It may be subject to licensure and regulation by the AHJs
options.E: It removes the need for the A/E to review the submittals
options.F: It must be procured as a separate prime contract

questions.explanation: Specifying an entire system or assembly by performance may call for specialized engineering and performance-based criteria, and at that level the work can fall under AHJ licensing and regulation. Performance specifying does apply to complete assemblies, prototype-test expense belongs to developing new technology, and nothing requires in-house engineers, a separate prime contract, or the end of submittal review.

questions.question: An A/E must specify a building monitoring system. The system is not entirely new, but it has not yet evolved into settled configurations, and no alternatives are similar enough to describe without excluding other variations. Under which performance specifying context does this fall?

options.A: Developing new technology
options.B: Utilizing non-standard technologies
options.C: Construction systems and assemblies
options.D: Delegating responsibilities
options.E: Delegated design of engineered components
options.F: Expediting construction with complete systems

questions.explanation: Utilizing non-standard technologies covers products that have come out of research and development but have not settled into standard configurations, so no alternatives are similar enough to describe without excluding other variations; building monitoring systems are a typical example. Developing new technology applies when nothing available suits the owner, while systems and assemblies, delegated design, delegated responsibilities, and expediting construction all involve established products.

questions.question: Sustainable design certifications are increasing the need for alternatives to traditional construction. LEED is the certification usually cited for structures; which certification is cited for infrastructure?

options.A: Green Globes
options.B: WELL Building Standard
options.C: Envision
options.D: Living Building Challenge
options.E: Energy Star
options.F: CHPS (Collaborative for High Performance Schools)

questions.explanation: Envision is the sustainability rating system for infrastructure, paired with LEED (Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design) for buildings and other structures, and both increase the demand for non-traditional solutions. Green Globes, WELL, the Living Building Challenge, and CHPS are rating systems for buildings, and Energy Star is a source of product and energy information, not the infrastructure certification.

questions.question: Which group does industry guidance give as examples of products and systems whose stage of development may leave no alternatives similar enough to specify descriptively?

options.A: Alternative energy, environmental control, building monitoring, and data systems
options.B: Wood or metal trusses, precast concrete, and certain types of foundation systems
options.C: New materials made from recycled pre-consumer and post-consumer waste streams
options.D: Fire sprinkler systems, curtain walls, and sophisticated exterior cladding systems
options.E: Gypsum board partitions, acoustical ceilings, and resilient flooring
options.F: Roofing, HVAC, and other readily available building systems

questions.explanation: Products such as alternative energy, environmental control, building monitoring, and data and communication systems are still developing, so no alternatives are similar enough to describe without excluding other variations. Sprinklers, curtain walls, and complex cladding are typical delegated-design items, recycled-content materials fall under developing new technology, and common finishes and readily available systems are established products.

questions.question: A specifier's office master roofing section was written for conventional membrane roofs, but the project now includes a green roof to support a LEED goal. What point does the green roof example illustrate?

options.A: Green roofs are entirely new technology that must be prototype tested first
options.B: Green roofs must be specified descriptively in order to qualify for LEED
options.C: Green roofs shift roof design responsibility to the roofing system manufacturer
options.D: Non-traditional roofing calls for rethinking traditional roofing requirements
options.E: Green roofs fall outside MasterFormat and need a custom number
options.F: Green roofs must be specified as closed proprietary systems

questions.explanation: A green roof is a non-traditional roof, and sustainable design goals like LEED call for rethinking the requirements written for conventional roofing rather than reusing them. Green roofs are not wholly new technology needing prototypes, nothing requires descriptive or closed proprietary specifying to earn LEED credit, design responsibility does not shift automatically, and they do not need a custom numbering scheme.

questions.question: The owner of a single small office building wants to use performance specifications to spur development of a new exterior wall technology that no manufacturer currently produces. Which advice best reflects industry guidance?

options.A: Proceed, since performance specifying is practical even for smaller projects
options.B: Reconsider, since this use is generally limited to large, high-volume owners
options.C: Proceed, provided the AHJ agrees to issue a contingent building permit
options.D: Reconsider, since new materials cannot be described by salient characteristics
options.E: Proceed, since development costs are borne by the manufacturers
options.F: Reconsider, since new technology may be bid only under design-build

questions.explanation: Using performance specifications to develop new technology is generally feasible only for large corporations or public agencies that build in volume, because the owner bears the time and cost of requirements, research, design, and prototype tests and needs economies of scale. Practicality for small projects applies to existing technology, a contingent permit does not reduce the owner's cost and risk, and design-build is not a precondition.

questions.question: Shortcomings in available technology that lead an owner to encourage innovation may relate to which factors?

options.A: Aesthetic quality, long-term durability, or warranty duration
options.B: Code compliance, design licensure, or permit timing
options.C: Technical capabilities, construction cost, or expediency
options.D: Product availability, bidder competition, or labor participation
options.E: Sustainability goals, energy codes, or LEED certification
options.F: Maintenance cost, service life, or replacement cycle

questions.explanation: When existing products and processes do not meet an owner's needs, the gaps lie in technical capability, construction cost, or speed, and performance specifying can draw research and development from across the industry to close them. The other lists borrow terms from neighboring topics, such as licensure, competition, sustainability, and life cycle costs, that are not given as these shortcomings.

questions.question: A specifier wants to allow a newly developed panel product made from recycled pre-consumer and post-consumer waste. How can such new materials be utilized?

options.A: By stating performance requirements that describe their salient characteristics
options.B: By naming the developing manufacturer and excluding unproven alternatives
options.C: By referencing the industry standard that governs the conventional product
options.D: By deferring their use to substitution procedures after the contract award
options.E: By specifying them only as owner-furnished products
options.F: By including them only as an additive bid alternate

questions.explanation: New products made from recycled pre-consumer and post-consumer waste can be used by writing performance requirements that describe the characteristics they must have. Naming the one developer and excluding others is restrictive, a conventional product's standard may not fit, and deferring to substitutions, owner-furnished status, or a bid alternate does not tell anyone what the material must achieve.

questions.question: A public agency plans to use performance specifications to obtain a unique modular wall system for one building, with no plan to use the system again. Which concern applies most directly?

options.A: The system must be limited to products that manufacturers already produce
options.B: Performance specifying gives no access to industry research and development
options.C: The new system must first be described by detailed prescriptive requirements
options.D: The requirements must gain economies of scale to offset the production expense
options.E: The requirements must first be published as a reference standard
options.F: Performance specifying cannot be used by public agencies

questions.explanation: Requirements for newly developed technology must reach economies of scale, because producing a one-of-a-kind product, system, or assembly can be very costly, and a single building with no reuse gives none. Attracting research and development is an advantage of this approach, it is not limited to existing products, it needs no prior prescriptive description or published standard, and high-volume public agencies are among the owners who can use it.

questions.question: A national retail chain with an extensive, ongoing construction program maintains its own architectural department but does not want to assume full design or construction responsibilities. To whom may such owners pass those responsibilities?

options.A: The construction manager as advisor
options.B: The supplier
options.C: The authority having jurisdiction
options.D: The owner's facility manager
options.E: The independent testing agency
options.F: The commissioning authority

questions.explanation: Many owners with large, continuing construction programs keep in-house architectural or engineering staff but do not take on full design or construction responsibility, and may pass it to the supplier, using performance requirements to state what they need. A CM-advisor, an AHJ, a facility manager, a testing agency, or a commissioning authority does not take over design and construction responsibility.

questions.question: An owner intends to use performance specifying to establish its project requirements and then hand off the remaining design and construction work. Which project delivery method does industry guidance associate with this approach?

options.A: Design-bid-build
options.B: Construction manager as advisor/agent
options.C: Construction manager as constructor
options.D: Design-build
options.E: Owner-build
options.F: Integrated project delivery

questions.explanation: Design-build lets an owner state its requirements as performance criteria and then hand the remaining design and the construction to one design-builder, with well-developed performance specifications protecting the owner's needs. In design-bid-build the owner's A/E finishes the design before bidding, the CM methods add a manager without handing over design, owner-build keeps construction contracting with the owner, and integrated project delivery has the owner lead a collaborative team rather than step back.

questions.question: When responsibilities are delegated through performance specifying, which allocation of tasks is correct?

options.A: Owner sets requirements by performance criteria; design-builder does final design and construction
options.B: Design-builder sets the performance criteria; owner completes final design before construction begins
options.C: Owner completes the final design; design-builder writes the performance criteria for construction
options.D: Owner's A/E does final design; design-builder only verifies compliance with the performance criteria
options.E: Owner sets requirements by performance criteria; CM-advisor does final design and construction
options.F: Owner fixes the design in descriptive documents; design-builder only builds it

questions.explanation: When responsibility is delegated through performance specifying, the owner states what it needs as performance criteria and the design-builder carries out the final design and the construction, so a well-developed performance specification is what protects the owner. Reversing who writes the criteria, keeping final design with the owner or its A/E, or fixing the design descriptively defeats the delegation, and a CM-advisor coordinates the work rather than designing or building it.

questions.question: A project team member argues that moving some packages to performance-oriented procurement and contracting will not change anyone's role. Which statement reflects industry guidance?

options.A: Roles stay unchanged, because only the method of specifying is different
options.B: All design responsibility then transfers from the A/E to the contractor
options.C: Some customary roles and responsibilities of participants may be altered
options.D: Roles may shift, but only on projects using design-build delivery
options.E: Only the contractor's role changes, since it must now provide design
options.F: Only the A/E's role changes, since it no longer prepares drawings

questions.explanation: Moving design, documentation, procurement and contracting toward performance can change some of the roles participants have traditionally filled. The owner must define and communicate criteria, the A/E sets performance levels and may transfer design, a CM-advisor may coordinate performance packages, contractors and manufacturers take on design and proof of compliance, and AHJs review incomplete documents. The change is therefore neither absent nor total, not limited to design-build, and not confined to one party; the A/E still prepares drawings.

questions.question: An owner wants to issue performance criteria for a new laboratory but also expects to reject any compliant solution it finds unappealing. What should the A/E advise, consistent with industry guidance?

options.A: The owner may still reject any compliant solution during submittal review
options.B: The owner keeps full control because it alone writes the criteria
options.C: The owner should have the contractor write the criteria to share that risk
options.D: The owner gives up some control and must accept results meeting the criteria
options.E: The owner can keep control by also specifying each item descriptively
options.F: The owner gives up all control and must accept any proposed solution

questions.explanation: By stating its requirements as performance criteria, the owner surrenders part of its control over the solution and must be prepared to accept any result that meets those criteria, which is why it has to communicate the criteria completely. Rejecting compliant work or claiming full control does not fit the method, describing the same items descriptively as well invites conflicts, and the criteria express the owner's own needs. Control is not lost entirely: a solution that misses the criteria can still be rejected.

questions.question: An owner begins a project by defining its requirements as performance criteria and intends to use design-build delivery. The criteria might then be used to prepare which document?

options.A: An invitation to bid
options.B: A request for proposals
options.C: The instructions to bidders
options.D: A bid form and supplements
options.E: A request for qualifications
options.F: A request for information

questions.explanation: Performance criteria that define the owner's requirements can become the basis of a request for proposals, the solicitation that design-builders answer with their proposed solutions and prices. A request for qualifications only narrows the field to a short list before an RFP is issued, a request for information asks for a clarification, and invitations to bid, instructions to bidders and bid forms belong to bidding on a completed design.

questions.question: An owner's facilities director asks how relying on performance criteria might change the owner's own work during planning. Which effect does industry guidance describe?

options.A: It may prompt a more comprehensive analysis of needs than usual
options.B: It reduces the need to communicate the criteria in full detail
options.C: It increases the owner's control over the selected final solution
options.D: It shifts the burden of analyzing needs to the design-builder
options.E: It lets the owner postpone defining its needs until after award
options.F: It limits the owner's planning role to setting the project budget

questions.explanation: Because the owner must accept any result that meets its performance criteria, it has to spell those criteria out completely, and that can lead it to analyze its needs more thoroughly than it would in a traditional arrangement. The owner gives up some control rather than gaining it, must communicate the criteria in full rather than less, and cannot hand the analysis of its needs to the design-builder, reduce it to a budget, or put it off until after award.

questions.question: Performance specifying can effectively hand part of a project's design to someone other than the A/E. With which element does this kind of design transfer frequently occur?

options.A: Building monitoring systems
options.B: Green roof assemblies
options.C: Precast concrete
options.D: Data and communication systems
options.E: Cast-in-place concrete frames
options.F: Site-built wood stud walls

questions.explanation: Design transfer through performance specifying is common for engineered items like metal or wood trusses, precast concrete and some foundation systems, where the fabricator's engineer completes the design. Building monitoring and data and communication systems are examples of non-standard technologies, a green roof illustrates non-traditional roofing, and cast-in-place concrete frames and site-built stud walls are normally designed by the A/E's own team rather than by a manufacturer.

questions.question: An A/E plans to performance specify metal trusses so that the fabricator's engineer completes the truss design. What regulatory caution does industry guidance raise for this situation?

options.A: AHJs will not issue any permit until the truss design is complete
options.B: Some states may restrict shifting design away from the A/E of record
options.C: Design transfer is allowed only under design-build project delivery
options.D: The truss manufacturer must also provide its specialized installation
options.E: The fabricator's engineer becomes the A/E of record for the building
options.F: The truss design must be complete before bids are received

questions.explanation: Performance specifying engineered items such as trusses often transfers part of the design to the fabricator's engineer, and some states have regulations that limit how far design can be moved away from the A/E of record, so local rules must be checked. Nothing bars permits until truss design is done, confines design transfer to design-build, obliges the manufacturer to install, or makes the fabricator's engineer the A/E of record, and finishing the truss design before bidding would defeat the transfer.

questions.question: In the traditional design role, an A/E decides that certain elements will be performance specified. What must the A/E know?

options.A: Levels that yield a satisfactory solution, plus standards, tests, and verification methods
options.B: The specific products that each bidder will propose, and each such product's installed cost
options.C: The construction means, methods, and sequences the contractor will use for each element
options.D: The research history and prototype test results of every candidate system and assembly
options.E: The installers' qualifications and the labor rates in the local market
options.F: The manufacturers' advertised claims and standard warranty terms

questions.explanation: To performance specify an element well, the A/E has to know which performance levels will produce a satisfactory solution, and which standards, tests and verification methods will show that a proposal meets them. Bidders' products and costs, the contractor's means and methods, local labor rates, research histories of every candidate system, and advertising claims are not what the A/E needs; products compete on measured performance, not marketing.

questions.question: An owner with a facility manager on staff has retained an A/E of record and a construction manager as advisor/agent, and has let several prime contracts, including a general trades contract; some are for performance-specified systems and others for descriptively specified work. Which participant might assume the task of coordinating these multiple-prime contracts?

options.A: The A/E of record
options.B: The general trades prime contractor
options.C: The CM-advisor/agent
options.D: The owner's facility manager
options.E: The authority having jurisdiction
options.F: The performance-specified system's manufacturer

questions.explanation: When a construction manager as advisor/agent is part of the delivery, it may take on coordinating the multiple-prime contracts, handling both the performance-specified packages and their interfaces with the descriptively specified work. The A/E coordinates design matters with the CM, each prime contractor answers only for its own contract, the facility manager looks after the owner's space and operations, and neither AHJs nor manufacturers coordinate the prime contracts.

questions.question: Why does industry guidance say the CM-advisor/agent becomes involved in handling performance items and interfacing them with traditionally designed items?

options.A: AHJs require a single party to sign each permit application
options.B: The A/E is barred from involvement once documents go out for procurement
options.C: Manufacturers submit compliance proof only through the CM-advisor/agent
options.D: Details of some items may not be known before release for procurement
options.E: The CM-advisor/agent writes the performance criteria for these items
options.F: Performance items are exempt from review by the A/E of record

questions.explanation: Some details of performance-specified items cannot be known before the documents are released for procurement, because they depend on the solutions bidders propose. The CM-advisor/agent therefore administers procurement of those items, ties them into the traditionally designed work, and coordinates design matters with the A/E, who stays involved. The CM does not write the criteria or replace the A/E's review, permits need no single CM signature, and manufacturers submit compliance proof through contractual lines.

questions.question: On a multiple-prime project that includes performance-specified packages, which activity does industry guidance describe as part of the CM-advisor/agent's involvement?

options.A: Coordinating with the A/E on design matters
options.B: Completing traditional detailing after contract award
options.C: Submitting proof of compliance through contractual lines
options.D: Reviewing performance specifications for code conformance
options.E: Designing and engineering the performance-specified systems
options.F: Issuing permits contingent on final documentation approval

questions.explanation: On a multiple-prime project with performance packages, the CM-advisor/agent administers procurement of the performance items, ties them to the traditionally designed work, and coordinates with the A/E on design matters. Designing the systems and completing detailing after award fall to the successful contractors, proof of compliance comes from manufacturers through contractual lines, and code review and contingent permits belong to the AHJs.

questions.question: A mechanical firm wins one of several prime contracts, bidding only on a performance-specified system. Interfaces with other systems were unknown at bid time. How are these details resolved?

options.A: The A/E resolves them by issuing an addendum before bids are received
options.B: The contractor resolves them after award through traditional detailing
options.C: The owner resolves them by issuing change orders once construction starts
options.D: The AHJ resolves them while reviewing the definitive materials for permit
options.E: The manufacturer resolves them through its standard product literature
options.F: The bidders resolve them jointly at the prebid meeting before bidding

questions.explanation: A contractor that bids on just one performance-specified system under multiple-prime contracts can face interfaces with other systems that are unknown at bid time. After award, the successful contractor resolves those details and completes the traditional detailing, coordinating with the other systems once they are selected. The interfaces cannot be settled by addendum or at a prebid meeting because the other systems are not yet chosen, and change orders, the AHJ or product literature do not resolve them.

questions.question: A trade union representative asks whether a shift to performance-based requirements will reduce the work available to its members. Which response is consistent with industry guidance?

options.A: Yes; the overall amount of work decreases when performance criteria are used
options.B: Yes; manufacturers' own crews will perform all erection and installation
options.C: Generally no, except possibly with extensive use of factory-prefabricated systems
options.D: Generally no, except on projects where design-build delivery is used instead
options.E: Generally no, except where multiple-prime contracts are awarded
options.F: Yes; delegating design removes most of the site installation work

questions.explanation: Performance-based requirements generally do not change labor participation much, because the total amount of work stays essentially the same; the possible exception is heavy use of prefabricated systems built mostly in a factory instead of on site. Manufacturers' own erection crews still have to be coordinated with other trades rather than replacing them all, and neither design-build delivery, multiple-prime contracts nor delegated design is the named exception.

questions.question: A general contractor with no in-house design staff is considering joining a design-build entity that will respond to an owner's performance criteria. What does generating solutions within those criteria require?

options.A: Only traditional detailing, because the owner's criteria already fix the design
options.B: Design and engineering capability, perhaps with closer manufacturer collaboration
options.C: Licensure of the contractor by the AHJ before any proposal can be submitted
options.D: Reliance on the owner's A/E to develop the needed solutions after contract award
options.E: Prequalification by the owner's A/E based on past descriptive work
options.F: Only installation coordination, since manufacturers supply all design

questions.explanation: A contractor or design-builder answering performance criteria must produce its own solutions within their bounds, which takes design and engineering capability and may call for closer work with suppliers and manufacturers for extra engineering support. The criteria do not fix the design, the owner's A/E does not develop the solutions, manufacturers support rather than replace the team's design capability, and no AHJ licensure or A/E prequalification step is the stated requirement.

questions.question: A manufacturer whose product was selected to meet a performance-specified requirement wants to send its compliance test data straight to the owner. How should the manufacturer submit proof of compliance?

options.A: Directly to the owner, which must accept compliant results
options.B: Through the owner's independent testing agency for review
options.C: Directly to the AHJ along with the permit application
options.D: Through the contractual lines of the project
options.E: Directly to the A/E, bypassing the contractor
options.F: Through the trade association that publishes the standard

questions.explanation: Under performance specifications, manufacturers must prove that their products meet the specified criteria, and they submit that proof through the project's contractual lines, normally by way of the contractor to the A/E. Sending data straight to the owner, the A/E or the AHJ, or routing it through a testing agency or a trade association, skips that contract chain, even when a testing agency produced the reports.

questions.question: A manufacturer's sales director asks how products are chosen on projects whose specifications state required results rather than naming products. On what basis is a product's use then decided?

options.A: Its performance measured against the specified criteria
options.B: The owner's preference among the products proposed
options.C: The A/E's familiarity with the product from prior projects
options.D: The strength of its advertising and brand recognition
options.E: Its listing in the A/E's office master specification
options.F: The number of past projects on which it has been used

questions.explanation: Performance specifications put competing products on the common ground of performance, so whether a product is used depends on how it measures against the specified criteria, not on an effective advertising campaign. Owner preference, A/E familiarity, a place in the office master, brand recognition or a long project list do not decide compliance; the owner gives up some control and must accept results that meet the criteria.

questions.question: Which additional assistance does industry guidance say a manufacturer might provide on a performance-specified project?

options.A: Coordinating its work under the multiple-prime contracts
options.B: Determining which of the project elements will be performance specified
options.C: Engineering to size its products to meet specific criteria or codes
options.D: Reviewing the performance specifications for code conformance
options.E: Writing the owner's performance criteria for the project
options.F: Evaluating competing proposals on the owner's behalf

questions.explanation: Under performance specifications a manufacturer may end up giving extra help such as design services, for example engineering to size its products to meet particular criteria or codes, and sometimes specialized installation. Coordinating multiple-prime contracts is a CM-advisor/agent task, deciding what to performance specify belongs to the A/E, defining criteria and judging proposals are owner and A/E work, and code-conformance review is done by AHJs.

questions.question: A design-build team applies for a building permit while final documentation is still incomplete. What do AHJs review for code conformance in such cases?

options.A: The complete construction documents prepared by the A/E of record
options.B: The available definitive materials and the performance specifications
options.C: The contractor's shop drawings and product data for all trades
options.D: The owner's program statement and the approved project budget
options.E: The successful proposal's cost breakdown and schedule
options.F: The record documents submitted at project closeout

questions.explanation: In performance-based procurement the construction documents are usually incomplete when the permit is sought, because final documentation often follows award and the start of construction. The AHJ therefore checks whatever definitive materials exist, together with the performance specifications, for code conformance. Complete construction documents and record documents do not exist yet, and shop drawings, cost breakdowns and the owner's program are not what a code review relies on.

questions.question: After reviewing the available materials on a performance-based project, the AHJ finds no conflicts in evidence. What may the AHJ be asked to issue?

options.A: A temporary certificate of occupancy pending final review
options.B: Permits contingent on successful prototype testing of each system
options.C: A conditional variance from the applicable code requirements
options.D: Permits contingent on inspection and final documentation approval
options.E: A certificate of substantial completion for the work
options.F: A notice to proceed with construction

questions.explanation: When the AHJ's review of the available definitive materials and performance specifications shows no conflicts, it may be asked to issue permits that depend on later inspection and on approval of the final documentation. A temporary certificate of occupancy and a code variance serve other purposes, prototype testing is a development cost rather than a permit condition, and the notice to proceed and the certificate of substantial completion come from the owner and the A/E, not the AHJ.

questions.question: On a project procured on a performance basis, when does industry guidance indicate final documentation is often completed?

options.A: Before permit application, so that code review can occur
options.B: After contract award but before construction has begun
options.C: Sometime after award, once construction has already begun
options.D: Before the contract is awarded, while proposals are being reviewed
options.E: Before solicitation, so bidders can price a complete design
options.F: During design development, before construction documents begin

questions.explanation: Performance-based procurement leaves the final documentation unfinished at permit time; it is often completed only some time after award, once construction is under way, because the successful bidder or proposer develops the detailed solution. That is why AHJs review the definitive materials available, and why completion before solicitation, during design development, before permit application, before award, or before construction starts does not fit.

questions.question: An owner and A/E are deciding how to apply performance specifying on a new laboratory building. Determining the extent of a performance specification involves which two interdependent decisions?

options.A: Which delivery method to use, and which bidders can respond to the performance criteria
options.B: Which attributes to evaluate, and which tests will verify compliance with each criterion
options.C: Which elements to performance specify, and how far each of them is performance specified
options.D: Which organizational format to use, and which drawings will accompany the specifications
options.E: Which specifying method to use, and which reference standards to cite
options.F: Which elements to performance specify, and which bidders may propose on each

questions.explanation: Setting the extent of performance specifying takes two linked decisions: which elements, from pieces and parts up to assemblies and systems, will be performance specified, and how far each of those elements will be taken. Choosing bidders, delivery methods, formats, drawings, attributes, tests or reference standards comes up elsewhere in planning or after the extent is settled, so none of those pairs defines the extent.

questions.question: On a mid-rise office project, the owner wants only the curtain wall and HVAC system written as performance criteria, with descriptive methods for everything else. A consultant objects that performance specifying must cover the whole building or none of it. Which response is correct?

options.A: Selected subsystems may be performance specified, with other approaches used for the remainder
options.B: Selected subsystems may be performance specified only when the contract is design-build
options.C: Performance specifying applies to individual components and cannot address complete subsystems
options.D: Performance specifying must cover the entire structure so a single entity designs all interfaces
options.E: Selected subsystems may be performance specified only on public projects
options.F: Selected subsystems may be performance specified only if UniFormat organizes the manual

questions.explanation: Entire structures can be performance specified, though that is rarely practical; many projects state only selected subsystems in performance terms and use other methods where they suit the rest better. No design-build, public-project or UniFormat condition applies to this partial use, and performance specifying is not confined to components, since it can range from a single attribute to a whole project.

questions.question: An owner asks the A/E when they must decide how much of a new transit facility will be performance specified. When should this extent be determined?

options.A: During construction documents, once drawings are substantially complete
options.B: During procurement, after the capabilities of likely bidders are confirmed
options.C: After award, when the contractor makes final product selections
options.D: Early in the project life cycle, to suit the owner's needs
options.E: At the preconstruction conference, with the contractor present
options.F: During construction, as each system's submittals are reviewed

questions.explanation: The owner and A/E should settle how much of the project to performance specify early in the project life cycle, choosing the extent that best fits the owner's needs, because the decision shapes the design, the documents and the procurement that follow. Waiting for construction documents, procurement, award, the preconstruction conference or submittal review leaves no room to act on it.

questions.question: An A/E is evaluating four building elements for possible performance specifying. Which element's circumstances most favor performance specifications?

options.A: A storefront for which the owner has standardized on one recognized system as the exclusive choice
options.B: An exterior wall forming a large share of the work, with several reasonably cost-competitive solutions
options.C: A roof system for which one solution costs far less than every other acceptable option available
options.D: A small trim element whose configuration must exactly match the existing historic profile in every detail
options.E: A specialty item that forms a tiny share of the work and has one known source
options.F: An interior partition whose required configuration leaves room for only one material

questions.explanation: Where options exist, performance specifications are favored when no single solution is recognized as the exclusive choice, the options' costs are reasonably competitive, and the system is a substantial part of the project that does not need a configuration so specific it rules out options. The exterior wall meets all three; the storefront and the single-source item have an exclusive choice, the roof options are not cost-competitive, and the trim and partition need fixed configurations.

questions.question: The first determination in performance specifying project elements is which elements, if any, should be specified in performance terms. Which question frames that determination, and at what scale does it apply?

options.A: Which elements offer a range of options whose competition yields optimum solutions; at any scale from part to system
options.B: Which elements carry the greatest design liability for the A/E; at any scale from part to system
options.C: Which elements offer a range of options whose competition yields optimum solutions; at the system and assembly scales
options.D: Which elements can be verified by independent testing; at the system and assembly scales
options.E: Which elements offer a range of options whose competition yields optimum solutions; at the part and component scales only
options.F: Which elements cost the least to build; at any scale from part to system

questions.explanation: The first decision asks which elements offer a range of options whose competition will produce the best solutions, and that question is asked at every element scale, from a part or component through assemblies and systems. Design liability, independent testing and lowest construction cost are not the framing question, and limiting it to systems and assemblies, or to parts and components, wrongly drops some scales.

questions.question: An owner needs a blast-resistant glazing assembly with properties that no product currently on the market can deliver. How does this circumstance bear on the choice of specifying method?

options.A: It weighs against performance specifications, since no standard solution exists to set criteria from
options.B: It favors a proprietary specification naming the manufacturer most likely to develop the product
options.C: It favors performance specifications, as one of the conditions under which they offer advantages
options.D: It favors a descriptive specification, since the A/E must define the new configuration in detail
options.E: It favors a reference standard specification citing the nearest existing standard
options.F: It means the item cannot be specified until a product reaches the market

questions.explanation: Performance specifications may offer advantages when nothing on the market meets the owner's needs, when the state of the art has no standard solution yet, or when an existing product must be developed further. Having no standard solution is a reason to state performance criteria, not to avoid them; proprietary, descriptive and reference standard methods all presume a known product, configuration or standard, and the item need not wait for a product to appear.

questions.question: To speed production, a specifier proposes writing the building envelope sections in UniFormat order and the interior finishes sections in MasterFormat order, bound together in one volume. What is the correct guidance?

options.A: Combine them, provided each section title carries both the MasterFormat and UniFormat numbers
options.B: Combine them, provided overall performance requirements are collected in Section 01 80 00
options.C: Combine them only in design-build contracts using the broadest levels, H and J
options.D: Do not combine the two formats in a single project manual
options.E: Combine them, provided PageFormat is used for every section in the volume
options.F: Combine them, provided a table cross-references the two numbering systems

questions.explanation: Specifications organized by MasterFormat and those organized by UniFormat should not be combined in one project manual; a project picks one organizational format. Section 01 80 00 can state overall performance requirements within a MasterFormat manual, but that does not permit mixing formats, and dual numbers, a cross-reference table, a common page layout, or design-build delivery do not make the combination acceptable.

questions.question: A curtain wall performance criterion limits the deflection of metal framing members normal to the wall plane when tested per ASTM E330. What limit does such a criterion typically set where a plastered surface is affected?

options.A: 1/175 of clear span
options.B: 1/480 of span
options.C: 1/360 of span
options.D: 1/240 of span
options.E: 3/4 inch, regardless of span
options.F: The greater of 3/4 inch or 1/175 of clear span

questions.explanation: A typical curtain wall criterion caps framing deflection at 1/175 of the clear span or 3/4 inch, whichever is smaller, and tightens it to 1/360 of span where a plastered surface is affected. The general limit, the 3/4-inch cap alone and a 'whichever is greater' reading are not the plaster limit, and 1/480 and 1/240 belong to a broader exterior-enclosure criterion based on ASCE/SEI 7 loads.

questions.question: An A/E's UniFormat-based performance specification currently describes B20—Exterior Vertical Enclosures. The owner now wants only curtain walls, framed in aluminum or steel. How should the A/E revise the specification?

options.A: Narrow B20 to curtain wall assemblies (B2010.40) and list acceptable or unacceptable framing
options.B: Keep B20 and add an l/240 deflection limit so non-curtain-wall systems cannot comply
options.C: Keep B20 and rely on proposal evaluation to reject any bronze, timber, and fiberglass framing
options.D: Abandon performance specifying and name one curtain wall manufacturer's system
options.E: Narrow B20 to B2020.30, Exterior Window Wall, and list acceptable framing
options.F: Replace B20 with MasterFormat Section 08 44 13 in the same manual

questions.explanation: Broad UniFormat terms such as B20 let providers offer many enclosures, from curtain walls to precast panels or brick veneer. To gain control, the A/E narrows the element to curtain wall assemblies, classified under B2010.40, and limits framing by listing acceptable materials (aluminum, steel) or unacceptable ones (bronze, timber, fiberglass). A deflection limit does not restrict system type, evaluation cannot fairly reject what the criteria never excluded, window wall is a different element, and MasterFormat sections do not belong in a UniFormat manual.

questions.question: An A/E who wants to retain greater control over a performance-specified element's configuration should take which approach?

options.A: Use a broad degree, describing the subsystem in general terms with broad functional criteria
options.B: Use a broad degree, organizing the elements under UniFormat to integrate related subsystems
options.C: Use a narrow degree, naming a specific manufacturer and basing criteria on its published product data
options.D: Use a narrow degree, identifying the type of component and basing criteria on its intrinsic traits
options.E: Use the broadest levels, stating only the occupants' human requirements
options.F: Use a broad degree, relying on subjective evaluation to reject unwanted configurations

questions.explanation: A narrow degree of performance specifying keeps more control over an element's configuration: the specific type of component, such as an aluminum curtain wall, is identified, and the criteria are based on characteristics intrinsic to that type. Broad degrees, including broad UniFormat descriptions and statements of human requirements, deliberately allow more latitude, subjective evaluation is no substitute for stated limits, and naming a manufacturer makes the section proprietary.
questions.source: establishing the level of performance specifying

questions.question: An A/E proposes a broad level of performance specifying for a school in a rural market where few local contractors have design or engineering capability. What is the best course of action?

options.A: Keep the broad level and require each bidder to perform all design services in-house
options.B: Set the level according to the local construction community's capabilities to respond
options.C: Keep the broad level, since its advantages do not depend on the number of participants
options.D: Defer setting the level until bids are opened and actual participation is known
options.E: Use the broadest levels, H and J, to attract outside design-builders
options.F: Keep the broad level and rely on manufacturers for all design services
