questions.question: A consultant's draft PART 1 'Closeout Submittals' article in a plumbing fixtures section restates all of Division 01's general operation and maintenance data requirements. What is the best course of action?

options.A: Keep the restated text so the section can stand alone if issued separately
options.B: Delete the article entirely and rely on Section 01 78 00 for all closeout items
options.C: Move the restated requirements into the section's PART 3 Cleaning article
options.D: Keep only requirements unique to that work result and delete the rest
options.E: Move the restated requirements into the Maintenance Material Submittals article
options.F: Replace the article with a general note on the plumbing drawings

questions.explanation: The PART 1 Closeout Submittals and Maintenance Material Submittals articles should cover only what is particular to the section's own work result, leaving the general requirements to Division 01. Keeping or relocating the duplicated text, to another PART 1 article or to PART 3 Cleaning, still repeats Division 01; deleting the article loses the section-specific items; and general notes on drawings are not the place for administrative requirements.

questions.question: An A/E retains engineering consultants plus specialty consultants for roofing, food service, and hardware. The owner asks whether the A/E's coordination responsibility covers the specialty consultants' sections. What is the answer?

options.A: Yes; the A/E coordinates all of the specifications, specialists' included
options.B: No; each consultant coordinates its own sections with the contractor
options.C: Only for engineering disciplines; specialty consultants coordinate their own
options.D: Only for Division 01 and the conditions of the contract, not technical sections
options.E: No; the owner's project manager coordinates the specialty sections
options.F: Only for sections that interface with the architectural drawings

questions.explanation: The A/E takes responsibility for overall coordination of the specifications, including the sections written by engineering consultants and by specialists such as roofing and waterproofing, hardware and food service consultants. That duty does not pass to each consultant, the contractor or the owner's project manager, and it is not limited to engineering disciplines, to Division 01 and the conditions, or to sections that touch the architectural drawings.

questions.question: An A/E is about to engage consultants to write portions of the project manual. When should the conditions of the contract and Division 01 be made available to them?

options.A: After their first drafts, for a coordination review
options.B: Before they prepare any of their sections
options.C: At the final coordination review before issue
options.D: Once the drawings are substantially complete
options.E: When their sections are submitted for review
options.F: During the bidding period, with the addenda

questions.explanation: Consultants need the conditions of the contract and the Division 01 sections in hand before they write any of their own sections, so they can coordinate their work and avoid duplications and omissions; their input for Division 01 is requested at the same time. Supplying the documents after first drafts, at review, at final coordination, once the drawings are nearly done or during bidding comes too late to prevent duplication.

questions.question: When the A/E gives consultants the conditions of the contract and the General Requirements, what else should it request from them at that time, and for what purpose?

options.A: Copies of their office master sections, so formats can be aligned
options.B: Lists of proposed products, so substitutions can be controlled
options.C: Input for Division 01, to avoid duplicating it in their sections
options.D: Their cost estimates, so alternates can be identified early
options.E: Their drawing general notes, so administrative terms appear there
options.F: Lists of their reference standards, so editions can be checked

questions.explanation: When the conditions of the contract and Division 01 go to the consultants, the A/E should also ask for their input to the Division 01 sections, so that those general requirements are not repeated in the sections the consultants write. Office masters, product lists, cost estimates and reference lists are not what is requested at that point, and administrative matters belong in Division 01 rather than in drawing notes.

questions.question: Which pair of words is not recommended for use in specifications at all?

options.A: "Observe" and "supervise"
options.B: "Shall" and "will"
options.C: "Furnish" and "install"
options.D: "Must" and "is to"
options.E: "Amount" and "quantity"
options.F: "Either" and "both"

questions.explanation: Neither 'must' nor 'is to' is recommended in specifications; the imperative mood states the requirement directly. The other pairs are all usable when each word keeps its own meaning: shall for the contractor and will for the owner or A/E, furnish and install as defined terms, observe versus supervise, amount for money and quantity for measures, and either for a choice versus both for all.

questions.question: A draft paragraph reads: "The Contractor must remove and provide new any damaged units in a workmanlike manner as directed." Which element of the sentence follows recommended specification language?

options.A: "must" for the obligation
options.B: "any damaged units"
options.C: "remove and provide new"
options.D: "as directed" at the close
options.E: "The Contractor" as the subject
options.F: "in a workmanlike manner"

questions.explanation: 'Remove and provide new' is the recommended wording, because 'replace' could be read as reinstalling the removed units. Every other element is on the avoid list: 'must' is not recommended, 'any' leaves the number to the reader, 'as directed' is a phrase with a missing object, 'in a workmanlike manner' is a vague expression, and the contractor should not be the subject of the sentence.

questions.question: Why is "remove and provide new" preferred to "replace" in specifications?

options.A: "Replace" implies the owner furnishes all of the new material
options.B: "Replace" can be read as reinstalling the removed material
options.C: "Replace" is reserved for warranty corrections after completion
options.D: "Replace" shifts disposal costs to the owner
options.E: "Replace" obliges the contractor to match the original manufacturer
options.F: "Replace" applies only to work damaged by other trades

questions.explanation: 'Replace' could be taken to mean putting the removed material back in place, while 'remove and provide new' makes clear that new material must be furnished and installed. The word says nothing about who furnishes material, warranty work, disposal costs, matching the original manufacturer or who caused the damage; the specifier should simply state what is required for the replaced material.

questions.question: A requirement must reach subcontractors and suppliers who did not sign the owner-contractor agreement. Which term is recommended for them?

options.A: Entity
options.B: Party
options.C: Contractor
options.D: Bidder
options.E: Proposer
options.F: Subcontractor

questions.explanation: A party is a signer of the contract, such as the owner or the contractor, so the generic term entity is used when a requirement must also reach persons or companies that did not sign it, such as subcontractors and suppliers. Contractor names one party, subcontractor leaves out suppliers, and bidder and proposer describe firms during procurement rather than everyone taking part in the work.

questions.question: Which line follows recommended specification vocabulary?

options.A: Quantity of the flooring allowance: $25,000.
options.B: Balance of attic stock: Store on site.
options.C: Amount of batt insulation: 2,400 square feet.
options.D: Remainder of unused tile: Deliver to Owner.
options.E: Inflammable liquids: Store off site.
options.F: Extra stock: Deliver to Owner and/or store on site.

questions.explanation: Remainder is the preferred word for what is left over, so 'remainder of unused tile' is right. Amount and balance are for money and quantity is for numbers, length, area or volume, so the allowance, attic stock and insulation lines each use the wrong word. Flammable is preferred over inflammable, and 'and/or' lets the contractor choose which meaning applies.

questions.question: A specification needs a verb meaning "to make certain, leaving no possibility of error." Which word has that meaning in specification usage?

options.A: Insure
options.B: Warrant
options.C: Ensure
options.D: Assure
options.E: Guarantee
options.F: Certify

questions.explanation: In specification usage, ensure means to make certain so that no error is possible. Insure means to issue or obtain an insurance policy, and assure means to give a person confidence or convince them of something. Warrant and guarantee are promises to answer for a product or the work, and certify means to state formally that something is so, so none of them carries the meaning asked for.

questions.question: The A/E's role is to watch the execution of the work without having control and direction of it. Which term matches that role in specification usage?

options.A: Control
options.B: Observe
options.C: Supervise
options.D: Oversee
options.E: Direct
options.F: Inspect

questions.explanation: To observe is to watch the work as it is carried out, which fits an A/E that has no control over it. Supervise means to oversee with control and direction of the work, so supervise, oversee, control and direct all imply authority the A/E does not have, and inspect suggests the exhaustive checking of the work that the A/E is not required to make.

questions.question: Where should the definitions of furnish, install, and provide be placed?

options.A: In the supplementary conditions or Division 01
options.B: In the owner-contractor agreement
options.C: In Part 1 of each technical section
options.D: In the instructions to bidders
options.E: In the general notes on the drawings
options.F: In the bid form, ahead of the bid prices

questions.explanation: Furnish means to supply and deliver to the site ready for installation, install means to put in place for service or use, and provide means to furnish and install, complete and ready for use. Because these meanings govern the whole project, their definitions go in the supplementary conditions or Division 01, not in the agreement, each section's PART 1, the instructions to bidders, the bid form or drawing notes.

questions.question: When may "The Contractor shall" appropriately appear in a specification paragraph?

options.A: When the paragraph is in Part 1 rather than Part 3
options.B: When the requirement concerns jobsite safety
options.C: When the requirement exceeds the referenced standard
options.D: When the contractor and the owner or A/E are named in the same paragraph
options.E: When the paragraph begins a new article
options.F: When the work is performed by a subcontractor

questions.explanation: Because every instruction is addressed to the contractor, 'Contractor shall' is normally dropped in favor of the imperative mood. When the same article or paragraph also names the owner or the A/E, writing 'The Contractor shall,' 'Owner will' and 'A/E will' makes clear who does what. The part of the section, the topic, the referenced standard, the position in the article and who performs the work do not change that.

questions.question: "Equipment shall be installed plumb and level" is a poor specification sentence mainly because:

options.A: Installation requirements belong in Part 2
options.B: "Shall" may be used only for owner actions
options.C: Equipment has no legal duty, so "shall" loses its meaning
options.D: "Plumb and level" is an undefined tolerance
options.E: "Installed" should read "provided," which includes furnishing
options.F: The subject should be "all equipment" to cover every unit

questions.explanation: Shall traditionally means 'has a duty to,' and equipment cannot have a legal duty, so a sentence with equipment as its subject uses shall in a way that fails that meaning; the imperative 'Install equipment plumb and level' avoids it. Installation does belong in PART 3, 'will' is the word for owner actions, and switching to 'provided' or adding 'all' does not fix the problem.

questions.question: When two spellings are equally correct, which set shows the spellings preferred in contract documents?

options.A: facia, gauge, molding, catalogue
options.B: facia, gage, molding, catalog
options.C: fascia, gage, moulding, catalog
options.D: fascia, gauge, moulding, catalogue
options.E: fascia, gauge, molding, catalog
options.F: facia, gauge, moulding, catalog

questions.explanation: When two spellings are equally correct, the shorter one is preferred in contract documents, giving facia, gage, molding and catalog. Every other set keeps at least one longer form, such as fascia, gauge, moulding or catalogue. The rule does not extend to invented short forms such as 'thru' for 'through,' which should be avoided.

questions.question: Which is an accepted exception to the usual caution against abbreviations in specification text?

options.A: Units of measure such as psi, written without periods
options.B: "Galv." for galvanized
options.C: "Approx." for approximately
options.D: "w/" for with
options.E: "Mfr." for manufacturer
options.F: "Typ." for typical

questions.explanation: Abbreviations are generally kept to drawings and schedules, but a few are accepted in specification text: parts of a company's legal name, organization names such as ASTM without periods, times such as a.m., time zones, temperatures written as degrees F, and units of measure such as psi and mph without periods. Shortcuts such as galv., approx., w/, mfr. and typ. are not among them; when in doubt, spell it out.

questions.question: Abbreviations should be limited to:

options.A: Three or fewer letters
options.B: Four or fewer letters
options.C: Six or fewer letters
options.D: Five or fewer letters
options.E: Two or fewer letters
options.F: Seven or fewer letters

questions.explanation: An abbreviation should be no longer than five letters, and one that shortens a short word by only a character or two should not be used at all. Two, three, four, six and seven letters are not the guideline. Abbreviations should also match between the drawings and the specifications, and when in doubt the word should be spelled out.

questions.question: Which written form in specification text follows recommended practice for symbols and dimensions?

options.A: 10°F using the degree sign
options.B: 20% (percentage of the contract sum)
options.C: 8'-2-1/2" (feet and inches both used)
options.D: 2 x 4 using the times sign for lumber
options.E: 50 lb/sq ft using the slash for per
options.F: Joints @ 16 inches using the at sign

questions.explanation: Symbols such as %, the degree sign, plus and minus, the times sign, the slash for per and @ should not stand in for words in specification text. Dimensions are the exception: a dimension that combines feet and inches takes the foot and inch marks, as in 8'-2-1/2". So write 10 degrees F, 20 percent, 2 by 4, pounds per square foot and at 16 inches instead.

questions.question: How should a dimension of 8 feet with no inches be written in specification text?

options.B: 8 feet
options.D: eight feet
options.E: 8 ft
options.F: 8 ft 0 in

questions.explanation: When a dimension has feet but no inches, the word feet is spelled out after the numeral, as in 8 feet; the foot and inch marks are used only when feet and inches appear together. Figures, not words, are always used for dimensions, so 'eight feet' is wrong, and abbreviations such as ft and in are not the recommended form.

questions.question: Which phrase follows recommended practice for numbers that define both size and quantity?

options.A: three 1/2-inch holes
options.B: three one-half-inch holes
options.C: 3 half-inch holes
options.D: 3 1/2-inch holes
options.E: three ½-inch holes
options.F: (3) 1/2-inch holes

questions.explanation: Numerals are used wherever possible, but when one phrase gives both a quantity and a size, the quantity is written as a word and the size in figures, as in three 1/2-inch holes. Writing both in figures invites misreading as 3-1/2 inches, sizes are not spelled out, fractions are typed with ordinary keys rather than special characters, and parentheses should be avoided.

questions.question: Which money and time references are written correctly?

options.D: $200 and 9 p.m.
options.E: Two hundred dollars and 9 p.m.
options.F: $200 and nine p.m.

questions.explanation: Money and clock times are written in figures, and unneeded zeroes are left off, so $200 rather than $200.00 and 9 p.m. rather than 9:00 p.m. Spelling out the dollars or the hour breaks the rule that money and clock times take figures; noon and midnight are the only times written as words.

questions.question: A quantity of less than one expressed as a decimal is written:

options.E: Two hundred thirty-five thousandths

questions.explanation: Decimals are written in figures, and a quantity less than one takes a zero before the decimal point, as in 0.235, so the point cannot be missed. Leaving off the leading zero, writing a fraction or words, or using a comma as the decimal marker does not follow the rule.

questions.question: Under recommended capitalization practice, which word stays lowercase even when it refers to the specific project?

options.A: Work
options.B: subcontractor
options.C: Contractor
options.D: Project Manual
options.E: Owner
options.F: Drawings

questions.explanation: Words such as Contractor, Owner, Work, Drawings and Project Manual are capitalized when they refer to the specific project, because they name parties or documents defined for that contract. Subcontractor and subcontract stay lowercase, since a subcontractor is not a party defined in the owner-contractor agreement.

questions.question: When a specification refers to one of the three main divisions of a section under SectionFormat, how is that word capitalized?

options.A: PART, in all capitals
options.B: Part, except in Division 01
options.C: part, in lowercase
options.D: Part, with an initial capital
options.E: PART in headings only, part in running text
options.F: Part, in italics with an initial capital

questions.explanation: When it refers to one of SectionFormat's three parts, the word is written PART, in all capitals, as in PART 3—EXECUTION. Initial capitals, lowercase, italics, or switching to lowercase outside headings are not the convention, and Division 01 is no exception.

questions.question: How should each item in a list of subparagraphs end?

options.A: With a comma, except the last item
options.B: With a semicolon, adding "and" before the last
options.C: With no punctuation
options.D: With a period, showing no content is missing
options.E: With a colon, linking it to the next item
options.F: With a semicolon, except the last, which takes a period

questions.explanation: Every paragraph ends with a period or a colon, and a parent paragraph that introduces a list ends with a colon. Each item in the list then ends with a period, which shows that no content is missing. Commas, semicolons, colons or no punctuation at the end of items leave the list reading as one unfinished sentence.

questions.question: Which series is punctuated as recommended for specifications?

options.A: Clean walls, floors, & ceilings.
options.B: Clean walls; floors; and ceilings.
options.C: Clean walls, floors, and ceilings.
options.D: Clean walls, floors and ceilings.
options.E: Clean walls, floors, and/or ceilings.
options.F: Clean walls/floors/ceilings.

questions.explanation: Specifications are legal documents, so formal punctuation applies, including the serial (Oxford) comma: a comma follows each item in a series, the one before 'and' included. Dropping that last comma, or using semicolons, an ampersand, slashes or 'and/or,' each breaks a rule for punctuation, symbols or vocabulary.

questions.question: Why is "in lieu of" unacceptable in specifications?

options.A: It is an archaic adverb like "herewith"
options.B: It is a foreign-language expression
options.C: It implies an owner-approved substitution
options.D: It is a phrase with a missing object
options.E: It is an imprecise article like "any" or "such"
options.F: It is a vague expression like "as per" or "etc."

questions.explanation: Foreign-language terms and expressions should not appear in specifications, and 'in lieu of' is the standard example; write 'instead of.' Missing-object phrases such as 'as directed,' archaic adverbs such as 'herewith,' articles such as 'any' and expressions such as 'etc.' and 'as per' are separate entries on the avoid list, and the phrase says nothing about substitutions.

questions.question: "If tiles are cracked, the contractor shall replace same at no additional cost." Which revision is preferred under recommended specification language?

options.A: Remove cracked tiles and provide new tiles at no additional cost.
options.B: Replace any cracked tiles at no additional cost.
options.C: If tiles are cracked, replace with acceptable tiles at no additional cost.
options.D: If tiles are cracked, the Contractor shall replace them at no additional cost.
options.E: If tiles are cracked, the Contractor must replace same at no additional cost.
options.F: Remove and replace all cracked tiles as directed at no additional cost.

questions.explanation: 'Same' should not be used as a pronoun, and the noun is better than any pronoun. The preferred revision is a direct imperative that names the tiles and uses 'remove and provide new,' since 'replace' can be read as reinstalling the removed material. The conditional 'replace with acceptable tiles' version is better but wordier, and the others keep 'same,' 'them,' 'must,' 'any,' 'all' or 'as directed.'

questions.question: In a streamlined specification, the explanatory statement in Division 01 or the supplementary conditions says a colon stands for:

options.A: "will," for actions of the owner
options.B: "as indicated on Drawings"
options.C: "and/or," when items are listed
options.D: "shall," "shall be," or "shall comply with," as the context requires
options.E: "provide," meaning furnish and install complete
options.F: "as specified in Division 01"

questions.explanation: Streamlined specifications usually carry a statement in Division 01 or the supplementary conditions saying the text uses the imperative mood and streamlined form, and that a colon within a sentence or phrase stands in for 'shall,' 'shall be' or 'shall comply with,' whichever the context needs. The colon does not stand for 'will,' 'provide,' 'and/or,' or a reference to the drawings or Division 01.

questions.question: Streamlining is best suited to which content?

options.A: Narrative descriptions of the work
options.B: Statements of owner responsibilities
options.C: Lists of products, materials, and reference standards
options.D: Step-by-step installation instructions
options.E: Explanations of the design intent
options.F: Coordination requirements between sections

questions.explanation: Streamlining puts the subject first, followed by a colon and the requirement, which gives keywords for quick reference and suits itemized content such as products, materials and reference standards. It is hard to adapt to descriptions or instructions, so narratives, design intent, owner responsibilities, coordination requirements and step-by-step installation are better written as full sentences.

questions.question: "Store all millwork under shelter, etc." Which pair of specification language rules does this sentence break?

options.A: It names a party, and it uses "shall"
options.B: "All" is usually unnecessary, and "etc." is on the avoid list
options.C: It lacks the imperative mood, and it uses a symbol
options.D: It uses a foreign term, and it omits a colon
options.E: It uses a pronoun, and it lacks a reference standard
options.F: It uses a missing-object phrase, and it lacks the Oxford comma

questions.explanation: 'All' is usually unnecessary, since 'Store millwork under shelter' says the same thing, and 'etc.' is on the list of expressions to avoid because it leaves the scope open. The sentence already uses the imperative 'Store,' names no party, and has no shall, symbol, foreign term, pronoun, missing-object phrase or series that would need a comma.

questions.question: Applying the rule that modifiers can replace prepositional phrases, which wording is preferred?

options.A: Within manufacturer's recommended time limit.
options.B: Within the time recommended by manufacturer.
options.C: Within the time limit as recommended.
options.D: Within the time recommended by the manufacturer thereof.
options.E: Within the time limit recommended by the manufacturer.
options.F: Within time limit of manufacturer's recommendation.

questions.explanation: Specification sentences can be shortened by using modifiers in place of prepositional phrases, so 'manufacturer's recommended time limit' is preferred. 'Within the time recommended by manufacturer' is correct but longer, the other 'by' and 'of' versions still lean on prepositional phrases, the 'as recommended' version drops who recommends, and 'thereof' only adds words.

questions.question: Which is the preferred version of "Mock-ups shall be built to show finishes and demonstrating workmanship"?

options.A: Mock-ups shall be built to show finishes and to demonstrate workmanship.
options.B: Build mock-ups showing finishes and to demonstrate workmanship.
options.C: Mock-ups are to show finishes and demonstrate workmanship.
options.D: Build mock-ups to show finishes and to demonstrate workmanship.
options.E: Build mock-ups to show finishes and demonstrating workmanship.
options.F: Contractor must build mock-ups to show finishes and to demonstrate workmanship.

questions.explanation: The two purposes in a compound predicate should share the same grammatical form, so 'to show' pairs with 'to demonstrate,' and the preferred version also uses the imperative mood with the action verb first. The 'shall be built' version is parallel but wordy, the 'showing' and 'demonstrating' versions mix forms, 'are to' is not recommended, and 'Contractor must' adds a discouraged subject and verb.

questions.question: A designation such as "ASTM C270" or "Section 01 42 19" in specification text should be:

options.A: Written without the internal space, as one continuous designation
options.B: Set in italics
options.C: Kept on one line with a non-breaking space
options.D: Enclosed in parentheses
options.E: Set in bold type so that it stands out
options.F: Hyphenated between its parts to prevent a break

questions.explanation: Designations from industry standards, such as ASTM C270 or ACI 318, and MasterFormat numbers such as Section 01 42 19 must not be split across two lines, so a non-breaking space keeps each one together. Closing up or hyphenating the spaces alters the designation itself, and italics, bold type or parentheses do nothing to prevent a line break.

questions.question: Abbreviations used in a project should be defined:

options.A: Only in the supplementary conditions
options.B: On the drawings or in Division 01
options.C: In Part 1 of each section that uses them
options.D: In the instructions to bidders
options.E: In the owner-contractor agreement
options.F: In the bid form

questions.explanation: Abbreviations belong mainly on drawings and schedules, where space is limited, and the ones a project uses are defined on the drawings or in Division 01 so that one list serves the whole set. The supplementary conditions, the agreement, the instructions to bidders and the bid form are not where they are defined, and defining them section by section works against keeping them consistent between drawings and specifications.

questions.question: In specification text, underlines should be:

options.A: Not used
options.B: Used only for defined terms
options.C: Minimized, like parentheses
options.D: Used for section titles
options.E: Used to emphasize critical requirements
options.F: Used only for web addresses

questions.explanation: Underlining is not used in specification text at all, including for web addresses; parentheses and quotation marks are a separate matter and are kept to a minimum or avoided. Underlines are not reserved for defined terms, section titles, emphasis or URLs.

questions.question: "The Contractor shall install light fixtures which are to be purchased under an allowance." Which revision is preferred under recommended specification language?

options.A: Install light fixtures to be purchased under an allowance.
options.B: Install light fixtures, which are purchased under an allowance.
options.C: Contractor shall install the light fixtures purchased under the allowance in Division 01.
options.D: Install light fixtures purchased under the allowances in Section 01 21 00.
options.E: Install light fixtures which are purchased under Section 01 21 00.
options.F: Contractor shall install light fixtures that are purchased under an allowance.

questions.explanation: Relative pronouns such as 'which' and 'that' should be used sparingly, if at all, and the imperative mood drops 'Contractor shall.' The preferred revision is a direct imperative that also points to the section where allowances are specified, Section 01 21 00. 'Install light fixtures to be purchased under an allowance' improves on the draft but is less precise, and the other versions keep a relative pronoun or 'Contractor shall.'

questions.question: The "four Cs" for effective specification communication are:

options.A: Concise, correct, consistent, and complete
options.B: Clear, complete, correct, and coordinated
options.C: Clear, concise, complete, and correct
options.D: Clear, concise, consistent, and coordinated
options.E: Clear, correct, consistent, and coordinated
options.F: Concise, complete, coordinated, and consistent

questions.explanation: Effective specification communication follows the four Cs: clear, concise, complete and correct. Consistency and coordination matter in specifications too, but they are not among the four Cs, so any set that swaps one of them in for clear, concise, complete or correct is wrong. Being concise means cutting needless words without giving up clarity, correctness or completeness.

questions.question: A PPD describes a curtain wall under B2010.40 whose scope also covers aluminum-framed entrances, panic hardware, and low-E insulated glass. Those same entrances, hardware, and glass types also appear in storefronts and hollow metal doors elsewhere. How should this work be organized in MasterFormat sections?

options.A: All components in 08 44 13 Glazed Aluminum Curtain Walls, because the PPD describes a single system
options.B: All components in Section 08 44 00, following UniFormat's cross-reference for B2010.40
options.C: Framing in 08 44 13, entrances in 08 42 13, panic hardware in 08 71 00, glazing in 08 80 00
options.D: Framing and glazing in 08 44 13, with entrances and panic hardware together in 08 42 13
options.E: Framing in 08 44 13, entrances and glazing in 08 43 13, panic hardware in 08 71 00
options.F: Framing and entrances in 08 44 13, panic hardware in 08 71 00, glazing in 08 80 00

questions.explanation: A curtain wall's framing, entrances, hardware and glazing could share one section, 08 44 13 Glazed Aluminum Curtain Walls, but when storefronts or hollow metal doors use the same entrances, hardware and glass, each goes in its own section: 08 44 13 for framing, 08 42 13 for entrances, 08 71 00 for door hardware and 08 80 00 for glazing. Grouping any of them with the curtain wall or a storefront section leaves the other assemblies depending on it.

questions.question: A schematic-design PPD describes element B2010 Exterior Walls as metal stud framing, glass-mat sheathing, a fluid-applied air barrier, rigid insulation, and brick veneer. At design development, the specifier begins the outline specifications in MasterFormat. How should she treat this PPD description?

options.A: As a resource whose components will likely be split among several specification sections
options.B: As the text of one exterior wall section, since the PPD already describes a complete assembly
options.C: As a superseded document, since PPD content is not carried forward into outline specifications
options.D: As an attachment to the outline specifications, so the UniFormat element numbers remain in use
options.E: As binding contract text that the outline specifications must not change
options.F: As a cost-estimating tool only, with no use in writing the specifications

questions.explanation: The switch from UniFormat to MasterFormat usually comes at design development, when the PPDs from schematic design serve as a resource for the outline specifications. A PPD's element descriptions bundle materials, products and components that will likely be specified in several sections, so this wall will spread across framing, sheathing, air barrier, insulation and masonry sections. The PPD is not copied whole into one section, discarded, attached, treated as binding, or limited to cost estimating.

questions.question: A specifier is about to draft the Division 01 sections for a public library. Which procurement and contracting document has the most influence on Division 01, and which Parts of other sections may it also affect?

options.A: 00 70 00 Conditions of the Contract; PART 1 and PART 3 of some sections
options.B: 00 70 00 Conditions of the Contract; PART 2 of most product sections
options.C: 00 52 00 Agreement Forms; PART 1 and PART 3 of some sections
options.D: 00 52 00 Agreement Forms; PART 2 of most product sections
options.E: 00 21 13 Instructions to Bidders; PART 1 and PART 3 of some sections
options.F: 00 31 13 Preliminary Schedules; PART 2 of most product sections

questions.explanation: The conditions of the contract, 00 70 00, have the most influence on preparing the Division 01 sections and may also shape PART 1—GENERAL and PART 3—EXECUTION provisions in some sections. Agreement forms and instructions to bidders are not singled out this way, preliminary schedules help set the order for preparing sections, and PART 2 product requirements are not named as an area the conditions influence.
questions.source: reviewing the procurement and contracting requirements

questions.question: On a phased school addition, the specifier wants to know which work packages are planned so she can decide the order in which to prepare sections. Which Division 00 document may provide this?

options.A: 00 31 32 Geotechnical Data
options.B: 00 31 13 Preliminary Schedules
options.C: 00 31 19 Existing Condition Information
options.D: 00 31 21 Survey Information
options.E: 00 31 16 Project Budget Information
options.F: 00 31 43 Permit Application

questions.explanation: Preliminary Schedules, 00 31 13, may identify how the project is phased into work packages, which tells the specifier the sequence in which to prepare sections. Geotechnical data supports sections such as waterproofing, earthwork and pavements, and existing condition, survey, budget and permit information do not show the planned phasing.
questions.source: reviewing the procurement and contracting requirements

questions.question: A specifier is editing a stainless-steel fabrications section. It needs a No. 4 satin shop finish applied before delivery, and it also needs methods for touch-up finishing done in the field after installation. Under SectionFormat, where does each belong?

options.A: Both in the PART 2 Finishes article, which covers all of the section's finishes
options.B: Shop finish in the PART 2 Fabrication article; field finishing methods in PART 2 Finishes
options.C: Shop finish in the PART 2 Finishes article; field finishing methods described in PART 3
options.D: Shop finish in the PART 2 Finishes article; field finishing methods in PART 1 Field Conditions
options.E: Shop finish in PART 2 Source Quality Control; field finishing methods in PART 3
options.F: Both in PART 3, under the Installation article, since finishing follows fabrication

questions.explanation: The PART 2 Finishes article covers factory and shop finishes, and field finishing materials when the section includes them, with Shop Finishing Methods as a subordinate title; field finishing methods are described in PART 3. So the No. 4 shop finish goes in Finishes and the touch-up methods in PART 3. Fabrication covers assembly, Source Quality Control covers tests and inspections, and Field Conditions covers ambient and existing conditions.

questions.question: A specifier is coordinating the PREPARATION articles of individual sections with Division 01. Which requirement belongs in Section 01 71 00 Examination and Preparation?

options.A: Cleaning glazing channels and framing members just before the glass is set
options.B: Basic requirements for installing owner-furnished products in the work
options.C: Removing loosely bonded coatings from joint substrates before sealant work
options.D: Initial construction layout and surveying for the project
options.E: Cutting and patching existing construction to receive new work
options.F: Protecting finished work from damage while construction continues

questions.explanation: Section 01 71 00 covers requirements unique to preparing for construction, such as initial layout, surveying and protection of adjacent construction, plus the basic requirements for preparing to install products. Installing owner-furnished products and cutting and patching belong to Section 01 73 00 Execution, protecting finished work to 01 76 00, and readying one section's own substrate, such as glazing channels or sealant joints, to that section's PART 3 Preparation article.

questions.question: After issuing an addendum that revises six specification sections, the specifier must distribute and archive the revised sections. Which approach follows recommended version control?

options.A: Issue native word-processing files with tracked changes so bidders can see edits
options.B: Issue a neutral format such as PDF, secured against unauthorized modification
options.C: Issue only the changed pages, archiving superseded versions under the same file names
options.D: Issue editable files so the contractor can update the conformed set directly
options.E: Issue paper copies only, discarding the superseded electronic files
options.F: Issue an unsecured PDF so bidders can mark up and return the revised pages

questions.explanation: Revisions should go out, and be kept, in a neutral format such as PDF or an internet posting, with security features that stop the contract documents from being changed except by the means expressly designated, and with a consistent file naming protocol for version control. Native or editable files invite uncontrolled changes, an unsecured file can be altered, reusing the original file names defeats version control, and discarding superseded files loses the record.
questions.source: archive electronic files for version control

questions.question: At the close of a project, the specifier archives the project manual revision log along with the final documents. What is the main reason for archiving that log?

options.A: To help update the office master guide specifications with lessons learned
options.B: To give the contractor a basis for pricing change orders after contract award
options.C: To serve as part of the owner's record documents at substantial completion
options.D: To document each addendum for the bidders' acknowledgment on the bid form
options.E: To support the A/E's request for additional services fees
options.F: To give the authority having jurisdiction a record of code changes

questions.explanation: The revision log records the project name and number, each revised section's number and title, and a short description of the changes, and it is archived so the office master guide specifications can be updated with the lessons the project taught. It is not a basis for change-order pricing, a record document, a bid-form acknowledgment of addenda, a fee claim or a filing for the authority having jurisdiction.

questions.question: A specifier is setting up a project manual revision log template for the firm. Which set of entries should each record in the log capture?
